next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. AHO funds are awarded only through SHRA multifamily pre-application rounds; SHRA is not accepting pre-applications and has not posted a 2027 schedule (2026 pattern suggests a January 2027 pre-application deadline).
layering_notes: Unincorporated-county-only money (fee is charged only on unincorporated residential permits). Normally paired with 4% credits plus bonds or 9% credits, SHRA HOME, PLHA and the County Housing Trust Fund in one SHRA award. Developer side of the ordinance: market-rate projects may instead dedicate land, build units, enter a development agreement with an Affordable Housing Strategy, or buy banked unit credits from SHRA; multifamily projects with at least 20% affordable units at 17 or more units per acre are exempt from the fee, which is itself a meaningful incentive for mixed-income rental. AHO is a local below-market loan, so the Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption may apply if no HOME or CDBG is in the stack; confirm with counsel. The County is mid-way through an AHO amendment study (Housing Element Program E3): KMA found 2% to 14% affordable production versus the 10% target; Board workshop Oct 6, 2026, nexus study through spring 2027, ordinance hearings expected winter 2027, possibly adding an inclusionary option and resource-area targeting. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
cycle_notes: Lent through SHRA's twice-yearly multifamily rounds (County AHO fund $6.0M available as of June 1, 2026). Fee side: $3.91 per habitable square foot as of March 27, 2026 (3.24% increase), adjusted annually. AHO amendment study: Board workshop October 6, 2026; nexus study fall 2026 to spring 2027; ordinance hearings expected winter 2027.
prevailing_wage_basis: SHRA 2026 County Multifamily Lending Policies Section 6.1 (which govern AHO fund loans) state state prevailing wages apply to projects receiving benefits from a governmental entity, with the main exemption being a below-market loan where 40% of units are at 80% AMI for 20 years (Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E)); an AHO-only loan meeting that test may be exempt, and HOME (12+ units) or CDBG (8+ units) in the stack adds Davis-Bacon. https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-SHRA-Multifamily-Lending-Policies-County-final.pdf ; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Sacramento County Housing Trust Fund (commercial linkage fee)
administering_agency: County of Sacramento (Chapter 16.89, fee collected at building permit); SHRA administers and lends the fund
typical_award_size: $900,000 available as of June 1, 2026 (was $0 in June 2025). 2024 fee revenue $1,605,084; year-end 2024 balance $6.36M ($1.2M uncommitted). Since 1991: $33.1M in fees, 29 developments, 3,037 total units. Recent loans $816,000 to $5.25M per project (San Juan $5.25M for 21 HTF units; Terracina at Wildhawk $4.6M for 18 units).
per_unit_cap: None published; recent awards about $250,000 per HTF-restricted unit.
affordability_requirement: Households at 50% to 80% of county AMI who are in the labor force (jobs-housing linkage); 55-year regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Through SHRA multifamily pre-application rounds (next expected January 2027). Current fee schedule (2024 report): office and hotel $3.26, research and development and commercial $2.17, manufacturing and warehouse $1.08 per gross square foot, adjusted annually.
layering_notes: Oldest local source (1990). Revenue tracks commercial construction and is volatile, so the balance is usually smaller than the AHO fund. Used mainly for new construction workforce units at 50% to 80% AMI, which complements deeper-targeted HOME or MHP units in the same project. Local below-market loan; state prevailing wage exemption may be available absent federal funds. The companion City of Sacramento Housing Trust Fund (City Code 18.56) is a separate pool covered in Pass 3. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
prevailing_wage_basis: Project-dependent. 2026 SHRA Multifamily Lending Policies (County), Section 6.1: state and federal law require prevailing wages on projects receiving governmental benefits; 6.1.1 names the main state exemption, a below-market-rate loan on a project with at least 40% of units restricted at 80% AMI for at least 20 years (Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E)); 6.1.2 Davis-Bacon applies if the deal also has HOME at 12+ units or CDBG at 8+ units; 6.1.3 pay the higher rate when both apply. Loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b); the outcome depends on loan terms and the restricted-unit share of the project, so left unclear. Sources: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-SHRA-Multifamily-Lending-Policies-County-final.pdf ; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Left unclear: SHRA policy 6.1 and Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) make state prevailing wage turn on project facts (below-market loan, 40% of units at 80% AMI for 20 years); Davis-Bacon only if HOME or CDBG is layered.

program_name: HOME Investment Partnerships Program, Sacramento County HOME Consortium
administering_agency: SHRA for the County of Sacramento (lead entity) and consortium cities Citrus Heights, Folsom, Rancho Cordova, Galt and Isleton
typical_award_size: 2027 Action Plan: $2,825,253 annual allocation plus $900,000 program income ($3.73M total). 2024 entitlement $2,965,817; year-end 2024 balance $15.7M ($9.1M uncommitted). $2,500,000 posted as available June 1, 2026. Recent project loans $1.5M to $8.9M (Arden Star $8.9M for 48 HOME units; Madison Square $4.45M; San Juan Phase II $4.2M).
per_unit_cap: HUD 221(d)(3) per-unit subsidy limits under 24 CFR 92.250; recent awards roughly $170,000 to $210,000 per HOME unit.
affordability_requirement: 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI (Low HOME rents), remainder at or below 60% AMI with rents at 65% AMI; federal affordability period 5 to 20 years but SHRA records 55-year restrictions. 15% CHDO set-aside.
next_deadline: Through SHRA multifamily pre-application rounds (next expected January 2027); HUD program year is the calendar year, 2027 Action Plan drafted August 2026.
layering_notes: Applies to the unincorporated county and the five consortium cities (Elk Grove and the City of Sacramento are separate HUD entitlements). HOME on 12 or more units triggers Davis-Bacon, and SHRA policy requires the higher of state or federal wage by trade when both apply; applicants must flag wage assumptions in the SHRA narrative. HOME units stack with CTCAC units but the HOME rent and income rules are the binding constraint on those units. SHRA may assign HOME rather than local fee funds to a request, so underwrite wages conservatively. Environmental review (NEPA) deadline falls two months after SHRA's application deadline. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
audit_note: Spot check Nov 9, 2026: 2027 Action Plan shows HOME $2,825,252.91 allocation plus $900,000 program income; SHRA June 1, 2026 funds list shows County HOME $2,500,000; pre-applications run 2 or 3 times a year and SHRA is not currently accepting them; County lending policies require the higher of state or Davis-Bacon wages. Action Plan lists Citrus Heights and Rancho Cordova as HOME Consortium members and Folsom, Isleton and Galt as cooperative agreement cities. Project loan figures and 2024 balances were not re-checked on these pages.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), Urban County of Sacramento
administering_agency: SHRA for the County of Sacramento
typical_award_size: 2027 Action Plan: $6,151,763 allocation plus $2,025,000 prior-year resources ($8.18M); about $3.63M targeted to the housing development, preservation and homeownership goal (27 rental units rehabilitated, 10 constructed, 100 owner rehabs), the rest to infrastructure and public services. June 2025 notice listed $0 County CDBG for multifamily; June 2026 notice did not list CDBG.
affordability_requirement: At least 51% of assisted units for households at or below 80% AMI.
next_deadline: Through SHRA rounds when offered (rehabilitation projects only); 2027 program year begins January 2027.
layering_notes: Limited developer value: CDBG cannot fund new construction unless carried out by a Community Based Development Organization, and SHRA offers it only for rehabilitation. Davis-Bacon applies at 8 or more units. Useful for acquisition-rehab or preservation deals paired with 4% credits and CalHFA or SHRA bonds. CDBG-CV balances are committed to the Mather Community Campus shelter.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County of Sacramento
administering_agency: County of Sacramento (HCD entitlement recipient); SHRA administers the multifamily share
typical_award_size: 2024 PLHA income $6,666,613; year-end 2024 uncommitted multifamily balance $2,245,525 and single-family (down payment assistance) balance $2,804,135. Recent multifamily commitments: Arden Star $2.42M (13 units), San Juan $1.7M (7 units), San Juan Phase II $2.7M then increased to $4.7M (70 units). $0 posted as available for County projects June 1, 2026.
per_unit_cap: None published; recent awards about $185,000 to $245,000 per PLHA unit.
affordability_requirement: Multifamily share for households at or below 60% AMI (with workforce flexibility under the County's PLHA plan); 55-year restriction. At least 25% of each allocation is reserved for down payment assistance below 50% AMI.
next_deadline: Through SHRA multifamily rounds as annual HCD PLHA disbursements arrive (SB 2 recording-fee revenue, variable). Next SHRA round expected January 2027; check the funds-available notice for a PLHA line.
layering_notes: State formula money without federal strings, so it is the preferred SHRA source when Davis-Bacon must be avoided (state prevailing wage still applies unless the below-market-loan exemption is met). Often paired with HOME in the same SHRA award (San Juan Phase II). The separate HCD Local Housing Trust Fund match program is no longer funding; the County's last LHTF award was 2024. SB 802 negotiations included language keeping PLHA flowing to all jurisdictions once the regional agency forms. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
prevailing_wage_basis: Project-dependent. 2026 SHRA Multifamily Lending Policies (County), Section 6.1: state and federal law require prevailing wages on projects receiving governmental benefits; 6.1.1 names the main state exemption, a below-market-rate loan on a project with at least 40% of units restricted at 80% AMI for at least 20 years (Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E)); 6.1.2 Davis-Bacon applies if the deal also has HOME at 12+ units or CDBG at 8+ units; 6.1.3 pay the higher rate when both apply. PLHA is state money with no Davis-Bacon trigger of its own, and the PLHA annual report states no labor rule. Loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b); the outcome depends on loan terms and the restricted-unit share of the project, so left unclear. Sources: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-SHRA-Multifamily-Lending-Policies-County-final.pdf ; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Left unclear: SHRA policy 6.1 and Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) make state prevailing wage turn on project facts (below-market loan, 40% of units at 80% AMI for 20 years); Davis-Bacon only if HOME or CDBG is layered.

program_name: SHRA Multifamily Mortgage Revenue Bonds (Housing Authority of the County of Sacramento conduit issuance)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of Sacramento, staffed by SHRA
typical_award_size: No minimum or maximum bond amount; sized to the senior lender's loan. Issuance fee 25 bps of the bond amount at closing; annual administration fee 5 bps of outstanding bonds (minimum $15,000) plus $100 per SHRA-regulated non-bond unit per year; when another issuer is used SHRA still charges up to 0.25% for TEFRA review. CDLAC fees and 0.5% performance deposit pass through.
affordability_requirement: Federal and state minimum: 20% of units at 50% AMI, or 30% at 60% AMI plus 10% at 50% AMI (H&S Code 34312.3); non-competitive CTCAC projects targeting above 60% AMI must average no more than 59% AMI. Rents capped at 30% of 50% or 60% AMI. Bond regulatory agreement for the qualified project period or 55 years from 50% occupancy, incorporating the CDLAC resolution.
next_deadline: Pre-application and full application on the SHRA schedule tied to CDLAC rounds (2026: applications March 2 and Sept 1 for the July/Sept and March/May 2027 CDLAC rounds). Inducement resolution and TEFRA hearing go to the Board of Supervisors or City Council before the CDLAC filing.
layering_notes: Local alternative to CalHFA, CSCDA and CMFA for 4% deals in the City and unincorporated county (other cities by cooperation agreement). SHRA requires projects using other issuers to meet SHRA affordability and due diligence standards and pays for TEFRA review. Nonprofit owners seeking the welfare exemption must show ongoing day-to-day involvement (services, management or maintenance) under SHRA policy 9.1.11. Bonds alone are generally not treated as public funds for state prevailing wage, but SHRA gap loans or HOME in the same deal usually are. Private placements waive the investment-grade rating requirement. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
prevailing_wage_basis: False for the bond financing itself. DIR coverage determinations PW 2006-001 Horizons at Indio (https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-001.pdf) and PW 2006-020(A) Heber (https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-020(A).pdf), following PW 2004-016 Rancho Santa Fe, hold that conduit multifamily revenue bonds, where the issuer assigns its rights to a private trustee that advances proceeds to the borrower and receives repayments directly, are not payment of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and not a public below-market loan under 1720(b)(4). SHRA's structure matches: 2026 SHRA County Multifamily Lending and Bond Policies Section 9.1.3 state there is no liability to or pledge of the County's, the Housing Authority's or SHRA's faith, credit or taxing power, repayment is limited to private project revenues, and the program is self-supporting with the developer paying all costs; Section 9.4.11 provides a bank bond trustee as custodian of funds. Caveat: SHRA gap loans, HOME, CDBG or other public funds in the same deal are tested separately under SHRA policy 6.1 and Labor Code 1720 (1720(c)(5)(E) exemption; Davis-Bacon for HOME at 12+ or CDBG at 8+ units). Sources: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-SHRA-Multifamily-Lending-Policies-County-final.pdf ; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Set false on DIR determinations PW 2006-001 and PW 2006-020(A) for trustee-structured conduit bonds, which matches SHRA policy 9.1.3 and 9.4.11; other public funds in the deal still need their own prevailing wage test.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of Sacramento
administering_agency: SHRA (the County housing authority administers all vouchers for both the City and County)
typical_award_size: Competitive RFP awards from the tenant-based HCV allocation or HUD-VASH; no RFP anticipated in 2026. Cap of 25 units or 25% of a building, whichever is greater, with exceptions for elderly or disabled households and units with qualifying supportive services (common for PSH). HAP contract up to 20 years with extensions to 40 years total.
per_unit_cap: 25 units or 25% of units per project unless the supportive-services or elderly/disabled exception applies
affordability_requirement: HCV income limits (very low income, 75% of admissions at or below 30% AMI); PBV units leased through the Coordinated Access System for homeless set-aside units under a Housing First model.
next_deadline: SHRA states it does not anticipate a Project-Based Voucher RFP in 2026; updates come through the SHRA listserv. HUD's 2026 budget guidance also asked PHAs to pause new PBV commitments except for public housing repositioning, so a 2027 RFP is uncertain. Non-competitive PBV remains possible for SHRA-controlled sites and for adding units to existing HAP contracts.
layering_notes: PBV HAP contracts underwrite debt on PSH units (rents at the payment standard, up to 120% of FMR with approval) and were the operating engine for Homekey, NPLH and MHP supportive units in Sacramento. With no 2026 RFP, new PSH deals should plan on Homekey+ operating grants, BHSA rental subsidies or the County Flexible Housing Pool instead. Referral mechanics for PBV PSH run through Sacramento Steps Forward (see Continuum of Care record). SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (HUD PBV development requirements, labor standards): for development activity (new construction or rehabilitation) involving nine or more PBV contract units, the owner and its contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages and the PHA monitors compliance; existing-housing PBV contracts with no development activity do not trigger it. SHRA's draft 2027 HCV Administrative Plan (Chapter 21) states the PHA will project-base units in new construction, rehabilitation and existing projects as defined in an RFP, so PBV awards to new construction or rehab of 9+ contract units carry Davis-Bacon. https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/SHRA-HCV-2027-Admin-Plan-Draft.pdf https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.153

program_name: Sacramento County Affordable Housing Fee Deferral and Waiver Program (county impact fees and SacSewer impact fees)
administering_agency: County of Sacramento Department of Finance with SHRA certification; Sacramento Area Sewer District (SacSewer, formerly SASD and Regional San) for sewer impact fee waivers
typical_award_size: Deferral or waiver of county development impact fees (Antelope, North Vineyard Station, Vineyard and Florin Vineyard plan area fees, library facilities fees, county transportation development fees) and SASD/Regional San sewer impact fees. Waivers are proportional to the share of very low-income units. Annual cap on waivers: greater of 200 dwelling units or 5% of prior-year new residential permits in the unincorporated county. SacSewer reported over $900,000 waived across five projects as of October 2025. $1,000 application fee; deferrals require a 10% fee deposit.
affordability_requirement: Deferral: at least 10% of units affordable to very low income (50% AMI) or 49% affordable to low income (80% AMI). Waiver: at least 10% of units at or below 50% AMI. Fees become due with interest penalties if the units are not delivered within 24 months.
next_deadline: Rolling, before building permit issuance; requires an SHRA Certification Letter, preliminary title report, and a recorded agreement, note and deed of trust (subordinable to construction financing). Deferred fees are due at close of escrow or 24 months after the agreement, whichever is first.
layering_notes: County impact fee relief applies to unincorporated projects; SASD and Regional San sewer impact fee waivers are available in all cities in the county and the unincorporated area. Sewer impact fees in Sacramento run several thousand dollars per unit, so the waiver is worth roughly $5,000 to $10,000 per very-low-income unit; it reduces basis and improves the CTCAC cost-containment score. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees waived or forgiven by a public agency as public funds, so a waiver can itself trigger state prevailing wage unless the project is otherwise exempt; confirm with counsel. City of Sacramento has its own fee deferral and fee reduction program (Pass 3).
prevailing_wage_basis: Unresolved. The County fee deferral page (Chapter 16.100) states no prevailing wage rule. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, but 1720(c) exemptions (including de minimis and the 1720(c)(5) residential exemptions) and the other funding in the deal decide coverage. Sources: https://feedeferral.saccounty.gov/us/en/affordable-housing.html ; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Left unclear: only basis is Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (waived fees are public funds); outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts.

program_name: Sacramento County Affordable Housing Incentive Program (density bonus, Zoning Code Section 6.5.4)
administering_agency: Sacramento County Planning and Environmental Review
typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law as implemented in the County Zoning Code Section 6.5.4 (Table 6.4): 20% bonus for 5% very low income rising to 50% at 15%; 20% for 10% low income rising to 35% at 20% and 50% at 24%; 5% for 10% moderate income for-sale rising to 50% at 44%; 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects (up to 20% moderate) with no maximum density within a half mile of a major transit stop, plus a three-story or 33-foot height increase there; separate schedules for senior, special needs, low income college student and land donation. Up to five concessions (Table 6.5: VLI 1 at 5%, 2 at 10%, 3 at 15%, 4 at 16% to 99%; LI 1 at 10%, 2 at 17%, 3 at 24%; five for 100% affordable; one more for child care). Table 6.4.1 (added June 11, 2026) adds a further bonus for projects restricting no more than 50% of units that provide at least 15% very low, 24% lower or 44% moderate income units.
affordability_requirement: Minimum five units with 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate (for-sale), or special population set-asides; rental target units restricted 55 years with professional management; units built concurrently and dispersed on site.
next_deadline: Rolling; filed with the entitlement application together with an Affordable Housing Strategies Memorandum; the County does not charge a processing fee for eligible applications (Housing Element page). Affordable Housing Agreement must be recorded before grading and building permits.
layering_notes: Parking maximums: 1 space studio and 1-bedroom, 1.5 for 2- and 3-bedroom, 2.5 for 4-bedroom; within a half mile of major transit 0.5 per bedroom, 0.5 per unit for 100% lower-income rental, none for special needs housing. Waivers of standards that physically preclude the project are unlimited but do not count as concessions. Land donation (one acre or 40 units, zoned 30+ units per acre) earns bonus and can satisfy the AHO. Combine with the AHO fee exemption (20% affordable at 17+ du/ac) and the Countywide Rezone Program sites for by-right or streamlined approval. 100% affordable LIHTC projects typically use the 80% bonus and parking reductions to cut costs rather than add units.
audit_note: Spot check Nov 9, 2026: Table 6.4 shows the low income bonus reaches 50% at 24% low income units (35% at 20%), not at 20% as the record stated. Other terms (5-unit minimum, 55-year rental term, concurrent and dispersed units, Affordable Housing Strategies Memorandum, parking Table 6.6) match.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Welfare Exemption processing, Sacramento County Assessor
administering_agency: Sacramento County Assessor, Institutional Exemptions Section (BOE issues the Organizational Clearance Certificate)
typical_award_size: Exemption of the qualifying low-income share of assessed value from the roughly 1.1% to 1.2% total property tax rate in Sacramento County (plus any direct levies that remain). Annual filing with the Assessor.
affordability_requirement: Per state law: lower-income units (80% AMI, 140% continuation rule) under LIHTC or a recorded regulatory agreement; limited partnerships need a nonprofit or eligible LLC managing general partner with an OCC and a Supplemental Clearance Certificate.
next_deadline: Annual claims due February 15 (next Feb 15, 2027; postmark next business day if a weekend or holiday). First-time filers submit BOE-267 with the BOE-277 OCC and the low-income supplemental affidavit (BOE-267-L or 267-L1 for partnerships). Contact (916) 875-0720 or ASR-InstitutionalExemptions@saccounty.gov.
layering_notes: Sacramento assessor applies the statewide rules (see Pass 1 BOE record); no county-specific abatement JPA exists. SHRA bond policy 9.1.11 additionally requires the nonprofit owner to have material day-to-day involvement (services, management or maintenance) for bond-financed projects claiming the exemption, which aligns with BOE managing-GP scrutiny. File the construction-period claim as soon as the OCC is issued and the site is under development to avoid a year of taxes.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(4) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works requires construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, including fees, loans or other obligations normally required in executing the construction contract that are reduced or waived. The welfare exemption (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)) reduces property tax on the completed property; it pays no construction cost, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage.

program_name: Sacramento County Behavioral Health (MHSA/BHSA) housing capital for permanent supportive housing
administering_agency: Sacramento County Department of Health Services, Behavioral Health Services, with SHRA screening projects through its multifamily rounds
typical_award_size: Not published as a NOFA amount. The FY2026-29 BHSA Integrated Plan budgets about $200,000 per BHSA unit for its planned capital project (30 BHSA units of 120, about $6M) and states 2 capital projects. Prior MHSA practice: SHRA's June 2025 funds notice said projects could be considered for County MHSA housing financing for PSH units; example $2.5M MHSA to Auburn Oaks PSH. BHSA requires 30% of county funds for housing interventions, up to 25% of that for capital.
affordability_requirement: PSH units restricted to persons with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk, referred through County Behavioral Health; typically 30% AMI or below with rental or operating subsidy.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No stand-alone BHSA capital NOFA or solicitation is posted; housing requests ride on SHRA multifamily pre-applications (2027 schedule not yet posted, likely January 2027).
layering_notes: BHSA classification: the Integrated Plan funds housing capital and rental subsidies, so this is a deployable capital source (kept as loan, consistent with prior MHSA capital practice through SHRA). Successor to the CalHFA Special Needs Housing Program and county NPLH allocations (NPLH is closed; Sacramento County ran its last Request to Partner in 2020). BHSA capital and operating subsidies can underwrite PSH units in 4% and 9% deals and support CTCAC homeless priority and the CDLAC Homeless set-aside. Pair with Homekey+ and HHAP. County funds are public funds for prevailing wage. Amounts and process should be confirmed with Behavioral Health Services and SHRA before underwriting.
cycle_notes: The County BHSA Three-Year Integrated Plan FY2026-27 to FY2028-29 commits BHSA Housing Interventions to capital development: 2 projects planned; the detailed entry is an unidentified braided-funding project with 30 BHSA units in a 120-unit permanent supportive housing development at about $200,000 BHSA per unit (state cap $450,000), by-right approval, units expected by July 1, 2029. BHSA housing is 30% of county BHSA funds (half for chronically homeless), with up to 25% of housing funds allowed for capital. BHS will coordinate with SHRA on SHRA-funded developments; DHSH administers other housing capital (HHAP).
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); the DHCS BHSA County Policy Manual capital development section (https://policy-manual.mes.dhcs.ca.gov/behavioral-health-services-act-county-policy-manual/V1.0.0/7-bhsa-components-and-requirements) states no prevailing wage rule, and when deployed through SHRA, SHRA Lending Policies Section 6.1 (https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-SHRA-Multifamily-Lending-Policies-County-final.pdf) restate state law with the 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption.
audit_note: PW citation pass 2026-11-09: true was uncited and no program-specific rule was found; set unclear per Tier 3 rule (1720(b) alone does not support true).

program_name: Sacramento Continuum of Care (CA-503) funding and PBV PSH referral system
administering_agency: Sacramento Steps Forward (CoC lead agency and HMIS lead) for the City and County of Sacramento
typical_award_size: HUD CoC Program awards described as tens of millions per round across more than 30 renewal projects; competition now runs every other year. 2026 competition: local letters of intent for new projects due July 2, 2026, local applications July 14, 2026, consolidated application to HUD Sept 30, 2026. Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program total $8,082,381 across seven projects (as of 2025).
affordability_requirement: CoC PSH serves households experiencing homelessness (chronic homelessness priority) through the Coordinated Access System; rental assistance and leasing, not capital.
next_deadline: 2026 round closed (HUD submission Sept 30, 2026). Next local competition expected 2028 under the every-other-year cycle, with renewals in between.
layering_notes: CoC dollars rarely fund capital, but CoC PSH rental assistance or leasing can replace PBV as the operating subsidy on a share of units, and CoC participation is required for Homekey+ and HHAP coordination. For PBV PSH buildings, SSF runs the lease-up: referrals begin 120 days before the temporary certificate of occupancy, are over-referred by 20%, and target full occupancy within 60 days of TCO, with SHRA paying the subsidy within 30 days of move-in. The 2023 City-County Affordable Housing Plan (SHRA, SSF, City, County) tracks a 649-unit PSH pipeline and a proposed joint PSH fund.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 578.99(h): the provisions of the Davis-Bacon Act do not apply to the HUD CoC Program (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/578.99). State prevailing wage could still apply if other public funds pay for construction.
audit_note: PW fix Nov 9, 2026: false confirmed under 24 CFR 578.99(h) (Davis-Bacon does not apply to the CoC Program). The record is CoC funding plus the PBV PSH referral system; the PBV subsidy itself is SHRA's (record 6936e589cd), where 24 CFR 983.153(c) applies to PBV development of 9+ contract units. State prevailing wage can still apply through other public construction funds.

program_name: County Fund for Housing (CFH)
administering_agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC)
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 NOFA: $8,000,000 available (up from $1,500,000 in FY 2025-26 and $1.5M in FY 2024-25). FY 2025-26 awards: Freebird Development, Healdsburg, 42 units, $1,340,417; Burbank Housing, Guerneville, 21 units, $159,583. Minimum loan $100,000; maximum limited to one program year's funds unless the Board commits future years. Since 2003 the fund has invested over $24M in more than 550 homes.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap; CFH-assisted unit count is set using the HOME per-unit subsidy limits (0-bdrm $153,314 to 4-bdrm $303,490 as of Sept 2021).
affordability_requirement: Rental: all assisted units affordable 55 years, initially to very low income (50% AMI), may float up to low income (80% AMI) on turnover. Priorities: most units at lowest incomes, geographic distribution across cities and unincorporated area, Housing Opportunity Sites, integration with health and human services, PSH and special needs. Homeownership: first-time buyers at or below 120% AMI with 20% of units at 80% AMI.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2027-28 combined CDC NOFA (CDBG, HOME, ESG, CFH, LMIHAF) has not been posted. Based on the FY 2026-27 schedule, expect a late February 2027 release with an early April 2027 application deadline; the agency has not announced dates.
layering_notes: Sonoma's main local gap source, capitalized by County General Fund, Reinvestment and Revitalization Funds (former RDA), developer in-lieu fees from the residential Affordable Housing Program, non-residential Workforce Housing fees, countywide transient occupancy tax, and loan repayments. Residual receipts loans structured to be compatible with LIHTC investor requirements; interest set by the Commission. Awarded in one annual NOFA together with HOME, CDBG, ESG and LMIHAF so applicants file once. Funds may go to projects inside cities only where the city has a RHNA Sharing Agreement with the County (shelters and congregate facilities exempt). Sponsors must comply with the County Living Wage Ordinance; the policy is silent on prevailing wage, so the Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) below-market-loan exemption may apply unless HOME or CDBG is also used. The County does not act as a conduit bond issuer; recent Sonoma deals used CMFA (Burbank Housing $8.12M) and CalHFA. CFH awards are typically $1M to $3M and are counted as local leverage for CTCAC tiebreaker and CDLAC readiness.
cycle_notes: Single combined annual CDC NOFA with a mandatory technical assistance workshop. FY 2026-27 round: issued February 21, 2026, applications due April 3, 2026 at 5 pm, CD Committee and CTAC recommendations May 13, 2026, final hearings June 17, 2026, Board adoption July 7, 2026. No FY 2027-28 NOFA posted as of November 8, 2026. FY 2026-27 CFH amount confirmed in NOFA: $8,000,000.
audit_note: Deadline refreshed November 8, 2026. Prevailing wage left unclear: CFH Policy (11/7/2023) cites only the County Living Wage Ordinance, and CDC Loan Policies (10/8/2024) section III.M.2 requires compliance with State prevailing wage law only as applicable, so no rule settles coverage for a CFH-only loan.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The CFH Policy (adopted November 7, 2023, sections 6.3 and 6.4) requires compliance with the CDC Loan Policies and the County Living Wage Ordinance but states no prevailing wage mandate (https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/County-Fund-Housing-Policy-Adopted-11-7-2023.pdf); CDC Loan Policies (October 8, 2024) section III.M.1 applies Davis-Bacon only where loan proceeds come from a federal source, and III.M.2 requires sponsors to follow state prevailing wage law as applicable and certify compliance, which defers to Labor Code 1720 rather than imposing wages (https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/Plans%20Policies%20and%20Reports/CDC-Loan-Policies-10-08-2024.pdf). CFH is local money (General Fund, former RDA funds, in-lieu fees, TOT), so below-market residual receipts loans may fall under the 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption (below-market loan, at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI; see DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: HOME Investment Partnerships Program, Sonoma Urban County
administering_agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC) for the Urban County
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 estimate: HOME $743,322 plus CHDO set-aside $99,090 (Consolidated Plan expects about $660,693 per year plus $60,000 program income). FY 2025-26: $495,519 HOME (George's Hideaway, Burbank Housing, $185,519; tenant-based rental assistance $310,000) plus $99,103 CHDO to George's Hideaway.
per_unit_cap: HUD HOME per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250).
affordability_requirement: HOME rules: 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI (Low HOME rent), remainder at or below 60% AMI; affordability period 5 to 20 years by subsidy, CDC loan policies extend to 55 years. Ready-to-proceed projects preferred.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2027-28 combined CDC NOFA (CDBG, HOME, ESG, CFH, LMIHAF) has not been posted. Based on the FY 2026-27 schedule, expect a late February 2027 release with an early April 2027 application deadline; the agency has not announced dates. NEPA review, Section 3 and Build America Buy America compliance required before agreement.
layering_notes: Urban County entitlement area = unincorporated county plus Cloverdale, Cotati, Healdsburg, Rohnert Park, Sebastopol, Sonoma and Windsor; Santa Rosa and Petaluma are separate HUD entitlements (Pass 3). Small allocation (well under $1M a year), so HOME is usually a minor layer on one project per year alongside CFH and PLHA. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. The County routinely uses HOME for TBRA, leaving even less for development. Programs are awarded in the single CDC NOFA with CFH and CDBG.
cycle_notes: Single combined annual CDC NOFA with a mandatory technical assistance workshop. FY 2026-27 round: issued February 21, 2026, applications due April 3, 2026 at 5 pm, CD Committee and CTAC recommendations May 13, 2026, final hearings June 17, 2026, Board adoption July 7, 2026. No FY 2027-28 NOFA posted as of November 8, 2026. FY 2026-27 estimates confirmed in NOFA: HOME $743,322 and CHDO $99,090.
prevailing_wage_basis: Sonoma County CDC FY 2026-27 Federal Funding Policies section 7.5 (Davis-Bacon applies to any HOME-funded project with 12 or more HOME-assisted units, 24 CFR 92.354) and CDC Loan Policies section III.M.1: https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/Plans%20Policies%20and%20Reports/BOS%20Approved%202026-2027%20Federal%20Funding%20Policies.pdf

program_name: Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), Sonoma Urban County
administering_agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC) for the Urban County
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 estimate: $3,145,583 for affordable housing projects, non-housing capital projects and microenterprise assistance, plus $247,872 for fair housing public services (the FY 2026-27 figure includes reprogrammed prior-year funds; the Consolidated Plan expects about $1.66M annual allocation). FY 2025-26: $1.88M total, with $941,605 to the countywide housing rehabilitation program and the rest to infrastructure and child care.
affordability_requirement: Units for households at or below 80% AMI (51% of units in assisted rental projects); affordable housing projects ready to proceed to construction preferred.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2027-28 combined CDC NOFA (CDBG, HOME, ESG, CFH, LMIHAF) has not been posted. Based on the FY 2026-27 schedule, expect a late February 2027 release with an early April 2027 application deadline; the agency has not announced dates.
layering_notes: Urban County entitlement area = unincorporated county plus Cloverdale, Cotati, Healdsburg, Rohnert Park, Sebastopol, Sonoma and Windsor; Santa Rosa and Petaluma are separate HUD entitlements (Pass 3). CDC lists affordable housing projects as a CDBG eligible use, but new construction remains limited by federal rules (CBDO carve-out) and most housing CDBG goes to the CDC's rehabilitation program and off-site infrastructure. Davis-Bacon applies at 8 or more units. Useful for site infrastructure or acquisition-rehab tied to a 4% deal.
cycle_notes: Single combined annual CDC NOFA with a mandatory technical assistance workshop. FY 2026-27 round: issued February 21, 2026, applications due April 3, 2026 at 5 pm, CD Committee and CTAC recommendations May 13, 2026, final hearings June 17, 2026, Board adoption July 7, 2026. No FY 2027-28 NOFA posted as of November 8, 2026. FY 2026-27 estimates confirmed in NOFA: CDBG $3,145,583 capital and housing, $247,872 fair housing public services.
prevailing_wage_basis: Sonoma County CDC FY 2026-27 Federal Funding Policies section 7.5 (CDBG-funded construction triggers Davis-Bacon except rehabilitation of properties with fewer than 8 units or force account labor, 24 CFR 570.603): https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/Plans%20Policies%20and%20Reports/BOS%20Approved%202026-2027%20Federal%20Funding%20Policies.pdf

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County of Sonoma
administering_agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC) for the County of Sonoma
typical_award_size: FY 2025-26 distribution $979,795 (Burbank Housing Guerneville 21 units $555,795; Habitat for Humanity Sebastopol 4 ownership units $424,000). Separate NOFAs: Sept 10, 2025 for rental or ownership projects (due Oct 30, 2025); Sept 17, 2026 for affordable owner-occupied workforce housing only, $674,360 over the counter. Residual receipts loans.
per_unit_cap: None published; recent rental award about $26,500 per unit.
affordability_requirement: County PLHA Five-Year Plan: 75% to multifamily rental for households at or below 50% AMI, 20% to owner-occupied workforce housing up to 120% AMI, 5% administration. 55-year restrictions.
next_deadline: Rental PLHA next expected in the CDC's fall 2026 or early 2027 NOFA (2025 pattern: September release, Oct 30 deadline); AOWH PLHA open over the counter since Sept 17, 2026 until the $674,360 is exhausted. Geography excludes the City of Santa Rosa and City of Petaluma, which receive their own PLHA.
layering_notes: State formula money with no federal strings; small annual amounts (under $1M) make it a top-up to CFH rather than a primary source. Mandatory technical assistance workshop before applying. Nonprofit and government applicants only. Below-market residual receipts loan, so the Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) prevailing wage exemption may apply absent other public funds that carry their own requirement.
prevailing_wage_basis: Neither the County FY 2025-26 PLHA NOFA nor HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines and Formula Allocation NOFA mention prevailing wage. Coverage rests on the general Labor Code 1720(b) public-funds definition; PLHA residual receipts loans may fall under the 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption (below-market loans, at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI) or 1720(c)(3) de minimis, depending on project facts and other sources. Source: https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Prevailing wage left unclear: PLHA NOFA and HCD guidelines are silent, and the outcome depends on Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Corrected exemption citation from 1720(c)(6)(E) to 1720(c)(5)(E).

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Sonoma County Housing Successor
administering_agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission as housing successor to the former County redevelopment agency
typical_award_size: Services: up to $250,000 per year for homeless prevention and rapid rehousing (FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 CDC NOFAs). Development: LMIHAF housing development spending was $3,837,187 in FY 2024-25 and $1,316,702 in FY 2023-24; the annual reports do not break this out by project or award size. Balance available for all other uses $2,509,338 at June 30, 2025 (down from $7,248,573 at June 30, 2024), of which $1,509,338 is excess surplus; loans and grants receivable $31,242,980.
affordability_requirement: Community Redevelopment Law housing provisions as applied by HSC 34176.1 (very low and low income). For development spending, at least 30 percent must go to rental housing for households at or below 30% AMI (FY 2024-25 report, Note 9); the report states Casa Roseland, under construction, has 32 percent of units at or below 30% AMI. Current NOFA awards are homeless services.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. LMIHAF is offered only for homeless prevention and rapid rehousing services in the combined CDC NOFA; the FY 2027-28 NOFA has not been posted (expected about late February 2027 based on the prior cycle). No capital round is offered.
layering_notes: The Sonoma County Community Development Commission, parent entity of the Sonoma County Housing Authority, is the housing successor. The fund pays for services through the annual CDC NOFA and also finances development directly: $3,837,187 of housing development spending in FY 2024-25 and $1,316,702 in FY 2023-24. The FY 2024-25 report lists Roseland Village (665 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, a former RDA property) and Casa Roseland as under construction but does not tie the development spending to a named project. Its plan for the $1,509,338 excess surplus (held more than 6 years) is reinvestment in affordable homeownership loans and/or new construction or preservation of affordable rental developments, so capital money is possible but is not offered through a posted competitive round. Former RDA Reinvestment and Revitalization money flows into CFH instead. Loan repayments ($31.2M receivable) replenish the fund. The FY 2025-26 report was not posted as of November 10, 2026.
cycle_notes: Awarded in the combined annual CDC NOFA. FY 2026-27: $250,000 for homeless prevention and rapid rehousing services, issued February 21, 2026, due April 3, 2026. Fund balance available for all other uses $2,509,338 at June 30, 2025.
audit_note: Corrected November 10, 2026: the FY 2024-25 and FY 2023-24 Housing Successor annual reports show LMIHAF development spending ($3,837,187 and $1,316,702), so the record no longer says the fund is not used for development. FY 2025-26 report not yet posted. Prevailing wage left unclear: no LMIHAF document states a rule, 1720(c)(1) likely unavailable because the housing successor is the CDC (parent of the Housing Authority), and 1720(c)(5)(E) turns on project facts.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The FY 2024-25 Housing Successor Agency Annual Report (https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/Successor%20Agency/Housing%20Successor%20Agency%20Annual%20Reports/Remediated_FY%2024-25%20Housing%20Successor%20Agency%20Annual%20Report.pdf) states no prevailing wage rule. Homelessness prevention and rapid rehousing grants are not construction under 1720(a)(1), but the fund paid $3,837,187 for housing development in FY 2024-25. The 1720(c)(1) private residential exemption does not apply to projects built under an agreement with a successor agency to a redevelopment agency or a local public housing authority, and the housing successor here is the Community Development Commission, parent entity of the Sonoma County Housing Authority, so a development agreement with it should not be assumed exempt under 1720(c)(1). 1720(c)(4) names only the former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund, not housing successor asset funds. Below-market loans can be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), as DIR PW 2019-018 applied (https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf). Land transfers below fair market value are public funds under 1720(b)(3).

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers for Permanent Supportive Housing, Sonoma County Housing Authority
administering_agency: Sonoma County Housing Authority (division of the CDC); jurisdiction is all of Sonoma County except the City of Santa Rosa
typical_award_size: 2025 PSH RFP: up to 100 project-based vouchers for studio, one- and two-bedroom PSH units in new construction or substantial rehab; applications were due June 24, 2025; 20-year HAP contract with automatic 20-year renewal; one-time $500 per voucher administrative fee plus billed-back environmental and legal review. Board of Commissioners committed 150 future PBVs to PSH (Nov 20, 2024) to support Homekey+ applicants. The authority administers about 2,988 vouchers and roughly $45M a year.
per_unit_cap: HUD limits: 20% of voucher funding may be project-based plus 10% more for units serving homeless or other special populations; per-project cap of 25 units or 25% unless units serve elderly, disabled or supportive-services households.
affordability_requirement: PSH for chronically homeless households referred through the Sonoma County Coordinated Entry System under its PSH prioritization policy; HCV income limits.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No new PBV RFP is posted on the CDC Doing Business page; the Housing Authority has not announced timing for an RFP for the 150 vouchers committed to PSH.
layering_notes: PBV HAP revenue is the operating subsidy that makes Homekey+, MHP supportive units and CFH-funded PSH underwritable in Sonoma; the 150-voucher commitment was adopted specifically to strengthen Homekey+ applications. Santa Rosa projects must use the Santa Rosa Housing Authority (Pass 3). Prior RFPs: 2018 and 2023 general rounds (up to 100 vouchers, $1,000 fee), 2022 existing-housing round (110 vouchers to 8 projects).
cycle_notes: Irregular competitive PBV RFPs (2018, 2022, 2023, 2025). 2025 PSH RFP: released May 20, 2025, up to 100 vouchers; the RFP schedule lists proposals due June 17, 2025 while its introduction says June 24, 2025; staff recommendations July 16, 2025, Board approval August 12, 2025.
prevailing_wage_basis: Davis-Bacon applies to development (including rehabilitation) of PBV projects with 9 or more assisted units: 24 CFR 983.4 labor standards cross-reference (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.4); the 2025 Sonoma County PSH PBV RFP section C requires meeting all 24 CFR 983 requirements including prevailing wage: https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/2025%20RFP%20for%20PSH%20PBV.pdf

program_name: Affordable Housing Program fees (residential in-lieu fee and non-residential Workforce Housing fee)
administering_agency: Permit Sonoma (collection and compliance); fees deposited to the County Fund for Housing administered by the CDC
typical_award_size: Residential: every unit in unincorporated Sonoma County must build affordable units or pay an in-lieu fee graduated by size; 2026 schedule $3,108 for units of 1,000 sq ft or less rising roughly $155 per 10 sq ft (about $19,000 at 2,000 sq ft, about $29,000 at 2,750 sq ft), paid before building permit final. Non-residential (Workforce Housing Program) 2026: office, commercial and hotel $3.69 per sq ft; industrial, warehousing and agricultural processing $3.80; retail and services $6.38; first 2,000 sq ft exempt. Both adjust each January 1 by the ENR Bay Area construction cost index.
affordability_requirement: On-site alternative for rental projects: at least 15% of units affordable to low and very low income, or 10% to very low and extremely low income; ownership projects 20% split between low and moderate income. Exemptions include ADUs, farmworker and agricultural employee housing, replacement of fire-destroyed homes within 10 years, and projects complying through other approved means (Code 26-89-045).
next_deadline: Compliance method must be selected with the first permit application; fee schedules reset every January 1 (2027 schedule due January 2027).
layering_notes: This is the revenue engine for CFH and the inclusionary rule that mixed-income rental developers in the unincorporated county must satisfy; a 100% affordable LIHTC project satisfies the requirement outright and pays no fee. Developers of market-rate or mixed projects can also meet it by land dedication or restricting existing units. The fee is separate from the traffic and parks impact fees that the Board waived for affordable projects in 2025-2026.
audit_note: Reclassified from other to regulatory requirement: this record is the inclusionary in-lieu fee and nonresidential linkage fee obligation, not a deployable source; fee revenue is deployed through the County Fund for Housing record. 2026 residential and Workforce Housing fee rates re-checked against Permit Sonoma pages on November 8, 2026.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Traffic and Parks Impact Fee Waiver for Affordable Housing (2025-2026)
administering_agency: Sonoma County Board of Supervisors; administered through Permit Sonoma
typical_award_size: Waiver of County traffic mitigation and parks impact fees for affordable projects in the unincorporated area that received building permits from Feb 1, 2025 through Dec 31, 2026; staff estimated up to $19.5M in fees waived across 15 eligible projects (over 1,900 affordable units) with a $1.5M General Fund backfill.
affordability_requirement: Units reserved for moderate-, low- and very low-income renters or buyers; recorded deed restriction of at least 55 years for rental and 45 years for ownership units. Minimum affordable percentage not stated in the County release; confirm with Permit Sonoma.
next_deadline: Expires Dec 31, 2026 unless extended; the County is studying its fee structure and may adopt a permanent program. Permits must be issued before the sunset.
layering_notes: Worth several thousand dollars per unit in the unincorporated county and reduces basis for the CTCAC cost containment score. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts fees waived or forgiven by a public agency as public funds, so a waiver can itself trigger state prevailing wage unless the project is otherwise exempt; most LIHTC projects taking HCD money already pay prevailing wage. Does not cover the affordable housing in-lieu fee, school, water agency or sanitation district fees. Multi-family fee deferral (separate record) remains available after the waiver sunsets.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule found. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts fees waived, reduced or charged at less than fair market value by a public agency as public funds, so the County traffic and parks fee waiver can make a private project paid for in part with public funds; coverage then turns on project facts and the 1720(c) exemptions, including 1720(c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost) and 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI). Most LIHTC deals with HCD money pay prevailing wage anyway. Source: https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Prevailing wage left unclear: only basis is Labor Code 1720(b)(4) and the result depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts; confirm with counsel or a DIR coverage determination.

program_name: Multi-Family Development Fee Deferral Program
administering_agency: Permit Sonoma
typical_award_size: Deferral of County development fees (traffic impact and parkland dedication fees; not school, water agency or sanitation district fees) from building permit final until permanent financing closes, under a recorded Fee Deferral Agreement.
affordability_requirement: Affordable rental or ownership housing for low- or very low-income households, or special needs housing (elderly or disabled) with at least 20% of units for low-income households.
next_deadline: Rolling; request by letter with the permit application. Approval requires a Director finding that the fees are not needed for near-term programmed improvements; agreement signed before building or grading permit.
layering_notes: Bridges construction-period cash flow so impact fees are paid from permanent sources at conversion, a common pairing with CalHFA or bond-financed 4% deals. Deferral terms (interest, security) are not published; a deferred fee charged at less than market terms may be treated as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Separate single-family ADU affordable-fee deferral exists for restricted ADUs.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule found. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts fees waived, reduced or charged at less than fair market value by a public agency as public funds, so the fee deferral, if charged at less than fair market terms, can make a private project paid for in part with public funds; coverage then turns on project facts and the 1720(c) exemptions, including 1720(c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost) and 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI). Most LIHTC deals with HCD money pay prevailing wage anyway. Source: https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 Permit Sonoma does not publish deferral interest or security terms.
audit_note: Prevailing wage left unclear: only basis is Labor Code 1720(b)(4) and the result depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts; confirm with counsel or a DIR coverage determination.

program_name: Sonoma County Density Bonus Program (Code Chapter 26, Sections 26-89-050 and 26-89-060)
administering_agency: Permit Sonoma
typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law (Gov. Code 65915 to 65917) applied directly: the County acknowledges its Chapter 26 provisions are out of date and states it will comply with current state law until Housing Element Program 15 amendments are adopted (adding lower-income student housing, 100% affordable bonuses, and updated bonus and incentive calculations). Affordable Housing Incentives under Section 26-89-060 also available to projects building inclusionary units on site.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable, senior, special populations); county inclusionary units may be counted toward the bonus.
next_deadline: Rolling with the entitlement application; code update timing not published (Housing Element 2023-2031 Program 15). Contact Permit Sonoma Housing at (707) 565-1391.
layering_notes: Because the local code lags the statute, rely on Gov. Code 65915 as amended (up to 80% bonus and unlimited waivers for 100% affordable projects, 3-story height bonus near major transit, reduced parking) and expect staff to process requests case by case. Pair with the inclusionary on-site option so the same units earn the bonus and satisfy the Affordable Housing Program with no in-lieu fee. Permit Sonoma also maintains Streamlined Housing Developments (SB 35 and AB 2011 style) and Rezoning Sites for Housing pages for by-right sites.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: Permit Sonoma page confirms Chapter 26 lags state Density Bonus Law and the County will comply with current state law pending a Housing Element program amendment. The page lists (707) 565-1900 as the contact number, not 565-1391. prevailing_wage_trigger false has no prevailing_wage_basis cited; a density bonus is not a public subsidy, but no rule is cited in the record.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Welfare Exemption processing, Sonoma County Assessor
administering_agency: Sonoma County Clerk-Recorder-Assessor, Exemption Unit
typical_award_size: Exemption of the qualifying low-income share of assessed value from the roughly 1.1% to 1.2% property tax rate plus voter-approved debt in Sonoma County.
affordability_requirement: Per state law: nonprofit or eligible LLC owner, or limited partnership with a qualifying managing general partner holding an Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement or deed restriction; tax savings must maintain affordability or reduce rents; plus government financing, LIHTC, or at least 90% lower-income occupancy.
next_deadline: Annual claims Jan 1 to Feb 15 (next Feb 15, 2027). First filing on newly acquired property due within 90 days after the first day of the month following acquisition or by Feb 15 of the following year, whichever is first; property must be in exempt use or under construction within 180 days of acquisition. File BOE-267 with the OCC, regulatory agreement and the low-income supplemental affidavit. Exemption Unit (707) 565-1881, assessor@sonomacounty.gov.
layering_notes: Standard statewide rules (see Pass 1 BOE record). Sonoma's assessor page is unusually explicit about the 180-day use requirement and first-filing deadline, which matters for construction-period exemptions on land acquired mid-year. No county property tax abatement JPA exists.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: Assessor page matches the 180-day exempt use rule, first filing within 90 days after the first of the month following acquisition or February 15 whichever is first, January 1 to February 15 annual filing, OCC and regulatory agreement requirements, and (707) 565-1881. Page adds that the 90% lower-income occupancy path is capped at $100,000 of tax per year.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(4) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works requires construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, including fees, loans or other obligations normally required in executing the construction contract that are reduced or waived. The welfare exemption (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)) reduces property tax on the completed property; it pays no construction cost, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage.

program_name: Measure O Behavioral Health and Homelessness sales tax, housing category
administering_agency: Sonoma County Department of Health Services
typical_award_size: Quarter-cent countywide sales tax (approved 2020, 10-year term) generating about $30M to $33M a year across five categories, one of which is Transitional and Permanent Supportive Housing. Pathways to Sustainability NOFA (released Aug 14, 2025) awarded $10M in Measure O plus $2.4M HHAP to 26 projects on Feb 10, 2026; PSH awards went to Committee on the Shelterless ($392,034 Measure O and $196,017 HHAP) alongside city, shelter and services grants.
affordability_requirement: Transitional and permanent supportive housing for people with behavioral health conditions experiencing homelessness; awards to date are predominantly operating and services, not capital.
next_deadline: 2025-26 round awarded Feb 10, 2026. The County says it hopes applicants 'continue to submit proposals for future projects' but has not announced a 2026-27 NOFA; the February 2026 release noted doubts about future funding levels. Measure sunsets around 2030-2031.
layering_notes: Best viewed as an operating and services subsidy for PSH units rather than a capital source; pair with HCD Homekey+, MHP supportive units and PBVs. Sonoma's BHSA (Prop 1) housing interventions requirement (30% of BHSA funds, half for chronically homeless) begins July 2026 and is administered by the same department; no BHSA capital NOFA was found. County funds are public funds for prevailing wage purposes if used for construction.
prevailing_wage_basis: No Measure O program rule on prevailing wage found; awards to date fund operations and services, which are not construction. If Measure O money paid for construction or rehabilitation it would be public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1), with coverage depending on 1720(c) exemptions (for example 1720(c)(3) de minimis or 1720(c)(5)(D) nonprofit shelters with at least 50 percent nonpublic funding). Source: https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Prevailing wage left unclear: no program rule; only the general Labor Code 1720 definition applies and the result depends on use of funds and 1720(c) exemptions.

program_name: Sonoma County Homeless Coalition (CoC CA-504) funding: HUD CoC competition and Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (HHAP, ESG, HHIP)
administering_agency: Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Homelessness Services Division, as CoC collaborative applicant
typical_award_size: 2026 HUD CoC competition: about $4.9M in renewal funding; HUD had not announced CoC Bonus or DV Bonus amounts; local applications due July 21, 2026. Annual Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (state ESG, one-time HHAP, DHCS HHIP and local sources): about $5.5M expected in the 2025-26 cycle (applications due Feb 7, 2025). HHAP rounds 1 to 5 brought $32.2M to the Sonoma area; HHAP Round 5 allowed one CoC Builds PSH construction project.
affordability_requirement: Homeless households via Coordinated Entry; CoC PSH rental assistance and services; HHAP permits permanent housing capital as an eligible use.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2026 CoC collaborative application and final priority listing have been submitted; the FY 2027 HUD CoC competition and the next Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA are not yet announced (the prior Consolidated NOFA cycle had a February deadline).
layering_notes: Operating-side partner for PSH: CoC rental assistance or HHAP operating subsidy can replace or supplement PBVs on supportive units. HHAP capital for permanent housing is allowed but Sonoma has directed most HHAP to shelter, outreach and rehousing. Developers should engage the Homelessness Services Division early so a PSH project appears in the CoC's regional action plan and Coordinated Entry referral agreements.
cycle_notes: HUD CoC competition: FY 2026 local RFP published July 1, 2026, about $4.9M renewal funding, local applications due July 21, 2026 at 5 pm; new projects limited to TH, SSO and DV Bonus, no new permanent housing accepted. Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA runs separately on a winter cycle.
audit_note: Deadline refreshed November 8, 2026. Prevailing wage left unclear: CoC and Consolidated NOFA pages state no prevailing wage rule, and coverage depends on whether a project uses HHAP or CoC funds for capital.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Sonoma 2026 CoC NOFO and local RFP page (https://sonomacounty.gov/2026-notice-of-funding-opportunity-coc-program-competition-and-sonoma-county-coc-request-for-proposals-(rfp)) states no wage rule. HUD CoC rule 24 CFR 578.99(h) states the Davis-Bacon Act does not apply to the CoC program (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/578.99), and the HHAP Round 6 NOFA contains no prevailing wage provision (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/calich/hhap-6-nofa.pdf). Most funds here pay rental assistance, services and operations, which are not construction under 1720(a)(1), but HHAP permits permanent housing capital (Round 5 allowed one CoC Builds PSH construction project), so state prevailing wage on any HHAP-funded capital work depends on 1720 facts (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720).

program_name: RED Housing Fund (Renewal Enterprise District, PG&E wildfire settlement capital)
administering_agency: RED Housing Fund, a nonprofit capitalized with $10M each from the County of Sonoma and the City of Santa Rosa (PG&E 2017 fire settlement), affiliated with the Renewal Enterprise District JPA
typical_award_size: Round 2 (NOFA issued March 4, 2026, due April 1, 2026): up to $5,000,000 in loans. Loan size up to 10% of project cost. Affordable projects: subordinate or senior loan at 3% interest, interest only during construction and up to 36 months after conversion, then amortizing, up to 18-year combined term, sized at minimum 1.05 combined DSC. Market rate or middle income: construction loan at senior rate plus 1% (4% floor), up to 3 years; permanent loan at first-position rate plus 1% (4% floor), up to 10 years. 1% origination fee ($10,000 minimum); commitments expire 18 months after Board approval. Round 1 (December 21, 2021 NOFA) awards: Acme Family Apartments $800,000, Aviara $2,400,000, Casa Roseland $4,200,000, 420 Mendocino Avenue $7,000,000, Pullman Lofts $2,300,000 (reduced to $1,300,000), South Park Commons $4,000,000.
affordability_requirement: Infill, mid- to high-density residential or mixed-use projects in transit-rich or planned areas meeting RED criteria; income mix may be affordable (up to 80% AMI), middle income (80% to 120% AMI), market rate, or mixed.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The NOFA page still shows the 2026 round; no future round has been announced. Email apply@redhousingfund.org for an upload link when a NOFA is open.
layering_notes: Lender of last resort (recycling repaid settlement capital) for projects the County and Santa Rosa want built in downtown Santa Rosa and other priority development areas; it accepts market-rate and middle-income deals that cannot use CFH or LIHTC. Capital is public settlement money, so prevailing wage exposure depends on loan terms. The separate private Sonoma County Housing Fund ($10M, Housing Trust Silicon Valley with the Santa Rosa Metro Chamber, predevelopment and acquisition loans up to five years) belongs in Pass 4.
cycle_notes: Irregular NOFAs as repaid capital allows: Round 1 issued December 21, 2021; Round 2 issued March 4, 2026, due April 1, 2026, recommendations by May 18, 2026. Concurrent closing with all other construction financing required.
audit_note: Deadline and loan terms refreshed November 8, 2026. Prevailing wage left unclear: the 2026 NOFA treats prevailing wage only as an optional evaluation criterion (Criterion I) and states no requirement; State law coverage of these below-market settlement-funded loans is not addressed.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The RED Housing Fund 2026 NOFA lists prevailing wage only as an optional Step Two evaluation criterion (criterion I: project provides prevailing wage, labor certification or apprenticeship programs) and imposes no wage requirement; the NOFA page and Q and A state none (https://redhousingfund.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/RED-Housing-Fund-NOFA-2026.pdf; https://redhousingfund.org/notice-of-funding-availability/). Whether loans from a nonprofit capitalized with County and Santa Rosa settlement money are public funds under 1720(b) is not settled by any opened document; affordable-deal loans at 3 percent may be below market under 1720(b)(4), in which case the 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption (below-market loan, at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI; DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf) could apply, while market-rate and middle-income loans would not qualify for it. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Napa County Affordable Housing Fund
administering_agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services (County Executive Office)
typical_award_size: Gap loans historically $500,000 to $2,000,000 per project: $2,000,000 requested for Burbank Housing Stoddard West (51 units, 2017), $650,000 plus $148,000 for Turley Flats in St. Helena (8 units, 2017-2018), $500,000 for SAHA Manzanita Family Apartments (51 units, 2019, with $750,000 HEAP), $200,000 for 963 Pope Street in St. Helena (5 units, 2025). The 2010 NOFA offered $5,000,000 plus $2,000,000 reserved for farmworker housing. By 2017 the fund had loaned $22,000,000 for more than 1,000 units since 1992; fee revenue runs about $2,000,000 a year and the fund also pays for farmworker centers, homeless services and fair housing.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap. The joint City and County Multi Family Transaction Underwriting Guidelines (Jan 21, 2020) size the subsidy by gap analysis against comparable projects; developer fee for small projects capped at $25,000 per unit for units 1-10, $15,000 for units 11-30, $12,000 above 30.
affordability_requirement: 55-year affordability covenant for rental projects (40 years for County-assisted ownership). County preference for projects in the unincorporated area, deeper affordability, permanent affordability and local workers where allowed by law. Loans may be forgiven after 40 to 55 years by Board action.
next_deadline: Rolling since the 2010 NOFA; the County accepts applications year-round under the 2010 application and the 2020 joint underwriting guidelines. Requests go to the Napa County Housing Commission and then the Board of Supervisors; time them to the CTCAC round.
layering_notes: Capitalized by residential inclusionary in-lieu and impact fees and nonresidential housing impact fees under County Code Chapter 18.107 (Ordinance 1026, 1992); the October 21, 2025 fee overhaul (phased in from Jan 16, 2026) should raise annual revenue. Terms per the joint guidelines: 3.0% simple interest (lower if needed for feasibility), 55-year term from permanent loan conversion, 50/50 split of residual receipts between the City/County and developer, balance due at maturity, subordinate to senior debt, 90% maximum LTV on senior debt, monitoring fee $100 per unit for the first 40 units. Deferred developer fee may be repaid from cash flow within 15 years before residual receipts split. Most funded projects are inside the cities; the County obtains RHNA transfer credits in exchange (80% of County RHNA goes to the City of Napa under the Napa Pipe agreement through 2058), which limits funds for other jurisdictions. County loan is public money, so state prevailing wage applies under Labor Code 1720 unless an exemption fits. napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the program page is https://www.napacounty.gov/443/Affordable-Housing-Projects and the source given is the joint underwriting guidelines hosted by the City of Napa.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost). The joint Napa City and County Multi Family Transaction Underwriting Guidelines (Jan 21, 2020) contain no prevailing wage provision, so the outcome turns on loan terms (3% residual receipts, possible forgiveness) and project facts. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee and Inclusionary Requirements (County Code Chapter 18.107)
administering_agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services; Planning, Building and Environmental Services
typical_award_size: Not a subsidy; it capitalizes the Affordable Housing Fund. Fees adopted Oct 21, 2025 (3-2 vote), effective Jan 16, 2026, phased 50% in 2026, 75% in 2027, 100% in 2028: residential per sq ft $0 up to 2,500 sq ft, $43 for 2,501-3,500 sq ft (was $10.75), $86 above 3,500 sq ft (was $12.25); ADUs under 751 sq ft exempt. Nonresidential per sq ft: hotel $100 (was $9), retail and restaurant $58.40 (was $7.50), office $14.68 (was $5.25), industrial $7.70 (was $4.50), warehouse $7.50 (was $3.60).
affordability_requirement: Ownership projects: 20% of single-family detached units or 17% of attached units for moderate income (120% AMI) households, 40-year restrictions. Rental projects pay housing fees or elect the alternative of 12% of units at low income rents under a rent regulatory agreement. Exempt: farmworker units of 1,200 sq ft or less, 100% affordable projects, certain multifamily and SRO projects, projects of four or fewer units may pay a per-unit fee. Equivalency proposals (off-site units, land dedication) allowed with Planning Commission approval.
next_deadline: Fees apply to applications filed after Jan 15, 2026 at 50% of the new schedule; 75% in 2027; full schedule in 2028. The Board also directed staff to create a fee deferral program for owners who rent units as affordable housing; terms not yet published.
layering_notes: Relevant to developers two ways: 100% affordable multifamily is exempt from the fee, and the fee stream funds the County Affordable Housing Fund.
