next_deadline: No open round as of November 10, 2026. No Boomerang-specific solicitation found; ask HCD whether Boomerang dollars are included in current development or services RFPs.
layering_notes: Recorded as needs_confirmation because the only document opened is the 2017 EveryOne Home implementation deck describing the five-year commitment; the acgov HCD page that listed boomerang funds now redirects to achcd.org without that text. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Housing successor (LMIHAF) reporting for the former Alameda County Redevelopment Agency was not found.
cycle_notes: No standalone application. The 2017 Board policy set a five-year annual allocation starting FY 2016-17; HCD's March 2026 consultant RFQ (achcd.org Current Funding Opportunities, Past Opportunities) still lists Boomerang among the funds HCD administers, and the HCD staff page names the Community Development manager as overseeing HOME, CDBG, ESG and Boomerang initiatives. No current Boomerang amount, policy or developer solicitation was found, so the closed/inactive cycle tag may be wrong; treat as an internal County source routed through HCD programs.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: 2017 EveryOne Home deck re-read and matches the 20 percent, $5 million minimum, $7.5 million maximum policy and initial allocations. achcd.org (March 2026 RFQ text and staff page) shows HCD still administers Boomerang, which conflicts with closed/inactive; no current amount or guideline found (2025 Housing Plan and March 2026 bidders deck have no Boomerang text). Reviewer should decide whether to reopen the cycle tag.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. No County boomerang fund guideline or agreement with a wage term was found; County grants to private affordable projects may fall under 1720(c)(3) de minimis or other 1720(c) exemptions depending on the deal.

program_name: San Mateo County Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) annual NOFA (Measure K, County impact fees, MHSA/BHSA, PLHA, HOME)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing (DOH), Housing and Community Development division, 264 Harbor Blvd, Building A, Belmont; Raymond Hodges, Director; applications through OpenGov (procurement.opengov.com/portal/smcgov)
typical_award_size: AHF 14.0 (released April 20, 2026, pre-application meeting by April 30, applications due May 20, 2026): $29,347,311 offered, made up of $24,247,311 Measure K ($19,000,000 new FY 2026-27 plus $5,247,311 recaptured), $100,000 County impact fees (unincorporated projects only) and $5,000,000 MHSA/BHSA. Ten applications sought more than $70,000,000 for 810 units. Board awards Aug 25, 2026: $24,347,311 to six projects totaling 459 units: Sand Hill Rise City, Redwood City $9,389,000 (94 units); Mercy Housing 555 Kelly, Half Moon Bay $6,575,000 (40); Related 1051 Mission, South San Francisco $3,545,414 (158, plus $9,495,420 from AHF 11); MidPen 626 Walnut, San Carlos $3,000,000 (95, County-owned site); Novin 3051 Edison, North Fair Oaks $1,537,897 Measure K and impact fees (70); Habitat Ladera, Portola Valley $300,000 (2 ownership units). AHF 13.0 (NOFA June 2, 2025, due July 3, 2025): $41,146,470 to nine projects on Oct 7, 2025 from $19,000,000 new Measure K, $18,022,198 recaptured Measure K, $824,272 PLHA, $100,000 impact fees, MHSA and HHAP. Since 2013 the AHF has awarded more than $400,000,000 to 63 projects and 4,522 units (2,339 occupied, 588 under construction, 1,595 in predevelopment).
per_unit_cap: No general per-unit cap. MHSA/BHSA units capped at $200,000 per restricted unit; minimum award $100,000 per project; projects in incorporated cities that are not supportive housing are capped at 15% of total development cost in cumulative County funds; first-time homeownership projects share a $1,000,000 cap and rehabilitation projects a $2,000,000 cap per round.
affordability_requirement: AHF 14 Affordability Threshold (NOFA Section IV.D): 100% of units (excluding manager unit) restricted to Low Income (80% AMI) and at least 15% of total units restricted to Extremely Low Income, for at least 55 years from completion under a County regulatory agreement (57 years from recording of the deed of trust); homelessness preference units count toward the 15% ELI threshold. The greater of 5% of low-income units or two units carry a preference for people experiencing homelessness at 30% AMI rents with tenant-based subsidies and a 60-day referral hold. MHSA/BHSA units serve behavioral health referrals at 30% AMI with PBVs or 20% AMI without. Senior studio and one-bedroom units may not assume rents above 50% AMI. The Board staff report describes typical project incomes of 30% to 60% AMI.
next_deadline: The DOH funding page lists the next Affordable Housing Development NOFA for fall 2027; AHF 14 closed in May 2026 and its awards were approved Aug 25, 2026. Recaptured funds are offered between rounds through an over-the-counter process (NOFA Appendix C). Pre-application meetings are mandatory and applications require third-party commitments of at least the lesser of $1,000,000 or $20,000 per unit.
layering_notes: The Peninsula's main gap source: about $19,000,000 of new Measure K sales tax a year plus recaptured funds, MHSA/BHSA capital, HACSM Moving to Work money and whatever HOME and PLHA the County holds, all run through one annual NOFA. Terms (Appendix D): 3% simple interest from certificate of occupancy, 55-year term, annual payments of at least 50% of residual receipts to the County (two-thirds pooled pro rata when other public soft lenders share), deferred developer fee paid only from the borrower share, DOH will not cut its rate unless the host city and state lenders do the same. Measure K and impact fees do not trigger Davis-Bacon, but the application requires a state prevailing wage determination and all projects must comply with the County Living Wage Ordinance, so budget prevailing wage. Awards are explicitly sized to make 4% and 9% tax credit, AHSC and Homekey+ applications competitive and ranked on readiness. The NOFA does not award PBVs; HACSM must issue its own commitment letter. Documents opened: AHF 14 NOFA PDF and Appendix D underwriting guidelines, the July 29, 2026 HCDC hearing deck, and Board items 25-838 and 26-679 via the Legistar API.
prevailing_wage_basis: AHF 14 NOFA Table 3 states Measure K and County impact fees do not trigger Davis-Bacon (the County requires certain other federal requirements); the NOFA states no state prevailing wage rule. State prevailing wage under Labor Code 1720 depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts; federal HOME or CDBG layered in from the Winter NOFA would trigger Davis-Bacon at 12+ HOME units or 8+ CDBG rehab units.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: AHF 14 NOFA (smcgov.org/media/159002) and Aug 25, 2026 Board item 26-679 confirm the $29,347,311 offer, $24,347,311 awards, May 20, 2026 deadline and caps. The $5,000,000 MHSA in AHF 14 was not awarded and is to be offered over the counter or in a later NOFA. Added the 100% low income and 15% ELI threshold and changed prevailing wage from true (uncited) to unclear.

program_name: Winter NOFA: HOME Consortium, Urban County CDBG, ESG and PLHA (annual federal and state funds round)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing, Housing and Community Development division, as HOME Consortium lead and Urban County CDBG grantee
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 Winter NOFA (issued Dec 2, 2025, applications due Jan 15, 2026, HCDC hearing March 12, Board April 21, 2026) sources: CDBG $2,315,528 plus $347,644 program income and returned funds; HOME $1,485,482 plus $1,428,857 program income and returned funds; federal ESG $208,430; state ESG $165,356; PLHA $0 (held pending housing element compliance); City of East Palo Alto minor home repair $125,000; total $6,076,297. Uses: $2,000,000 HOME for new affordable housing and preservation, $717,035 HOME CHDO set-aside left unallocated for an over-the-counter award, $620,815 CDBG rehab and public facilities, $493,716 Section 108 loan repayment (Trestle Glen). The December 2025 notice estimated about $5,000,000 in total CDBG, HOME and related funds; a separate capital projects guideline listed about $3,317,010 CDBG for capital and $1,738,713 for community development based on FY 2025-26 levels.
per_unit_cap: HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits (HUD bulletin effective Feb 13, 2024) apply to HOME-assisted units.
affordability_requirement: HOME: households at or below 80% AMI at HOME rents, 55-year County regulatory agreement (HOME units become AHF-restricted units for the balance of the 55 years when the HOME period is shorter); CDBG: low and moderate income benefit; County loan terms as in the AHF underwriting guidelines.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 Winter NOFA to be released Dec 1, 2026 after the HCDC needs hearing on Oct 22, 2026; applications are typically due mid-January with Board approval in April. Housing capital applicants should also watch the fall AHF round.
layering_notes: Urban County: unincorporated area plus Atherton, Belmont, Brisbane, Burlingame, Colma, East Palo Alto, Foster City, Half Moon Bay, Hillsborough, Menlo Park, Millbrae, Pacifica, Portola Valley, San Bruno, San Carlos and Woodside. HOME Consortium: the Urban County plus Redwood City, San Mateo and South San Francisco (Daly City is its own entitlement, Pass 3). Federal money is small next to Measure K, so HOME usually appears as a $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 piece inside an AHF-funded project. Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects with 12 or more assisted units and CDBG projects with eight or more; state prevailing wage on County loans turns on the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions, and the County Living Wage Ordinance may also apply. Sources opened: Winter NOFA page, FY 2026-27 Action Plan sources and uses PDF, FY 2027-28 hearing notice.
prevailing_wage_basis: Winter NOFA FY 2026-27 Capital Projects Guidelines: Davis-Bacon applies to HOME-funded projects with 12 or more HOME-assisted units (24 CFR 92.354), to CDBG-funded housing rehab of 8 or more units, and to CDBG non-residential construction contracts over $2,000; where State funds are also invested the stricter of State or Federal wage determinations applies.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: April 21, 2026 Board staff report (item 26-305) confirms $6,076,296.79 total, $2,620,815.39 for housing and public facilities, $493,716.26 Section 108 repayment and $783,177.51 unallocated for CHDO and rapid rehousing over the counter. NOFA guidelines set HOME covenants at a 20-year minimum for new construction and 15 for rehab and CDBG at 55 years; the County 55-year term comes from its underwriting guidelines. FY 2027-28 release date not yet posted on the NOFA page.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), San Mateo County entitlement
administering_agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing (HCD entitlement grantee)
typical_award_size: 2019-2023 five-year formula estimate $7,257,300 (CY 2021 funds $2,068,889). Calendar year 2022 and 2023 funds of $1,831,715 ($1,036,938 plus $794,777) were authorized Dec 2, 2025 and awarded by HCD in July 2026 after the County's housing element came into compliance; $824,272 is committed through AHF 13 (moved from Laurel Landing to Rotary Gardens on Aug 25, 2026) and the balance is being allocated over the counter. HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA estimates: CY 2024 $849,022, CY 2025 $909,428, five-year $5,306,388.
affordability_requirement: County PLHA plan funds Activity 1 (rental development for extremely low to moderate income households with 55-year covenants through the AHF process) and Activity 6 (homeless services, shelter and navigation center operations and case management). HCD 2024-2028 Formula Guidelines consolidate eligible uses into Rental, Affordable Owner-Occupied Workforce Housing (up to 120% AMI, 150% in high-cost areas) and Homelessness Assistance activities; rental projects need 55-year regulatory agreements and plans must prioritize households at or below 60% AMI. Neither the 2024-2028 guidelines nor the NOFA sets a mandatory owner-occupied share.
next_deadline: PLHA is offered through the AHF NOFA, the Winter NOFA and over-the-counter processes as HCD releases each year's funds; CY 2022 and 2023 money must be spent on HCD's deadlines, which drove the Aug 2026 reallocation. Ask DOH whether CY 2024 and 2025 funds will appear in the fall 2027 AHF round.
layering_notes: Small and lumpy because HCD withheld San Mateo's PLHA for several years over housing element compliance; the County treats it as a swap source inside AHF awards (PLHA to the project closing soonest, Measure K to the slower one). PLHA states no wage rule of its own; construction use is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Figures from Board items 25-1006 and 26-706 read through the Legistar API and the HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines and Formula Allocation NOFA contain no prevailing wage provision (only the separate Non-Entitlement Competitive NOFA does). https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf San Mateo County routes PLHA through AHF awards; the AHF 14 NOFA states state and local funds do not trigger Davis-Bacon and states no state prevailing wage rule. https://www.smcgov.org/media/159002/download?inline=

program_name: Housing Endowment and Regional Trust of San Mateo County (HEART) developer loans
administering_agency: HEART of San Mateo County, joint powers authority of the County and 20 cities and towns; 2905 S. El Camino Real, San Mateo; Armando Sanchez 650-204-5640
typical_award_size: HEART reports $57,000,000 invested in affordable housing development. Two products: QuickStart (up to five years, predevelopment, acquisition, construction or rehab, principal deferred to maturity) and SemiPerm (five to 15 years including extensions, interest-only or amortized on a 30-year schedule with balloon, for acquisition, predevelopment, refinancing and rehab). Rates are described as favorable and competitive and quoted on request; origination fee 2% of loans up to $2,000,000 and 1.5% above, $3,000 application fee, borrower pays lender legal and third-party costs; loan size depends on project financials and repayment source. Recent County relationships: a $2,400,000 agreement (June 16, 2026) for HEART to run the County's mobile home replacement loan program, and a $450,000 HEART loan in HEART-SV's plan to take over Visitacion Gardens in Brisbane (May 2026). Funded projects include Montara at Bay Meadows, Ocean View, Peninsula Station, Trestle Glen, Hillcrest Senior, Serenity Senior, Fair Oaks Commons, The Village at the Crossing and 2000 South Delaware.
affordability_requirement: Up to 120% AMI (workforce) with a 55-year affordability covenant on a number of units commensurate with HEART's share, deferring to other funders' covenants when sufficient; projects must be in a member jurisdiction (the County and 20 cities and towns: Atherton, Belmont, Brisbane, Burlingame, Colma, Daly City, East Palo Alto, Foster City, Half Moon Bay, Hillsborough, Menlo Park, Millbrae, Pacifica, Portola Valley, Redwood City, San Bruno, San Carlos, San Mateo, South San Francisco, Woodside and the County) with an adopted or under-review housing element.
next_deadline: Rolling; contact HEART for current rates and available funds. The 2026 Board report notes HEART is restructuring programs (first-time homebuyer loans ended Jan 28, 2026). HEART also runs an ADU design center and received state LHTF matching grants in past rounds.
layering_notes: HEART is bridge and acquisition money, not permanent gap financing: use QuickStart to tie up a site or carry predevelopment until an AHF award and tax credits close, then take out the loan. Member dues are population based and the County administers HEART, so it reads as a county-level source even though cities co-own it. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Term sheets (May 24, 2023) and member list opened on heartofsmc.org.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. The HEART program page and QuickStart and Semi-Permanent loan term sheets (May 24, 2023) contain no prevailing wage term. https://www.heartofsmc.org/programs/for-developers/

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo (HACSM, Moving to Work agency)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo, a division of the Department of Housing, 264 Harbor Blvd, Belmont, 650-802-3300; housing@smchousing.org
typical_award_size: HACSM assists about 4,600 households and project-bases 1,930 vouchers (FY 2027 MTW Plan), with 36 new PBVs planned for 493 Eastmoor Avenue in Daly City (72 units). As an MTW agency since 1998 HACSM may project-base up to 40% of budget authority (raised from 35% in FY 2021) and awards PBVs through periodic RFPs: the last offered 200 Section 8 PBVs and 35 HUD-VASH PBVs for new construction (released Dec 2022, due Dec 30, 2022, awards Jan 2023), with at least 25% of PBVs as supportive housing units, 50% on two- and three-bedroom units, and a per-project cap of about 50% of units (waivable for supportive housing). In Jan 2025 DOH told Homekey+ applicants no PBVs were available. HACSM also provides HAP contracts up to 20 years and the County Housing Voucher Program (local funds) for Homekey sites such as Casa Esperanza.
per_unit_cap: MTW cap of 40% of budget authority agency-wide; project cap about 50% of units except supportive housing; rents per HACSM payment standards and MTW rent policies.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission with ELI targeting; supportive housing units for homeless and special needs households referred through Coordinated Entry; new construction only in the last RFP; 20-year HAP contracts with extensions.
next_deadline: No PBV RFP open as of Nov 2026 and none since Dec 2022; the AHF NOFA states applications may not assume PBVs without an existing HACSM award letter. Watch the DOH NOFAs, Bids and Proposals page and the annual MTW Plan (FY 2027 plan posted 2026) for the next solicitation. HACSM covers the entire county; no city in San Mateo County runs its own housing authority.
layering_notes: HACSM is the operating subsidy partner for every County-funded PSH deal and uses MTW flexibility to award PBVs in bulk (1,930 outstanding), but supply is tight and awards come through RFPs rather than the AHF NOFA. A HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of nine or more contract units. HACSM also recycles MTW HAP reserves into the Affordable Housing Fund (separate record). Sources opened: 2022 RFP page and PDF, FY 2027 MTW Annual Plan, Homekey+ RFP Q&A.
prevailing_wage_basis: HACSM PBV RFP (Dec 2022), Federal Requirements, Labor Standards: Davis-Bacon Act, Contract Work Hours and Safety Standards Act and 24 CFR 983.154(b) apply to an AHAP covering nine or more assisted units. The RFP was new construction only under an AHAP, so development projects with 9 or more PBV units pay federal prevailing wages.
audit_note: Tier 4: RFP page and RFP PDF re-read; 200 Section 8 and 35 HUD-VASH PBVs, new construction only, December 30, 2022 deadline, late January 2023 awards, 50% project cap, 25% supportive housing and 50% two- and three-bedroom minimums, 50% AMI, 20-year HAP terms and about 4,600 households all match. Corrected prevailing_wage_trigger from false: the RFP itself names Davis-Bacon for AHAPs of nine or more units.

program_name: HACSM Moving to Work funds for affordable housing development (through the Affordable Housing Fund)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo (MTW Activity 2011-16 and development activity) with the Department of Housing
typical_award_size: HUD has approved HACSM's use of unspent HAP reserves (MTW funds) for affordable housing development in steps: $4,000,000 originally, $8,000,000 (FY 2013), $10,000,000 (FY 2016), $25,000,000 (FY 2020), $35,000,000 (FY 2024) and $65,000,000 (FY 2025). The FY 2027 MTW Plan reports $65,000,000 of MTW funds approved for the Affordable Housing Fund, including $7,900,000 for Ridge at Ralston in Belmont and $8,600,000 for 493 Eastmoor in Daly City.
per_unit_cap: None published; awards are sized with the AHF underwriting.
affordability_requirement: Low, very low and extremely low income rental housing in San Mateo County; HACSM loans are typically zero interest with principal repaid from residual receipts under the AHF loan documents, 55-year covenants.
next_deadline: Allocated through the AHF NOFA when HACSM has reserves to contribute; next AHF round expected fall 2027. Ask DOH whether HACSM funds are in the pool before applying.
layering_notes: Unusual source: HUD lets this MTW agency lend its unspent voucher money as capital, and the County has pushed the ceiling to $65,000,000. It arrives inside an AHF award as a zero-interest residual receipts loan, which helps cash flow versus the County's 3% Measure K loan. MTW-funded acquisition, rehab or construction carries federal Davis-Bacon on all units under HUD Notice PIH 2011-45 (Section 12 of the 1937 Act), plus Section 3; state prevailing wage turns on the County loan and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions. Read from the FY 2027 MTW Annual Plan PDF (opened).
audit_note: PW audit Nov 10, 2026: true confirmed from HUD Notice PIH 2011-45 (MTW local non-traditional activities); prior basis implied a nine-unit threshold that does not apply to MTW-funded development.
prevailing_wage_basis: HUD Notice PIH 2011-45 (Parameters for Local, Non-Traditional Activities under the MTW Demonstration, issued August 15, 2011, in effect until superseded), Labor standards: Davis-Bacon requirements under Section 12 of the 1937 Act apply at all units acquired, renovated and/or built using MTW funds; no nine-unit floor applies to MTW-funded development. 42 U.S.C. 1437j(a) is the underlying statute. If HACSM also attaches PBVs, 24 CFR 983.153(c) separately applies Davis-Bacon to PBV development with nine or more contract units. https://www.hud.gov/sites/documents/pih2011-45.pdf ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1437j ; https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-IX/part-983

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA, CSCDA and CEDA issuances (County not an active issuer)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Board of Supervisors with the County Attorney (TEFRA hearings); bonds issued by the California Municipal Finance Authority, California Statewide Communities Development Authority or California Enterprise Development Authority
typical_award_size: The County is a member of CMFA, CSCDA and CEDA and holds the required TEFRA hearings for projects in the unincorporated area or where it is the member jurisdiction: CMFA bonds up to $11,000,000 for Mercy Housing's 42-unit 903 Oceana Boulevard rehabilitation in Pacifica (April 7, 2026), plus CMFA (May 6, 2025), CEDA and CSCDA (June 10, 2025) hearings. CMFA shares part of its issuance fee with the County. No County-issued multifamily housing revenue bonds were found in 2025 or 2026 Board records.
affordability_requirement: CDLAC and Section 142(d) minimums (20% at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI) under the JPA issuer's regulatory agreement; County loans in the same project add 55-year County restrictions.
next_deadline: Schedule the TEFRA hearing with the County Attorney's office at least seven days after newspaper notice and before the CDLAC application; the Board hears these on consent. For projects inside cities, the city holds the hearing.
layering_notes: Expect to use CMFA or CSCDA as issuer in San Mateo County; the County's role is the TEFRA approval and a small fee share, with no County credit or staff involvement. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; AHF, HOME or HACSM money in the deal does. Board item 26-255 read through the Legistar API.
prevailing_wage_basis: False for the JPA conduit bond issuance itself: DIR Public Works Case No. 2006-001, Horizons at Indio (March 12, 2007), https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-001.pdf, following PW 2004-016 Rancho Santa Fe Village, held that publicly offered multifamily housing revenue bonds issued by a conduit issuer (CSCDA), with proceeds and repayments assigned to a private trustee, are not a payment of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and are not a below-market public loan under 1720(b)(4); even if they were, the affordable housing loan exemption (40% of units at or below 80% AMI for 20 years, 1720(c)(5)(E), formerly (c)(6)(E)) would apply. The County staff report for item 26-255 states CMFA debts are not obligations of the County, and the County only holds the TEFRA hearing. Applies to the bond issuance only; County AHF, HOME, CDBG, HACSM vouchers or other public money in the same deal is analyzed separately and can trigger state prevailing wage or Davis-Bacon.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage set false for the conduit bond issuance alone based on DIR coverage determination PW 2006-001 (consistent with other county bond records). Privately placed bond structures were not separately confirmed; layered public loans can still trigger coverage.

program_name: Inclusionary Affordable Housing Ordinance (2004) with 2026 rezoning amendments, County affordable housing impact fees, and state density bonus
administering_agency: San Mateo County Planning and Building Department, 455 County Center, Redwood City; impact fees deposited to the Department of Housing's Housing Trust Fund
typical_award_size: Multifamily projects of five or more units in the unincorporated area must make 20% of units affordable, typically to lower income households (a rental project of five to nine units may provide its one required unit at moderate income; ownership projects may provide half at moderate income), with in-lieu fees, off-site units, land dedication or rehabilitation of existing affordable units allowed at the County's sole discretion. Ordinance 4927 (adopted Oct 6, 2026) removes those alternatives and the moderate-income option in the new R3-MD, PC-HD and TS-MU districts rezoned April 21, 2026 in Colma, Broadmoor and the Harbor Industrial area: 20% on site at low, very low or extremely low income. Affordable housing impact fees on residential and non-residential development were adopted in 2016 from a multi-jurisdictional nexus study and fund the AHF ($100,000 offered in each of AHF 13 and 14 for unincorporated projects); a new Multi-Jurisdictional Inclusionary Housing and Non-Residential Linkage Fee Study (Strategic Economics, $619,135, Dec 2025 to June 2027, County share $51,681) will reset fee levels for the County and ten cities. Density bonus follows Government Code 65915; the County enforces state law and has no local bonus beyond it.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units at lower income rents or prices for the ordinance term (long-term covenants recorded at entitlement); state density bonus units 55 years for rental.
next_deadline: Not applicable; applies at entitlement. Expect revised impact fee levels after the nexus study concludes in mid-2027. Unincorporated areas include North Fair Oaks, Colma, Broadmoor, Harbor Industrial, the Midcoast and Emerald Hills.
layering_notes: North Fair Oaks and the Colma and Broadmoor rezoning areas are where County inclusionary rules bite; 100% affordable projects satisfy them automatically and take the state density bonus. In-lieu fees and impact fees are small (about $100,000 a year reaches the AHF) because unincorporated development volume is low. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage. Sources: County inclusionary ordinance page (the ordinance PDF is image-only), Board items 26-817 and 25-1053 and the Oct 6, 2026 Board presentation and Ordinance 4927 (opened).
audit_note: Tier 4: the smcgov.org ordinance page carries only a summary and the image-only 2004 ordinance PDF; Board file 26-817 (Ordinance 4927, adopted October 6, 2026) staff report confirms the 20% lower income requirement for five or more units, the moderate income options for five to nine unit rentals and ownership projects, the County's sole-discretion alternatives, and their removal in the R3-MD, PC-HD and TS-MU districts adopted April 21, 2026. Impact fee and nexus study figures not re-read. prevailing_wage_trigger false is uncited.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Development fee waiver for affordable housing (no countywide program)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: No standalone fee waiver or deferral program for affordable housing, but the County Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Ordinance Code Chapter 5.154; rates and exemptions in Resolution 074532, Exhibit C) exempts new units rented or sold at affordable cost to very low, low or moderate income households under a deed restriction meeting County standards, housing for the elderly or disabled, and property eligible for the welfare exemption. Projects with an Area Standard Wage Participation Agreement get a 25% fee reduction, and the ordinance allows waiver or modification requests. Base rate for apartments: $10 per square foot of net new residential floor area. Planning and building permit fees still apply. The AHF NOFA scores host city land, fee waivers or inclusionary contributions toward its $1,000,000 or $20,000 per unit third-party commitment threshold.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Deed-restricted affordable units in unincorporated San Mateo County are exempt from the County affordable housing impact fee at permit; other County planning and building fees apply. Ask host cities about their own fee waivers.
layering_notes: Negative finding. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts waived fees as public funds for prevailing wage purposes. Planning fees page is linked from the County inclusionary ordinance page (opened).
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: the cited inclusionary page has no fee waiver content. The County impact fee page and Resolution 074532 Exhibit C (smcgov.org/media/73946) show deed-restricted affordable units are exempt from the County affordable housing impact fee, contradicting the prior text that told users to budget full County fees. Program name still reads no countywide program; consider renaming to the impact fee exemption.
prevailing_wage_basis: No standalone fee waiver program exists. The developer-relevant feature is the County Affordable Housing Impact Fee exemption for units rented or sold at affordable cost (Resolution 074532, Exhibit C). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Mateo County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder
administering_agency: San Mateo County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder and Elections (ACRE), Mark Church, Assessor; 555 County Center, Redwood City; 650-363-4500; institutional exemptions unit via smcacre.gov contact page
typical_award_size: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area. ACRE posts the full BOE-267 series (267, 267-L, L1, L2, L3, L4, H, O, R and income worksheets) and notes the annual BOE-267-A is issued by the office rather than downloaded.
per_unit_cap: Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g)(1)(C) caps the exemption at $20,000,000 of assessed value per taxpayer per fiscal year (single or multiple properties), and only where the exemption rests solely on the 90 percent lower income occupancy test for a property not owned by a limited partnership. Projects with tax-exempt bonds, government loans or grants (214(g)(1)(A)) or low-income housing tax credits (214(g)(1)(B)) are outside the cap; LP-owned projects with a nonprofit managing general partner must have tax credits or government financing to qualify (BOE Publication 149). Not a statewide cap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit or LP with eligible nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate (plus a Supplemental Clearance Certificate for LP low-income housing); units restricted by recorded regulatory agreement or occupied by households at or below 80% AMI; BOE-267 first filing and annual supplemental affidavits by Feb 15 (late claims receive a reduced exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 270).
next_deadline: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). File the first claim on acquisition so the construction period is covered.
layering_notes: Standard in every tax credit operating budget; San Mateo's high assessed values make this the largest operating subsidy most projects receive. ACRE's institutional exemptions and forms pages (opened) list forms and the OCC and SCC requirements but no local deadline text or direct phone; the BOE county contacts page gives the main number.
prevailing_wage_basis: Property tax exemption; no construction funds are provided, so the exemption itself does not make a project public works.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: ACRE page lists BOE-267, 267-L, L-B (100% AMI worksheet), L1, L2, L3 (140% AMI over-income), L4 (100% AMI over-income), H, O and R and says BOE-267-A is omitted; Feb 15 deadline per Rev. and Tax. Code 255 and BOE Publication 149 (late claims: 90% relief if filed by Jan 1 of the next year, 85% after). The prior per_unit_cap described a statewide cap for LP projects; the statute applies it per taxpayer to non-LP claims under the 90% occupancy test.

program_name: Daly City/San Mateo County Continuum of Care (CA-512) and HHAP
administering_agency: San Mateo County Human Services Agency, Center on Homelessness (CoC lead agency and HHAP administrative entity for the County and CoC)
typical_award_size: HHAP joint County and CoC allocations: Round 1 $3,431,246 (Feb 2020), Round 2 $1,597,106, Round 3 $4,375,129, Round 4 $4,658,201, Round 5 $5,237,946 (County $2,564,722, CoC $2,673,224), Round 6 $5,026,361 (County $2,430,522, CoC $2,595,839; accepted June 10, 2025, awarded March 2, 2026, usable through June 30, 2029), about $24,300,000 in all. State accountability site: $19,300,000 HHAP rounds 1 to 5 to the County ($13,800,000 obligated, $11,800,000 spent by mid-2025); Encampment Resolution Funding $16,000,000 in the area, $14,100,000 to the County. HHAP-6 supports operations of the 240-unit Navigation Center in Redwood City. next_deadline: HHAP-7 is available to HHAP-6 grantees; the CoC runs the HUD NOFO each summer. For capital, the County route is the Homekey+ co-applicant process through the Department of Housing and the AHF NOFA's homelessness preference units; HHAP itself funds shelter and services.
layering_notes: A small CoC (about $800,000 a year in HUD renewals) and modest HHAP, so homeless capital comes from Measure K and Homekey rather than CoC money; the County uses its own Housing Voucher Program and HACSM PBVs for operating subsidy at Homekey sites. HHAP figures from the County HSA HHAP page and Board item 25-554 (opened), HCD allocation lists and accountability.ca.gov; Homekey details from Board item 25-249 and the Homekey+ RFP page.

HHAP used for rapid rehousing, bridge housing operations and services is not construction under 1720(a)(1); HHAP capital work would be tested on project facts (Homekey carries its own state rule). https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/578.99 ; https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/calich/hhap-6-nofa.pdf

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions and MHSA/BHSA capital through the Affordable Housing Fund
administering_agency: San Mateo County Health, Behavioral Health and Recovery Services (BHRS), with the Department of Housing administering capital awards
typical_award_size: Three-Year Integrated Plan FY 2026-27 to FY 2028-29 approved by the Board June 9, 2026 (Behavioral Health Commission hearing closed March 5, 2026). Housing Interventions expenditures $24,427,542 (FY 2026-27), $24,374,720 (FY 2027-28), $24,374,720 (FY 2028-29); capital development $6,152,822 then $6,100,000 a year (24% of the component, near the 25% cap) delivered through the DOH Affordable Housing Fund NOFAs, where the AHF 14 round carried $5,000,000 of MHSA/BHSA capital at up to $200,000 per restricted unit; the plan lists nine capital projects and a 65-unit PSH pipeline at up to $450,000 per unit. Operating subsidies $3,540,627 plus $2,182,327, bundled rental and operating subsidies about $1,160,000 to $1,460,000, rental subsidies $1,000,000; $12,900,025 a year (51%) dedicated to chronically homeless people; 64 people a year in operating-subsidized units. per_unit_cap: MHSA/BHSA capital capped at $200,000 per restricted unit in the AHF NOFA; BHSA statute caps the housing intervention share at $450,000 per unit.

BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) but carries no wage rule of its own; coverage turns on the 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (see prevailing_wage_basis). Plan read from the Board attachment on Legistar (final plan PDF, opened); the smchealth.org copies returned 404.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The DHCS BHSA County Policy Manual chapter 7 (housing interventions, capital development) states no prevailing wage requirement, and the San Mateo County AHF 14 NOFA, which carries MHSA/BHSA capital (Table 3), states state and local funds do not trigger Davis-Bacon and gives no state prevailing wage rule. https://policy-manual.mes.dhcs.ca.gov/behavioral-health-services-act-county-policy-manual/V1.0.0/7-bhsa-components-and-requirements ; https://www.smcgov.org/media/159002/download?inline=

program_name: Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Fund) and the annual federal and state housing NOFA
administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Housing and Federal Grants Division, 3501 Civic Center Drive, San Rafael; affordablehousing@marincounty.gov
typical_award_size: The Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Fund, created 1988) is capitalized by inclusionary in-lieu fees, the single-family Affordable Housing Impact Fee, commercial linkage fees and County General Fund contributions (Guidelines 2023-2027, adopted Dec 12, 2023). It funds seed and catalyst costs, land acquisition, predevelopment, construction and gap financing; awards are generally $50,000 per unit, up to $100,000 per unit depending on funds, project type, location, bedrooms, affordability depth and restriction term, with higher amounts considered in high-resource areas. About 25% of funds are prioritized for preservation and rehab and 75% for new construction or conversion. Funds are generally loans (3 months to 55 years); the Board may award grants for smaller requests. The Fund also supplies the 1:1 local match for PLHA through the annual NOFA. The 2026-27 NOFA estimated about $3,100,000 total ($1,500,000 CDBG, $700,000 HOME, $900,000 PLHA inclusive of Trust Fund match). On June 23, 2026 the Board approved FY 2026-27 allocations: $676,641 HOME, $1,611,279 CDBG, and $476,762 estimated PLHA matched 1:1 by $476,762 from the Trust Fund (Oak Hill, Eden Housing, $553,524 combined; Bayfront Terrace, EAH, $400,000 combined); staff reported a Housing Fund balance of $14,032,062 after the match. Standalone Board actions recorded in earlier agendas include a $5,239,098 Trust Fund loan to Habitat for Humanity Greater San Francisco (April 15, 2025) and a $3,000,000 Golden Gate Village predevelopment loan restructured April 14, 2026.
per_unit_cap: Generally $50,000 per unit; up to $100,000 per unit in some circumstances (Affordable Housing Fund Guidelines 2023-2027).
affordability_requirement: Low, very low and extremely low income households; affordability restrictions in perpetuity unless the Board approves a shorter term required by a public financing source. Priorities: AFFH, leverage, high-resource areas, unincorporated Marin, RHNA, homeownership. Projects in cities and towns must waive all planning and building fees and, if the jurisdiction has a housing trust, provide a match from it.
next_deadline: No open NOFA round as of November 8, 2026; the 2027-28 NOFA is expected to open early in calendar 2027 per the County funding page. Affordable Housing Fund requests are accepted year-round.
layering_notes: marincounty.gov, marincounty.org, assets.marincounty.gov, marinhhs.org and arcc.marincounty.gov sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so County program pages could not be opened; Board agendas were read on marin.granicus.com and staff reports through its MetaViewer links where available. Marin's county money is small and project-specific: the Trust Fund mostly supplies PLHA match (about $500,000 a year) and five- to six-figure gap grants, with occasional larger loans for County-priority sites (Habitat in Novato, Oak Hill workforce housing next to San Quentin, Golden Gate Village). The County also weighed joining an Affordable Housing Guarantor Financing Program for Oak Hill in April 2025. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Sources opened: Board agendas for April 15, 2025, June 10, 2025, Dec 5 and 12, 2023, April 7 and 14, 2026 and June 23, 2026 on Granicus, the April 14, 2026 Golden Gate Village loan staff report, and the Local News Matters reports of April 6 and June 24, 2026. NOFA amounts and dates come from search engine excerpts of the County NOFA page, which is why this record is needs_confirmation.
cycle_notes: Two tracks. Affordable Housing Fund applications are accepted throughout the year through the Neighborly portal and go to the Board individually. PLHA plus Trust Fund match, HOME and CDBG are awarded through the annual NOFA: the 2026-27 window ran January 19 to February 19, 2026, with PSC review May 19 and Board approval June 23, 2026. The County states it opens the NOFA toward the beginning of each calendar year.
audit_note: County site now opens; guidelines, NOFA and funding pages read 2026-11-08. Measure W removed from the list of Trust Fund revenue sources because the guidelines list four sources and Measure W is a separate fund. The 60% AMI PLHA priority claim was not found and was removed. Prevailing wage trigger left as found; not in audit scope. PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true changed to unclear. The Affordable Housing Fund guidelines page on marincounty.gov returned 403 (Cloudflare) to WebFetch and curl, so the 2023-2027 guidelines were not read; if they require prevailing wage, restore true with that citation.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans and grants are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) and (b)(5) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market interest rate loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (applied to an NPLH loan in DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf), and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidies (under $600,000 and under 2 percent of project cost). Affordable Housing Fund awards that are grants or land acquisition funds fall under 1720(b)(1); homeownership aid to households is exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C).

program_name: HOME and CDBG, Marin County Urban County (countywide entitlement with city planning areas)
administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Housing and Federal Grants Division, with the Countywide Priority Setting Committee
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27: about $1,600,000 CDBG and $676,000 HOME approved June 23, 2026. Housing awards: Eden Housing Oak Hill (unincorporated, between San Quentin and Larkspur Landing, about 230 units with more than 130 for educators and school employees) $531,000 CDBG; Eden Housing Mill Valley rental development $360,000 HOME; Homeward Bound of Marin permanent supportive housing for formerly homeless seniors in San Rafael $317,000 HOME; Habitat for Humanity Greater SF home rehabilitation program $70,000 CDBG (requested $296,000); Homeward Bound shelter capital repairs about $132,000 CDBG; the balance to child care facilities, a San Rafael preschool and public services. FY 2025-26 CDBG entitlement was $1,512,738; that NOFA drew 33 applications requesting about $3,940,000 CDBG, $1,600,000 HOME and $1,390,000 PLHA. CDBG is split into planning-area shares (San Rafael's 2026-27 share about $508,000) recommended by the cities and the County.
per_unit_cap: HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits apply; awards are typically $300,000 to $600,000 per housing project.
affordability_requirement: HOME: households at or below 80% AMI at HOME rents with a County regulatory agreement; CDBG: low and moderate income benefit. The Consolidated Plan for FY 2025-2029 (adopted June 10, 2025) sets priorities including family, rental, special needs and homeowner housing and an eastern Marin land trust with specific inclusion for African American households.
next_deadline: Next NOFA expected January 2027 (applications due February 2027, PSC in May, Board in June) alongside PLHA and Trust Fund match; a two-year funding cycle covers 2026-27 and 2027-28 for services.
layering_notes: marincounty.gov, marincounty.org, assets.marincounty.gov, marinhhs.org and arcc.marincounty.gov sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so County program pages could not be opened; Board agendas were read on marin.granicus.com and staff reports through its MetaViewer links where available. Marin is the HUD entitlement for the whole county, including its cities, so a project in San Rafael or Novato competes for the same CDBG and HOME as unincorporated sites and needs the planning-area committee's support first. Federal money is a few hundred thousand dollars per project and is used to complete 9% deals (Homeward Bound) or as early money for large 4% deals (Oak Hill). Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Figures from the Local News Matters report of June 24, 2026 (opened), the June 23, 2026 Board agenda (opened) and the Dec 5, 2024 Priority Setting Committee packet on GovDelivery (opened).
audit_note: Nov 9, 2026 spot check: replaced news source with the June 23, 2026 Board staff report (item 8c, file 26-1733). Figures match: CDBG $1,611,279 ($1,610,959 entitlement plus $320 program income), HOME $676,640.92, CDBG $531,106.80 to the Oak Hill project, $70,000 Habitat, about $131,738 Homeward Bound shelter repairs, San Rafael planning area $508,032.03; FY 2026-27 NOFA opened January 19, 2026 and public services run on a two-year cycle. Wording fix: the $360,000 Mill Valley HOME award went to EAH Inc. (Bayfront Terrace, the CHDO set-aside project), not Eden Housing; Homeward Bound seniors PSH received $316,640.92.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Marin County entitlement, matched 1:1 by the Affordable Housing Fund
administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Housing and Federal Grants Division (HCD entitlement grantee)
typical_award_size: 2020 five-year plan estimated $4,353,426 from HCD, each dollar matched by the County Affordable Housing Fund; Formula Round 5 award $476,762 (March 2025); 2026-27 cycle about $477,000 PLHA plus match. HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA estimates: CY 2024 $509,302, CY 2025 $545,537, five-year $3,183,138. Example award: $605,062 to EAH Housing in 2024 ($302,531 PLHA plus $302,531 Trust Fund). program_name: Inclusionary housing, affordable housing impact fee and commercial linkage fee (Development Code Chapter 22.22) with state density bonus (Chapter 22.24)
administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Planning Division (unincorporated area); fees deposited to the Affordable Housing Fund
typical_award_size: Chapter 22.22: 20% of units or lots in new residential projects must be affordable (projects of four or fewer units round up only above 0.70 of a unit), restricted in perpetuity unless shortened to match financing; income tiers very low (30% to 50% AMI), low (50% to 80%), moderate (80% to 120%) and middle (120% to 150%); alternatives in priority order are off-site units, land dedication and an in-lieu fee set at 125% of the requirement when a waiver is granted; single-family homes over 2,000 square feet pay an Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Ordinance 3500, 2008); non-residential projects pay a jobs-housing linkage fee by floor area and use (Ordinance 3798 and Resolution 2023-102 of Sept 19, 2023; Resolution 2016-122 for residential care and skilled nursing). Fees are indexed annually to the California Construction Cost Index; the June 23, 2026 adjustment was 3.9% and the FY 2026-27 in-lieu fee is $421,886.99 per required unit per the County fee page (2023-24 fee was $399,654). Chapter 22.24 implements Government Code 65915: base 20% bonus at 10% low or 5% very low income units, one to five concessions by affordability level, unlimited waivers of standards that physically preclude the project, height increases up to three stories near major transit for 80% lower income projects; the County may offer incentives to deed-restricted projects without a bonus but is not required to give fee waivers.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units restricted in perpetuity (or the maximum financing allows); density bonus rental units 30 years minimum under 22.24, moderate-income for-sale units in perpetuity. Rents capped at 50%, 65% and 100% of AMI levels for very low, low and moderate tiers.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement (rolling); fees adjust annually by the CCCI, next adjustment expected effective July 1, 2027.
layering_notes: Marin's unincorporated inclusionary rule is one of the strictest in the state (20% in perpetuity, in-lieu fee only after off-site and land dedication are shown infeasible), and fee receipts flow to the Affordable Housing Fund that this database records separately. Fee revenue is modest because unincorporated development is small. A 100% affordable project satisfies the chapter automatically and uses the state density bonus. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; Labor Code 1720(b)(4) would treat any fee waiver as public funds. Sources opened: Zoneomics mirror of Development Code Article III (Chapters 22.22 and 22.24) and the June 23, 2026 fee adjustment staff report on Granicus; the County fee calculator page was blocked.
cycle_notes: FY 2026-27 fees adopted by the Board June 23, 2026 (3.9% CCCI), effective July 1, 2026. Multi-jurisdictional Affordable Housing Impact Fee Study authorized April 15, 2025; County infrastructure impact fee study public hearing was March 10, 2026.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: staff report and Attachment 2 (Understanding Affordable Housing Fees 2026-27) confirm $421,886.99 in-lieu fee, 20% requirement, AMI tiers 30-50/50-80/80-120/120-150 and rent caps 50/65/100% AMI. Prevailing wage false is uncited; density bonus alone carries no stated prevailing wage rule. Past study hearing date moved from next_deadline to cycle_notes.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) covers only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. An inclusionary requirement, impact fee or linkage fee imposes an obligation on a private developer and pays nothing toward its construction, and a density bonus grants units and concessions, not funds, so this record does not trigger prevailing wage. Fee revenue later lent or granted from the Affordable Housing Fund is public funds analyzed under that record, and any fee waiver would be public funds under 1720(b)(4) subject to 1720(c)(3) de minimis.

program_name: ADU and JADU development fee waiver, unincorporated Marin County (up to $10,000 for deed-restricted affordable ADUs; no countywide affordable multifamily fee waiver)
administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency
typical_award_size: No fee waiver program exists for affordable multifamily housing. The only adopted County development fee waiver is the ADU and JADU program: a Board resolution of March 11, 2025 extends the Community Development Agency Director's delegated authority to waive or reduce building permit fees through December 31, 2026, up to $1,500 per JADU, $2,500 per ADU, $5,000 for an ADU deed restricted to a moderate-income household (81 to 100 percent AMI) and $10,000 for an ADU deed restricted to a low-income household (up to 80 percent AMI). In 2024 the County processed 27 ADU waivers (one affordable deed-restricted) and 1 JADU waiver totaling $78,000.
affordability_requirement: Base ADU and JADU waivers: owner affirms the unit will not be a short-term rental. Higher tiers: recorded deed restriction renting the ADU to a low-income (up to 80 percent AMI) or moderate-income (81 to 100 percent AMI) household.
next_deadline: Rolling until December 31, 2026, when the current delegation expires unless the Board extends it.
layering_notes: Corrected from a negative finding: Marin County has an adopted fee waiver, but only for ADUs and JADUs; there is still no countywide fee waiver or reduction for affordable multifamily projects. Development Code 22.24.020(C)(2) says nothing requires direct financial incentives such as fee waivers and leaves them to County discretion, so a multifamily developer would request fee relief case by case (Affordable Housing Fund or a density bonus concession). Separately, the County policies page describes reductions of the affordable housing impact fee or in-lieu fee for projects with affordable units beyond the minimum; that is an inclusionary compliance option under Chapter 22.22 (record 02b451fc33), not a development fee waiver. The ADU waiver stacks with the ADU Center technical assistance pilot.
cycle_notes: Delegated waiver authority runs January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2026 (Board action March 11, 2025, extending Resolution 2021-34 and the JADU authority first granted in 2017). Applicants request the waiver with the building permit application to the Building and Safety Division. The General Fund reimburses CDA for non-deed-restricted waivers; the Affordable Housing Fund reimburses waivers for deed-restricted units.
eligible_project_detail: accessory dwelling units and junior ADUs in unincorporated Marin, with higher waivers for deed-restricted affordable ADUs
audit_note: 2026-11-09: marincounty.gov and marincounty.org (policies and fees page, fee guide PDFs) still return Cloudflare 403. prevailing_wage_basis: Waived or reduced fees are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects built on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment agency or local public housing authority, which typically fits an owner-built ADU. The March 11, 2025 Board letter (https://marin.granicus.com/MetaViewer.php?view_id=33&event_id=3961&meta_id=1365949) states no wage rule. Development Code 22.24.020(C)(2) (https://www.zoneomics.com/code/marin-county-unincorporated-CA/chapter_3) notes that direct financial incentives such as fee waivers may require prevailing wages if State law requires.

Eliseo PSH in Larkspur) but has issued no developer PBV RFP recently; 94 Emergency Housing Voucher households were told in Oct 2025 that funding ends in 2026. The 2027 PHA Annual Plan comment period closed in July 2026 and the plan was due to HUD in October 2026. HAP contracts up to 20 years.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (HUD PBV development requirements, labor standards): for development activity (new construction or rehabilitation) involving nine or more PBV contract units, the owner and its contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages and the PHA monitors compliance; existing-housing PBV contracts with no development activity do not trigger it. MHA has awarded PBVs to new construction (CTCAC staff report CA-21-164: Vivalon Healthy Aging Campus, San Rafael, new construction with 66 PBV units), so third-party PBV awards to development of 9+ contract units carry Davis-Bacon. MHA's own RAD and Section 18 conversions follow the separate RAD notice labor rules. https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/ctcac/meeting/2021/20211020/staff/7/21-164.pdf https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.153

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), Marin County Assessor-Recorder-County Clerk
administering_agency: Marin County Assessor-Recorder-County Clerk, Shelly Scott, Marin Civic Center, San Rafael; 415-473-7215
typical_award_size: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area. The Assessor-Recorder posts the BOE-267 series including BOE-267-L, L1 and L2 for low-income housing.
per_unit_cap: Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g)(1)(C) caps the exemption at $20,000,000 of assessed value per taxpayer per fiscal year (single or multiple properties), and only where the exemption rests solely on the 90 percent lower income occupancy test for a property not owned by a limited partnership. Projects with tax-exempt bonds, government loans or grants (214(g)(1)(A)) or low-income housing tax credits (214(g)(1)(B)) are outside the cap; LP-owned projects with a nonprofit managing general partner must have tax credits or government financing to qualify (BOE Publication 149). Not a statewide cap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit or LP with eligible nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate (plus a Supplemental Clearance Certificate for LP low-income housing); units restricted by recorded regulatory agreement or occupied by households at or below 80% AMI; BOE-267 first filing and annual supplemental affidavits by Feb 15 (late claims receive a reduced exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 270, and the County FAQ confirms partial relief for late filings).
next_deadline: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). File the first claim on acquisition so the construction period is covered.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions, Marin County Behavioral Health and Recovery Services
administering_agency: Marin County Health and Human Services, Behavioral Health and Recovery Services (BHRS)

Housing Interventions receive 30% of base allocations: $5,854,517 in year one, $5,733,901 in year two and $5,695,539 in year three (plus $125,000 of unspent MHSA moved to housing). Planned uses: rental and operating subsidies at four PSH programs, 16 to 22 local Behavioral Health vouchers, continuation of transitional rent and Bridge Housing programs after they end, a peer respite facility, and capital development for a new PSH project in year one. per_unit_cap: BHSA statute: capital development up to 25% of the housing component and at most $450,000 per unit.

next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. Watch County HHS RFP postings and the annual plan update; ask BHRS about capital match or operating subsidies for PSH units.
layering_notes: funding_type grant: the plan funds housing capital (forgivable capital grants such as Carmelita House) and rental and operating subsidies. Marin's BHSA housing money is about $5,700,000 to $5,900,000 a year and is being used as the local match that makes Homekey+ and small PSH conversions work, plus scattered-site rental subsidies and operating subsidies. Sources: HHS BHSA page and DHCS-approved Integrated Plan PDF, April 14, 2026 Carmelita House staff report, RFP HHS-2026-02.
cycle_notes: Plan in effect July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029 with annual updates. Capital is awarded project by project (Homekey+ match) and subsidies and services through County RFPs (HHS-2026-02 closed April 17, 2026), not a standing NOFA.

The $321,425 Carmelita operating figure from the prior pass was not found in the documents read and was dropped. Prevailing wage trigger left as found; not in audit scope. PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true changed to unclear. hhs.marincounty.gov returned 403 (Cloudflare) this pass, so the plan PDF was not re-read; capital uses are taken from the record.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The BHSA statute section read (Welfare and Institutions Code 5830, https://california.public.law/codes/welfare_and_institutions_code_section_5830) contains no prevailing wage or Labor Code provision. Rental and operating subsidies fund no construction (1720(a)(1), https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but the Integrated Plan also funds capital development for a new PSH project and capital match for Homekey+ projects; those capital grants are public funds under 1720(b)(1), and Homekey+ carries its own requirement in that program record.

program_name: Traffic Impact Fee (TIF) Offset Program for Developments with Affordable Housing Units (Board Policy B-14)
administering_agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Affordable Housing Unit, with the Department of Transportation and the Chief Administrative Office; Housing@edcgov.us; 330 Fair Lane, Placerville (Housing Unit moving to 768 Pleasant Valley Road, Diamond Springs)
typical_award_size: Up to $1,000,000 of TIF offsets authorized each year from federal and state transportation revenues, with unused balances carried forward; Board may award more than the annual amount. Since December 2007 about $4.7 million of offsets have supported 344 affordable units. Recent awards: Diamond Village Apartments Phase II $436,632 for 30 units at 80% AMI (about 94% of the project TIF, May 12, 2026); Racquet Way Phase 2 recommended at 50% ($139,098 of $278,196) in February 2026 and denied by the Board. Staff reported about $13 million of offset capacity remaining in the program.
per_unit_cap: Offset is a share of the TIF per income-restricted unit: 100% for very low (50% AMI), 75% for low (80% AMI), 25% for moderate (120% AMI) units. 2025 Zone B multifamily TIF is $15,456 per unit, so the full offset is about $15,456 (very low) or $11,592 (low) per unit, subject to each TIF schedule update. Only income-restricted units count.
affordability_requirement: Developments of 5 or more units in the unincorporated county with a submitted planning application and at least 20% of units affordable to very low, low or moderate income households. Deed restriction through a TIF Offset Affordable Housing Agreement: 55 years for rental units, 45 years for ownership units (lengthened from 20 years in the September 29, 2026 revision). Must be able to pull permits within 2 years of award (extensions in 1-year increments, up to 3).
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. Round 37 applications were accepted January 1 to 15, 2026 with Board awards in spring 2026. Revised Board Policy B-14 (approved September 29, 2026) reviews offset requests twice a year in February and August; the County TIF Offset page still posts only the Round 37 notice, so watch for a new public notice ahead of the February 2027 review.
layering_notes: This is the County's only recurring development incentive and it is an offset, not cash, so it reduces the fee line of the sources and uses rather than adding a source. A 30-unit project at 80% AMI saved $436,632 in 2026. Scoring criteria: complete packet, site control, developer capacity, benefit to lower income households, Housing Element alignment, mixed income, services and infrastructure, likelihood of construction within 2 years. The Advisory Committee docked Racquet Way for a market-rate developer's limited affordable housing experience, so bring a compliance track record. The 2026 revisions also changed TIM to TIF, removed ADU language and asked the Affordable Housing Task Force to study eligibility up to 150% AMI, 100% offsets for low income units and CAO-delegated awards; none of those were adopted as of September 2026. Fee reductions under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) have an unsettled prevailing wage effect, but most projects using this offset also carry tax credits or state funds that trigger it anyway. Other impact fees (school, fire) still apply. Cities (Placerville, South Lake Tahoe) are outside the program.
cycle_notes: Competitive rounds announced by public notice on the County TIF Offset page (Round 37: pre-submission meeting December 10, 2025, questions December 15 to 30, 2025, applications January 1 to 15, 2026 by email to housing@edcgov.us, Advisory Group review January 20 to February 28, 2026, Board awards April 2026). The September 29, 2026 revision of Policy B-14 moves to reviews twice a year in February and August.
audit_note: T2 audit 2026-11-08: deadline refreshed from the County page, Round 37 notice and the Legistar copy of revised Policy B-14 (file 26-1443, approved September 29, 2026). Prevailing wage left unclear: neither the program page, the 2017 procedure manual, the Round 37 notice nor revised B-14 mentions prevailing wage, and the Labor Code 1720 text (fee reductions as public funds, de minimis exception) could not be opened this pass (california.public.law and Justia returned 403).
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. The TIF offset pays the fee from federal and state transportation revenues (Board Policy B-14), which is also a payment on behalf of the developer under 1720(b)(1). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Affordable Housing Trust Fund and Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund (no development NOFA)
administering_agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Affordable Housing Unit (program administration contracted to Housing Group LLC dba HousingINC through December 31, 2026); Housing@edcgov.us
typical_award_size: Small and discretionary. The Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund held about $600,151 in April 2026, fed by building permit activity, and the Board committed $550,151 of it to the Caldor Fire Grizzly Flats Homeowner Rebuild Program (forgivable loans up to $73,318 for about 12 fire-displaced households, administered by HomeAid Sacramento). The separate Affordable Housing Trust Fund receives the County's share of CMFA bond issuance fees (for example $6,000 from the Diamond Village II issuance). No multifamily development award from either fund was found.
affordability_requirement: None codified. Staff describe the Special Revenue Fund as having no specific restrictions, with use at the Board's discretion for affordable housing purposes. The Trust Fund is designated for studies, program development or contributions toward creating housing.
next_deadline: No NOFA. A request would go through the Affordable Housing Unit and require Board action.
layering_notes: Reclassified from other to loan in the November 8, 2026 audit: the Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund is deployable at Board discretion and its only recent use was forgivable loans (up to $73,318 per household) under the Caldor Fire Grizzly Flats Homeowner Rebuild Program (Resolution 064-2026, April 7, 2026). Do not underwrite County gap money in El Dorado. The county has no inclusionary fee revenue yet, no housing bond and no sales tax measure, so the Trust Fund is capitalized only by occasional conduit issuance fees and permit-related deposits. The planned Affordable Housing Ordinance (inclusionary with an in-lieu fee set by a fee nexus study now being procured) is intended to expand the Trust Fund, which is the only path to a real county gap source in the next few years. County housing staff capacity is thin: a single Administrative Analyst position was reinstated in April 2026 and HousingINC runs the program in the interim, so allow time for any County action (Board Policy A-6 resolutions, TIF offsets, TEFRA hearings).
audit_note: PW pass Nov 9, 2026: no County rule found; changed true to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. No County fund rule with a wage term was found; the only recent use was forgivable loans to individual homeowners rebuilding after the Caldor Fire, and 1720(c)(5)(C) exempts assistance to a household for rehabilitation of a single-family home.

program_name: State HOME and CDBG (non-entitlement county) and Affordable Housing County Participation Requests for HCD applications
administering_agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Affordable Housing Unit; Loans@edcgov.us; Board approval of resolutions under Board Policy A-6
typical_award_size: El Dorado County is a non-entitlement jurisdiction, so HOME and CDBG come through state HCD competitions and the County has used them for homeownership, not rental development: HOME $500,000 First-Time Homebuyer award (Resolutions 058-2026 and 080-2026) and a 2025 CDBG application for up to $1,500,000 for the First-Time Homebuyer Program (Resolution 180-2025). Developers seeking state funds that require a County co-applicant or resolution file an Affordable Housing County Participation Request Form at least 10 weeks before the HCD deadline.
per_unit_cap: State HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply if the County sponsors a rental project; none has been sponsored recently.
affordability_requirement: HOME: at or below 80% AMI with HOME rents and affordability periods; CDBG: low and moderate income benefit. A developer-sponsored state HOME rental application through the County would carry HCD's 55-year regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Follows HCD's HOME and CDBG NOFA calendar (hcd.ca.gov/grants-and-funding/nofa-calendar). Submit the County Participation Request Form at least 10 weeks before the HCD deadline so the Board can adopt the resolution.
layering_notes: The County's HOME and CDBG dollars are committed to first-time homebuyer loans, so a rental project should not count on them. The practical value of the County here is as a resolution sponsor or co-applicant for state programs (HOME rental new construction, CDBG public infrastructure, Joe Serna farmworker, MHP) in a non-entitlement area where a local government signature is required. Build the 10-week lead time plus Board calendar into the HCD application schedule. State HOME in a project triggers Davis-Bacon on 12 or more HOME units and HOME cross-cutting requirements (environmental review, Section 3); state prevailing wage turns on other public funds and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 92.354(a) (HOME): every construction contract for housing with 12 or more HOME-assisted units must require Davis-Bacon wages. Applies to a developer-sponsored state HOME rental project; the County's current HOME and CDBG awards are for homebuyer assistance with no construction contract. https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 9, 2026: Collaborative Opportunities page confirms the Participation Request Form and the 10-week lead time (Board Policy A-6); Legistar items 26-0477, 26-0661 and 25-1885 confirm the $500,000 HOME FTHB award (Resolutions 058-2026 and 080-2026) and the up to $1,500,000 CDBG FTHB application (Resolution 180-2025).

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), El Dorado County formula allocation
administering_agency: El Dorado County Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA), Community Services Division; hhsa-grants@edcgov.us
typical_award_size: 2019-2023 five-year estimate $2,990,478 (Resolution 143-2025, October 21, 2025; years 1-3 were $479,995, $729,477 and $973,923). HCD's 2024-2028 formula NOFA lists El Dorado County at $308,950 (2024), $318,390 (2025) and a five-year estimate of $1,930,938. All of it is programmed to homelessness operations, not development.
affordability_requirement: PLHA guidelines allow rental housing at or below 60% AMI (up to 80% AMI) with 55-year covenants, but the County's plan directs the funds to operating the navigation center and interim housing services rather than capital.
next_deadline: Not available to developers. The 2024 plan amendment moved all PLHA to a single capital activity for a permanent navigation center, and in 2025 staff said the Forni Road housing services site will likely not use PLHA capital, so the money is being reallocated to navigation center operations. A new five-year plan for the 2024-2028 allocations is required by HCD and could revisit uses.
layering_notes: El Dorado's PLHA is about $300,000 to $1,000,000 a year and is entirely absorbed by homeless services, so there is no PLHA capital for multifamily deals in the unincorporated county. The only PLHA capital nearby came through the City of Placerville's competitive PLHA award (Middletown Apartments, about $1,050,000), which is a Pass 3 item. If the County restructures its 2024-2028 PLHA plan, a developer could ask HHSA to carve out a capital or operating subsidy line for a permanent supportive housing project; HHSA, not Planning and Building, controls PLHA here.
audit_note: PW pass Nov 9, 2026: PLHA formula rules are silent on prevailing wage; changed true to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines and Formula Allocation NOFA contain no prevailing wage provision; El Dorado currently spends its PLHA on homeless services, which are not construction under 1720(a)(1). https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Zoning Ordinance Chapter 130.31) and the Affordable Housing Ordinance in development (inclusionary with in-lieu fee)
administering_agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Planning Division (530-621-5355), with the Affordable Housing Task Force (established April 2, 2024, Resolution 046-2024)
typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law (Government Code 65915) as implemented in Chapter 130.31: up to 50% density bonus for the standard affordability tiers, up to 80% or unlimited density for 100% affordable projects, plus concessions, waivers and reduced parking. No local bonus beyond state law was found.
affordability_requirement: State tiers: 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, or 100% affordable.
