The draft Affordable Housing Ordinance presented to the Task Force October 14, 2026 would require, for West Slope residential projects of 5 or more units or lots, 10% of rental units at 80% AMI for 55 years or 10% of for-sale units at 120% AMI for 45 years, with alternatives (in-lieu fee, off-site units, land dedication, conversion of market-rate units) and exemptions including deed-restricted affordable projects, mixed-use projects that are two-thirds or more residential, shelters and transitional housing, and projects where 51% or more of units are 1,600 square feet or less.
next_deadline: Density bonus is by right with the planning application. Resolution of Intention 163-2025 (November 4, 2025) started the Chapter 130.31 amendments; the Task Force's fee nexus study consultant was being selected in October 2026 and the ordinance and in-lieu fee will return to the Board after the study. No adoption date set.
layering_notes: Entitlement tools, not money. Diamond Village II (31 units) was approved under SB 35 by the Planning Commission in January 2025, which shows the ministerial path works in the unincorporated county. Watch the inclusionary ordinance: a 100% affordable project is exempt, but mixed-income workforce projects on the West Slope would pick up a 10% at 80% AMI obligation or an in-lieu fee once adopted, and the Task Force is also studying Community Facilities Districts and Enhanced Infrastructure Financing Districts as infrastructure tools. Staff flagged litigation risk around inclusionary exactions. The Tahoe Basin portion of the county is also subject to TRPA allocations and coverage rules, which this ordinance would not cover (West Slope only).
audit_note: Nov 9, 2026 spot check: ROI 163-2025 (Nov 4, 2025) and the October 14, 2026 Task Force slides match (West Slope 5+ units or lots, 10% rental at 80% AMI for 55 years, 10% for-sale at 120% AMI for 45 years, listed exemptions; fee nexus consultant RFP closed Oct 14, then Board funding request). Legistar detail page returns Invalid parameters to curl; read through the Legistar web API. prevailing_wage_trigger false is uncited (density bonus confers no public funds).
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA issuances (County not an issuer)
administering_agency: El Dorado County Board of Supervisors (TEFRA host approval, agenda through the Planning and Building Affordable Housing Unit); issuer California Municipal Finance Authority (CMFA), JPA member since October 2014; CSCDA also available
typical_award_size: Project-sized conduit issuances. CMFA TEFRA approved March 10, 2026 for up to $12,000,000 for Diamond Village Apartments II (31 units, 750 Black Rice Road, Placerville area, paired with $3,560,000 of HOME-ARP). CMFA closed $37,800,000 of bonds for SNO Foundation and Kingdom Development in El Dorado County in 2026. No County-issued multifamily bonds.
affordability_requirement: Federal 4% LIHTC and bond rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: TEFRA hearings are placed on regular Board agendas with published notice; allow 6 to 8 weeks from request to Board action and align with CDLAC rounds. County receives a share of the CMFA issuance fee for its Affordable Housing Trust Fund.
layering_notes: The County has no bond program of its own and does not take financial risk on conduit issues, so the TEFRA approval is procedural. Staff reports are prepared by the Affordable Housing Unit, which is stretched; submit the TEFRA request package early. Diamond Village II is the current template for an unincorporated El Dorado 4% deal: SB 35 ministerial approval, CMFA bonds, HOME-ARP from the state, TIF offset for the affordable units, and PBVs through the County PHA for the NPLH or homeless set-aside units. Private activity bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but tax credits plus state funds in the same deal usually do.
prevailing_wage_basis: DIR Public Works Case No. 2010-008 (April 8, 2010, CMFA conduit revenue bonds), applying PW 2004-016 Rancho Santa Fe Village Senior Affordable Housing (CSCDA conduit bonds for affordable housing): conduit bond proceeds and loan repayments never enter public coffers, so conduit bond financing is not payment out of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b). CDLAC QRRP evaluation criteria (4 CCR 5230) contain no prevailing wage condition. This covers the CMFA bonds and County TEFRA approval only; other public sources in the same deal (HOME 24 CFR 92.354 at 12+ HOME units, PBV 24 CFR 983.153(c) at 9+ units, state loans or a County fee offset) can trigger prevailing wage independently. https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2010/2010-008.pdf
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage set false for the conduit bond itself based on DIR coverage determinations PW 2010-008 and PW 2004-016; check every other funding source in the stack separately.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers and Housing Choice Vouchers, El Dorado County Public Housing Authority (HHSA)
administering_agency: El Dorado County Public Housing Authority, a division of HHSA (Board of Supervisors is the governing board); 530-621-6300; 330 Fair Lane, Placerville (moving to 768 Pleasant Valley Road, Diamond Springs, effective May 20, 2026)
typical_award_size: Small agency: 417 Housing Choice Vouchers, no public housing, qualified PHA exempt from annual plans. The PHA conducted a competitive Project-Based Voucher selection process in the 2020-2025 plan period and used PBVs with special-purpose vouchers to support the El Dorado Haven development (No Place Like Home units). Special-purpose vouchers: VASH, Mainstream, FUP, FYI; Emergency Housing Vouchers are winding down. No PBV RFP open as of November 6, 2026.
per_unit_cap: HUD PBV program cap: up to 20% of the PHA's authorized units (about 83 vouchers), with exceptions for supportive housing and other eligible units; contract rents at reasonable rent up to 110% of FMR.
affordability_requirement: HCV eligibility at 50% AMI or below (75% of admissions at 30% AMI); PBV HAP contracts up to 20 years with extensions. HCV waitlist has been closed since 2016.
next_deadline: No open PBV competition as of November 8, 2026. The 2026-2030 Five-Year PHA Plan (adopted September 29, 2026) reports a prior competitive PBV selection and PBVs committed to El Dorado Haven, and its section B.5 contains no statement of intent to make non-competitive PBV selections, so a non-competitive award would need a plan amendment first. Contact the PHA (530-621-6300) to ask about a future PBV RFP.
layering_notes: PBVs are the one County-controlled operating subsidy available for supportive housing in El Dorado, and with about 417 vouchers the pool is about 80 PBVs at most, several already committed to El Dorado Haven. A project with 10 to 20 PSH units should open the conversation with HHSA early and align with the EDOK Continuum of Care Coordinated Entry, which the PHA references. PBVs on a newly built or rehabilitated project with nine or more contract units trigger federal Davis-Bacon wages under 24 CFR 983.153(c); they do not by themselves trigger state prevailing wage, but state funding layered in usually does. The HCV program is federal; the PHA has no local rental assistance money. The Tahoe Basin is in the county PHA's jurisdiction but check overlap with the City of South Lake Tahoe programs.
cycle_notes: PBVs are awarded through PHA-issued competitive selections when vouchers are available, not on a fixed schedule. Non-competitive selection under 24 CFR 983.51(c) requires a statement of intent in the 5-Year Plan or an amendment; the 2026-2030 plan has none.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (HUD PBV development requirements): for new construction or rehabilitation under a PBV Agreement involving nine or more contract units, the owner and contractors must pay federal Davis-Bacon wages and the PHA must monitor compliance. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-IX/part-983/subpart-D. PBVs on existing housing with no development activity are not covered.
audit_note: T2 audit 2026-11-08: deadline text refreshed from the PHA page and the Legistar copy of the adopted 2026-2030 PHA Plan (file 26-1446, approved September 29, 2026); prevailing wage set from 24 CFR 983.153(c).

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), El Dorado County Assessor
administering_agency: El Dorado County Assessor, Jon DeVille, 360 Fair Lane, Placerville; 530-621-5719; with the California State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
typical_award_size: Exemption of property taxes on the share of units restricted to lower income households (Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g)): full exemption for units at or below 80% AMI in LIHTC or publicly financed projects, partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In El Dorado the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt applies to the exempt value.
per_unit_cap: No cap for projects that receive LIHTC or are financed with tax-exempt bonds or local, state or federal loans or grants (R&T 214(g)(1)(A)-(B)). The $20 million assessed-value cap per taxpayer applies only to exemptions claimed solely under the 90 percent lower income occupancy rule (R&T 214(g)(1)(C)).
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate, recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, HOME, PLHA, local agreement) restricting rents to lower income households.
next_deadline: File BOE-267 (first year) or BOE-267-A (annual) with the Assessor by February 15 each year. Late claims filed by January 1 of the next year can cancel 90 percent of tax, penalty and interest, and later claims 85 percent, with the combined tax, penalty and interest capped at $250. Property acquired after the January 1 lien date must file within 90 days of the first of the month after acquisition or by February 15 of the following year, whichever is earlier. Supplemental forms BOE-267-L or BOE-267-L1 attach as applicable.
layering_notes: Standard underwriting item. The Racquet Way staff report noted the project does not currently qualify for a welfare tax exemption because it is developed by a market-rate developer rather than a nonprofit, which is a reminder that a for-profit TIF offset recipient without a nonprofit managing general partner pays full property tax; the developer can instead request a restricted assessed value under Revenue and Taxation Code 402.1 that reflects the rent restrictions. The County's 55-year TIF offset agreement counts as a recorded restriction for the 402.1 valuation but does not by itself qualify for 214(g).
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: source_url only confirms the Assessor contact (Jon DeVille, 530-621-5719); substantive rules checked against BOE Publication 149 and R&T 214. The $20 million cap was misattributed to all non-LIHTC regulatory-agreement projects; it applies only to the 90 percent occupancy route, not to government-financed projects. 80 percent AMI (lower income per HSC 50079.5) is correct. prevailing_wage_trigger false is uncited; it is a property tax exemption, not construction funding.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(4) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works requires construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, including fees, loans or other obligations normally required in executing the construction contract that are reduced or waived. The welfare exemption (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)) reduces property tax on the completed property; it pays no construction cost, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage.

program_name: El Dorado Opportunity Knocks Continuum of Care (CA-525) and HHAP, El Dorado County region
administering_agency: El Dorado County HHSA as Administrative Entity for HHAP and as Collaborative Applicant (through the County PHA) for the EDOK CoC; edokcoc.org; Front Door access 530-600-2822
typical_award_size: HHAP Round 6: $670,181.51 accepted June 23, 2026 (County $324,069.60, CoC $346,111.91; HCD agreement 10349 through June 30, 2030). HHAP rounds 1-5 totaled about $5.4 million to the County and CoC, with $5.3 million obligated and $2.7 million spent per the state accountability dashboard. FY 2026 HUD CoC renewal competition: $160,797. State ESG 2024: $359,633 to the region. 2024 point-in-time count 284 people (135 unsheltered), 416 beds.
affordability_requirement: HHAP: people experiencing or at risk of homelessness; HHAP-6 requires a regionally coordinated homelessness action plan, encampment policy and Housing Element compliance plan. HUD CoC: Permanent Supportive Housing and Rapid Rehousing for homeless households.
next_deadline: HHAP-6 is committed to bridging Navigation Center operations during its wind-down and the gap before the treatment-focused campus at 300 Forni Road opens; no competitive local HHAP NOFA. HUD CoC competition annually (FY 2026 round applied for in 2026). HHAP Round 7 timing depends on the state budget.
layering_notes: The region is small and the money is spoken for: HHAP has historically funded the 60-bed Navigation Center (operated by Volunteers of America) and the County is pivoting to a treatment-based interim housing campus at 300 Forni Road. A permanent supportive housing developer would use the CoC for Coordinated Entry referrals and possibly a HUD CoC PSH renewal or new project, rather than county HHAP capital. HHAP-6 dollars could fund rental assistance or operating subsidy for PSH units if HHSA agrees, but the staff report commits them to interim housing and transition services. Coordinate with HHSA Community Services, not Planning and Building, for anything homelessness-related.
audit_note: PW pass Nov 9, 2026: no HHAP or CoC rule supports true; changed to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. 24 CFR 578.99(h): Davis-Bacon does not apply to the CoC program; the HHAP Round 6 NOFA states no prevailing wage requirement. HHAP here supports navigation center and interim housing activity that may include County-contracted capital work, which would be a public work under 1720(a)(1), so coverage depends on the use. https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/578.99 ; https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/calich/hhap-6-nofa.pdf

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions, El Dorado County HHSA Behavioral Health
administering_agency: El Dorado County Health and Human Services Agency, Behavioral Health Division (Integrated Plan FY 2026-27 through 2028-29 adopted June 23, 2026)
typical_award_size: Housing Interventions budget about $4,050,000 per year (30% component). Capital Development Projects line $500,000 in FY 2026-27 and $500,000 in FY 2027-28 (about 12% of housing interventions, under the 25% cap), both for the Forni Road Housing Services Site (county-owned interim housing with temporary tiny homes and a congregate services building, partly funded from Capital Facilities and Technological Needs). Remaining housing dollars go to rental subsidies, operating subsidies (about 15 people), a Flexible Housing Subsidy Pool, transitional rent and outreach and engagement.
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible population: adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk of homelessness; at least 50% of housing interventions for chronically homeless people; no more than 25% of housing interventions for capital.
next_deadline: Capital line is fully committed to the County's own Forni Road site for FY 2026-27 and 2027-28; no developer NOFA. The Integrated Plan can be revised annually (draft due to DHCS each March 31) and the next three-year plan starts FY 2029-30.
layering_notes: Unlike larger counties, El Dorado's BHSA capital is reserved for a county-owned interim housing campus, so a developer cannot expect BHSA gap funding for PSH before FY 2029-30. The operating subsidy and Flex Pool lines are the realistic ask: a PSH project with units set aside for BHSA clients could request a multi-year rental or operating subsidy agreement and services contract from Behavioral Health, which also strengthens an MHP or NPLH-style supportive housing application. BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) but carries no wage rule of its own; coverage turns on the 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (see prevailing_wage_basis). Contact Behavioral Health early in the annual update cycle (fall) to be included in the following year's plan.
audit_note: PW pass Nov 9, 2026: BHSA policy manual is silent on prevailing wage; changed true to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The DHCS BHSA County Policy Manual chapter 7 (Housing Interventions, section C.10 capital development) states no prevailing wage requirement. Rental and operating subsidies are not construction under 1720(a)(1); the Forni Road capital line is a County-owned project, which would be a public work if the County contracts the construction. https://policy-manual.mes.dhcs.ca.gov/behavioral-health-services-act-county-policy-manual/V1.0.0/7-bhsa-components-and-requirements

program_name: County development fee waivers and deferrals for affordable housing beyond the TIF offset (none found)
administering_agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: None. The County Developer Programs page lists only the Traffic Impact Fee (TIF) Offset and Collaborative Opportunities; no general affordable housing fee waiver or reimbursement program is offered to developers. The TIF offset (Policy B-14) is the only fee incentive. The separate Building Fee Deferral Program (listed under Homebuyers, page live on November 8, 2026) lets very low-income applicants defer building fees on new construction or health and safety repair permits until refinancing, resale or change in ownership; new guidelines are marked coming soon and it is aimed at individual homeowners, not multifamily developments. School, fire and other agency impact fees are not waived: Racquet Way Phase 2 (24 units) still owed about $87,360 to the Office of Education and $36,240 to the fire district after a 50% TIF offset was recommended.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: Not applicable. The Affordable Housing Task Force's Phase 2 tools work could add fee incentives; none proposed as of October 2026.
layering_notes: Negative finding recorded so the fee line is budgeted in full. Use the full 2025 TIF schedule less the B-14 offset on income-restricted units, plus full school, fire and County building and planning fees. The Building Fee Deferral Program is a homebuyer-side program for very low-income applicants; confirm with the Planning and Building Department (530-621-5824, Loans@edcgov.us) before assuming it covers a multifamily project.
audit_note: Reclassified fee waiver to negative finding because no waiver program exists. Building Fee Deferral page was reachable via WebFetch on November 8, 2026 (curl returns 403 Access Denied).
prevailing_wage_basis: No program exists, so nothing here pays for construction; Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) applies only to construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. Any fee waiver or deferral granted case by case would be public funds under 1720(b)(4) and is tested on the project. The Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) is tested in its own record.

program_name: HCDS Affordable Housing NOFA (NOFA 2026-03): IHTF, HOME, HOME-ARP, CDBG and PLHA capital loans
administering_agency: County of San Diego Health and Human Services Agency, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS), Community Development; 3989 Ruffin Road, San Diego 92123; community.development@sdcounty.ca.gov; (858) 694-4885; NOFA contact Felipe Murillo (858) 694-4807
typical_award_size: NOFA 2026-03 (released October 1, 2026, due November 19, 2026 at 2:00 pm, awards March 2027) offers about $16.0 million: $9.0M Innovative Housing Trust Fund, $2.5M HOME, $1.5M HOME-ARP, $1.8M CDBG, $1.2M PLHA. HCDS allocates sources at its discretion across awarded projects. Recent IHTF loans have ranged from $400,000 to $7.25 million per project (median about $3.5 million); HCDS's portfolio averages about $1.4 million of County-administered money per development. The prior round (NOFA 2024-01, due December 20, 2024) offered $6.5M HOME/HOME-ARP/CHDO, $3.5M IHTF, $1.5M PLHA plus 100 PBVs and 25 VASH PBVs.
per_unit_cap: No County per-unit cap stated. HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply to HOME-assisted units. The share of rent-restricted units must at least equal HCDS's share of total development cost.
affordability_requirement: 55-year minimum affordability for every award regardless of source. IHTF at or below 80% AMI regionwide; HOME and PLHA at or below 60% AMI (20% of HOME units at Low HOME rents); HOME-ARP at or below 30% AMI for people experiencing or at risk of homelessness; CDBG at or below 80% AMI for acquisition or rehabilitation only. Preferences: unincorporated area or County-owned land, projects applying to the 2027 second CDLAC/TCAC round, green building (LEED Silver, 50% onsite renewable), homeless units with secured services funding (HOME-ARP).
next_deadline: NOFA 2026-03 applications due November 19, 2026 at 2:00 pm (USB plus electronic copy); virtual industry day was October 15, 2026; awards March 2027. HCDS has run at least one capital NOFA each year since 2018 and plans to award its newest $22 million IHTF allocation through NOFAs in FY 2026-27, so expect another round in 2027.
layering_notes: This is the main county gap source for the whole San Diego region, including the City of San Diego for IHTF money (HOME, HOME-ARP, CDBG and PLHA are limited to the Urban County and HOME Consortium cities listed in the NOFA). Loan terms: 3% simple interest, 55-year term, 50% residual receipts shared proportionally with other public lenders, GP loans may not be repaid ahead of the County, TCAC developer fee limits, replacement reserves $375 per unit (new construction), $500 per PSH unit, $720 per unit (rehab), $4,000 initial compliance monitoring fee. All other local funds must be committed before applying and senior lenders must subordinate to the regulatory agreement. Funds are reserved for 24 months and the County will not split or combine awards if a deal converts between 9% and 4%. Scoring (165 points) weights geographic location 30, financing gap 20, experience 20, target population 15, services 15, overall 15. Federal sources carry Davis-Bacon, NEPA, Section 3, BABA (HOME) and relocation rules; state prevailing wage on County loans turns on the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions. PSH or PBV projects must fund a one-year transition reserve. No Place Like Home was offered through earlier County NOFAs and is exhausted.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Innovative Housing Trust Fund (IHTF), County of San Diego
administering_agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS); established by the Board of Supervisors October 10, 2017 (Administrative Code Article XV, Sections 230.8 and 232.5)
typical_award_size: Board allocations total over $129 million through seven allocations since 2017 (General Fund one-time money, plus redirected grant balances such as $2 million of Capital ESG in June 2025). $112 million has been awarded to 36 developments with 3,054 units in 22 communities, leveraging $1.6 billion. The newest $22 million allocation is being awarded through NOFAs in FY 2026-27: a $12 million IHTF NOFA for County-owned sites ran July 6 to August 10, 2026, and $9 million is in NOFA 2026-03 (due November 19, 2026). Loans to date range from $200,000 (Vista Lane) to $7.25 million (Terrasini, 95 units); most are $3 million to $7 million.
per_unit_cap: None stated in the ordinance or NOFAs. Awards have ranged from about $2,000 to $112,000 per unit, typically $30,000 to $75,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 80% AMI (extremely low, very low and low income). NOFA 2024-01 required 99-year affordability for IHTF-funded units; NOFA 2026-03 states a 55-year minimum for all sources. Eligible anywhere in San Diego County, including all 18 cities.
next_deadline: Through NOFA 2026-03, due November 19, 2026. The Board's October 7, 2026 five-year report directs staff to identify a dedicated ongoing revenue source for the IHTF; no ballot measure or fee is adopted yet, so future rounds depend on one-time Board allocations.
layering_notes: IHTF is the only County money usable inside the City of San Diego and the larger cities, which makes it the typical County piece of a City of San Diego deal alongside SDHC funds and Housing Authority of the City of San Diego bonds. It is a 3% simple, 55-year residual receipts loan under HCDS standard terms. HCDS also deposits ground lease revenue from County land deals (for example about $500,000 of initial rent from 3177 Ocean View Boulevard) and will deposit inclusionary in-lieu fees from the unincorporated ordinance into HCDS trust funds, so the fund will grow modestly from those streams. County-owned sites get a scoring preference and had their own $12 million round in summer 2026. Expect state prevailing wage on any IHTF-funded construction.
audit_note: Nov 9, 2026 spot check: Attachment C shows Genesis (9 units, $1,350,000 IHTF) at about $150,000 per unit, above the $112,000 top of the per-unit range in per_unit_cap, and Vista Lane at about $1,300 per unit; about 15 of 36 loans are under $3 million. Not material to screening.
prevailing_wage_basis: County of San Diego HCDS NOFA 2026-03 (Capital IHTF, HOME, HOME-ARP, CDBG and PLHA), section 9 Prevailing Wage Rates/Davis-Bacon: all developments funded through this NOFA process are public works within the meaning of Labor Code 1720 and the applicant, developer and owner must comply with state prevailing wage law (Labor Code 1770 et seq.); federal Davis-Bacon also applies where HOME (12+ assisted units) or CDBG funds are used. https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/sdhcd/new-docs/CD/01%20NOFA_2026-03_Capital_IHTF_HOME_FINAL.pdf

program_name: CDBG acquisition and rehabilitation NOFA (NOFA 2026-01) and HOME Consortium entitlement, San Diego Urban County
administering_agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS), Community Development; community.development@sdcounty.ca.gov
typical_award_size: NOFA 2026-01 (released June 1, 2026, due July 10, 2026, awards November 2026) offered $1.7 million of CDBG for acquisition and/or rehabilitation of existing affordable multifamily units or land acquisition for affordable housing; new construction is not eligible. FY 2027-28 CDBG applications for public facilities, infrastructure and services ran September 21 to October 30, 2026. HOME and HOME-ARP ($11.9 million HOME-ARP allocation) flow through the capital NOFA; the County's loan portfolio holds about $82 million of federal funds across 123 developments.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits for HOME-assisted units; none stated for CDBG.
affordability_requirement: CDBG: households at or below 80% AMI, HUD minimum 5 years but HCDS imposes 55 years. HOME: at or below 60% AMI with 20% Low HOME units, 20-year HUD minimum, 55 years enforced by HCDS. Eligible areas: Urban County (unincorporated plus Coronado, Del Mar, Imperial Beach, Lemon Grove, Poway, Solana Beach) for CDBG and PLHA; HOME Consortium adds Carlsbad, Encinitas, La Mesa, San Marcos, Santee and Vista.
next_deadline: Next acquisition-rehab CDBG NOFA expected around June 2027 if HCDS repeats the 2026 schedule; HOME and HOME-ARP are in NOFA 2026-03 (due November 19, 2026). CDBG public facilities applications open each September for the following fiscal year.
layering_notes: Terms match the capital NOFA: 3% simple, 55 years, 50% residual receipts, $720 per unit replacement reserve for rehab, 12-month reservation with no extensions, $4,000 compliance fee. Federal money brings Davis-Bacon, Uniform Relocation Act, NEPA release of funds before any choice-limiting action, lead-based paint and Section 3. Useful for preservation buys of small existing properties in the Urban County cities where IHTF is the only other County option. The larger cities (San Diego, Chula Vista, Oceanside, Escondido, El Cajon, Carlsbad for CDBG) are their own entitlements for Pass 3.
audit_note: Spot check Nov 9, 2026: NOFA 2026-01 confirms $1.7M CDBG, release June 1, 2026, due July 10, 2026, award November 2026, 80% AMI, 55 years, 3% simple 55-year 50% residual receipts, $720 per unit reserve, 12-month reservation, $4,000 monitoring fee, Davis-Bacon and state prevailing wage (stricter applies), new construction ineligible. HCDS NOFA page shows NOFA 2026-03 (IHTF, HOME, HOME-ARP, CDBG, PLHA) due November 19, 2026 at 2:00 PM. New construction and supportive housing tags reflect the HOME capital NOFA, not the CDBG acquisition-rehab NOFA.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County of San Diego formula allocation
administering_agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS)
typical_award_size: HCD's 2024-2028 formula NOFA lists San Diego County at $1,389,802 (2024), $1,488,682 (2025) and an estimated $8,686,263 over five years (the City of San Diego is separate at about $4.1 to $4.4 million a year). HCDS puts PLHA into its capital NOFAs ($1.2 million in NOFA 2026-03, $1.5 million in NOFA 2024-01) and into a moderate-income down payment assistance program.
affordability_requirement: Rental housing at or below 60% AMI with 55-year affordability under HCDS's NOFA; PLHA guidelines allow up to 80% AMI rental and 120% to 150% AMI ownership. Eligible only in the Urban County (unincorporated plus Coronado, Del Mar, Imperial Beach, Lemon Grove, Poway, Solana Beach).
next_deadline: Through NOFA 2026-03, due November 19, 2026. HCDS is preparing the County's new five-year PLHA plan and application for the 2024-2028 allocations (Board action expected in the coming months), which sets how much goes to development versus down payment assistance.
layering_notes: Small relative to the IHTF but it is the one County source that can be used for moderate-income ownership. For rental projects it rides along with IHTF and HOME in the same application, same 3% 55-year loan terms. NOFA 2026-03 treats all funded developments as Labor Code 1720 public works (see prevailing_wage_basis). Cities with their own PLHA (San Diego, Chula Vista, Oceanside, Escondido and others) are Pass 3.
audit_note: Spot check Nov 9, 2026: HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA lists San Diego County $1,389,802 and $1,488,682 and $8,686,263 five-year estimate (City of San Diego $4,064,317 and $4,353,481). NOFA 2026-03 lists $1.2M PLHA, due November 19, 2026. Prevailing wage true is uncited (no PLHA or NOFA rule named); add a basis in a PW citation pass.
prevailing_wage_basis: County of San Diego HCDS NOFA 2026-03, which awards the County PLHA formula funds alongside IHTF and HOME, section 9: all developments funded through this NOFA process are public works within the meaning of Labor Code 1720 and must pay state prevailing wage. The County adds this term; HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines contain none. https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/sdhcd/new-docs/CD/01%20NOFA_2026-03_Capital_IHTF_HOME_FINAL.pdf

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers and HUD-VASH PBVs, Housing Authority of the County of San Diego (HACSD)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Diego, administered by HCDS Rental Assistance Division (Board of Supervisors sits as the Board of Commissioners); 3989 Ruffin Road, San Diego
typical_award_size: Since the Board's September 1, 2021 direction to expand PBVs, HACSD has awarded 768 PBVs (HCV PBVs plus VASH PBVs); 479 PBV units are operating and 327 more open within one to four years. The FY 2026 Agency Plan lists 387 PBV units in 13 developments operating, 119 units in four developments opening in 2026 (Union Tower 24 VASH, Villa Serena II 15, Alvarado Senior Village 53, Palomar Point 27) and 333 units in eight developments opening 2027 or later. PBVs are awarded through HCDS NOFAs (NOFA 2024-01 offered 100 PBVs and 25 VASH PBVs; 65 additional VASH vouchers were secured in 2025). HACSD assists over 11,000 households and pays about $21 million a month to about 4,000 landlords.
per_unit_cap: PBV contract rents at reasonable rent up to 110% of FMR (HACSD payment standards); HUD program cap of 20% of authorized vouchers with exceptions for PSH and other eligible units. Minimum 10% of PBV units in a project must be VASH when VASH PBVs are requested.
affordability_requirement: PBV units at or below 50% AMI (30% to 50% AMI homeless or special needs populations in recent awards); VASH PBVs for veterans up to 80% AMI. Initial HAP contract of 20 years renewable for up to 20 more at HACSD's discretion. HACSD jurisdiction: unincorporated area plus Chula Vista, Coronado, Del Mar, El Cajon, Escondido, Imperial Beach, La Mesa, Lemon Grove, Poway, San Marcos, Santee, Solana Beach and Vista (not the cities of San Diego, Carlsbad, Encinitas, National City or Oceanside).
next_deadline: No PBVs are offered in NOFA 2026-03 (due November 19, 2026). The HCV program closed to new applicants February 20, 2026 because of federal funding levels, so a PBV round depends on HUD appropriations; HACSD's 121 public housing units in Chula Vista are converting to PBVs through RAD/Section 18 with a developer RFP for ground lease and renovation expected after HUD approval (18-month process started November 2025).
layering_notes: PBVs are the County's operating subsidy for PSH and are usually requested in the same HCDS NOFA as the capital loan, with Coordinated Entry referrals through the Regional Task Force on Homelessness. HCDS requires a transition reserve sufficient to hold rents for one year if PBV assistance is not renewed. Nine or more PBVs in a project trigger Davis-Bacon under HCDS rules; PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage. Projects inside the City of San Diego use San Diego Housing Commission vouchers instead (Pass 3). Watch the Chula Vista public housing repositioning: four sites (Dorothy Street, L Street, Melrose, Town Center Manor, 121 units) will be offered to an affordable developer under a ground lease with PBVs attached.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal Davis-Bacon applies by rule: 24 CFR 983.153(c)(2) requires the owner and its contractors to pay Davis-Bacon wages for PBV development (new construction or rehabilitation under an AHAP) involving nine or more contract units, whether or not completed in stages. PBVs attached to existing housing are not development and do not trigger it. State prevailing wage depends on the other public funds in the deal under Labor Code 1720. https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.153

program_name: Affordable housing on County-owned excess land (ground leases through Disposition and Development Agreements)
administering_agency: County of San Diego Department of General Services, Real Estate Services (RFP issuance and DDA), with HCDS (regulatory agreement and IHTF capital); Board of Supervisors approval
typical_award_size: 12 County-owned surplus sites are in the pipeline for 100% affordable housing totaling about 1,762 homes (595 completed, 126 under construction, 1,043 upcoming), with $51.8 million of County capital committed to the sites. Nine sites are in the City of San Diego, plus Fallbrook, Ramona and Escondido. Terms are long-term ground leases (99 years at 620 E. Valley Parkway, Escondido, 134 senior units; 3177 Ocean View Boulevard, San Diego, 122 units with BRIDGE Housing and a San Ysidro Health clinic, about $500,000 initial rent then $300 a year escalating 3.5%). Next starts: 6255 Mission Gorge Road (337 units) and 5001 73rd Street (120 units) in early 2027, 4588 Market Street (138) in 2027, Ramona 12th and Main (100) and 5202 University Avenue (90, via SDHC) in 2028.
affordability_requirement: 100% affordable at or below 80% AMI under a County regulatory agreement (55 years or longer); specific populations (seniors, families, PSH) set in each RFP. Developer must comply with the County Working Families Ordinance (prevailing wage, skilled and trained workforce, paid sick leave) on County property.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026; the County General Services Development Opportunities page lists only an RFP for a Behavioral Health Wellness Campus. Housing site RFPs are issued site by site after the Board declares a property surplus; expected next solicitations are the ground lease and renovation of the four Chula Vista public housing sites after HUD RAD/Section 18 approval and the Fallbrook North Orange and East Ivy site (program TBD).
layering_notes: County land deals come packaged: nominal ground lease, IHTF or other County capital (County sites had their own $12 million IHTF NOFA in July 2026 and get a location preference in every HCDS NOFA), PBVs where HACSD has jurisdiction, and Board support for state applications. In exchange the County requires 100% affordability, Working Families Ordinance labor terms (prevailing wage plus skilled and trained workforce on work over $1 million), ground lease payments to the IHTF, and a County regulatory agreement senior to other restrictions. Mission Gorge (337 units) and Ramona are the largest unincorporated or near-term opportunities; Ramona and Fallbrook sites test rural feasibility. Faith-based land partnerships (three developments, 220 units) are a parallel track.
cycle_notes: Site-by-site RFPs posted on the County DGS Real Estate Development Opportunities page; no housing RFP open as of November 8, 2026.
prevailing_wage_basis: County of San Diego HCDS NOFA 2026-03 section 8: all developments on County-owned property are subject to the Working Families Ordinance (Ord. 10771), which requires County lessees to pay prevailing wage and use a skilled and trained workforce on construction they perform on County property over $1 million (stated exemptions include non-profit entities, projects already in process and projects with bargaining agreements); section 9 adds that NOFA-funded developments are Labor Code 1720 public works. https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/sdhcd/new-docs/CD/01%20NOFA_2026-03_Capital_IHTF_HOME_FINAL.pdf
audit_note: Working Families Ordinance lists an exemption for non-profit entities; confirm whether a nonprofit ground lessee is exempt in the specific DDA.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, In-Lieu Fee and expanded density bonus, unincorporated San Diego County (Zoning Ordinance Sections 6341 and 7430)
administering_agency: County of San Diego Planning and Development Services (ordinance and affordable housing plans) with HCDS (in-lieu fee trust fund and affordable housing agreements)
typical_award_size: Adopted June 24, 2026 (Ordinance 11009), effective October 22, 2026; projects with a complete or SB 330 preliminary application submitted by October 21, 2026 are exempt. Applies to residential and mixed-use projects of 10 or more primary units in the unincorporated area. Incentives: density bonus doubled relative to state law up to a 50% maximum (10% low income units earns 40% instead of 20%) plus two extra concessions, and 30-day priority discretionary review for projects providing 50% more low income units than required. In-lieu fees: $18.69 per interior square foot (rental, 95% market share assumed, effective $17.76), $21.37 (for-sale, effective $19.23), $41.82 (General Plan Amendment projects, effective $33.46), paid at building permit and deposited to an HCDS trust fund for affordable housing anywhere in the county including cities. Staff estimate 15 to 60 deed-restricted units a year.
affordability_requirement: For-rent: 5% extremely low (30% AMI) or 5% very low (50% AMI) or 10% low (80% AMI). For-sale: 5% very low or 10% low or 15% moderate (120% AMI). General Plan Amendment projects: 20% low. Units calculated on base density before bonus, rounded up at 0.5. Alternative compliance in Board priority order: land donation, affordable for-sale ADUs (up to 50% of requirement or 5 units), in-lieu fee for 50%, in-lieu fee for 100%, off-site units in the same community plan area, a village, a TCAC High or Highest Resource area or a VMT-efficient area (cities allowed). 100% affordable projects are exempt but record an affordable housing agreement. Market-rate permits are held until affordable units are permitted (50% rule) and finaled (75% rule).
next_deadline: In effect for applications submitted on or after October 22, 2026. Senior Housing and Small Lot zoning updates and Housing Unlocked zoning amendments are scheduled for the Board in fall 2026 and 2027; a programmatic EIR for low-VMT housing streamlining comes in 2027.
layering_notes: For a 100% affordable deal the ordinance is a zero-cost exemption plus access to the doubled density bonus if the project also meets a set-aside; for mixed-income workforce deals in the unincorporated area it adds a 5% to 10% affordable obligation or roughly $18 to $19 per square foot in fees. The in-lieu fee revenue becomes new County gap money administered by HCDS (the Board asked staff for a dedicated IHTF revenue source and this is the first one). Land donation sites must be suitable for multifamily at the displaced density with utilities, outside slopes, floodplains, farmland and habitat; donations over $1 million go to the Board. Density bonus and inclusionary agreements do not trigger prevailing wage; the Working Families Ordinance applies only on County-owned land. 2026 San Diego County AMI is $130,900.
audit_note: Nov 9, 2026 spot check: next_deadline holds the October 22, 2026 effective date, not an application deadline, so the computed past date is not a missed round.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; the inclusionary ordinance (Zoning Ordinance 6341) and density bonus (7430) provide density and processing incentives only (Applicant Guide, Incentives section) and pay no public funds, so they do not by themselves trigger prevailing wage. County funds layered on a project are tested separately. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA, CSCDA and other JPA issuances (County not an issuer)
administering_agency: County of San Diego Board of Supervisors (TEFRA host approval through the Finance and General Government Group, Debt Advisory Committee concurrence); issuers California Municipal Finance Authority, California Statewide Communities Development Authority, California Public Finance Authority, California Enterprise Development Authority
typical_award_size: Project-sized conduit issuances approved as consent items roughly monthly. 2026 approvals include CMFA bonds for 2581 Commercial Street Apartments (70 units, up to $13 million, March 24 and August 18, 2026), four CMFA issuances on March 24, 2026 (up to $20M, $13M, $40M and $72M), Island Family Housing (CSCDA, August 18, 2026), Fallbrook Trails, Promenade and Seaward Affordable Apartments (CMFA, September 2026), Vista Lane Family Apartments reissuance (165 units, up to $55 million, December 9, 2025) and Fallbrook Senior Apartments (up to $26 million, November 4, 2025). The County collects about $991 per approval to recover staff costs and takes on no debt.
affordability_requirement: Federal bond and 4% LIHTC rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Request the County TEFRA approval through the issuer (CMFA or CSCDA handle the notice and hearing); allow six to eight weeks before the CDLAC application deadline. Approvals appear on regular Board agendas; the Board also reapproves when terms change (reissuance on conversion to permanent, address corrections).
layering_notes: Neither the County nor the Housing Authority of the County of San Diego issues multifamily bonds; CMFA is the usual issuer, with County Board approval for projects in the unincorporated area and, in practice, for several City of San Diego addresses as well. Inside the City of San Diego the Housing Authority of the City of San Diego (through SDHC) is an active issuer and will be covered in Pass 3. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but County IHTF, HOME or PLHA in the same deal does. Pair the TEFRA timeline with the HCDS NOFA award (March 2027) and the 2027 second CDLAC/TCAC round that the NOFA rewards.
prevailing_wage_basis: DIR Decision on Administrative Appeal, PW 2006-020 Heber Family Apartments (April 5, 2007), following PW 2004-016 Rancho Santa Fe Village and PW 2006-005 Central Village Apartments, holds that loans of tax-exempt conduit bond proceeds for affordable housing, whether publicly offered or privately placed, are not a payment out of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and are not a public below-market loan under 1720(b)(4), because the proceeds and repayments never enter public coffers; reaffirmed in PW 2010-008 and PW 2015-008. Bond financing alone does not trigger state prevailing wage; other public funds in the same deal (city or county loans, fee waivers, land) are tested separately, and federal sources such as HOME or 9+ PBVs carry their own Davis-Bacon rules. https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-020(A).pdf

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Diego County Assessor
administering_agency: San Diego County Assessor/Recorder/County Clerk, Jordan Z. Marks; Institutional Exemptions unit, 1600 Pacific Highway, Suite 103, San Diego, CA 92101; (619) 531-5772; with the State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
typical_award_size: Exemption of property taxes on units restricted to lower income households under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g): full exemption for qualifying units in LIHTC or publicly financed projects and partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In San Diego County the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt applies to the exempt value, typically worth 1.1% to 1.25% of assessed value a year.
per_unit_cap: Statewide $20 million assessed-value cap on the 214(g) exemption for non-LIHTC projects relying only on a regulatory agreement; no cap for LIHTC projects. AB 84 (2024) added the 100% AMI over-income category reported on BOE-267-L4.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit owner or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, HOME, PLHA, IHTF or County regulatory agreement) restricting rents to lower income households; BOE-267-L2 tenant data for projects without government financing or tax credits.
next_deadline: Next annual filing due February 15, 2027 (claims for fiscal year 2027-2028); the Assessor form states claims must be filed each year by 5:00 p.m. on February 15. Claims filed February 16 through January 1 of the following year receive 90 percent of the exemption.
layering_notes: Standard underwriting item for every LIHTC or County-financed deal in the region. The County's 55-year regulatory agreement and the inclusionary affordable housing agreements qualify as recorded restrictions. File the Organizational Clearance Certificate copy with the first claim and use the San Diego forms posted at sdarcc.gov. Mixed-income inclusionary projects owned by for-profits do not qualify and should instead seek a restricted assessed value under Revenue and Taxation Code 402.1.
cycle_notes: Annual claim due February 15 each year; first-year claims on BOE-267 with L-series supplements; current posted form is for fiscal year 2026-2027 (due February 15, 2026).
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(4) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works requires construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, including fees, loans or other obligations normally required in executing the construction contract that are reduced or waived. The welfare exemption (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)) reduces property tax on the completed property; it pays no construction cost, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage.

program_name: San Diego City and County Continuum of Care (CA-601, Regional Task Force on Homelessness) and HHAP, County of San Diego share
administering_agency: Regional Task Force on Homelessness (RTFH, CoC lead and HMIS lead); County of San Diego HHSA, HCDS Office of Homeless Solutions (County HHAP administrative entity); City of San Diego (large city allocation)
typical_award_size: HHAP Round 6 (FY 2026-27 through 2028-29): County $12.1 million (accepted December 9, 2025), RTFH CoC $12.9 million, City of San Diego $25.8 million, from a joint regional application filed August 29, 2025. County HHAP rounds 1 to 6 total about $64 million ($9.99M, $4.57M, $12.79M, $10.5M, $14.1M, $12.1M); the region received $220.6 million in rounds 1 to 5 plus $46.2 million of Encampment Resolution Funds. County HHAP pays for Housing Our Youth, the Local Rental Subsidy Program ($6.6 million in Round 5), shallow rent subsidies, housing stability case management and harm reduction contracts, not capital. 2025 point-in-time count: 9,905 people, 5,714 unsheltered.
affordability_requirement: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness; HHAP-6 requires a regionally coordinated action plan, 10% youth set-aside, and allows Category 1 permanent housing uses including housing development and capital funding, rental assistance and operating support.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 9, 2026. County HHAP-6 is programmed to existing contracts; the next HUD CoC NOFO and any HHAP Round 7 depend on HUD and the state budget.
layering_notes: County HHAP is operating money, not a capital source, and the County's BHSA plan says it will spend all of it on existing youth, regional housing assistance and local rental subsidy programs as ARPA expires. A PSH developer should look to RTFH for CoC PSH or Rapid Rehousing operating funds and to the City of San Diego's much larger HHAP allocation for capital or operating subsidies inside the city (Pass 3). Coordinated Entry through RTFH is the referral source required by HCDS for homeless units in County-funded projects, and RTFH's CES is the official front door for BHSA housing interventions tied to homelessness.
cycle_notes: FY 2026 HUD CoC NOFO: RTFH local project application deadline July 13, 2026; HUD paused the NOFO in August 2026 and reopened it with a September 30, 2026 deadline. HHAP-6 joint regional application filed August 29, 2025 (amended October 29, 2025); County accepted $12.1M on December 9, 2025. RTFH's HHAP page lists no open solicitation.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: changed true to false; CoC rule 578.99(h) and HHAP 6 operating-only use. Revisit if the County funds HHAP or CoC capital.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 578.99(h): the Davis-Bacon Act does not apply to the CoC program. The County HHAP Round 6 Board letter (item 25-661) commits the funds to the Housing Our Youth program, emergency housing in the unincorporated area, permanent housing rental subsidies with housing stability services, administration and HMIS; none is construction, and Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction only. Any CoC or HHAP capital award would be tested separately. https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/578.99

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions and Flexible Housing Pool, County of San Diego Behavioral Health Services
administering_agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Behavioral Health Services (Integrated Plan FY 2026-2029 approved June 9, 2026); Flexible Housing Pool Pilot administered by Brilliant Corners under a single-source contract approved November 18, 2025
typical_award_size: BHSA budget about $329.5 million in FY 2026-27, with the housing component at 27% of the local allocation (roughly $89 million a year by that percentage; the plan does not publish a single housing dollar total). Rental subsidies for about 2,672 people a year: 290 permanent slots (250 Flexible Housing Pool subsidies for ACT clients plus 40 operating subsidies at Starling Place, a Homekey+ site in the City of San Diego) and about 2,382 interim placements from a $23.6 million interim housing budget; 4,305 units a year funded in total. Flex Pool Pilot costs $3.45 to $5.35 million in FY 2026-27 (Behavioral Health Bridge Housing and BHSA). Capital development: none in FY 2026-27.
affordability_requirement: Medi-Cal eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk; at least half of housing funds for chronically homeless people; permanent settings include supportive housing, master-leased apartments, shared housing, board and care and recovery residences; Transitional Rent (six months, Medi-Cal managed care) feeds into BHSA subsidies.
next_deadline: No developer NOFA. The plan states the County will not fund capital development with BHSA in year one (to sustain treatment services) and will reassess in future years; operating subsidies are limited to the 40 Homekey+ units. Annual plan updates start FY 2027-28 (draft due to DHCS each March 31), and BHSA will absorb Behavioral Health Bridge Housing programs when that grant ends in FY 2028-29.
layering_notes: Unlike Orange or Contra Costa, San Diego County is spending its BHSA housing money on subsidies and a Flex Pool rather than capital, so do not underwrite County BHSA capital for PSH in 2026-27. The realistic asks are: Flex Pool tenant-based subsidies for units set aside for ACT clients (Brilliant Corners master-leasing or direct placements), a Homekey+ style operating subsidy agreement if the County co-applies (it has co-applied with Wakeland in Chula Vista and Casa de Amparo in Vista), and Medi-Cal Transitional Rent through the managed care plans for move-in. Community input asked the County to dedicate the full 25% to capital, so the FY 2027-28 update is the moment to request a capital line. BHSA capital, if used, would be public funds under Labor Code 1720(b); the County is not using BHSA Housing Interventions for capital development in the first plan year (see prevailing_wage_basis).
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: changed true to false because the plan funds no capital; revisit in later plan years if BHSA capital is added.
prevailing_wage_basis: San Diego County BHSA Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Board item 26-366, Attachment A, Capital Development Projects, Chapter 7 Section C.10): the County will not use BHSA Housing Interventions for capital development in the first year and is using the Flexible Housing Pool and operating subsidies instead. Rental and operating subsidies are not construction under Labor Code 1720(a)(1); the DHCS BHSA Policy Manual chapter 7 states no prevailing wage term. If the County later funds BHSA capital, coverage would be unclear under 1720(b). https://policy-manual.mes.dhcs.ca.gov/behavioral-health-services-act-county-policy-manual/V1.0.0/7-bhsa-components-and-requirements

program_name: State CDBG and HOME (non-entitlement county) and County housing programs, Yolo County Administrator's Office
administering_agency: Yolo County Administrator's Office (Mark Bryan, housing programs; housingprograms@yolocounty.gov) with grant administration contracted to Thurmond Consulting LLC through November 30, 2026; Yolo County Housing formerly administered the County CDBG program
typical_award_size: Small. Yolo County is a non-entitlement jurisdiction and applies to HCD's state CDBG and HOME competitions. The Board held the required housing public hearing on March 24, 2026 and authorized a $300,000 application for the 2025 state CDBG funding year (Resolution 26-34). Current CDBG use is an owner-occupied housing rehabilitation program with loans up to $100,000 for low and moderate income homeowners in the unincorporated area. Earlier HOME and CDBG awards funded first-time homebuyer assistance. No County loan to a multifamily development was found.
per_unit_cap: State HOME per-unit subsidy limits would apply if the County sponsored a rental project; none found.
affordability_requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI (low and moderate income benefit) in the unincorporated area only (not Davis, Woodland, West Sacramento or Winters). HOME at or below 80% AMI with HCD's affordability covenants.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. HCD's 2025 state CDBG NOFA portal closed April 3, 2026 and the next CDBG NOFA has not been posted; HCD's HOME Program Activities draft guidelines finished public comment September 9, 2026 with no new HOME NOFA open. A developer wanting the County as applicant or co-applicant should contact the County Administrator's Office before the next HCD NOFA opens.
layering_notes: Yolo County has no county gap loan program for rental housing and no development NOFA. Its state CDBG and HOME capacity is small and committed to homeowner rehab and homebuyer programs, and the County issued an RFP in September 2026 for housing program consulting (loan management, grant writing) to run these programs. The practical County role for a developer is the resolution or co-applicant for state programs (HOME rental, Joe Serna farmworker housing, MHP) in the unincorporated communities (Esparto, Madison, Knights Landing, Dunnigan, Clarksburg). The Board created a Farmworker Housing Ad Hoc Subcommittee in May 2025 and the March 2026 Board calendar listed hearings on a farmworker housing planning grant application. The three cities (Davis, Woodland, West Sacramento) run their own programs and are Pass 3. HOME and CDBG carry Davis-Bacon at their unit thresholds and federal cross-cutting rules; state prevailing wage turns on state or local funds and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis).
cycle_notes: Tied to HCD's state CDBG and HOME NOFA calendar. 2025 CDBG funding year: County public meeting March 18, 2026, Board hearing and $300,000 application authorization March 24, 2026 (Resolution 26-34), HCD portal closed April 3, 2026. HOME Program Activities draft guidelines were out for comment August 10 to September 9, 2026; the last HOME Program Activities NOFA was 2024 (amended to over-the-counter).
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Yolo County formula allocation
administering_agency: Yolo County (Board of Supervisors resolutions; County Administrator's Office and Health and Human Services Agency)
typical_award_size: 2019-2023 five-year formula allocation $819,661 (Board resolution adopted February 27, 2024 with the PLHA plan). HCD's 2024-2028 formula NOFA lists Yolo County at $270,934 (2024), $303,869 (2025) and an estimated $1,693,338 over five years. For comparison the cities receive their own allocations: Davis about $1.33 million, Woodland about $1.09 million and West Sacramento about $1.04 million over five years.
affordability_requirement: PLHA guidelines: rental housing at or below 60% AMI (up to 80% AMI) with 55-year covenants, or homeownership and homelessness activities as chosen in the County's five-year plan. The County's adopted plan activities were not readable in the opened documents.
next_deadline: The County must adopt a new five-year plan and resolution for the 2024-2028 allocations under HCD's amended formula NOFA; no 2026 Board action was found in the minutes reviewed. Ask the County Administrator's Office which activities the plan funds before counting on PLHA.
layering_notes: At $270,000 to $300,000 a year, Yolo County PLHA is a small, deal-specific source and the County's plan uses have not been published in a readable form online. It could support a single predevelopment or gap contribution for a project in the unincorporated area, or be subgranted to Yolo County Housing. PLHA states no wage rule of its own; construction use is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis).
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on public-funds logic only; no program or local rule found, changed to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines and Formula Allocation NOFA contain no prevailing wage provision; the Yolo County PLHA resolution and plan (February 27, 2024) add no wage term. https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (County Code Chapter 8-8), in-lieu fee and the Affordable Housing Program account, unincorporated Yolo County
administering_agency: Yolo County Community Services Department, Planning Division (ordinance and affordable housing agreements); in-lieu fees held by the County in the Affordable Housing Program account
typical_award_size: Regulatory requirement, not a funding source. Ordinance 1451 (effective January 1, 2015) requires on-site affordable units: for-sale projects of 10 or more units set aside 20% (half low income, half moderate income); rental projects of 20 or more units set aside 25% very low income plus 10% low income; rental projects of 7 to 19 units set aside 15% very low plus 10% low. Smaller projects (9 or fewer single-family, 7 or fewer multifamily) pay an in-lieu fee assessed on a unit percentage basis. The in-lieu fee equals a percentage of the estimated cost to construct the required units, is set in the County Master Fee Schedule (last adopted June 24, 2025) and may be reduced up to 50% based on available subsidy; the current per-unit amount was not published in the opened documents (the 2009 schedule was $12,920 for-sale and $17,610 rental per required unit).
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units must be permanently affordable (Sec. 8-8.108(b)); for-sale units carry a 20-year covenant that resets at each resale to a qualified buyer. Alternatives, only if on-site is shown infeasible: off-site units in the unincorporated county, land dedication (2 acres minimum), in-lieu fee, or housing credits transferable within 3 miles and 5 years. Density bonus units do not generate an inclusionary obligation.
next_deadline: Applies at discretionary approval; fee estimate given at approval and paid before final map, first building permit or certificate of occupancy. In-lieu fees must be spent or encumbered within five years of receipt unless the Board extends.
layering_notes: The Affordable Housing Program account (Sec. 8-8.116) is the County's only local housing fund and it is fed solely by in-lieu fees from small unincorporated projects, so expect a balance in the low hundreds of thousands at most; no NOFA or award from it was found. For a 100% affordable project the ordinance imposes no obligation and offers the incentives in Sec. 8-8.118 (fee waiver, standards modifications, streamlining, density bonus). For a mixed-income rental project of 20 or more units the 35% combined set-aside (25% very low plus 10% low) is one of the steepest in the region and is a real feasibility constraint in Esparto, Madison and Dunnigan; the ordinance predates current state density bonus law and the Latinos Unidos v. Napa decision, so confirm how the County applies it today. Davis, Woodland and West Sacramento have their own inclusionary programs (Davis in-lieu fee about $215,000 per unit) covered in Pass 3.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: official code host codelibrary.amlegal.com still returns 403 to curl and WebFetch, and yolocounty.gov is 403; the 2021 Housing Element Board presentation on public.destinyhosted.com does not restate the ordinance terms. Terms remain mirror-only (zoneomics).
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this inclusionary ordinance (County Code Chapter 8-8) provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any public loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on a project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Development fee incentives for affordable units: 50% application and processing fee waiver (Sec. 8-8.118) and Housing Density Bonus (Chapter 8-12), unincorporated Yolo County
administering_agency: Yolo County Community Services Department, Planning Division; fee waivers subject to Board of Supervisors approval
typical_award_size: Section 8-8.118(a) allows a fifty percent waiver of development-related application and processing fees for affordable units, subject to Board approval, plus modified standards for road widths, parking, lot coverage and lot size, priority processing and a density bonus. Chapter 8-12 (Ordinance 1445, August 14, 2014) codifies state density bonus law as of 2014: 20% base bonus for 10% low or 5% very low income units, rising to a 35% maximum, one to three concessions, parking caps of 1 space (studio and 1 bedroom), 2 spaces (2 to 3 bedrooms) and 2.5 spaces (4 or more bedrooms). No impact fee waiver program exists; County development impact fees are not waived for affordable housing.
affordability_requirement: Fee waiver applies to the affordable units in an inclusionary or 100% affordable project. Density bonus tiers per Government Code 65915 (the County code's 35% cap is superseded by current state law allowing 50% and unlimited density for 100% affordable projects).
next_deadline: Request with the planning application; the fee waiver needs a Board action. Chapter 8-12 has not been updated since 2014 and state law controls where more generous.
layering_notes: The waiver covers planning application and processing fees only, not the County's development impact fees, school fees or the cities' fees, so the dollar value is modest (tens of thousands on a typical project). Waived fees are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), which is why the prevailing wage flag is unclear; most projects using the waiver also carry state funds that trigger it anyway. Use state density bonus law directly rather than the 2014 County chapter, and expect staff to process it under Government Code 65915 as amended.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program rule found. Yolo County Code Chapter 8-12 (density bonus, read on gocodebook.com) contains no prevailing wage provision. Waived fees are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), but under 1720(c)(3) a subsidy that is both under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost is de minimis and does not by itself make a private project a public work, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property absent an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority. A 50 percent planning fee waiver will usually fall under the de minimis test, but the outcome depends on project facts and other funding sources.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear. Only basis is the general Labor Code 1720(b)(4) public funds definition with outcome set by 1720(c)(3) de minimis and 1720(c)(1) exemptions; no DIR determination or County rule on point found. Section 8-8.118 text could not be located on gocodebook (404 at the expected chapter URL).

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers and HUD-VASH PBVs, Yolo County Housing (YCH)
administering_agency: Yolo County Housing (Housing Authority of the County of Yolo, CA044), 147 West Main Street, Woodland; (530) 662-5428; Executive Director Ian Evans; Housing Program Manager Anisa Vallejo
typical_award_size: YCH leases about 1,500 to 1,600 Housing Choice Vouchers countywide and owns 431 public housing units. It awarded 155 PBVs over the three years to January 2026 (84 to new construction) through RFPs, most recently a December 2023 pair of RFPs (existing housing, and new construction or rehabilitation) offering up to 40 PBVs with up to 3 HUD-VASH vouchers. The FY 2026 Agency Plan commits to allocating additional PBVs to new and existing projects until YCH reaches HUD's PBV cap (about 30% of vouchers) by the end of 2029, and to project-basing about 36 tenant protection vouchers from a 2026 Section 18 disposition at its Tupelo development in Woodland.
per_unit_cap: PBV contract rents at reasonable rent up to YCH payment standards (110% of FMR); HUD program cap of 20% of authorized vouchers plus 10% for PSH and other exception units.
affordability_requirement: Very low and extremely low income households (at or below 50% AMI); PBV HAP contracts up to 20 years with extensions. The PBV waiting list has been closed since February 2023 and the HCV program has had intermittent voucher shortfalls since 2023 while Emergency Housing Voucher households are moved onto HCV.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. YCH's Doing Business page lists only RFP P26-011 (landscape maintenance) and IFB B26-04 (exterior painting), no PBV RFP. YCH issues PBV RFPs as voucher budget allows and its FY 2026 Agency Plan targets reaching the 30% PBV cap by Q4 2029; contact Anisa Vallejo (avallejo@ych.ca.gov) to be notified.
layering_notes: PBVs are the one countywide operating subsidy for PSH in Yolo and YCH is unusually willing to project-base (goal of reaching the HUD cap by 2029), but federal HCV funding shortfalls since 2023 limit new awards; the County's BHSA plan calls voucher capacity 'extremely limited.' Nine or more PBV units in a project trigger Davis-Bacon under HUD rules; PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage. Coordinated Entry through the Homeless and Poverty Action Coalition (HPAC, CoC CA-521) supplies referrals for homeless set-aside units. YCH is also converting or disposing of public housing (Vista Montecito, Yolito, Ridgecut in 2026; Yolano Village and Donnelly Circle in 2027 or later), which will generate more PBVs tied to its own redevelopment.
cycle_notes: Irregular PBV RFPs rather than a fixed annual cycle; most recent PBV RFPs were December 2023 (existing housing, and new construction or rehabilitation, up to 40 PBVs with up to 3 HUD-VASH). About 36 tenant protection vouchers from the 2026 Section 18 disposition of Vista Montecito, Yolito and Ridgecut are planned to be project-based at YCH's own Tupelo site in Woodland. Jurisdiction is countywide including Davis, Woodland, West Sacramento and Winters.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (PBV development requirements, labor standards): for development (new construction or rehabilitation) involving nine or more contract units, the owner and its contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages, and the PHA must monitor compliance; existing housing placed under a HAP contract without development activity is not covered. Federal Davis-Bacon only; PBVs alone do not trigger California prevailing wage. Source: eCFR 24 CFR part 983, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-IX/part-983/subpart-D/section-983.153

program_name: Yolo County Housing and New Hope CDC development partnerships, surplus land and farmworker housing sites
administering_agency: Yolo County Housing (YCH) with its nonprofit affiliate New Hope Community Development Corporation; Executive Director Ian Evans, ievans@ych.ca.gov, (530) 669-2219
typical_award_size: YCH acts as co-developer, land owner and partner rather than lender. Current pipeline: Tupelo, 73 units in Woodland (one to three bedrooms, 30% to 60% AMI) with a $27,999,100 AHSC award announced December 10, 2025 (City of Woodland $1.5 million loan commitment, Sutter Health $1.5 million, Brinshore Development and Operative Office as partners, construction as early as 2027, about 36 project-based TPVs); 641 5th Street, West Sacramento, 37 units (New Hope CDC, groundbreaking planned 2026, completion target 2027); Yolano and Donnelly redevelopment in Woodland (HUD Choice Neighborhoods Planning Grant, September 2024, over 240 mixed-income units planned, three phases by 2029); El Rio Villa Phase I by 2029. YCH posted a Surplus Land Act Notice of Availability for its Dunnigan property on September 10, 2026 (60-day response window, priority to proposals with at least 25% affordable units) and is seeking developers for its vacant Esparto lots for farmworker homeownership by 2027. In December 2025 YCH partnered with Fulcrum Property and Pacific Housing to deed-restrict 30 existing West Sacramento units for moderate income households for 35 years using the welfare exemption.
affordability_requirement: Set deal by deal: 30% to 60% AMI at Tupelo (AHSC and tax credit rules); moderate income (80% to 120% AMI) in the acquisition and deed-restriction model; farmworker households at the Esparto lots. YCH's strategic plan targets a 15% increase (about 390 units) in affordable units it owns, manages or supports by 2029.
next_deadline: No open solicitation confirmed as of November 9, 2026. The Dunnigan Surplus Land Act response window closes about now and could not be re-confirmed on ych.ca.gov. Next expected openings: developer partnerships for the Esparto vacant lots (farmworker homeownership target Q4 2027) and Section 18 redevelopment of Yolano Village and Donnelly Circle (2027 or later).
layering_notes: In Yolo the housing authority, not the County, is the development partner that brings land, PBVs, migrant center operating experience and public housing repositioning capital. A developer can join as YCH's co-developer (Brinshore model at Tupelo), buy or ground lease YCH surplus land under the Surplus Land Act, or use YCH or New Hope CDC as the nonprofit managing general partner to qualify existing buildings for the welfare exemption (the KIND West Sacramento structure, where YCH provided a $25,000 operating loan and the deed restriction). Tax credits do not trigger state prevailing wage (DIR PW 2006-001); state prevailing wage turns on the local and state funds in these deals and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions, and HOME or CDBG add Davis-Bacon at their unit thresholds. YCH also operates the Davis, Madison and Dixon migrant centers for the state Office of Migrant Services, so it is the natural partner for Joe Serna farmworker housing applications in the unincorporated area.
cycle_notes: Dunnigan Surplus Land Act Notice of Availability reported posted September 10, 2026 with a 60-day response window (not found on ych.ca.gov or by search on November 9, 2026). YCH FY 2026 Annual Plan: Section 18 disposition application for Vista Montecito, Yolito and Ridgecut around mid-2026, about 36 TPVs to be project-based at Tupelo.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on public-funds logic only; no program or local rule found, changed to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. YCH land conveyed below fair market value is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(3), and the 1720(c)(1) private-property exclusion does not apply to projects built under an agreement with a local public housing authority; whether a given project is a public work depends on its land terms, funding sources (each with its own rules) and 1720(c) exemptions. No YCH or Surplus Land Act disposition term requiring prevailing wage was found, and the Surplus Land Act has no general wage rule. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), Yolo County Assessor
administering_agency: Yolo County Assessor/Clerk-Recorder/Elections (ACE), Jesse Salinas, 625 Court Street, Woodland, CA 95695; (530) 666-8135; ace.yolocounty.gov; with the State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
typical_award_size: Exemption of property taxes on units restricted to lower income households under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g): full exemption for qualifying units in LIHTC or publicly financed projects and partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In Yolo County the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt applies to the exempt value.
per_unit_cap: Units stay exempt if an existing tenant's income rises to 140% AMI in tax credit units or to 100% AMI in other agreement-restricted units (100% rule runs FY 2024-25 through 2028-29; reported on BOE-267-L3 and L4). Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g)(1)(C) caps the exemption at $20,000,000 of assessed value per taxpayer per fiscal year (single or multiple properties), and only where the exemption rests solely on the 90 percent lower income occupancy test for a property not owned by a limited partnership. Projects with tax-exempt bonds, government loans or grants (214(g)(1)(A)) or low-income housing tax credits (214(g)(1)(B)) are outside the cap; LP-owned projects with a nonprofit managing general partner must have tax credits or government financing to qualify (BOE Publication 149). Not a statewide cap.
