affordability_requirement: Nonprofit owner or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, HOME, PLHA, housing authority or County agreement) restricting rents to lower income households; BOE-267-L2 tenant data where there is no government financing or tax credits.
next_deadline: File BOE-267 (first year) or BOE-267-A (annual) with the Assessor by February 15 each year (next: February 15, 2027) with BOE-267-L, L1, L2 and worksheets as applicable. Late claims: 90% of tax canceled if filed by January 1 of the next calendar year, 85% after (BOE Publication 149). The Yolo ACE website does not post exemption instructions; call the Assessor's office.
layering_notes: Standard underwriting item. Yolo County Housing is actively using the exemption as a financing tool: its FY 2026 plan commits to working with private investors to build affordable workforce housing 'utilizing the benefits of the welfare exemption,' and the December 2025 KIND West Sacramento deal deed-restricted 30 units for moderate income households with a YCH operating loan structured to meet exemption requirements. Check carefully that moderate income (above 80% AMI) units qualify only within the AB 84 over-income allowance; the core exemption is for lower income units.
prevailing_wage_basis: Property tax exemption; no construction funds are provided, so the exemption itself does not make a project public works.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: the cited BOE county contacts page is only an assessor directory. Checked BOE Publication 149 and Rev. and Tax. Code 214 and 255. The $20 million cap is per taxpayer, not statewide, and applies only to non-LP claims under the 90% occupancy test.

program_name: Davis, Woodland/Yolo County Continuum of Care (CA-521, Homeless and Poverty Action Coalition) and HHAP, Yolo County share
administering_agency: Yolo County Health and Human Services Agency (County HHAP administrative entity and HPAC staff; HMIS lead) with the Homeless and Poverty Action Coalition (CoC board) and the City of Davis
typical_award_size: HHAP Round 6 allocations (HCD, based on the 2024 count): Yolo County $1,074,906.92 and the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC $1,148,019.07. HHAP Round 7 preliminary allocations (FY 2026-27, disbursed as third and fourth disbursements of HHAP 6 under the NOFA amended August 7, 2026): Yolo County $1,231,712.43 and the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC $1,319,691.89. HHAP rounds 1 to 5 brought $8.1 million to the Yolo area, $3.9 million of it to the County ($2.6 million spent). Round 5 County subawards approved March 3, 2026 include $135,000 to the City of West Sacramento for interim housing operating subsidies and $15,000 for rapid rehousing, both through February 2028. 2024 point-in-time count: 942 people, 633 unsheltered, 983 year-round beds.
affordability_requirement: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness; HHAP-6 requires a regionally coordinated action plan, a 10% youth set-aside and allows permanent housing capital, operating subsidies and rental assistance among its categories.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. HCD's HHAP application window is closed; HHAP 7 is a formula allocation to existing HHAP 6 grantees (County and CoC), not a competitive developer NOFA. Developers access these funds only through local County or HPAC subaward RFPs, posted on yolocounty.gov (blocked to automated access on November 8, 2026). Key grantee dates: Regionally Coordinated Homelessness Action Plan update due January 31, 2027; HHAP 6 initial disbursement 75% obligated and 50% expended by June 30, 2027.
layering_notes: Yolo's HHAP is about $1 million a year each to the County and the CoC and goes to operations, not capital. For a PSH project the value is Coordinated Entry referrals through HPAC, possible HHAP or CoC operating subsidies for a handful of units, and the County's Behavioral Health Bridge Housing and Transitional Rent pipeline for tenants. The City of Davis receives its own HHAP (about $1 million in Round 6) and the City of West Sacramento has run interim housing with County HHAP pass-throughs; both are Pass 3.
cycle_notes: State formula rounds to the County and CoC; local subawards follow County HHSA and HPAC RFPs. HHAP 6 contracted 2026 through 2029; HHAP 7 ($829.35 million statewide, FY 2026-27) added by NOFA amendment August 7, 2026 with Round 7 initial disbursement fully expended by December 31, 2032 and second disbursement by December 31, 2033. County BHSA plan says HHAP supports existing youth transitional housing, rapid rehousing and interim housing operations.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 578.99(h): the Davis-Bacon Act does not apply to the CoC program. The HHAP Round 6 NOFA states no prevailing wage requirement, and Yolo HHAP goes to operations and services (interim housing operating subsidies, rapid rehousing), not capital, so it pays for no construction under Labor Code 1720(a)(1). A future HHAP or CoC capital award would need a project-level 1720 analysis. https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/578.99 ; https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/calich/hhap-6-nofa.pdf ; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: changed true to false; the record states Yolo HHAP funds operations, not capital.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions and capital set-aside, Yolo County HHSA Behavioral Health
administering_agency: Yolo County Health and Human Services Agency, Behavioral Health (Director Tony Kildare); Integrated Plan FY 2026-2029 approved by the Board of Supervisors June 23, 2026
typical_award_size: Projected BHSA funding $19.4 million in FY 2026-27 with Housing Interventions at 30% ($5,834,453); the Board's March 3, 2026 budget approach (Scenario 3) transfers 7% of housing interventions to Behavioral Health Services and Supports, leaving about $4.4 million for housing in FY 2026-27. The adopted plan commits to a procurement to allocate 25% of Housing Interventions funds (roughly $1.1 to $1.5 million a year) to capital development: property acquisition, new construction, and rehabilitation or renovation of existing units. Remaining funds pay rental subsidies after Transitional Rent ends, landlord damage mitigation, participant assistance and a new Housing Interventions Team. The Board also added 8 behavioral health case managers ($1 million a year) for permanent supportive housing sites.
affordability_requirement: Medi-Cal eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk; at least half of housing funds for chronically homeless people. BHSA housing interventions are available only after CalAIM Community Supports and the six-month Medi-Cal Transitional Rent benefit (provider Turning Point Community Programs) are exhausted.
next_deadline: The capital procurement (25% of housing interventions) has not been released as of November 6, 2026; the plan says it will be conducted during FY 2026-27. Behavioral Health Bridge Housing funding expires June 30, 2027, after which BHSA absorbs those costs. Annual plan updates begin FY 2027-28 (draft due to DHCS March 31).
layering_notes: Yolo is one of the few small counties committing the full 25% capital share, but at about $1.1 to $1.5 million a year it buys a handful of units: realistic uses are acquisition of small existing properties, a capital contribution to a PSH project with a BHSA referral agreement, or rehab of existing supportive housing (the Board asked staff whether capital can go to existing facility needs). Pair with YCH PBVs and the County's PSH case management staffing (8 FTE) to make a small PSH deal pencil. BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) but carries no wage rule of its own; coverage turns on the 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (see prevailing_wage_basis). Behavioral Health is also the County's lead on Homekey+ interest and on the Encampment Resolution Fund application.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on public-funds logic only; no program or local rule found, changed to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The DHCS BHSA County Policy Manual chapter 7 (Housing Interventions, section C.10 capital development) states no prevailing wage requirement, and the Yolo FY 2026-29 Integrated Plan adds none. Rental and operating subsidies are not construction under 1720(a)(1); the capital set-aside is public funds whose coverage depends on 1720(c) and the other sources in the deal. https://policy-manual.mes.dhcs.ca.gov/behavioral-health-services-act-county-policy-manual/V1.0.0/7-bhsa-components-and-requirements

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: no County or YCH conduit program; CMFA and CSCDA issuances with local TEFRA approval
administering_agency: Issuers California Municipal Finance Authority and California Statewide Communities Development Authority; TEFRA approval by the host city council or, in the unincorporated area, the Yolo County Board of Supervisors
typical_award_size: Project-sized conduit issuances. Example: CMFA issued $6,668,698 of tax-exempt financing for Esperanza Crossing Apartments (Mercy Housing, a 40-unit new construction project on Woodland Avenue in Yolo County, 39 units restricted at or below 55% AMI for 55 years). No County of Yolo or Yolo County Housing bond issuance and no County TEFRA resolution appeared in the 2026 Board minutes reviewed in Pass 2 (January 27, March 3 and March 24, 2026).
affordability_requirement: Federal bond and 4% LIHTC rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Request the TEFRA hearing through the issuer; allow six to eight weeks before the CDLAC application. For unincorporated sites the hearing goes on a Board of Supervisors consent agenda; for Davis, Woodland and West Sacramento sites the city council holds it (Pass 3).
layering_notes: Neither the County nor YCH runs a bond program, so budget issuer fees for CMFA or CSCDA. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but tax credits plus state or County funds in the same deal usually do. The County's TEFRA practice in the unincorporated area could not be confirmed from opened documents because no recent unincorporated bond-financed project was found.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: CMFA Esperanza Crossing page re-read and matches the amount, unit count, 55% AMI and 55-year term (CMFA describes it as new construction). Verified on the CMFA page for the bond terms; the negative finding on County TEFRA items rests on the Pass 2 minutes review and was not re-opened.
prevailing_wage_basis: False for the conduit bond financing itself. DIR Decision on Administrative Appeal, Public Works Case No. 2006-020, Heber Family Apartments (April 5, 2007), following PW 2004-016 Rancho Santa Fe, held that privately placed and publicly offered conduit housing revenue bonds are not payment out of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) because the issuer never holds the proceeds or repayments, and that federal LIHTCs are not public funds (https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-020(A).pdf; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The CMFA Esperanza Crossing release states no wage term (https://www.cmfa-ca.com/mercy-housing-preserves-affordable-housing-using-tax-exempt-financing-issued-cmfa/), and a County or city TEFRA approval adds no public funds. Other public sources in the same deal (City or County loans, land, HOME at 12 or more HOME-assisted units, PBVs at 9 or more assisted units) are tested separately and can trigger state or federal prevailing wage.

program_name: County affordable housing gap loans funded by Affordable Housing in-lieu fees (Hope Way and Destination at Placer One commitments)
administering_agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing Division (Gloria Stearns, Director; Nikki Streegan, Housing Manager); 145 Fulweiler Avenue #100, Auburn; (530) 886-2642; housing@placer.ca.gov
typical_award_size: Project-by-project Board commitments, no NOFA. On August 25, 2026 the Board approved a Funding Commitment Letter for Hope Way Apartments Phase 1 (Penryn 721, L.P., an affiliate of USA Properties Fund; 132 units of a 240-unit entitlement at 3130 Penryn Road) for a loan of up to $7,260,000 at 3% simple interest over 55 years, funded by affordable housing in-lieu fees (reported as Bickford Ranch in-lieu fees), and a Preliminary Funding Letter for Destination at Placer One (360 units north of Roseville) framing a potential $8,900,000 loan at 3% simple interest for which no funding source has been identified. Earlier County loans include Sabre City (Parkside at Sabre City, 44 homes with ADUs, Housing Trust Placer) and $500,000 in 2025 to a North Lake Tahoe housing trust.
per_unit_cap: None stated. Hope Way works out to about $55,000 per Phase 1 unit; Destination at Placer One to about $24,700 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Set in each Funding Agreement and Use Deed Restriction: tax credit income tiers (30% to 80% AMI), 55-year term, and the Placer County Affordable Housing Priority Applicant Policy (adopted May 12, 2026, effective July 1, 2026) giving preference to current residents, local workers and past residents of Placer County or the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District area for new deed-restricted units.
next_deadline: No NOFA. Developers request a commitment letter through the Economic Development and Housing Division and the Board acts on each project; Hope Way's Funding Agreement, Deed of Trust and deed restriction follow the commitment letter, and both 2026 projects still must win tax credits. The Board's Ad Hoc Committee for Housing Funding and Fee Implementation is working on new funding sources, and the nexus study update that would raise the in-lieu fee was due to the Board in 2026.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. Placer County's only gap money is the pool of in-lieu fees collected under its 2020 Affordable Housing and Employee Accommodation Ordinance, and the Board has committed most of it: Hope Way Phase 1 ($7.26 million) exhausted the identified balance, and Destination at Placer One is waiting on a source (a supervisor noted the County has never used General Fund for affordable housing loans). Terms are 3% simple, 55 years, residual receipts style repayment. Expect Board politics: Hope Way needed appeals, a 3-2 vote in December 2025 and a lawsuit settlement cutting it to 132 units with a four-year pause on the rest. The County's 2025-2029 Housing Action Plan targets 1,300 units by mid-2029, and the Prohousing Designation (reapplying fall 2026) gives projects state scoring advantages. Cities (Roseville, Rocklin, Lincoln, Auburn) run their own funds and are Pass 3.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost). No Placer County in-lieu fee loan prevailing wage rule was found in the sources read. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Affordable Housing and Employee Accommodation Ordinance (County Code Chapter 15.65): 10% inclusionary requirement, in-lieu fee and employee accommodation fee
administering_agency: Placer County Community Development Resource Agency (entitlement review) and Economic Development and Housing Division (fee collection and use); nexus study update by BAE Urban Economics under a February 4, 2025 contract
typical_award_size: Regulatory requirement and the County's only local housing revenue. Ordinance 6050-B (October 27, 2020), effective January 1, 2021: new private residential projects of more than 100 units must make 10% of units affordable; projects of 8 to 100 units may instead pay an in-lieu fee per habitable square foot of each market-rate unit. The fee was $2.00 initially and is indexed; the Board's April 7, 2026 annual impact fee adjustment raised it from $2.73 to $2.84 per square foot effective July 1, 2026. An Employee Accommodation Fee of $2.84 per net building square foot applies to new non-residential development in the Sierra Nevada and Lake Tahoe area (Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary). Exempt: projects of 7 or fewer units or where most units are under 1,600 square feet, deed-restricted affordable housing, ADUs, infill sites, transit priority areas, mixed-use projects at least 70% residential, and others in Section 15.65.050. Fee revenue funds construction of affordable housing, preservation, acquisition-rehab of multifamily projects and first-time homebuyer assistance.
affordability_requirement: 10% of units affordable for projects over 100 units, with the in-lieu fee option for 8 to 100 units; compliance terms set in a development agreement or affordable housing agreement. A BAE Urban Economics nexus study update (draft, not approved) and ordinance amendments are scheduled on the County's project page for a Board update in fall or winter 2026 to 2027 and final Board adoption in spring or summer 2027.
next_deadline: No application deadline; applies at entitlement with fee paid before building permit issuance. Nexus study and ordinance amendments are scheduled for final Board adoption in spring or summer 2027 per the County project page as of November 8, 2026.
layering_notes: For a 100% affordable or deed-restricted project the ordinance is not a cost (exempt). For a mixed-income project over 100 units it is a 10% set-aside; between 8 and 100 units the fee is $2.84 per square foot (about $2,840 on a 1,000 square foot unit), low relative to Bay Area counties. The fee revenue is the pool behind the County's gap loans, so a higher fee from the 2027 nexus update would expand the only local source. The infill and transit priority area exemptions remove many western Placer multifamily sites from the requirement. Density bonus and inclusionary agreements do not trigger prevailing wage. placer.ca.gov program pages opened directly on November 8, 2026.
cycle_notes: Not an application program. Requirement applies at entitlement; the fee is calculated at complete building permit application and paid before permit issuance. Fee is adjusted annually by the Board (current $2.84 per square foot from July 1, 2026).
eligible_project_detail: market-rate residential projects of 8 or more units in unincorporated Placer (compliance)
fee revenue funds new construction, preservation, acquisition-rehab and first-time homebuyer assistance
audit_note: Replaced news-article source with the County program page; fee updated to $2.84; funding_type changed from density bonus to regulatory requirement per SCHEMA meanings; nexus adoption moved to 2027.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Launchpad workforce housing incentive, eastern Placer County (Transient Occupancy Tax through the TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program)
administering_agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing (Timothy Cussen, Housing Specialist); Tahoe City office 775 North Lake Boulevard; funding recommended by the North Tahoe Community Alliance (NTCA) TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program
typical_award_size: $200,000 per unit for category one (condos, townhomes, multifamily units and conversions of non-residential or non-code-compliant space; single-family homes are not eligible), $125,000 per ADU and $50,000 per SRO unit, paid at completion once the 55-year workforce Use Deed Restriction is recorded. Funding: $1,000,000 inaugural NOFA LP-001 (released April 16, 2025; 8 applications) reserved $725,000 for two Kings Beach projects (Steelhead Avenue Cottage Court, 3 tiny homes, $600,000; accessible ADU, $125,000). NOFA LP-002, posted February 6, 2026, offered $3,275,000 ($3,000,000 of new TOT approved February 3, 2026 plus $275,000 carryover), drew 12 applications (55 units, $10,550,000 requested) and reserved $3,250,000 for four projects: Lake Forest Multifamily (12 studios, Tahoe City, $2,400,000), Dollar Hill Tiny Homes (3 units, $600,000) and two tiny home ADUs in Lake Forest and Cedar Flat ($125,000 each).
per_unit_cap: $200,000 per unit (new construction or conversion of non-residential or non-code-compliant space), $125,000 per ADU, $50,000 per SRO.
affordability_requirement: Units must be in unincorporated eastern Placer County within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary, outside avalanche hazard areas, with entitlements in place or allowed by right. A 55-year Use Deed Restriction (restarting on each transfer) requires occupancy as a primary residence by a qualified household with a local worker employed within the TTUSD area; no income limit or sales price cap. Units used to meet the Affordable Housing and Employee Accommodation Ordinance are ineligible.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 10, 2026. The February 2026 NOFA LP-002 (applications February 25 to March 18, 2026) is fully reserved. The May 11, 2026 Board memo says staff will bring revised guidelines to the Board later in 2026, and the County opened a community survey in August 2026; a future NOFA depends on new TOT funding recommended through the NTCA TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov sits behind Cloudflare; the same County pages and DocumentCenter files open on the placerair.org host, and Board memos are on content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER. Launchpad is a per-unit grant rather than a loan and is sized for small infill projects in Kings Beach, Tahoe City and the North Shore; a 10-unit workforce project could draw $2 million, which is meaningful against TRPA coverage and construction costs in the Basin. It pays only at completion, so it is bridge-financed. Guidelines Section III.f bars combining Launchpad with any other County program or subsidy unless the Board approves. The workforce (not income) restriction means it does not fit LIHTC deals directly but can fund unrestricted middle-income units in a mixed-income project. North Lake Tahoe TOT also funds the Workforce Housing Preservation Program and the Dollar Creek Crossing effort.
cycle_notes: NOFA rounds when TOT funding is approved (LP-001 April 2025, LP-002 February 2026); 3-week application windows; randomized lottery prioritizing categories one and two when oversubscribed (used in 2026); projects have 2 years from the award letter to complete. Guidelines under revision after the August 2026 survey. The LP-001 and LP-002 NOFA PDFs are no longer posted (DocumentCenter links return 404); the program page and Guidelines remain the current sources.
audit_note: PW pass B November 10, 2026: program page, Reserved Projects page, Guidelines PDF, January 14 and August 27, 2026 news releases and the May 11, 2026 Board memo read. NOFA LP-001 and LP-002 PDFs return 404 and no later NOFA was found; Legistar 'placerca' holds matters only through August 11, 2026 and lists no Launchpad item. Prevailing wage stays unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific rule. The Launchpad Guidelines (April 2025, Section III) require compliance with all applicable federal, state and local laws but do not mention prevailing wage; the program page, Reserved Projects page and May 11, 2026 Board memo also say nothing on it; the LP-002 NOFA PDF is no longer posted. Only the general Labor Code 1720 framework applies (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): the TOT grant paid at completion is public funds under 1720(b)(1) and is not a loan, so 1720(c)(5)(E) does not apply, but 1720(c)(1) excludes private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency or local public housing authority, and 1720(c)(3) excludes de minimis subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost. Most Launchpad awards (ADUs at $125,000, tiny home projects at $600,000) sit at or near these thresholds; a larger award such as Lake Forest Multifamily ($2,400,000) would need a project-specific determination.

program_name: Workforce Housing Preservation Program (WHPP), eastern Placer County deed-restriction purchases
administering_agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing; down payment assistance component administered by Housing Trust Placer
typical_award_size: $4,100,000 allocated since 2021 ($500,000 General Fund and TOT in 2021, $600,000 TOT in 2023, $3,000,000 TOT in April 2024 through the NTCA TOT-TBID program); 17 deed restrictions purchased for $1,852,400 (average $108,965 per property; three in FY 2025-26 for $329,600). $2,247,500 remained through FY 2025-26, with staff seeking to extend it into FY 2026-27. May 12, 2026 amendments opened the program to multifamily properties of more than four units: maximum aggregate disbursement 16% of fair market value with a $75,000 per-unit cap (single-family cap $150,000), local businesses eligible as buyers, and a termination fee that declines over time.
per_unit_cap: $75,000 per unit for multifamily properties (and 16% of fair market value aggregate); $150,000 per single-family property.
affordability_requirement: Permanent deed restriction requiring occupancy by a household with at least one member of the local workforce (employed within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District area); no income limit. Applies to existing homes, condos, duplexes and now multifamily rental properties in eastern Placer County.
next_deadline: Applications accepted while funds last; $2,247,500 available as of May 2026, subject to NTCA extension into FY 2026-27. Multifamily eligibility is new as of May 2026, so no multifamily transaction had closed when the guidelines were amended.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. The 2026 change makes WHPP a small acquisition subsidy for buying existing North Shore apartment buildings and restricting them to local workers: a four-unit building worth $2 million could draw $300,000. It fills the preservation gap the County identified as redevelopment pressure on long-term rentals. The restriction is workforce occupancy rather than income, so it does not combine with LIHTC or state programs that require income limits, but it can pair with Launchpad for added units and with the welfare exemption only if a nonprofit owner also records income restrictions. No construction, so no prevailing wage.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: May 12, 2026 Board memo and amended guidelines match on $4.1M total allocation, 17 deed restrictions for $1,852,400, $2,247,500 remaining, 16% of FMV aggregate with $75,000 per-unit multifamily cap and $150,000 single-family cap, local business eligibility, and no minimum AMI in East County (eliminated June 28, 2022). Minor wording: 2021 allocation was $250,000 General Fund plus $250,000 TOT, and the deed restriction runs 55 years renewed with each conveyance rather than being permanent on its face. Prevailing wage false is uncited; program purchases deed restrictions with no construction.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction, alteration, demolition, installation or repair paid with public funds; WHPP pays owners for workforce deed restrictions on existing homes and multifamily properties and funds no construction, and homebuyer payments are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Placer County formula allocation
administering_agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing Division
typical_award_size: County formula allocations confirmed on HCD documents: 2019-2023 five-year estimate $2,730,542 (2024 amended formula NOFA); 2019 allocation award $455,090 on October 21, 2020 (activities 1 and 9); 2022 and 2023 allocations ($385,467 and $247,060, total $632,527 with $31,626 admin) awarded April 30, 2026 for activity 9 only. HCD's CY 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA (July 16, 2026) lists Placer County at $489,950 (CY 2024) and $538,105 (CY 2025), about $3,062,188 over five years. Cities receive their own allocations.
affordability_requirement: 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines Section 301: rental activities up to 120% AMI (150% in high-cost areas), owner-occupied workforce housing up to 120% AMI, homelessness assistance up to 30% AMI; rental development assistance must be a low-interest deferred loan with a regulatory agreement of at least 55 years. The County's 2019-2023 plan used activity 1 (multifamily rental) in 2020 but only activity 9 (homeownership opportunities including down payment assistance) for the 2022-2023 award.
next_deadline: No open County PLHA developer round as of November 8, 2026. The County's HCD application for its CY 2024 allocation is due February 29, 2028 (final business day of February 2028).
layering_notes: At about $500,000 a year, County PLHA is modest. The 2022-2023 allocations awarded April 30, 2026 went to homeownership activity 9, not multifamily rental, so a developer should ask the Economic Development and Housing Division to include rental activities and a developer NOFA in the 2024-2028 plan. Prior record text saying state funds trigger prevailing wage had no cited rule.
cycle_notes: Formula grant to the County from HCD. The County must adopt a 2024-2028 five-year plan and apply to HCD; CY 2024 funds released spring 2026 with an HCD application deadline at the end of February 2028, CY 2025 by February 2029. Any developer competition is a County decision; the County last ran a developer NOFA in 2020.
prevailing_wage_basis: The 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf) contain no prevailing wage provision; coverage of a County PLHA loan is a Labor Code 1720 question, including the 1720(c)(5)(E) affordable housing exemption (numbered (c)(6)(E) when DIR PW 2006-020 applied it).

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers and special-purpose vouchers, Placer County Housing Authority (PCHA)
administering_agency: Placer County Housing Authority, operated by Health and Human Services, Human Services Division (Robert Oldham, Director; Alexis Madera, Staff Services Manager); Board of Supervisors sits as the Board of Commissioners
typical_award_size: PCHA assists 435 very low and low income households through Housing Choice, Mainstream, VASH, Family Unification and Foster Youth to Independence vouchers; it owns no public housing. PBVs are awarded from the existing inventory through periodic RFQs (RFQ 20387 closed May 30, 2023 for new construction, rehabilitated and existing units) and project agreements: 8 PBVs to The Frances (formerly University Avenue Apartments, 2160 University Avenue, Rocklin, USA Properties Fund, occupancy expected 2029; HAP agreement approved July 28, 2026) and 16 PBVs committed to two Pacific Street partnerships in Rocklin (November 2025). The HCV waiting list is closed.
per_unit_cap: PBV contract rents at reasonable rent up to PCHA payment standards (110% of FMR); HUD cap of 20% of authorized vouchers (about 87) plus exceptions for PSH and other eligible units.
affordability_requirement: Very low and low income households (at or below 50% AMI at admission); PBV HAP contracts up to 20 years with extensions. PCHA's jurisdiction is all of Placer County except the City of Roseville, which has its own housing authority.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The PCHA Project-Based Vouchers page still lists RFQ 20387 (closed May 30, 2023; awards August 29, 2023 to USA Properties Fund and Community Housing Works) as the latest solicitation; contact PCHA@placer.ca.gov about future PBV commitments.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. With only 435 vouchers, PCHA can project-base perhaps 8 to 16 units per project, which is the pattern in Rocklin. Treat PBVs as a small PSH set-aside subsidy rather than a project-wide operating source, and plan on a transition reserve. Nine or more PBV units trigger Davis-Bacon; PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage. Roseville Housing Authority (City of Roseville) is covered in Pass 3. Coordinated Entry runs through the Homeless Resource Council of the Sierras (CoC CA-515).
cycle_notes: PBVs are offered through periodic competitive RFQs posted on placer.bidsandtenders.net (last RFQ 20387, 2023), followed by project-specific agreements approved by the Housing Authority Board (for example The Frances, July 28, 2026, 8 PBVs from existing inventory).
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (HUD PBV rule, Subpart D): for PBV development activity involving nine or more contract units, owners and contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages; existing housing and development with fewer than nine PBV units are not covered. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-IX/part-983/subpart-D
audit_note: T2 audit 2026-11-08: PBV page read on the placerair.org host (placer.ca.gov 403); Legistar matter 1355 text confirms 435 households, 8 PBVs for The Frances and occupancy in 2029. Prevailing wage trigger is federal Davis-Bacon and applies only to new construction or rehab with 9 or more PBV units.

program_name: County-owned land for affordable housing: Dollar Creek Crossing (3205 North Lake Boulevard, Tahoe City)
administering_agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing, with the Community Development Resource Agency; developer Related California (Related Norcal Development, LLC) under a preliminary agreement
typical_award_size: County-owned site at 3205 North Lake Boulevard, Tahoe City, acquired in 2019. After mixed-use and mixed-income concepts, the Board directed an affordable-only project of at least 80 lower income units in April 2025; the developer's June 2026 financial report said the County would need to contribute about $18,500,000 (land plus gap). The Exclusive Right to Negotiate with Related expired June 30, 2026, and the County is now preparing a new developer RFP; land contribution plus any gap funding will be set in the RFP terms.
affordability_requirement: Low income (at or below 80% AMI) rental housing, 80 units, with the County's Affordable Housing Priority Applicant Policy for local workers and residents.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The County held a community meeting on future RFP terms on September 2, 2026 and is collecting survey feedback; staff expect to bring RFP terms to the Board in early 2027 and to issue the developer RFP before July 2027.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. Dollar Creek is the County's only land contribution in the Tahoe Basin and shows the limit of its resources: the land is in hand but the County has no fund large enough for an $18.5 million gap, so the deal will depend on state money (MHP, IIG, AHSC, TRPA bonus units) plus TOT programs. A developer answering a future RFP should price the TRPA coverage and allocation process and the County's requirement for workforce preference. Public land conveyed below fair market value and local loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and (b)(3), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal (see prevailing_wage_basis).
cycle_notes: One-time developer RFP for a County-owned site; the prior Exclusive Right to Negotiate with Related expired June 30, 2026. Board hearing on RFP terms expected early 2027; RFP to issue before July 2027. Affordable Housing Priority Applicant Policy (Resolution 2026-077, May 11, 2026) gives local residents and workers priority.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. County land at less than fair market value is public funds under 1720(b)(3), and any County gap money would add 1720(b) funds, but no County or program prevailing wage rule was found; state sources later awarded carry their own rules. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Housing Trust Placer (nonprofit housing trust seeded and funded by Placer County)
administering_agency: Housing Trust Placer, Inc. (Robyn van Ekelenburg, CEO; robyn@housingtrustplacer.org); County contributions through the Economic Development and Housing Division
typical_award_size: Nonprofit trust formed in 2020 that provides gap financing, acquisition and fundraising; Placer County pledged $575,000 with its 2021 Housing Element and selected the trust to administer its First-Time Homebuyer and Workforce Housing Preservation down payment programs (2025). Projects: Parkside at Sabre City (44 homes each with an ADU, manufactured housing, County and HCD financing, leasing 2025-2026) and the Hope Way site at 3130 Penryn Road (240 units with USA Properties Fund). No published NOFA, loan amounts or terms for developers; financing is arranged deal by deal from public and private sources.
affordability_requirement: Set per project; Sabre City serves low income renters and the trust's homebuyer programs serve first-time and workforce buyers.
next_deadline: No NOFA; approach the CEO directly. The County also approved $500,000 in 2025 for a new North Lake Tahoe housing trust (separate from Housing Trust Placer).
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. Housing Trust Placer is the County's chosen intermediary for homebuyer programs and a co-developer or site holder for County-backed projects rather than a lender with a fund balance, so do not underwrite a trust loan without a conversation. It is useful as a nonprofit partner for the welfare exemption and for assembling County, SMUD, hospital and foundation gap money on western Placer projects. It qualifies as a Local Housing Trust Fund for HCD matching grants only if it meets the LHTF program's dedicated-revenue test, which was not confirmed.
prevailing_wage_basis: No stated rule. Housing Trust Placer is a private nonprofit that publishes no NOFA or loan guidelines and its website says nothing on prevailing wage. Coverage follows the public sources it assembles: County funds can make a project public works under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to 1720(c)(3) de minimis (under $600,000 and under 2% of project cost) and 1720(c)(5)(E) below-market loans with 40% of units at 80% AMI or below for 20 years; its down payment programs fall under the 1720(c)(5)(C) exemption for down payment assistance. Any HOME, CDBG or state money layered in carries that program's own rule.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies and the outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project funding mix.

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), Placer County Assessor
administering_agency: Placer County Assessor, Matt Maynard; (530) 889-4300; with the State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
typical_award_size: Exemption of property taxes on units restricted to lower income households under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g): full exemption for qualifying units in LIHTC or publicly financed projects and partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In Placer County the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt and direct assessments applies to the exempt value.
per_unit_cap: Statewide $20 million assessed-value cap on the 214(g) exemption for non-LIHTC projects relying only on a regulatory agreement; no cap for LIHTC projects. AB 84 (2024) allows a share of units occupied by households up to 100% AMI to remain exempt.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit owner or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, County Use Deed Restriction with income limits, PLHA) restricting rents to lower income households.
next_deadline: Next annual filing due 5:00 p.m. February 16, 2027 (the statutory February 15, 2027 date falls on Presidents' Day, a holiday, so it moves to the next business day). File BOE-267 (first year) or BOE-267-A (annual) with the Placer County Assessor with BOE-267-L and L2 supplements as applicable; claims filed after the deadline through December 31 get 90 percent of tax, penalty or interest canceled.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. Standard underwriting item for Hope Way, Placer Creek and similar LIHTC deals. Note that the County's eastern Placer workforce deed restrictions (Launchpad, WHPP) restrict occupancy to local workers without income limits and do not by themselves qualify a property for the welfare exemption.
cycle_notes: Annual claim due February 15 each year (next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday); BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate required; late claims filed February 16 to December 31 receive 90 percent relief under Revenue and Taxation Code 270.
audit_note: T2 audit 2026-11-08: deadline confirmed in BOE Publication 149, the BOE-267-A sample form and the Placer County BOE-267-L2 affidavit (read on placerair.org). Placer Assessor Matt Maynard, 530-889-4300, confirmed on the BOE county contacts page.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(4) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works requires construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, including fees, loans or other obligations normally required in executing the construction contract that are reduced or waived. The welfare exemption (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)) reduces property tax on the completed property; it pays no construction cost, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage.

program_name: Roseville, Rocklin/Placer County Continuum of Care (CA-515, Homeless Resource Council of the Sierras) and HHAP, Placer County share
administering_agency: Homeless Resource Council of the Sierras (HRCS, CoC lead and HMIS lead for CA-515 and Nevada County CA-531); Placer County Health and Human Services (County HHAP administrative entity; homeless outreach with the City of Roseville)

HHAP Round 7 allocations follow the 2026-27 state budget ($900 million statewide).
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. Placer's HHAP is under $1 million a year each to the County and the CoC and is used for subsidies and services, not capital. audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

HUD CoC rule 24 CFR 578.99(h) states the Davis-Bacon Act does not apply to the CoC program, and the HHAP Round 6 NOFA, amended NOFA and FAQ contain no prevailing wage provision; state prevailing wage on any HHAP-funded capital work depends on 1720 facts. Placer uses these funds mainly for subsidies and services, which are not construction under 1720(a)(1). https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/578.99 ; https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/calich/hhap-6-nofa.pdf

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CalPFA, CMFA and CSCDA issuances (County not an issuer)
administering_agency: Placer County Board of Supervisors (TEFRA host approval for unincorporated projects); issuers California Public Finance Authority (CalPFA), California Municipal Finance Authority and California Statewide Communities Development Authority
typical_award_size: Project-sized conduit issuances. Placer Creek Affordable Apartments (St. Anton Communities, 168 units at Baseline Road and Westbrook Boulevard, unincorporated Placer, 30% to 70% AMI): CDLAC allocation of $32,320,000 and $3,073,371 of annual federal credits approved April 8, 2025 with CalPFA as issuer; County TEFRA hearing August 19, 2025 for up to $37,000,000; construction August 2025 to September 2026. Earlier County TEFRA approvals covered CMFA and CSCDA issuances for senior and assisted living projects.
affordability_requirement: Federal bond and 4% LIHTC rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Request the TEFRA hearing through the issuer six to eight weeks before the CDLAC application; the County places hearings on regular Board agendas. Hope Way Phase 1 and Destination at Placer One will need TEFRA approvals when they apply for bonds.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. Neither the County nor the Placer County Housing Authority runs a bond program, so budget issuer fees for CalPFA, CMFA or CSCDA. Placer Creek is the current template for an unincorporated western Placer 4% deal: Lennar-provided site in a specific plan, CalPFA bonds, average income set-aside up to 70% AMI, County affordable housing agreement, no County cash. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; County in-lieu fee loans and state funds in the same deal do.
prevailing_wage_basis: DIR Decision on Administrative Appeal, PW 2006-020 Heber Family Apartments (https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-020(A).pdf), following PW 2004-016 Rancho Santa Fe: loans of conduit tax-exempt bond proceeds (publicly offered or privately placed) and federal LIHTCs are not payment out of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b). Other public loans in the same deal are evaluated separately.

program_name: 2016 Measure A Affordable Housing Bond (Housing Bond)
administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Office of Supportive Housing (OSH), Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: $950 million general obligation bond approved November 8, 2016. As of October 2026 the Board had committed $879.2 million; 65 multifamily rental developments in 12 cities received about $747 million ($714.3 million in Supportive Housing Development Program rounds 1 through 14 and off-cycle awards plus $11.9 million acquisition loans and $90.5 million County acquisitions). Individual commitments range from $1.0 million (The Veranda, Cupertino, 19 units) to $42.3 million (Mosaic Court, Milpitas, 134 units); Gateway Tower (220 units, San Jose) revised January 13, 2026 to $25,560,000, about $116,182 per unit.
per_unit_cap: No published cap. Awards have averaged roughly $100,000 to $200,000 per unit in recent rounds; $116,182 per unit at Gateway Tower (2026).
affordability_requirement: Board goals by category: PSH for persons with disabling conditions, rapid rehousing units, ELI (30% AMI) and VLI (50% AMI) units, plus 300 mixed-income units and homeownership. 4,800 rental unit goal exceeded (5,255 goal units approved, 109%). Long-term County regulatory agreement recorded on each project.
next_deadline: No new application round. As of October 2026 the remaining $67.8 million is reserved for three developments on County-owned land and one affordable homeownership development (Branham Station, VTA TOD). About $6.4 million of program-generated income is available to recommit to multifamily rental projects.
layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. The County's November 3, 2026 implementation report (first annual report, year 10 of a 10-year plan) states the bond is nearly fully deployed: 65 approved rental developments with 6,846 units (2,693 supportive), 38 in operation, 17 under construction, four fully financed and six in predevelopment; $30.5 million in program-generated income received, $23.5 million recommitted. Measure A averaged about $6 of outside funding per $1 of County bond money and has been the standard local soft source behind 4% and 9% tax credit deals in Santa Clara County; in 2025, 11 County-funded projects won tax credit awards. Awards are made through the over-the-counter Supportive Housing Development Fund NOFA (see separate record) and paired with SCCHA project-based vouchers (3,000 plus PBVs deployed). Do not confuse with the November 4, 2025 Measure A, a five-eighths cent County sales tax for safety-net services that is not a housing fund. The Board is studying a future housing fund (June 2, 2026 report) but no successor measure is on the November 2026 ballot; the statewide $10 billion housing bond (AB 736/SB 417) is the near-term pipeline source. County loans require state prevailing wage as public funds.
audit_note: PW audit Nov 10, 2026: basis moved from the 2017 Housing Trust guidelines to the County's current Board-approved Supportive Housing Development Program Guidelines (Version 7, Nov 16, 2021), still cited as operative in a Sept 15, 2026 Board report; trigger true unchanged, with the guidelines' exemption carve-out noted.

program_name: Welfare exemption (property tax) processing, Santa Clara County Assessor
administering_agency: Santa Clara County Assessor, Exemptions Division (Assessor Neysa Fligor, 408-299-5500)
typical_award_size: Full exemption of property tax on qualifying low-income rental units owned by a nonprofit or by a limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; worth roughly 1.1 to 1.2 percent of assessed value per year plus most direct levies.
per_unit_cap: Statutory: lower income units under Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g); units stay exempt if an existing tenant's income rises to 140% AMI in tax credit units or to 100% AMI in other agreement-restricted units (the 100% rule runs FY 2024-25 through 2028-29). Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g)(1)(C) caps the exemption at $20,000,000 of assessed value per taxpayer per fiscal year (single or multiple properties), and only where the exemption rests solely on the 90 percent lower income occupancy test for a property not owned by a limited partnership. Projects with tax-exempt bonds, government loans or grants (214(g)(1)(A)) or low-income housing tax credits (214(g)(1)(B)) are outside the cap; LP-owned projects with a nonprofit managing general partner must have tax credits or government financing to qualify (BOE Publication 149). Not a statewide cap.
affordability_requirement: Recorded regulatory agreement with a public agency or tax credit restriction; annual BOE-267 (first filing) or BOE-267-A (annual) with BOE-267-L, L1 or L2 supplemental affidavits and tenant income data.
next_deadline: February 15, 2027 for the 2027-28 lien date (late filings accepted with reduced exemption through the following year).

program_name: Conduit multifamily and nonprofit housing bonds, County TEFRA approvals (CSCDA, CMFA)
administering_agency: County of Santa Clara Board of Supervisors; TEFRA hearings delegated to the Director of Finance
typical_award_size: The County does not issue its own multifamily housing bonds; it is a member of CSCDA (joined July 13, 1993) and approves conduit issues for projects in unincorporated territory or multi-site plans. 2026 example: CSCDA plan of finance up to $125,000,000 for Odd Fellows Home of California (Saratoga Retirement Community, $110 million, plus a Napa facility), approved February 24, 2026 after a February 4, 2026 teleconference TEFRA hearing. Affordable projects inside cities obtain TEFRA approval from the city council (for example CMFA issues for Sunnyvale Block 15, Sango Court in Milpitas, Santa Clara Apartments $33.5 million CDLAC allocation in 2026). SCCHA itself used CMFA for the Laurel Grove Lane acquisition.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable; sized by CDLAC allocation and the 50 percent test.
affordability_requirement: Federal 20 percent at 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at 60 percent AMI plus CDLAC requirements; County approval carries no additional covenant.
next_deadline: None. TEFRA hearings are held by Administration before the Board meeting at which the approval resolution is placed on the consent calendar; allow four to six weeks.
layering_notes: santaclaracounty.gov subdomains (osh, asr, bhsd, news, files) returned HTTP 403 to automated access on 2026-11-07; records were built from the Board of Supervisors IQM2 legislative files (sccgov.iqm2.com), the County Housing Element, Santa Clara County Housing Authority documents, HCD and BOE pages. Expect to go to CMFA, CSCDA or CalHFA for bonds and to the host city for TEFRA. The County's role is procedural and fee-free (the County incurs no cost or liability). SCCHA historically issued its own housing bonds (Blossom River 1998A still outstanding) but now acts as borrower through CMFA. Conduit bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; County, state or federal subsidy in the same deal does.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: IQM2 file 127492 (BOS-2026-25) confirms the CSCDA plan of finance up to $125,000,000 for Odd Fellows Home of California, adopted Feb 24, 2026 after a Feb 4, 2026 teleconference TEFRA hearing, County CSCDA membership since July 13, 1993, and the 2020 delegation to hold TEFRA hearings before the Board meeting. Prevailing wage false is uncited.
prevailing_wage_basis: DIR Public Works Case No. 2006-001, Horizons at Indio (March 12, 2007), following PW 2004-016: multifamily housing revenue bonds issued by a conduit issuer, with proceeds and repayments held by a private trustee, are not a payment of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) or a below-market public loan under 1720(b)(4), and LIHTCs are not public funds; the County only holds the TEFRA hearing. Other public subsidy in the same deal is tested separately. https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-001.pdf

program_name: CDBG and HOME, San Joaquin Urban County (Neighborhood Preservation Division NOFA)
administering_agency: San Joaquin County Human Services Agency, Neighborhood Preservation Division
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 Urban County entitlements requested by jurisdiction: CDBG $2,948,080 (County share $1,740,858; Escalon $75,000; Lathrop $97,358; Manteca $420,911; Ripon $92,270; Tracy $521,683), HOME $973,290 (County share $663,627) and ESG $258,552, plus about $500,000 CDBG and $500,000 HOME program income. Historic averages per the division: CDBG about $2.4 million a year, HOME about $700,000 a year, ESG about $200,000 a year.
per_unit_cap: No local cap published; HOME subsidy limits per 24 CFR 92.250 apply.
affordability_requirement: HUD CDBG national objective (51% low and moderate income benefit) and HOME rent and income limits with HOME affordability periods; at least 15% of HOME to CHDOs. Lodi Commons (54 restricted senior units plus manager) is the current HOME-assisted rental example.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The 2027-28 Urban County CDBG, HOME and ESG NOFA has not been posted on the Neighborhood Preservation page; based on prior cycles (December posting, late January deadline) the next NOFA is expected around December 2026. Confirm with Neighborhood Preservation at (209) 468-3175 or neighborhood@sjgov.org.
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The Urban County covers unincorporated San Joaquin County plus Escalon, Lathrop, Manteca, Ripon and Tracy (qualification package for FY 2027-28 through 2029-30 authorized August 4, 2026); Stockton and Lodi are separate HUD entitlements with their own NOFAs (Pass 3). Roughly half of CDBG and HOME passes through to the five cities, so County HOME available for rental development is typically under $1 million a year including program income; the 2026-27 draft Action Plan says requests far exceeded funds. HOME is used as a small soft loan behind 4% and 9% tax credit deals. Lodi Commons (Housing Authority, 55 units, TDC $28,463,882) stacks $3,031,559 of County HOME from three fiscal years, $2,000,000 County HOME-ARP, $1,000,000 County HHAP, $5,400,000 HACSJ funds, $665,000 City of Lodi CDBG, $2,000,000 Health Net, $3,000,000 San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund, $500,000 HUD CPF and about $10.7 million LIHTC equity, with 32 PBVs and 22 ACC units (FONSI dated November 4, 2026). Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). The Neighborhood Preservation pages moved from sjgov.org to sjchsa.org in 2026; the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan are posted there.
cycle_notes: Annual NOFA for the Urban County (unincorporated area plus Escalon, Lathrop, Manteca, Ripon, Tracy). 2026-27 cycle: NOFA and application posted December 8, 2025, virtual workshop December 17, 2025, applications due January 23, 2026 at 4:00 pm, Board public hearing May 12, 2026. Stockton and Lodi run separate NOFAs. Expected timing for 2027-28 is inferred from prior cycles, not an agency announcement.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The SJRHF board is the SJCOG board (Escalon, Lathrop, Lodi, Manteca, Mountain House, Ripon, San Joaquin County, Stockton, Tracy). administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (PHA code CA024), 2575 Grand Canal Boulevard, Suite 100, Stockton

PBVs are awarded through Requests for Proposals for existing, new construction or substantially rehabilitated housing serving persons with disabilities, veterans and families; a past RFP offered up to 130 PBVs for existing units. FY 2026-27 project-basing: Tracy Apartments Phase I 32 PBVs plus 22 RAD and tenant protection vouchers (54 units), Lodi Commons 32 PBVs plus 22 ACC units (estimated PBV subsidy $152,172 a year), Edison House 19 PBVs plus 14 HUD-VASH (33 units), Grant Street Apartments 24 PBVs.
per_unit_cap: Payment standards set annually by HACSJ; PBV rents capped at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR per 24 CFR 983.
affordability_requirement: HUD PBV rules: households at or below 50% AMI at admission with 75% at or below 30% AMI; 15 to 20 year HAP contracts; HACSJ is not a Moving to Work agency so the 20% program cap and PBV competitive selection rules apply (exception for projects selected through a prior competitive public process).
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No PBV Request for Proposals is posted on hacsj.org; HACSJ issues PBV RFPs periodically through Public Purchase and its FY 2026-27 Annual Plan reports it cannot apply for additional vouchers because of funding shortfalls. Monitor hacsj.org/resources/procurement and Public Purchase.
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). PBVs are the main operating subsidy for PSH and senior deals in the county and underwrite debt on Measure-K and Regional Housing Fund projects; HACSJ attaches PBVs to its own Delta Community Developers Corp. projects and to partner projects. Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction and rehabilitation of nine or more units. HACSJ also runs HUD-VASH, Family Unification and Emergency Housing Vouchers (EHV sunset noted in 2026) and launched CASH SJC in August 2026, a $4.75 million CDSS-funded direct cash program for about 250 seniors on its waitlists. The 2026-27 Annual Plan (effective October 1, 2026) is the source; PBV program description is on hacsj.org/portfolio-item/project-based-voucher.
cycle_notes: PBVs are awarded through periodic Requests for Proposals (existing, new construction or substantial rehabilitation) rather than a fixed annual cycle; no announced schedule.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (current eCFR, as amended by the HOTMA rule): labor standards apply to PBV development activity; for development involving nine or more contract units (whether or not completed in stages), the owner and its contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages and comply with CWHSSA and 29 CFR part 5. If the PHA lets development start before an Agreement or HAP contract (983.154(f) or 983.157(b)(2)), labor standards run from proposal submission or the PHA board resolution approving project-basing. 24 CFR 983.4 cross-references the same labor standards for development of nine or more assisted units. Statutory basis is 42 U.S.C. 1437j(a), which covers projects with nine or more units assisted under section 1437f where the agreement is made before construction or rehabilitation begins. Does not apply to PBV on existing housing or to developments with eight or fewer PBV units. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-IX/part-983 ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1437j
audit_note: PW audit Nov 10, 2026: true confirmed for PBV new construction or rehab with nine or more contract units (24 CFR 983.153(c), 983.4, 42 U.S.C. 1437j(a)); not triggered for existing housing PBV.

program_name: HACSJ public housing repositioning and co-development (Delta Community Developers Corp.)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin and Delta Community Developers Corp. (DCDC), its nonprofit instrumentality

Pipeline from the FY 2026-27 Annual Plan and development page: Tracy Apartments Phases I and II (55 units each, replacing 17 demolished Tracy Homes units; sources include Health Plan of San Joaquin, HOME, Capital Fund loan, Freddie Mac permanent loan, U.S. Bank, LIHTC); Lodi Commons and Danny Drive (110 senior units each in two phases); Edison House (33 PSH units, Homekey+, Stockton PIP, HHAP); Grant Street Apartments (24 behavioral health units, MHSA, HHAP, ARPA); Sierra Vista Phase III (106 units, Section 18 disposition of 26 units in process, up to 80 approved vacancies); Conway Homes phased redevelopment. Sierra Vista Phase I was co-developed with CCHC, and HACSJ has sought a development partner for Sonora Square.
affordability_requirement: Public housing and PBV income limits with long-term use restrictions under RAD or Section 18 conversion; LIHTC restrictions on mixed-finance phases.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026; HACSJ procurement page lists no open solicitations and directs bidders to Public Purchase. Partner solicitations are issued project by project.
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; Alternative In Lieu Fees are due in full at building permit issuance. In-lieu fees are set by Council resolution (current posted schedule is Resolution 18-174). Daly City is a participant in the 2026 multi-city nexus study.

program_name: Residential Impact Fee and Commercial Linkage Fee ordinances with on-site affordable alternative (BMC 25.44 and 25.45)
administering_agency: City of Burlingame Community Development Department, Planning Division

On-site alternative allowed as of right: rental projects providing 10% low income plus 5% very low income units in perpetuity, or for-sale projects providing 15% low income units for 55 years, are deemed mitigated; off-site units, preservation conversions, land dedication or other alternatives need Council approval. Commercial linkage fee (Chapter 25.44) on hotel, retail, restaurant, service and office projects adding 5,000 square feet or more: retail $7 ($5), hotel $12 ($10), office up to 50,000 square feet $18 ($15), office over 50,000 square feet $26 ($21) per square foot. Uses are tenant-based rental subsidies for about 6,015 people a year (1,015 permanent, 5,000 interim) and operating subsidies for about 725 people in PSH, assisted living and interim settings; no BHSA capital development (the County reports housing funds fully subscribed and points to 399 new interim and recuperative care units at the Mead Valley Wellness Village opening 2027). The DHCS BHSA County Policy Manual capital development rules (Section 7.C.10, https://policy-manual.mes.dhcs.ca.gov/behavioral-health-services-act-county-policy-manual/V1.0.0/7-bhsa-components-and-requirements) state no prevailing wage requirement.

program_name: Development impact fee waiver for affordable housing (Ordinance 659) and density bonus (Ordinance 348)
administering_agency: Riverside County Transportation and Land Management Agency, Planning and Building and Safety
typical_award_size: The County Housing Element states that all affordable housing projects receive a waiver of all County development impact fees under Ordinance 659 (fees unchanged since 2015 and higher in the eastern Coachella Valley); the County also commits to fee deferrals and fast-track processing for County-assisted affordable projects (Program 1.1d). Density bonus: Ordinance 348 was amended in March 2021 to adopt state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 and 65917.2) with incentives, concessions and waivers; the R-6 Residential Incentive Zone offers case-by-case density above the General Plan for projects with 15% of units at 80% AMI or 25% at 120% AMI. Projects in the unincorporated area are also exempt from most city-level fees.
affordability_requirement: Affordable housing as defined by the DIF ordinance and the Housing Element; density bonus tiers per state law.
next_deadline: Claimed at building permit (DIF waiver) and at entitlement (density bonus). School, regional transportation (TUMF and WRCOG) and special district fees are not County DIFs and are not waived.
layering_notes: Riverside County's Housing and Workforce Solutions (HWS) department runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA, HHAP, Homekey+ sponsorships and project loans, while the Housing Authority of the County of Riverside (HACR, same Board sitting as Commissioners) supplies project-based vouchers, housing successor funds and land; rivcohws.org and harivco.org block automated access, so records were built from Board of Supervisors files on riversidecountyca.iqm2.com and media.rivcocob.org, RUHS Behavioral Health, the Assessor and the County Housing Element. The blanket DIF waiver is the County's most valuable standing incentive for unincorporated sites (DIFs run several thousand to over ten thousand dollars per unit by area plan); confirm the current Ordinance 659 text and the waiver procedure with Building and Safety because the Housing Element statement is the only source opened this pass and planning.rctlma.org blocks automated access. Prevailing wage is marked unclear because waived fees can be read as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Source is the County 2021-2029 Housing Element HCD submittal (Programs 1.1d and 1.2b and the constraints chapter).
eligible_project_detail: affordable multifamily new construction in unincorporated Riverside County
mixed-income projects using state density bonus
prevailing_wage_basis: No program rule found. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees waived or reduced by a political subdivision as public funds, but 1720(c)(3) excludes de minimis subsidies (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost) and 1720(c)(1) excludes private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment successor or housing authority; density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 is not public funds. Coverage depends on the size of the waiver and project facts.
audit_note: Leave unclear: only basis is the general Labor Code 1720(b) public funds definition; coverage turns on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Riverside County Housing Element and Labor Code 1720 read 2026-11-08; Ordinance 659 text not reachable (planning.rctlma.org) and no DIR determination on DIF waivers found.

audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 9, 2026: Assessor welfare exemption page confirms the OCC (BOE-277) first, then BOE-267 first filing with the Findings Sheet for each year of use; Important Dates page confirms the February 15 exemption claim deadline. Project type tags widened because the exemption covers qualifying nonprofit or LIHTC low-income rental housing generally (as the record's own detail says), not only supportive housing. Prevailing wage false is uncited.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(4) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works requires construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, including fees, loans or other obligations normally required in executing the construction contract that are reduced or waived. PLHA loans and grants are public funds under 1720(b)(1) and (b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), 1720(c)(5)(C) (mortgage, down payment or single-family rehab aid to a household) and 1720(c)(3) de minimis can apply. Davis-Bacon applies only if HOME (12+ HOME units, 24 CFR 92.354) or CDBG (8+ units, 24 CFR 570.603) is layered. program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 21.03 Affordable Housing Regulations) and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: San Benito County Resource Management Agency, Planning and Building (sbcplan@sanbenitocountyca.gov, (831) 637-5313)
typical_award_size: Requirement rather than a subsidy: 15% of units affordable on site (for-sale and rental) or 20% off site under Sections 21.03.006 and 21.03.007; developments of 1 to 5 units exempt, 6 to 10 units pay the in-lieu fee automatically, 11 or more units build on or off site and pay the fee on fractions below 0.7 unit. In-lieu fee adopted December 13, 2022 (Ordinance 1052, Resolution 2022-149): $30 per square foot for for-sale homes based on the 15% requirement (Vernazza Wolfe affordability gap study). affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80% AMI) and moderate (120% AMI) income units per Section 21.03.003; off-site rental projects of 24 or more lots carry an updated income breakdown (Ordinance 1059, September 12, 2023); affordable housing plans are approved by the Planning Commission and Board (Housing Advisory Committee dissolved 2023).

The County has no HOME or CDBG entitlement, no housing trust fund NOFA and no County loan program; Hollister runs its own PLHA and CDBG programs (Pass 3). sanbenitocountyca.gov and the amlegal code library block automated access, so records were built from Board of Supervisors packets on cosb.granicus.com (attachments on d2kbkoa27fdvtw.cloudfront.net), HCD allocation tables and hacosantacruz.org. In-lieu fees go to an affordable housing fund (see separate record). Other public funds layered in the same deal (for example project-based vouchers or local loans) are evaluated separately and can trigger prevailing wage.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers for San Benito County projects, Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz

program_name: Welfare exemption from property tax for nonprofit-owned affordable housing, Madera County Assessor
administering_agency: Madera County Assessor, Brett Frazier ((559) 675-7710, assessor@maderacounty.com)
typical_award_size: Full or partial property tax exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g), prorated to the share of units occupied by lower income households. The owner needs a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate (and a Supplemental Clearance Certificate for a nonprofit or eligible LLC managing general partner) and files with the Madera County Assessor: BOE-267 (first filing) or BOE-267-A (annual), plus BOE-267-L for nonprofit-owned lower income housing or BOE-267-L1 for a limited partnership with an eligible managing general partner.
affordability_requirement: Lower income households as defined in HSC 50079.5 (80% AMI). Units must be restricted by a regulatory agreement with a public agency, recorded deed restriction or other legal document; the property must have tax credits or government financing, or, for a nonprofit owner without them, 90% or more lower income occupants; and the tax savings must be used to maintain affordability or reduce rents. The exemption covers only the qualifying share of units.
next_deadline: File BOE-267 or BOE-267-A with the supplemental affidavit at the Madera County Assessor by February 15, 2027 for the 2027-28 roll (that date is Presidents' Day, so if the office is closed the filing moves to the next business day).
layering_notes: Madera County is a small non-entitlement county: the Community and Economic Development Department (planning, state CDBG and HOME applications) and Behavioral Health Services (BHSA, bridge housing) are the only County housing actors, the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (HACM) is the PHA for the county, and the Fresno Madera Continuum of Care (CA-514, led by Fresno County) handles HHAP and CoC funds. There is no County housing trust fund, NOFA, inclusionary ordinance or impact fee waiver program. The City of Madera is a separate CDBG and HOME entitlement with its own PLHA plan (Pass 3). maderacounty.com blocks automated access (403 on pages and documents), the PrimeGov and IQM2 portals returned no 2026 meetings, and Board agendas were read from PDFs mirrored on maderacountywater.com; other sources were HCD allocation tables, maderaha.org, zoneomics (County Code Title 18), CEQAnet and press coverage. Confirmation needed: the Assessor's pages on maderacounty.com returned 403, so local filing notes were not read; the exemption itself is state law.
cycle_notes: Annual claim due to the County Assessor by February 15 each year (next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday). Late claims: 90% of tax, penalty and interest may be cancelled if filed by January 1 of the next year, 85% after that.
eligible_project_detail: LIHTC rental housing with nonprofit managing general partner
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: Madera County Assessor pages still return 403, so terms were verified against the statewide rules the Assessor applies: BOE Publication 149 (forms, February 15 deadline, late-filing relief, supplemental affidavits) and Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g) (lower income definition, proration, managing general partner rule). Removed the unverified claim that the County posts a BOE-267-L2 form. Source URL moved to BOE Publication 149.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(4) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works requires construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, including fees, loans or other obligations normally required in executing the construction contract that are reduced or waived. The welfare exemption (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)) reduces property tax on the completed property; it pays no construction cost, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage.
