program_name: Folsom legacy housing funds: Oaks at Willow Springs inclusionary fund (Fund 274) and former redevelopment bond proceeds (Fund 280)
administering_agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services
typical_award_size: Largely spent. Fund 274 held $25,672 at June 30, 2025 from a 2006 $3.1M inclusionary payment ($2.7M went to the Granite City Apartments site on Sibley Street). Fund 280 held $149,695 of pre-2011 redevelopment bond proceeds that SB 107 (2015) let the City use for housing; over $9.6 million was invested in multiple affordable projects after redevelopment dissolved in 2012.
affordability_requirement: Low and very low income housing per the original sources.
next_deadline: No new rounds; residual balances may be folded into an AHL Program loan.
layering_notes: Recorded as negative information: Folsom's redevelopment successor housing money is essentially exhausted, so the City's capacity now rests on the in-lieu fee fund. Figures from the August 26, 2025 Housing Fund update staff report.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The August 26, 2025 Housing Fund update staff report (https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/folsomca-meet-20667254009747e4aa5f68a4d63539d6/ITEM-Attachment-001-54dff11a603148f68a0203d4b6b13245.pdf) states no wage rule for Fund 274 or Fund 280; it notes only that state HCD programs such as Homekey and Infill Infrastructure require prevailing wage. Fund 280 holds former redevelopment bond proceeds released by SB 107, not the former Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund that 1720(c)(4) names, and Fund 274 paid for a project on City-owned land, where below-market land transfers are public funds under 1720(b)(3) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). Below-market loans can be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), as DIR PW 2019-018 applied (https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (City Code Chapter 6.27, Ordinance 1180) and Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees
administering_agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Planning Division and Housing Division (fund held by the Finance Director); 1052 Tata Lane, 530-542-7417
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential construction, redevelopment of 50% or more of a building with dwellings, or condo conversion must provide inclusionary units or pay an in-lieu fee scaled to unit size (habitable square feet): 2,000 sq ft or less exempt; 2,001 to 2,500 sq ft 5% of units or $5.29 per sq ft; 2,501 to 3,000 sq ft 6% or $5.84 per sq ft; 3,001 to 5,000 sq ft 9% or $16.77 per sq ft; over 5,000 sq ft 17% or $17.65 per sq ft. Fees are paid before building permit issuance (by phase for phased projects) into the Workforce Housing Fund for housing affordable to low and moderate income households. Fund balance and collections to date are not published; the 2027-2035 draft Housing Element commits the City to post requirements, fee amounts and annual collections by mid-2027 and to publish a five-year in-lieu fee report under AB 2663.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units deed restricted for rent or sale to lower income households (80% AMI or below, El Dorado County), priced at no more than 30% of gross income including utilities, dispersed on site, comparable in exterior quality and bedroom mix, built concurrently with market-rate units. No affordability term is stated in the chapter text that was read.
next_deadline: Applies at building permit. The Master Fee Schedule adopted May 5, 2026 keeps the in-lieu rates unchanged from the March 26, 2024 schedule ($5.29, $5.84, $16.77 and $17.65 per square foot by size tier) plus a $157 inclusionary housing plan check fee. Draft Housing Element Program 2-10 commits to posting requirements and fee amounts by mid-2027 and annual monitoring; first AB 2663 fee report due in 2027.
layering_notes: This is the only locally generated housing fund in South Lake Tahoe. Multifamily rental projects are exempt from both the unit requirement and the fee (chapter text on the gocodebook mirror), so apartment developers owe nothing; the fund is fed by large single-family and condo construction, which is the dominant product in the Basin. Spending the Workforce Housing Fund is at Council discretion with no NOFA or guidelines published; pair requests with the City's HOME program income, PLHA formula and Prohousing Incentive Program dollars (see the City direct financing record) and with the County Affordable Housing Trust Fund, County PLHA and County HOME/CDBG records, which also have no standing NOFA. The ordinance grew out of Housing Element Program 2-11 (2022 to 2027 cycle) and the January 2023 Analysis of Local Funding Sources. Adoption date conflict: the August 2026 draft Housing Element says Council adopted the ordinance in December 2024, but the March 26, 2024 Master Fee Schedule already lists the inclusionary fee tiers, so the fee was in place by early 2024. Fee amounts are confirmed on the official Master Fee Schedule; unit percentages and exemptions were read on the gocodebook mirror because codepublishing.com returns 403.
eligible_project_detail: single-family and condominium projects over 2,000 sq ft per unit (compliance)
deed-restricted units at or below 120% AMI (exempt)
long-term multifamily rental projects of two or more units (exempt)
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: in-lieu fee tiers ($5.29, $5.84, $16.77, $17.65 per square foot; 2,000 sq ft or less exempt) confirmed on the official Master Fee Schedules adopted March 26, 2024 and May 5, 2026; the August 2026 draft Housing Element confirms the ordinance, the 2,000 sq ft threshold, in-lieu fees restricted to affordable housing and Program 2-10. Percentages and the multifamily rental exemption rest on the gocodebook mirror (codepublishing 403). The December 2024 adoption date conflicts with the fee appearing in the March 2024 schedule. Manual edit Nov 10, 2026: adoption date dropped from program_name pending the ordinance text.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: City direct gap and predevelopment financing for affordable housing (HOME program income, Housing Successor and Redevelopment Agency program income, PLHA formula funds, Prohousing Incentive Program funds, general fund, residential units of use) and state application sponsorship
administering_agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager, mmanuel@cityofslt.gov, 530-542-7417); City Council approves each commitment
typical_award_size: Deal-by-deal Council commitments, no NOFA or written guidelines. Track record: over $2.5 million of HOME program income, Redevelopment Agency program income and general fund to Sugar Pine Village (248 units, Related California and Saint Joseph Community Land Trust on state surplus land; Phase 1A 68 units opened fall 2024, Phase 2A 60 units fall 2025, Phase 1B 60 units summer 2026, Phase 2B seeking financing), plus City-sponsored AHSC ($17,359,470), MHP ($19.6 million), IIG, LGMG, HOME and PLHA awards; a $564,073 predevelopment loan plus $500,000 of Prohousing Incentive Program funds to Novin Development for the 75-unit 3900 and 3908 Lake Tahoe Boulevard project (SB 35 approval 2025, AHSC pending); about $1,791,669 CDBG-CV and $120,000 PIP for rehabilitation of three Homekey properties (72 supportive units) with Tahoe Coalition for the Homeless; 21 multifamily residential units of use donated to Lake Tahoe Community College's 100-bed dorm (about $315,000 market value); three Al Tahoe lots donated to Saint Joseph Community Land Trust. City awards 2020 to 2025 included PLHA formula about $880,000 total, PLHA competitive $15 million over three awards, HOME $6,538,240 and PIP Round 2 $620,000. Legacy RDA Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund loans (AB 987 database) total $16.46 million HOME, $2.15 million RDA and $1.18 million CDBG across 296 units in eight projects.
affordability_requirement: Follows the state source layered in: Sugar Pine Village and 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard are 55-year deed restrictions at 30% to 80% AMI; TRPA deed restriction also required when bonus units are used. HOME program income follows HOME rules.
next_deadline: No NOFA; no open round as of November 8, 2026. Approach the Housing Division (housing@cityofslt.us) ahead of the AHSC, MHP and PLHA competitive rounds; the draft Housing Element commits the City to apply for at least one grant per year. The draft 2027-2035 Housing Element was open for public comment through September 12, 2026 and no adopted version was posted on the City Housing Element page as of November 8, 2026; Phase 2B of Sugar Pine Village is still pursuing financing.
layering_notes: South Lake Tahoe is a non-entitlement city that has out-raised most small cities by sponsoring state applications (PLHA competitive, AHSC, HOME, IIG, LGMG) for a nonprofit or private developer, so the City's own cash is small but its sponsorship is the key to the state layer. Gap order used on Sugar Pine Village: LIHTC and bonds, AHSC and MHP, IIG and LGMG, HOME and PLHA, City program income last. County layers available in the Tahoe Basin: El Dorado County PLHA formula and County HOME/CDBG participation requests, County Affordable Housing Trust Fund (no development NOFA), County PHA project-based vouchers, CMFA TEFRA approvals, welfare exemption, BHSA housing funds; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city because the City levies its own fees. TRPA layer: bonus units and the allocation exemption are required for any deed-restricted project (see the TRPA record), and TRPA application fees are waived for affordable projects. Residential allocations are scarce (33 market-rate per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), which is why deed-restricted projects using bonus units are the only route to scale. Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees (inclusionary record) are a separate, newer pool. No local housing trust fund, no city NOFA, no local tax-exempt issuer. Source is the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter; the City's CivicPlus pages opened directly but council packets were not reachable (Granicus and Legistar hosts not found).
cycle_notes: Deal-by-deal City Council commitments with no NOFA or written guidelines; timing follows the state program rounds the City sponsors (AHSC, MHP, PLHA competitive, HOME, IIG).
audit_note: T2 audit 2026-11-08: the earlier statement that final Housing Element adoption was set for a September 8, 2026 Council hearing is not supported; the City Housing Element page shows the draft comment period ran through September 12, 2026 and posts no adopted 2027-2035 element. That page names Jessica Wackenhut Lomeli as Housing Manager (housing@cityofslt.us), which differs from the contact in administering_agency.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: City permit fee waiver for nonprofit and public agency affordable housing (City Code Section 6.55.090), lot consolidation fee waiver for deed-restricted units (Housing Element Program 1-7) and Sugar Pine Village inspection fee reduction
administering_agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions); waivers approved by the City Council at a public hearing
typical_award_size: Case by case. Nonprofits and public agencies developing affordable housing may request waiver of City permit fees, granted by Council resolution (about 45 days from request to approval, run concurrently with permit review). The City also reduced building inspection fees for Sugar Pine Village because HCD inspects the modular units. Program 1-7 commits the City to waive the lot line adjustment fee when the resulting project includes deed-restricted affordable units. City planning fees are modest relative to TRPA fees; City multifamily impact charges are mainly utility connection fees set by South Tahoe Public Utility District (not waived; $7,500 deposit and 10% of capacity fees at plan review). No waiver of TRPA water quality ($1.86 per sq ft) or excess coverage mitigation fees ($8.50 per sq ft), though TRPA application fees are waived for affordable, moderate and achievable bonus-unit projects and the mobility mitigation fee may be waived.
affordability_requirement: Affordable housing project sponsored by a nonprofit or public agency; deed restriction consistent with TRPA affordable, moderate or achievable definitions when bonus units are used. No specific AMI threshold published for the City waiver.
next_deadline: Request with the entitlement or building permit application; Council hearing required. Verify current practice with the Housing Division (530-542-7417) because the code text could not be opened.
layering_notes: Fee relief is small in dollar terms; the real cost drivers in the Basin are TRPA mitigation fees, land coverage purchases and development rights, which the TRPA bonus unit program (separate record) addresses. Combine with the TRPA application fee exemption and with the Phase 2 Housing Amendments height, coverage and density relief. Private for-profit developers are not eligible for the 6.55.090 waiver unless partnered with a nonprofit or public agency. The County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) is not available inside the city. The City's code host (codepublishing.com) returned 403 and the gocodebook mirror had no Chapter 6.55 page, so Section 6.55.090 was not read directly; the description is taken from the fees and exactions analysis in the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element (pages 4-203 to 4-206) and from Program 1-7 of the adopted 2022-2027 Housing Element.
audit_note: PW pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on 1720(b)(4) alone; changed to unclear per the consistency rule.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Waived permit fees are public funds under 1720(b)(4), but the 1720(c)(3) de minimis test (under $600,000 and under 2% of project cost) will usually exempt small waivers; City Code 6.55.090 could not be read (codepublishing 403).

program_name: TRPA Residential Bonus Unit Program (TRPA Code Chapter 52), allocation exemption (Chapter 50.5.1) and Phase 2 Housing Amendments as applied in South Lake Tahoe Town Centers (Tourist Core, Tahoe Valley and Midtown Area Plans)
administering_agency: Tahoe Regional Planning Agency (TRPA), with City of South Lake Tahoe Planning Division as lead reviewer inside Area Plan boundaries; City holds a voting seat on the TRPA Governing Board
typical_award_size: Regulatory, not cash, but it substitutes for development rights that otherwise must be bought. Deed-restricted affordable (80% AMI), moderate (120% AMI) or achievable (TRPA-set percentage tied to median home price) units receive residential bonus units at no cost in place of a residential unit of use (potential unit plus allocation), are exempt from the City's annual allocation (33 market-rate allocations per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), and are exempt from TRPA application fees. About 946 of the 1,124 bonus units set aside in 2018 remained as of the 2026 draft Housing Element, all reserved for deed-restricted housing and prioritized for Centers and multifamily zones. Phase 2 Housing Amendments (TRPA Governing Board, December 2023; MAP settlement July 2024) remove the maximum density cap for 100% deed-restricted projects in Town Centers, allow heights up to 65 feet in Centers (step-back, shade and scenic findings above 56 feet), allow 100% deed-restricted projects outside Centers to transfer in coverage up to 70% of high-capability land if runoff is treated by a public stormwater system, and allow use of the TRPA basin-wide parking study to reduce parking. Affordable projects using these tools have reached 61 to 67 units per acre in the city (Sugar Pine Village, 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard).
per_unit_cap: One bonus unit per deed-restricted unit; no dollar cap. Market value of a multifamily residential unit of use is about $15,000 (the City valued 21 units given to Lake Tahoe Community College at about $315,000).
affordability_requirement: Permanent TRPA deed restriction recorded as a permit condition: occupancy limited to affordable, moderate or achievable households (or local employees for achievable units), no second-home or vacation rental use, annual compliance report to TRPA (penalties up to $5,000 per day), real estate disclosure on transfer; project within one half mile of transit. Height, coverage and density incentives under Phase 2 require 100% deed-restricted units plus stormwater and transportation contributions.
next_deadline: Bonus units assigned at TRPA permit (about 120 days of TRPA review, or City-only review for qualifying projects inside the TCAP and TVAP). Watch: TRPA Phase 3 (Cultivating Community, Conserving the Basin) EIS scoping closed March 16, 2026 with further code changes pending; City Midtown Area Plan (MTAP) adoption was pending a September 2026 hearing; TRPA 2025-2026 income limits and achievable percentages are updated each July.
layering_notes: Flag for every South Lake Tahoe deal: the Tahoe Basin is dual-jurisdiction. The City cannot grant a state density bonus law bonus or concessions that exceed TRPA standards; TRPA gives full density relief only to 100% deed-restricted projects and gives no comparable benefit or mandatory concessions to mixed-income projects that set aside a share of units, which the draft 2027-2035 Housing Element names as a continuing constraint (Program 2-8 asks TRPA to allow state density bonus compliance). Land coverage (Bailey system, 30% base outside Area Plans, 70% inside TCAP and TVAP), scenic and height limits and the allocation system govern feasibility more than zoning. Projects using bonus units must carry a TRPA deed restriction in addition to TCAC, HCD or City covenants; coordinate the three so income limits (TRPA uses county AMI for a family of three) and terms do not conflict. The TRPA application fee waiver stacks with the City Section 6.55.090 waiver (separate record). County layers (PLHA, Trust Fund, PBVs, welfare exemption) apply as in the rest of El Dorado County. Source pages at trpa.gov opened directly; City-specific figures (946 bonus units remaining, 61 to 67 du per acre, 65-foot height, MTAP status) come from the City's August 2026 draft Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter.
eligible_project_detail: motel or hotel conversion to residential
acquisition-rehab (coverage and density relief for 100% deed-restricted)
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Placerville City Code Title 10 Chapter 12 (Sections 10-12-1 to 10-12-13; 2015 text, state-law update ZC 24-05 pending under ROI 2024-01)
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division, 3101 Center Street, (530) 642-5252, pv.planning@gmail.com
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The local chapter still reflects the 2015 version of Government Code 65915: bonus up to 35% for 5% very low, 10% lower or 10% moderate (for-sale) units, 20% for senior housing, land donation bonus up to 35% combined; one to three incentives (reduced lot size, setbacks, lot coverage, height, parking, mixed-use zoning, other cost-reducing regulatory relief) and by-right parking ratios of 1 space (0 to 1 bedroom), 2 (2 to 3 bedrooms) and 2.5 (4 or more). Where the chapter conflicts with state law, state law controls (10-12-1), so the current 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects, unlimited bonus near major transit and up to five concessions apply by operation of state law. The 2025 Annual Progress Report (March 2026) reports the full density bonus ordinance update was deferred to 2026 because of evolving state law.
affordability_requirement: Per state law: income-restricted units for very low (50% AMI), lower (80% AMI) or moderate (120% AMI, for-sale) households with a recorded density bonus housing agreement (10-12-12); rental affordability term per Government Code 65915 (55 years).
next_deadline: Request with the entitlement application (optional pre-application conference). Watch for the Planning Commission and City Council hearings on text amendment ZC 24-05 (density bonus update), dates still TBD on the City's project list; adoption targeted in 2026.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law. Placerville has no local housing trust fund, no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee, no commercial linkage fee, no city NOFA and no redevelopment successor housing funds; the City's affordable housing tools are this chapter, the Housing Opportunity Overlay by-right sites, fee deferral under SB 937, SCIP impact fee financing and sponsorship of state CDBG, HOME and PLHA applications (separate records). Stack with the El Dorado County density bonus and the County PLHA, Trust Fund, HOME/CDBG, PBV and welfare exemption records; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city, which levies its own traffic impact mitigation fee. Chapter text read from the City's own zoning ordinance PDF; the City page links the amlegal code library, which was not opened.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Housing Opportunity Overlay Zone (HO, Title 10 Chapter 5 Section 24, Zone Change 2016-01) by-right affordable sites and Housing Element Programs A-3 and A-5
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory. Sites in the HO overlay (and the R-5 Very High Density Multi-Family zone) allow owner-occupied or multifamily housing by right at a minimum 20 and maximum 24 units per acre with compliance with local design standards and no discretionary action (Government Code 65583.2 sites). The overlay covers about 17 acres with three additional sites proposed for 2026. Two of the four original HO parcels produced Mallard Apartments (72 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years) and Middletown Apartments (82 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years), both by Pacific Southwest Community Development Corporation and under construction in 2025 (82 Middletown permits issued in 2025). Objective design standards (LEAP $65,000 and SB 2 $160,000 funded) were still being completed as of March 2025.
affordability_requirement: By-right status is tied to lower income housing need under state law; projects on HO sites have been 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI with 55-year covenants. No local inclusionary percentage.
next_deadline: Ministerial site plan review on HO or R-5 sites at any time. Three additional HO sites were proposed for 2026 rezoning; confirm status and the objective design standards with Planning.
layering_notes: The HO overlay is where Placerville's deal flow has actually occurred; both recent projects paired by-right siting with City-sponsored CDBG and CPLHA loans, IIG and MHP (see the City state-funding record). The 2025 APR reports 244 lower income units of site capacity against a 90-unit lower income RHNA, so no-net-loss is not a constraint. Combine with the state density bonus (Chapter 12) and SB 35 or AB 2011 streamlining. Source is the City's 2021-2029 Housing Element policy document (Programs A-3 and A-5); the 2016 draft HO ordinance was also read on the City's EvoGov agenda host. No local trust fund or NOFA exists in Placerville.
eligible_project_detail: mixed-income multifamily on HO or R-5 sites
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this zoning overlay provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any City or County loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on the project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Development impact fee deferral for affordable projects (SB 937 implementation, Housing Element Program C-5), ADU impact fee reductions, and Statewide Community Infrastructure Program (SCIP) impact fee financing (Program C-7)
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions) and Finance; SCIP bonds issued by California Statewide Communities Development Authority (CSCDA)
typical_award_size: Timing relief, not a reduction, for multifamily: the City reports it implemented fee deferrals under SB 937 in 2025 so impact fees on qualifying affordable projects are collected at certificate of occupancy rather than permit issuance. Housing Element Program C-5 also offers deferment to completion or occupancy, payment over 12 months or longer after completion, or fee reductions where the applicant documents lower facility demand. Impact fee reductions (water, sewer, traffic impact mitigation, park fees) have been implemented only for ADUs and JADUs consistent with state law. SCIP lets a developer finance City impact fees and public improvements through tax-exempt CSCDA bonds repaid by a special assessment on the parcel; the City intends to offer it for all projects, especially housing, but no development had used SCIP as of the 2023 and 2025 progress reports. No general fee waiver for affordable housing exists.
affordability_requirement: SB 937 deferral applies to projects meeting the statute's affordability definitions (generally 100% affordable or qualifying mixed-income projects); Program C-5 options are for affordable housing providers. SCIP has no affordability requirement.
next_deadline: Request deferral at building permit; SCIP participation requires a City resolution and CSCDA application ahead of permit issuance. Confirm the current fee schedule and deferral form with the Building Division.
layering_notes: Placerville levies its own traffic impact mitigation, park and utility fees, so the El Dorado County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) does not apply to city projects; deferral is the only local fee tool. SCIP assessment financing of impact fees is senior to other liens and must be cleared with TCAC and permanent lenders. Pair with the HO overlay by-right sites and City-sponsored CDBG, PLHA and HOME loans (separate records). Sources read: the March 24, 2026 City Council staff report accepting the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report (SB 937 deferral statement), the City's Housing Resources page describing SCIP (updated March 4, 2025) and Programs C-5 and C-7 of the 2021-2029 Housing Element.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific rule found. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees that are paid, reduced, waived or forgiven by a public agency as public funds, but SB 937 deferral only changes timing and is not listed; ADU fee reductions and any Program C-5 reduction could count under 1720(b)(4) subject to the 1720(c)(3) de minimis test (under $600,000 and under 2% of project cost) and the 1720(c)(1) and (c)(5) private residential exemptions. No DIR determination on fee deferral or SCIP assessment financing was located. Outcome depends on project facts. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Tier 3: left unclear; only the general Labor Code 1720(b)(4) definition applies and the result turns on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts.

program_name: City-sponsored state CDBG, Competitive PLHA and HOME loans for affordable multifamily (non-entitlement city; Housing Element Program C-4) and partnership with Housing El Dorado
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (applicant and lender of record for state CDBG and PLHA competitive funds) with El Dorado County Housing Authority (HHSA) and Housing El Dorado
typical_award_size: Pass-through loans sized to each state award, no local cash. Mallard Apartments (Mallard Lane and MacIntosh, 72 units): City CDBG loan $756,000 for acquisition, Competitive PLHA (CPLHA) loan $756,000 for architecture and engineering, IIG $1,105,000 for frontage and offsite work, MHP $11,000,000. Middletown Apartments (Cold Springs Road and Middletown Road, 82 units): CDBG loan $861,000 for acquisition, CPLHA loan $861,000, IIG $2,158,000, MHP $13,000,000. The 2025 progress report adds a $400,000 PLHA loan secured for Mallard/Middletown. Program C-4 commits the City to meet annually with nonprofit developers, apply or co-apply for state and federal funds (CDBG, HOME, PLHA, Section 202 and 811, CalHome), and to establish priority processing and fee deferrals for extremely low income projects.
per_unit_cap: None; limited by the state program caps (state CDBG and PLHA competitive NOFAs).
affordability_requirement: Follows the state source: Mallard and Middletown are 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI for 55 years; CDBG and PLHA require at least 55-year covenants for rental new construction.
next_deadline: Tied to HCD state CDBG and PLHA competitive NOFAs (typically fall or late winter per the Housing Element) and HUD rounds in late spring. Contact Planning at least one cycle ahead so the City can adopt the required resolutions; no city NOFA exists.
layering_notes: Placerville competes in the same non-entitlement state CDBG, HOME and competitive PLHA pools as El Dorado County, so coordinate with the County's Affordable Housing Unit (Housing@edcgov.us) to avoid both jurisdictions applying for the same project; the County's own records cover County HOME/CDBG participation requests, County PLHA formula funds and the County Trust Fund (no development NOFA). County PHA project-based vouchers and the welfare exemption apply inside the city. Gap order used on the two Placerville projects: 4% LIHTC and bonds (CMFA TEFRA via the County), MHP, IIG, City CDBG and CPLHA loans. The City has no local trust fund, inclusionary fee, linkage fee or RDA successor housing funds; a first-time homebuyer program and workforce housing study (Program C-8, CDBG planning grant by spring 2025) were not advanced as of the 2025 progress report. Source is the City's 2023 Housing Element Annual Progress Report tables (October 8, 2024 Council packet); the 2025 APR staff report of March 24, 2026 was also read.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Davis Municipal Code Article 18.05, Ordinance 2646) and Rental Housing Inclusionary Guidelines (Resolution 25-002, in-lieu fee)
administering_agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Affordable Housing Manager Iris Grace and Director Dana Bailey; Community Development Department for entitlements
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of 20 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half low income and half very low income (ordinance adopted July 2023). Resolution 25-002 (adopted January 7, 2025, 4 to 1) set the in-lieu fee for non-discretionary rental projects at $250,000 per required affordable unit and $125,000 for a fractional unit when the whole units are built on site. Staff had proposed $608,000 per unit (cost of the most recent all-affordable project) and the Council rejected $369,000. The fee is indexed annually by the construction cost index with a one-time payment or a multi-year option at a 10-year net present value. Ownership projects have separate land dedication and in-lieu options approved case by case.
affordability_requirement: 15% of rental units (7.5% low income at 80% AMI and 7.5% very low income at 50% AMI) with long-term covenants; alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication, Project Individualized Plan) must deliver equivalent affordability value and discretionary projects need Council approval of the alternative.
next_deadline: None (ordinance). Council on December 16, 2025 directed staff to amend the land dedication option as soon as possible; an amendment requiring land dedicators to also provide funding was introduced in March 2026 per local coverage. A broader revision of the ownership inclusionary rules is in progress. Verify current text with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.
layering_notes: The ordinance is the engine behind Davis's two main local tools: in-lieu fees and negotiated contributions flow to the City Housing Trust Fund, and land dedication produces fully improved affordable sites (see the Housing Trust Fund and land dedication records). For a 100% affordable developer this means partnering with a market-rate applicant on a dedicated site, or seeking Housing Trust Fund gap money. Staff's October 21, 2025 informational report found production lagging RHNA and proposed a mandatory financial review when a developer claims infeasibility; Councilmembers asked staff to look at 10% extremely low income in place of part of the 15% requirement. Section 40.27.110 of the zoning code ties Article 18.05 to state density bonus law. Stack with county records: no Yolo County housing trust fund or county NOFA exists; Yolo County Housing project-based vouchers and the state CDBG and HOME competitions are the county-level layers. Access: cityofdavis.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and to WebFetch; the Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org open and were used. The Resolution 25-002 text (showpublisheddocument/20364) and the October 21, 2025 staff report could not be opened.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: funding_type changed from density bonus to regulatory requirement; this is an inclusionary ordinance, which SCHEMA.md classifies as a regulatory requirement. January 7, 2025 minutes confirm the 15% rental requirement and the $250,000 and $125,000 in-lieu fees under Resolution 25-002.

program_name: City of Davis Housing Trust Fund (in-lieu fees and negotiated developer contributions, Article 18.05)
administering_agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department (Housing Trust Fund administered by the Affordable Housing Manager; Social Services Commission reviews affordable housing plans)
typical_award_size: Project-specific gap contributions sized by Council; no published NOFA or guidelines found. Revenue is in-lieu fees under Resolution 25-002 ($250,000 per unit) plus negotiated contributions from peripheral Measure J/R/D projects: Village Farms Exhibit E (approved December 16, 2025, revised January 13, 2026) commits $6,000,000 to the Housing Trust Fund ($2 million with dedication of the first land site, $1 million at the first building permit, $3 million before any Phase 3 building permit); Willowgrove's plan reportedly adds $1.8 million. Earlier years the fund was small (the 2023 single-family in-lieu fee was about $82,000 per unit) and the City has historically funded projects such as Paul's Place and Creekside from it. Current balance not published in any document opened this pass.
affordability_requirement: Low and very low income units with long-term covenants; Council direction prioritizes very low and extremely low income and deed-restricted ownership.
next_deadline: No NOFA as of November 10, 2026. Village Farms contributions will not arrive because Measure V failed in June 2026 (press reports of the certified count). Willowgrove (Measure W) is passing in Yolo County unofficial results; confirm its Housing Trust Fund contribution and timing with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.
layering_notes: The only local soft money in Davis. Sized to projects on the dedicated land sites first (the Village Farms plan says the money should support affordable housing on the dedication sites but may be used elsewhere consistent with the plan). Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Councilmembers raised formalizing the fund into a structured trust (April 2026). Davis has no RDA successor housing fund. Blocked: cityofdavis.org pages and the Village Farms Exhibit E staff reports (403); facts are from the December 16, 2025 and January 13, 2026 Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org, which did open.
cycle_notes: No NOFA or published guidelines; Council sizes contributions project by project. Village Farms Exhibit E ($6 million to the fund) depended on Measure V, which failed June 2, 2026 per press reports. Willowgrove, Measure W on the November 3, 2026 ballot, had 14,166 yes (73.40%) to 5,135 no in Yolo County unofficial results as of November 6, 2026; certification is due by December 3, 2026.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: December 16, 2025 and January 13, 2026 Council minutes re-read and confirm the Village Farms $6 million schedule ($2 million with first land dedication, $1 million at first building permit, $3 million before Phase 3 permits). Yolo County Elections unofficial November 2026 results show Davis Measure W (Willowgrove) at 73.40% yes. Still unverified: the $250,000 in-lieu fee under Resolution 25-002, the Willowgrove $1.8 million figure and the official Measure V count (cityofdavis.org 403; no official June 2026 statement of vote found).
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. No City of Davis Housing Trust Fund NOFA, guideline, resolution or loan term requiring prevailing wage was found (no published guidelines exist; the December 16, 2025 Council minutes have no wage term). Loans are public funds under 1720(b)(1) or (b)(4), but qualifying below-market loans may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) and small subsidies under 1720(c)(3). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Affordable housing land dedication sites under Article 18.05 (Village Farms 16-acre dedication, Project Individualized Plan Exhibit E)
administering_agency: City of Davis Community Development Department and Social Services and Housing Department (Council subcommittee negotiates development agreements)
typical_award_size: Land, not cash. Village Farms Davis (Development Agreement Exhibit E, approved December 16, 2025 and revised January 13, 2026) dedicates 16 acres to the City for 280 low and very low income units on fully improved sites (no more than 4 parcels, none under 2.5 acres), to be developed with a qualified affordable housing developer selected by the City, with the City to endeavor to add 80 moderate income units. Baseline features now require construction to commence on 100 affordable units before Phase 3 and no permits beyond the first 150 until that starts; the City holds an option after 150 units. Together with the $6 million Housing Trust Fund payment the package is valued by the applicant at over $6 million plus land.
affordability_requirement: 280 low and very low income units (plus up to 80 moderate) on dedicated land; affordability covenants set in the City's developer agreement.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 10, 2026. Village Farms dedication will not proceed after the reported Measure V defeat; watch for the Willowgrove affordable housing plan if Measure W is certified and for any other Article 18.05 dedications.
layering_notes: This is how 100% affordable developers get sites in Davis: the inclusionary ordinance's land dedication option plus Housing Trust Fund money, then compete for 9% credits, MHP, AHSC or HCD Super NOFA money. Vice Mayor Vaitla's December 2025 direction to amend the land dedication option (so dedicators also provide resources) led to a March 2026 ordinance introduction, so later projects should carry cash with the land. Earlier dedications (Cannery, Chiles Ranch, Bretton Woods) produced sites now built or in pipeline. Davis has no city-owned surplus land program beyond these dedications. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the CoC HHAP money for supportive units.
cycle_notes: Village Farms land dedication approved by Council December 16, 2025 (revised January 13, 2026) depended on voter approval under Measure J/R/D; press reports say Measure V failed June 2, 2026, so the dedication will not occur unless the project returns. Willowgrove (Measure W, November 3, 2026) had 73.40% yes in Yolo County unofficial results as of November 6, 2026; its affordable housing terms were not reviewed in this pass. The general Article 18.05 land dedication option still exists.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: Exhibit E terms (16 acres, 280 low and very low units, no more than 4 parcels of at least 2.5 acres, 80 moderate units, 100 affordable units before Phase 3, City option after 150 units) re-confirmed in the December 16, 2025 and January 13, 2026 minutes. Measure V outcome still rests on press reports; no official June 2026 statement of vote could be opened (cityofdavis.org 403, ElectionStats is a script app).
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The January 13, 2026 City Council minutes on the Village Farms Exhibit E affordable housing plan (https://documents.cityofdavis.org/Media/CityCouncil/Documents/PDF/CityCouncil/CouncilMeetings/Minutes/2026/Minutes-2026-01-13-City-Council-Meeting.pdf) state no wage rule, and no Davis land dedication or developer agreement term on prevailing wage was found. Land the City receives under Article 18.05 and later conveys to an affordable developer for less than fair market price is public funds under 1720(b)(3) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), so coverage turns on the conveyance terms, the 1720(c) exemptions and the project's other public funds.

program_name: Density bonus (Davis Municipal Code Section 40.27.110, deviations under Article 18.05 and state density bonus law)
administering_agency: City of Davis Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory. Section 40.27.110 (Ordinance 2322, 2008) allows deviations from zoning standards in accordance with the density bonuses and incentives provided for affordable housing by Article 18.05 and state density bonus law (Government Code 65915). Davis has no local enhancement beyond the state schedule; Article 18.05 alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication) are the local layer.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 100% affordable up to 80% bonus and unlimited near transit) or Article 18.05 inclusionary units.
next_deadline: None; applied with the entitlement application. Davis is updating its General Plan (2025 to 2027), which may fold density bonus text into a zoning rewrite.
layering_notes: Standard state law implementation; Davis downtown zones (Article 40.13) are form-based and the 2021-2029 Housing Element rezoned sites to meet RHNA, so the bonus matters most on R-3 and R-HD infill sites. Davis is not Prohousing designated. No fee waiver program for affordable units exists at the City level; development impact fees are set by Council annually. The code mirror (zoneomics) was used because qcode.us is blocked; confirm against the official code.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: official Davis code host (library.qcode.us now redirects to resolve.ecode360.com) returns 403 to curl and WebFetch; ecode360 and municode also 403. Section 40.27.110 remains mirror-only (zoneomics).
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: CDBG and HOME entitlement allocations (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, Resolution 25-061) and PLHA formula allocation
administering_agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Housing and Grants Management (Director Dana Bailey)
typical_award_size: Davis is a CDBG entitlement city and a HOME participating jurisdiction. HUD formula allocations: FY 2025 CDBG $730,016 and HOME $323,760 (about $1.05 million combined); FY 2026 CDBG $700,471 and HOME $309,807 (about $1.01 million). Council adopted the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and the Program Year One (2025) Annual Action Plan on April 15, 2025 (Resolution 25-061). HOME has historically funded first-time homebuyer loans and rental project gap loans; CDBG funds public services, facilities and homelessness programs. PLHA: HCD's 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA (July 16, 2026) lists Davis at $212,632 for CY 2024 and $227,760 for CY 2025, with an estimated $1,328,950 over five years; staff said in February 2025 that PLHA would go to homeownership opportunities.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply (HUD 221(d)(3) limits for Yolo County).
affordability_requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI; HOME at or below 80% AMI with at least 90% of rental assistance at 60% AMI and 20% of units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more HOME units.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 10, 2026. The Program Year 2027 Action Plan process is expected winter to spring 2027 with a public hearing typically in April; confirm amounts and the HOME set-aside with Grants Management, (530) 757-5602.
layering_notes: Federal money is the only recurring Davis source for rental projects, but the annual HOME amount is small (hundreds of thousands) and competes with homebuyer uses; combine with Housing Trust Fund gap money and state credits. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Davis also receives HHAP through the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC (see county record) for supportive housing operations. Yolo County's own CDBG and HOME (state non-entitlement) cover only unincorporated areas, so there is no overlap. Blocked: the Grants Management page and the Consolidated Plan PDF on cityofdavis.org (403); the April 15, 2025 minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org were opened and record the adoption.
cycle_notes: CDBG and HOME follow an annual Action Plan adopted each spring after a public hearing. PLHA formula funds flow through the City's five-year plan; under HCD's 2024-2028 NOFA the City must apply for the CY 2024 allocation by the end of February 2028 and the CY 2025 allocation by the end of February 2029.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: April 15, 2025 minutes confirm Resolution 25-061; HUD FY 2025 and FY 2026 CPD formula allocation spreadsheets give Davis CDBG and HOME amounts (replacing the press figure); HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA Appendix A gives the Davis CY 2024, CY 2025 and five-year PLHA figures. Next cycle relabeled Program Year 2027.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Woodland Municipal Code Chapter 15.16, Ordinance 1662 of 2020) inclusionary requirements and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019) with the Community Services Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Citywide outside the Spring Lake Specific Plan: for-sale and multifamily rental projects of 30 or fewer units are exempt; 31 to 80 units provide 5% low income units; 81 or more units provide 10% low income, reduced to 5% if the project is built at 95% or more of maximum allowed density; in Downtown, Corridor Mixed Use and Neighborhood Commercial areas projects of at least 10 units built at maximum density (and at least 10 units per acre) owe 5% for-sale units. Very low income requirements were dropped in the April 2020 amendments. Alternatives: land dedication valued at the in-lieu fee times required units, or in-lieu fees per an adopted fee schedule (reviewed annually) or, if none is adopted, as negotiated in the inclusionary housing agreement and paid before building permits. Example: Ashley and Main (168 units, 2020) paid $469,413. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Fund (Fund 1327); up to 10% of annual income may fund administration.
affordability_requirement: Low income (80% AMI) rental units must be permanently affordable; for-sale affordable units 10 years minimum reset at each resale with a $1,000 silent second and equity share; rents calculated at 50% AMI for very low and 80% AMI for low income units.
next_deadline: None (ordinance). The 2020 temporary relief provisions were set to expire in April 2022 unless dwelling unit goals were met; the Housing Element (Program A.27) committed to a LEAP-funded study of a standardized square-foot in-lieu fee, including nonresidential. Confirm whether a fee schedule has been adopted with the Housing Analyst.
layering_notes: Woodland's inclusionary program feeds the only local soft money in the city (Fund 1327, see the in-lieu fund record). Thresholds are generous to market-rate builders (exempt to 30 units, 5% at 31 to 80), so most revenue has come from Spring Lake development agreements and large projects. Spring Lake has its own stricter rules (separate record). Rental inclusionary units must accept Section 8 vouchers (Yolo County Housing PBVs can layer). Chapter 15.16 also now contains the City's state density bonus procedures. No county inclusionary applies inside city limits (Yolo County Chapter 8-8 is unincorporated only). ecode360 hosts the official Woodland code and opened directly.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: funding_type changed from density bonus to regulatory requirement (inclusionary ordinance per SCHEMA.md). ecode360 returned 403, so the 2023 Housing Element public hearing draft was used; it confirms the 2020 citywide update outside Spring Lake, 10% low income for 81 or more units, the 5% requirement at 95% of maximum density and in-lieu fees on infeasibility.

administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department, Housing (Deputy Director Erika Bumgardner; Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019)

program_name: Spring Lake Specific Plan Affordable Housing Plan: inclusionary requirements, Off-Site Affordable Housing Fee and 25% density bonus
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Spring Lake Specific Plan area)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Multifamily projects in Spring Lake must make at least 20% of units affordable to and occupied by very low income households plus 10% low income, or alternatively 25% very low income, with a 25% density bonus for complying projects. For-sale projects owe 10% low income units (exempt under 10 units), with land dedication or, only at City initiative for projects under 50 units, an in-lieu fee equal to the appraised affordability gap per unit plus administration. All single-family market-rate units pay an Off-Site Affordable Housing Fee of $1,100 per unit (Council may reset it, not above $1,300), collected before final map approval and spent anywhere in the City on qualifying affordable units; up to 10% may fund administration.
affordability_requirement: Multifamily: 20% very low plus 10% low, or 25% very low income, permanently affordable; for-sale 10% low income for the longest feasible period.
next_deadline: None (specific plan requirement). The Housing Element (Program A.24) proposes amending the Spring Lake Specific Plan to clarify affordability provisions; several Spring Lake single-family projects have paid in-lieu fees under development agreements.
layering_notes: Spring Lake is where most of Woodland's affordable pipeline sits: Mutual Housing at Spring Lake (farmworker, 100 units), a 4.6-acre multifamily site dedicated in 2019 to a nonprofit in place of $900,000 of fees (112 lower income senior units required), and R-20 and R-25 sites intended for 25% very low income projects. A 100% affordable developer can acquire a Spring Lake R-20 or R-25 site and satisfy a market-rate builder's obligation, then draw on Fund 1327 and the off-site fee revenues as gap money. The Plan still names the Redevelopment Agency as fund recipient; the City is housing successor. Chapter 15.16 applies in Spring Lake only where the Specific Plan is silent.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: plan confirms 20% very low plus 10% low or 25% very low, permanent rental affordability, 25% density bonus, 10% low income for-sale (at least 10 years, reset on resale), City-initiated in-lieu fee only for detached for-sale projects under 50 units, and $1,100 Off-Site Affordable Housing Fee (cap $1,300) collected before final map. The stated for-sale exemption under 10 units was not found in the plan text (the attached ordinance applies the rental requirement to projects of 10 or more units). Prevailing wage false is uncited; this is a regulatory requirement with no public funds.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Density bonus ordinance (Woodland Code Sec. 25-21-25, now implemented in Chapter 15.16) with fee waiver and fee deferral incentives
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive. Projects of 5 or more units qualify with 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior housing or 10% moderate income condominiums; base bonus 20% rising 1.5% per 1% of lower income units (2.5% per 1% very low) to a 35% cap under the posted ordinance, and Chapter 15.16 now grants bonuses, concessions, waivers and parking ratios as a matter of right per current Government Code 65915 (up to 50% and unlimited near transit). Listed local incentives include use of local affordable housing funds, waiver or reduction of City building permit, plan check and inspection fees, and waiver or deferral of City impact fees until certificate of occupancy.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, senior or special needs) with covenants of 55 years for rental.
next_deadline: None; request with the planned development, design review or other entitlement application. The Housing Element (Program A.10) commits to keep the ordinance current with state law and to publish a one-page fact sheet.
layering_notes: The fee waiver and impact fee deferral incentives are the city's only fee relief for affordable units and are granted project by project with the density bonus agreement (see the fee deferral record). The 2021 Housing Element found the posted ordinance out of date with Government Code 65915; the ecode360 Chapter 15.16 density bonus section (Ordinance 1662, 2020) is the operative text. Woodland's realistic densities already run near maximums (Spring Lake 101-unit project at 80% of RM density), so the bonus matters most on CMU corridor sites such as Tupelo's CMU-A parcel. City fee waivers are public subsidy and can trigger prevailing wage; impact fee deferrals alone generally do not.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: City PDF of Sec. 25-21-25 matches the 5+ unit thresholds, 20% base with 1.5% and 2.5% steps to 35%, and the listed incentives (local funds, building fee waiver or reduction, impact fee deferral to certificate of occupancy). The posted ordinance sets a 30-year minimum term and a 5% base bonus for moderate condominiums; the record's 55-year rental term follows current Gov. Code 65915(c), which governs via Chapter 15.16 (not re-opened).
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Fee waiver and impact fee deferral are offered as density bonus incentives; the density bonus itself provides no public funds (1720(a)(1)). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Development Impact Fee Deferral Program (MPFP fee deferral for multifamily, December 2008 ordinance) and case-by-case deferrals for affordable projects
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department and Administrative Services (Finance)
typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver. Under Ordinance No. 1690 (adopted June 21, 2022, no expiration date) residential infill projects (single-family or multifamily on vacant or underutilized parcels in urbanized areas) may defer ten City impact and capacity fees (General City, Library, Police, Water Capacity, Roads, Administration, Storm Drain, Fire, Wastewater, Parks) under a recorded fee deferral agreement and lien; deferred fees are due at the earlier of the final inspection request or 12 months, at the rate in effect at permit issuance. Spring Lake Infrastructure Fees, permit and plan check fees and non-City fees are not deferrable. Approval by the City Manager or Council depending on amount. The Council has also approved case-by-case interest-free deferral to just before certificate of occupancy for affordable projects (Housing Element). The Prohousing application cites Vista Del Robles (72 units, 2024) as a user.
affordability_requirement: None for the general program; affordable projects may also get case-by-case Council deferrals.
next_deadline: Rolling, no deadline as of November 8, 2026. Apply through Community Development, (530) 661-5820.
layering_notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but is not a subsidy; combine with the density bonus fee waiver incentive and Fund 1327 loans. Woodland was designated Prohousing by HCD in 2025 (application March 21, 2025), which adds Prohousing points in state programs. Spring Lake has its own financing plan; Spring Lake Infrastructure Fees cannot be deferred.
cycle_notes: Ongoing program; apply to Community Development before permit issuance. Ordinance 1690 has no sunset (replaced the 2008 program that ran through June 30, 2022).
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts fees, loans or interest rates normally required that are reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven as public funds; an interest-free deferral of impact fees may fall within that language, and the deferral guidelines (Ordinance 1690) state no wage term. Coverage depends on the deferral terms, other public funds and 1720(c), including the 1720(c)(3)(B) de minimis test and 1720(c)(1) for private projects on private property. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: false was not supported by a rule; 1720(b)(4) may reach fee deferrals, changed to unclear.

program_name: CDBG entitlement program (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, annual Action Plan NOFA) and PLHA formula allocation
