The June 15, 2026 Transportation Mitigation Fee update (effective August 14, 2026) and the pending Park Impact Fee nexus study (hearing continued from May 18 to June 15, 2026) will set the fee base against which any waiver is measured.
affordability_requirement: Not codified in the documents read; waivers have been granted to 100% affordable projects on request. Program 36 commits the City to reduce fee burdens for affordable housing projects where possible by December 31, 2025 and is reported as in progress.
next_deadline: Request with the entitlement or building permit application; Council action required. Watch the Park Impact Fee adoption and any affordable housing exemption written into it (2026 to 2027).
layering_notes: Waived fees count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), so model prevailing wage on any waiver. Combined with the Trust Fund and County money this is a modest layer; the City is counting Program 36 and Resolution 11025 toward its Prohousing Designation points. Resolution 11025 and Resolution 14983 were not opened (the City's Laserfiche portal refused connections); terms come from the 2025 Annual Progress Report, the 2026 Prohousing draft application and Resolution 14891 Section H, all opened. marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. A waived or reduced fee that would normally be required is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(3) treats a subsidy as de minimis (so the project is not a public work on that basis) when it is under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost, and 1720(c)(5) exemptions can apply. The 2025 Annual Progress Report (https://storage.googleapis.com/proudcity/sanrafael/2026/07/3.b-general-plan-and-housing-element-annual-progress-reports.pdf) states no prevailing wage rule for Resolution 11025 waivers or the traffic mitigation fee exemption.

program_name: Prohousing Designation application (Resolution of October 5, 2026) and Prohousing Incentive Pilot eligibility
administering_agency: City of San Rafael Community and Economic Development Department (Greg Minor, (415) 680-4707, greg.minor@sanrafael.gov)
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. Designation gives City-sponsored projects scoring priority in AHSC, IIG, TCC, SCCP, LPP, TIRCP and STPG and lets the City apply to HCD's Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP); the staff report notes the smallest award in the most recent PIP round was $315,762.38 and that no Marin jurisdiction held the designation as of August 10, 2026. Draft application posted for public review October 9 to November 8, 2026, then submitted to HCD, which has 60 days to decide; designation lasts three years.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable. The City commits to implement Housing Element Programs 19 (City-owned lots), 20 (North San Rafael Precise Plan), 25 (Objective Design Standards), 36 (fee reductions for affordable housing) and 43 (parking standards) to keep its score.
next_deadline: HCD decision expected by early 2027 (60 days after formal submittal following the comment period that closed November 8, 2026). Check for a PIP NOFA in 2027.
layering_notes: If approved, San Rafael becomes the only Prohousing jurisdiction in Marin, which matters for AHSC and IIG scoring on transit-adjacent sites like Northgate and Downtown. PIP funds would likely be routed through the City's Affordable Housing Trust Fund process. Staff report and draft application PDFs opened on the City site.
cycle_notes: HCD PIP rounds once designated
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) requires construction paid for out of public funds. Prohousing Designation is a scoring preference that pays no funds to a project, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage; wage obligations come only from the funding programs used. Prohousing Incentive Pilot awards routed to projects would be tested as public funds.

program_name: Novato Affordable Housing Requirements (inclusionary), Novato Municipal Code Division 19.24 (Ordinances 1576, 1676 and 1718), with in-lieu fees to the City housing fund
administering_agency: City of Novato Community Development Department, 922 Machin Avenue, Novato, (415) 899-8989
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu fee amounts are set by Council resolution (not published on the code mirror); fees are paid before building permit issuance into a separate City fund earmarked for very low, low and moderate income housing (19.24.040). Council approval of an in-lieu payment is discretionary for projects of 7 or more units and by right for 3 to 6 unit projects and for fractions below 0.70.
affordability_requirement: Sliding scale by project size: 3 to 10 units 10%, then one percentage point per unit from 11 units (11%) to 20 or more units (20%). Rental projects: half of the required units at 50% AMI rents and half at 60% AMI rents (very low and low income). Ownership: half low income (65% AMI pricing) and half moderate income (90% AMI pricing). Fractions of 0.70 or more round up. Affordable units restricted for a minimum of 99 years from first occupancy (rental) or first sale (ownership) unless state law requires a shorter term (19.24.070E), through a recorded Inclusionary Housing Agreement; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units. Exempt: ADUs and JADUs, residential care facilities for the elderly, single or two-unit projects with homes of 3,000 square feet or less, and AHO overlay projects that meet the overlay's 20% requirement.
next_deadline: Ordinance 1718 (Sept 10, 2024) was the latest amendment read. Confirm the current in-lieu fee resolution and any Housing Element Program 3.F (Evaluate and Adjust Impact Fees) follow-up with the Planning Division.

program_name: Novato Affordable Housing Fund (inclusionary in-lieu fee fund) gap financing and development fee waivers for affordable projects
administering_agency: City of Novato Community Development Department, 922 Machin Avenue, Novato, (415) 899-8989
typical_award_size: No published guidelines or NOFA. The Affordable Housing Programs Fund (Fund 210) receives in-lieu fees, BMR resale and monitoring fees and interest, and mainly pays for BMR program administration, with occasional project support: past loans to Eden Housing ($1,500,000), Homeward Bound Oma Village ($600,000) and Habitat northwest quad ($427,438). For Habitat for Humanity's 80-unit Redwood Boulevard ownership project the Council granted $350,000 for development impact fees plus waivers of several City fees (March 14, 2023) and a further grant of up to $1,000,000 ($800,000 from Fund 210 plus $200,000 transferred from the General Fund) for processing fees (March 11, 2025). Staff projected a Fund 210 balance of $1,132,422 at June 30, 2025, leaving about $332,422 for other projects after reserving $650,000 for BMR buybacks, and said the fund no longer has large balances because developers build inclusionary units on site.

next_deadline: No open round; requests go to Council through the Community Development Department as of November 8, 2026.
layering_notes: Treat as a small, negotiated gap or fee-offset source, roughly $1,000,000 per project at most and limited by a low fund balance; mainly useful to meet the Marin County Affordable Housing Fund requirement that cities waive fees and provide a local match. CDBG and HOME for Novato flow through the Marin Urban County planning area, and Novato supplies PLHA match for its planning area. audit_note: novato.gov still 403; the March 11, 2025 Council agenda and staff report on novato.granicus.com were read and correct the prior figures ($350,000, not $1,000,000, in 2023; the $1,000,000 in 2025 was a grant, not fee reductions). Local loans and grants are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) and (b)(5) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market interest rate loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (applied to an NPLH loan in DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf), and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidies (under $600,000 and under 2 percent of project cost). program_name: Mill Valley Affordable Housing Trust Fund (MVMC 20.80.070, Ordinance 1295, Resolution 20-26 Administrative Guidelines, Resolution 24-60 Local Housing Trust Fund match)
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department (Danielle Staude, dstaude@cityofmillvalley.org), with Housing Advisory Committee priorities and City Council approval of every award
typical_award_size: Funded by the 1% affordable housing impact fee on residential permits at or above the construction valuation threshold ($142,000 since May 1, 2024) plus inclusionary in-lieu payments and donations; collections were $345,000 by Feb 2020, roughly $300,000 a year per the Housing Element and about $600,000 a year per the 2024 Annual Progress Report, with about $1,000,000 unencumbered in 2024. Resolution 24-60 (Sept 5, 2024) committed $1,000,000 of Trust Fund match for an HCD Local Housing Trust Fund application ($1,200,000 requested; HCD's Round 5 applicant list shows the City with a self-score of 60) so that $2,400,000 total would be available: $1,000,000 ($500,000 grant plus $500,000 match) for Bayfront Terrace at 1 Hamilton Drive and $1,400,000 for other projects to be solicited. Loans at simple interest of no more than 3% as construction or deferred-payment permanent financing; up to 5% administration. Ongoing uses: Marin Housing Authority BMR administration, Home Match contract (up to $30,000 a year), Bayfront Terrace predevelopment, and the Lease to Locals pilot ($3,500 to $14,000 per converted rental, running through 2027).
per_unit_cap: None published; LHTF-matched funds must put at least 30% toward extremely low income (30% AMI) units and no more than 20% toward 80% AMI units, with the remainder at or below 60% AMI.
affordability_requirement: Low income households per Chapter 20.80 covenants; LHTF-matched awards target 60% AMI and below with a 30% extremely low income set-aside. Projects must be inside Mill Valley, scored on feasibility, funding needed, unit count and location outside the very high fire severity zone. Council approves each award at a public hearing. The City adopted HCD's Uniform Multifamily Regulations for underwriting.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The City said it would announce a solicitation in early 2025 contingent on the HCD LHTF award; no award or solicitation was found on the City site as of November 2026, and the 2028 Mitigation Fee Act five-year review and impact fee extension decision are the next fixed milestones.
layering_notes: Mill Valley's fund is unusually well capitalized for a 14,000-person city because the 1% fee hits every large remodel; it is the only Marin priority city with a committed state LHTF match strategy. Money has gone almost entirely to the City's own site (Bayfront Terrace, EAH Housing, 45 units) and to tenure programs, so a third-party developer should expect the $1,400,000 remainder and future fee receipts (about $600,000 a year) as the ceiling. Layer under the Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (the County awarded 1 Hamilton $500,000 in 2022 and $1,000,000 total by 2024 per County documents cited in search results, not opened), County HOME ($360,000 to the Eden Housing Mill Valley rental project in FY 2026-27, see County record) and PLHA; CDBG and HOME flow through the Marin Urban County. City loans are public funds for prevailing wage. program_name: Mill Valley Affordable Housing Requirements: inclusionary units and affordable housing impact fee, MVMC Chapter 20.80 (Ordinance 1295 of 2017, inclusionary update adopted 2026 under Housing Element Programs 7 and 11)
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Impact fee: 1% of construction valuation on single-family and small multifamily residential work at or above the valuation threshold ($100,000 in 2018, $105,000 in 2020, $130,000 in 2023, $142,000 from May 1, 2024, indexed to the California Construction Cost Index), paid at building permit into the Affordable Housing Trust Fund; collection was extended five years by Council resolution on March 20, 2023. The 2026 update lowered the inclusionary requirement from 25% to 15%, exempted 2 to 6 unit projects from building affordable units and waived their impact fee when units stay under 850 square feet (one bedroom), 1,000 (two bedrooms) or 1,200 (three bedrooms), and eliminated micro-unit caps. Fractional units of 0.50 or more may be met by an in-lieu payment calculated by applying the fraction to the impact fee formula.
affordability_requirement: Projects of 7 to 9 units: 15% affordable with at least one unit for moderate income households. Projects of 10 or more units: 15% affordable, at least half of the affordable units for low income households and the rest moderate income. Rental affordable units restricted in perpetuity or the maximum term allowed by law (20.80.060). Exempt: ADUs, micro units, projects below the valuation threshold, projects vested before November 1, 2018. Off-site units, land dedication or acquisition-rehabilitation alternatives at the City's sole discretion; Chapter 20.80.080 allows reducing moderate income unit counts when units are instead restricted to very low or low income.
next_deadline: Threshold adjusts each calendar year. Housing Element Program 11 requires a further look at inclusionary ratios at the 2028 RHNA mid-point; Program 12 calls for considering a commercial linkage fee and single-family impact fee changes with other Marin jurisdictions.
layering_notes: The 2026 drop from 25% to 15% (half low, half moderate) brings Mill Valley below Novato (20%) and the County (20%) and closer to San Rafael's 5% to 10%; combined with the Housing Overlay Districts (17 to 40 units per acre) it is meant to make 7-plus unit infill feasible on commercial corridors. The impact fee is the engine of the Trust Fund record above; no commercial linkage fee exists yet. The 2026 ordinance PDF (Attachment 1, as adopted per the City zoning updates page), the Zoneomics mirror of Chapter 20.80, the 2024 APR and the Housing Element were opened; the City's eCode360 host was not needed.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Mill Valley development fee waivers for affordable housing (MVMC 5.32 as amended October 3, 2022, Housing Element Programs 14 and 23) and lot merger fee waiver in the Opportunity Site Housing Overlay
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department; City Council resolution for waivers

Separately, MVMC 5.32 provides a 50% reduction in City fees, licenses and taxes for units affordable to and occupied by lower and moderate income households. Lot merger fees are waived for projects using the Opportunity Site Housing Overlay (2024 overlay ordinance). Affordable projects are also exempt from the Chapter 20.80 impact fee. Dollar value depends on the City fee schedule.
affordability_requirement: At least 10% of units for very low or extremely low income households and operation by an affordable housing organization; the City also may consider a fee waiver program for ADUs under Program 30.
next_deadline: Request at application. Confirm the exact MVMC 5.32 threshold (very low versus extremely low) with Planning before underwriting; the two City documents read describe it differently.
layering_notes: A processing-fee waiver is worth tens of thousands of dollars on a Mill Valley project, not a gap closer, but it counts as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Stack with the Trust Fund, the housing overlays and State Density Bonus. Mill Valley's title 5 code text was not opened (eCode360 not attempted); terms come from the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element Chapter 4 (opened), the 2024 Annual Progress Report (opened) and the overlay ordinance (opened). marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.
audit_note: Link redirect is only a filename slug. Housing Element Chapter IV also states the 50% MVMC 5.32 reduction for lower and moderate income units, which the record omitted. PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true changed to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. A waived or reduced fee that would normally be required is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(3) treats a subsidy as de minimis (so the project is not a public work on that basis) when it is under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost, and 1720(c)(5) exemptions can apply. The certified Housing Element (https://www.cityofmillvalley.gov/DocumentCenter/View/7984) states no prevailing wage term for the fee waivers.

program_name: Mill Valley Density Bonus (MVMC Chapter 20.81) and Housing Overlay Zoning Districts (Small Lot, Office Conversion and Opportunity Site overlays, 2024 ordinance)
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: Requirement framework, not a cash subsidy. Chapter 20.81 applies Government Code 65915 by reference (bonus, incentives, waivers, parking ratios; senior projects get no concessions unless state law requires). The 2024 Housing Overlay Districts, applied on top of base zoning to Housing Element sites, allow 17 to 40 units per acre (20 to 40 in the Opportunity Site overlay), 40-foot height, one parking space for units of 1,000 square feet or less, waived lot merger fees, and let projects also use State Density Bonus to modify standards; projects reserving 20% of units for lower income households get streamlined review. Affordable units in overlay projects follow Chapter 20.80 deed restriction rules. Bayfront Terrace (45 units) was rezoned to RM-B and approved as a 100% affordable project using density bonus incentives but not the density increase.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds for Chapter 20.81; overlay projects must meet Chapter 20.80 inclusionary (15% since 2026) or provide 20% lower income units for the streamlined path. Density bonus affordability covenants recorded before building permit (20.81.050).
next_deadline: None. The 2026 inclusionary ordinance also updated the Opportunity Site overlay to the 15% standard and removed micro-unit restrictions; parking standards were updated November 3, 2025.
layering_notes: Mill Valley's overlays are the practical density path because base multifamily zoning is scarce; combine overlay density with the State bonus, the 15% inclusionary rule and the Trust Fund. No local bonus exceeds state law. Overlay ordinance (DocumentCenter 7829) and the Zoneomics mirror of Chapter 20.81 were opened; the City's eCode360 host was not attempted.
prevailing_wage_basis: Density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of development standards, not public funds; Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) covers only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011, Gov. Code 65912.130). The 2024 Housing Overlay ordinance (https://www.cityofmillvalley.gov/DocumentCenter/View/7829) waives lot merger fees for Opportunity Site projects; that waiver is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) but is de minimis under 1720(c)(3) (under $600,000 and under 2 percent of project cost) on any realistic project.

program_name: Concord Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Concord Development Code Chapter 18.185.040, Ord. 24-1) and in-lieu fee (Fees and Charges Schedule, Res. 26-6042.1)
administering_agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Sophia Huckabay, Housing Manager, 925-671-3387) with the Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 5 or more units: ownership projects 15% inclusionary (7.5% low, 7.5% moderate); rental projects 6% inclusionary (1% very low, 1% low, 4% moderate), with a fixed rotation order for each inclusionary unit. In-lieu fee effective July 1, 2026 (adjusted annually by a construction cost index): $20.13 per gross square foot of market-rate development for ownership projects and $15.10 per gross square foot for rental projects of 10 or more units; fractional-unit fee $256,497 x fractional unit (ownership) and $174,160 x fractional unit (rental). Rental projects may pay the fee for the whole obligation; ownership projects may pay only for fractional units or for 5 to 9 unit projects. In the five years before the 2023 Housing Element the City collected only about $170,000 in in-lieu fees.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted 55 years and ownership units 45 years under a recorded Affordable Housing Agreement; density bonus units meeting the table income levels count toward the inclusionary requirement; projects of 1 to 4 units, replacement of units lost to natural disaster, and office-to-residential conversions of buildings commercial for at least 5 years are exempt.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee rate in effect at building permit. Fee schedule last adopted April 28, 2026 (Res. 26-6042.1) effective July 1, 2026; the schedule is readopted each spring. Housing Element Program 12.4 called for a fee update by July 2024, which produced the March 14, 2024 fee basis now indexed annually.
layering_notes: Low rental percentage (6%) and a relatively low rental in-lieu fee ($15.10 per square foot) mean most Concord apartment projects either build a handful of moderate-income units or pay the fee; this is why the City's inclusionary fund is small relative to Walnut Creek's. In-lieu revenue goes to a restricted fund alongside the Concord Housing Fund (see the Concord Affordable Housing Fund record). Chapter 18.185.040(G) also lets the City grant development incentives, including deferral of development fees until first occupancy (approved by the City Manager) and expedited processing, when an affordable housing agreement is signed. County Chapter 822-4 inclusionary ordinance does not apply inside Concord. codepublishing.com (the City's code host) returns 403 to automated access; chapter text was read on the zoneomics mirror (https://www.zoneomics.com/code/concord-CA/chapter_4) and the City's 2024 Inclusionary Housing Ordinance Summary Sheet (https://www.cityofconcord.org/DocumentCenter/View/13659). Fee amounts were read from the adopted July 1, 2026 fee schedule (source_url).
eligible_project_detail: market-rate rental and ownership projects of 5 or more units (compliance)
off-site acquisition-rehab (2 rehabilitated units per required unit)
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: fee schedule (Res. 26-6042.1, adopted April 28, 2026) matches in-lieu fees $20.13 and $15.10 per gross sq ft and fractional fees $256,497 and $174,160; Summary Sheet matches 15% ownership and 6% rental splits and exemptions. prevailing_wage_trigger false has no cited rule in prevailing_wage_basis (regulatory requirement, no public funds); cite a basis when available.

This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

typical_award_size: Housing Successor fund at June 30, 2025: available cash $3,063,558; FY 2024/25 deposits $1,020,949 (including a $615,049 Pavilion loan repayment and $222,705 in loan payoffs); FY 2024/25 expenditures $596,214 (mostly $334,957 in first-time homebuyer loans; no multifamily loan issued); housing loans receivable $33.9 million. The City's Resources for Housing Developers page points developers first to County Measure X and HCD. program_name: Concord Affordable Housing Incentive Program (CDC 18.185.060), Density Bonus Program (CDC 18.185.050) and Transit Station Overlay density increase
administering_agency: City of Concord Community Development Department, Planning Division (zoning@cityofconcord.org, 925-671-3152)
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Local alternative to state density bonus law for projects with at least 40% affordable units on parcels of 10,000 square feet or more in RM, RH, CO, NC, CMX, DMX and DP districts: RM density rises from 32 to about 45 units per acre (1 unit per 970 square feet, a 40% bonus), RH from 100 to about 145 units per acre (45% bonus), NC from 24 to about 33 units per acre plus FAR increases; reduced parking and other standard modifications; bonuses under 18.185.060 are not additive with 18.185.050. Separately, the Transit Station Overlay District grants a 25% density and floor area increase (Housing Element program to make it by right with objective standards). State-law density bonuses (Gov. Code 65915) are processed by the Community Development Department under 18.185.050; written findings are required to deny; an affordable housing agreement is recorded before building permit.
affordability_requirement: 18.185.060 rental eligibility: at least 20% of units at very low income plus another 20% at low or very low income (40% total); for-sale: 20% at low or very low plus 20% at up to 100% AMI. 18.185.050 follows state density bonus thresholds.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; no deadline. Concord completed its AFFH rezoning (at least 1,000 lower-income units of capacity in higher-resource areas) in March 2026 and allows multifamily by right in commercial and mixed-use districts when objective design standards are met.
layering_notes: The 40% affordability threshold for the local incentive program is high, so most mixed-income projects use state density bonus law instead; 100% affordable projects (which qualify for an 80% state bonus or unlimited density near transit) get the most value from the local program's FAR and parking relief in downtown districts. No City fee waiver program exists; fee deferral to first occupancy is available under 18.185.040(G) by affordable housing agreement. Pair with the County's conduit bond issuer and HACCC project-based vouchers (county records). codepublishing.com returned 403; chapter text read on the zoneomics mirror (source_url) and confirmed against the City's Affordable Housing Toolkit page.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this incentive and density bonus program provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any City or County loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on the project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 The record notes fee deferral to first occupancy is available; a deferral is not itself a reduction or waiver, but any fee waiver or City funds would be assessed under 1720(b)(4).

program_name: Concord CDBG entitlement and Contra Costa Consortium three-year NOFA (FY 2027/28 to 2029/30)
administering_agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Sophia Huckabay, sophia.huckabay@cityofconcord.org) within the Contra Costa HOME Consortium
typical_award_size: Concord is a CDBG entitlement city. Its FY 2026/27 Action Plan (Expected Resources table) shows a CDBG annual allocation of $967,306 plus $23,392 program income and $214,094 prior-year resources, $1,204,792 total, and about $1,000,000 a year expected over the 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan; the City also has a small housing rehabilitation revolving loan fund and $88,200 of Cannabis Community Benefit Funds (non-housing). Concord's HOME share is pooled in the County-administered Contra Costa HOME Consortium (Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg, Walnut Creek and the Urban County). The Consortium released the FY 2027/28 CDBG and ESG RFP/NOFA on October 15, 2026 through City Data Services for a three-year cycle FY 2027/28 through 2029/30 (Concord awards are for FY 2027/28 with possible renewal through FY 2030); one joint application serves all five jurisdictions. Concord uses CDBG for public services, homeowner rehabilitation (including Habitat for Humanity's rehabilitation program), fair housing and public facilities, and requires a 20% match on CDBG projects; housing development is funded from the City's own funds.
affordability_requirement: CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit, 80% AMI); HOME requests go through the County (55-year County regulatory agreement).
next_deadline: Applications due Monday, December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM via City Data Services; Concord Council adopts the FY 2027/28 Action Plan in April or May 2027 for a July 1, 2027 program year.
layering_notes: For multifamily development, treat Concord CDBG as minor (rehab, fair housing and public facility set-asides) and apply to the County for HOME and Measure X (county record: Contra Costa County Affordable Housing Program: HOME and CDBG-Housing). Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-assisted projects of 8 or more units and HOME projects of 12 or more. Audit November 8, 2026: NOFA dates and the December 7, 2026 5:00 PM deadline read on Concord's Community Grants page and the Antioch Community Grants page; the $967,306 allocation read in the City's FY 2026/27 Action Plan (https://www.cityofconcord.org/DocumentCenter/View/15404).
cycle_notes: three-year cycle; applications due December 7, 2026
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Concord Naval Weapons Station Reuse Project affordable housing requirement (Concord Reuse Project Area Plan, 2012; 2026 Navy EDC Term Sheet; Brookfield master developer)
administering_agency: City of Concord Economic Development and Base Reuse Division, acting as Local Reuse Authority (1950 Parkside Drive MS/56, 925-671-3001)
typical_award_size: Requirement and future land pipeline, not a current subsidy. The Area Plan and Reuse Plan call for about 12,000 housing units on roughly 2,300 to 2,400 acres, of which 25% (about 3,000 units) must be affordable to low and very low income households, including 125 supportive housing units, 195 units for people experiencing homelessness and 20 self-help units. The Council approved the Navy financial Term Sheet and revised Brookfield Term Sheet on May 26, 2026 (reported Navy price $628 million over 30 years); the Navy executed the Economic Development Conveyance Term Sheet in September 2026; SB 328 (2026) was signed; Brookfield is now preparing the Specific Plan with community engagement starting early 2027.
affordability_requirement: 25% of all units affordable to low and very low income households per the Area Plan; specific income tiers, phasing and affordable-site delivery mechanics will be set in the Specific Plan and Disposition and Development Agreement.
next_deadline: No affordable developer solicitation yet. Brookfield-led Specific Plan work starts winter 2026-27; first phase entitlements likely 2028 or later. Monitor concordreuseproject.org news flashes and the semiannual CRP Program Report.
layering_notes: The largest single affordable pipeline in central Contra Costa (about 3,000 deed-restricted units over three decades), delivered through Brookfield's affordable-site dedications to nonprofit partners rather than City cash; Brookfield also has a project labor agreement with the Contra Costa Building Trades, so prevailing or union wages should be assumed on the affordable sites. Nonprofit developers should position for receiver-site selection and plan to layer County Measure X and HOME, HACCC project-based vouchers and 4% credits on each phase. The 25% figure and homeless and supportive sub-allocations were read in the City's certified Housing Element Programs Document (source_url); the term sheet milestone was read on the Concord Community Reuse Project site (http://www.concordreuseproject.org/m/newsflash/home/detail/95).
cycle_notes: future pipeline; Specific Plan expected 2027 or later
prevailing_wage_basis: The 25 percent affordability requirement itself provides no public funds (Labor Code 1720(a)(1), https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). Affordable sites are dedicated through the master developer from former Navy land conveyed to the City, so a dedication or conveyance below fair market value can be public funds under 1720(b)(3); coverage turns on the transfer terms and 1720(c). Separately, Brookfield has a project labor agreement with the Contra Costa Building Trades, a private contract rather than a statutory wage rule.

administering_agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division and Planning Division (surplus land inventory, Housing Element sites program)

A land write-down is public funds under 1720(b)(3), but coverage depends on 1720(c) exemptions and deal facts; the Surplus Land Act affordability section (Gov. Code 54233) contains no wage term. https://california.public.law/codes/government_code_section_54233

program_name: Richmond Inclusionary Housing and Affordable Housing Linkage Fee Ordinance (Richmond Municipal Code Article 15.04.603, readopted 2020) and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Richmond Community Development Department, Housing Division (Jesus Morales, Housing Manager, 510-620-6649) and Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential and mixed-use projects of 10 or more units. Compliance options: for-sale projects 7% of units at low income or 10% at moderate income; rental projects 9% at very low income or 10% at low income. The in-lieu fee is per square foot and geographically tiered, $0 to $12 per square foot (rental projects south of I-580 and on the Point San Pablo peninsula pay $12 per square foot; market-rate projects north of I-580 are exempt from on-site units and the fee after a 2020 feasibility study); for-sale projects south of I-580 and on Point San Pablo must build units and may not pay the fee. A non-residential affordable housing linkage fee was authorized in the same 2020 update. Collections: $803,055 in-lieu fees in calendar 2020 and $677,194 in 2021. Other alternatives: 10% very low income rental units in a for-sale project, off-site construction, or land dedication yielding at least 10% more units than required.
affordability_requirement: 45-year affordability for for-sale inclusionary units and 55 years for rental units under a recorded Inclusionary Housing Agreement; incentives include the Article 15.04.602 density bonus, clustering of units where a funding source requires it, and smaller or different unit types if at least 5% more affordable units result.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee due per the Inclusionary Housing Agreement. Housing Element Program 2.A called for reassessment of the ordinance and linkage fee by first quarter 2024 and any amendments by third quarter 2025, with annual performance reports; confirm with the Housing Division whether amendments were adopted.
layering_notes: Richmond's 2020 rewrite deliberately lowered requirements north of I-580 (Hilltop, North Richmond edge) to make market-rate housing feasible, so most inclusionary units and fees come from the south side (Marina Bay, downtown, Point San Pablo). Fees and linkage revenue fund the City Affordable Housing Fund (separate record). Richmond's Rent Program (Measure L, 2016) caps rent increases on pre-1995 multifamily and sets just-cause rules, which affects underwriting of acquisition-rehab deals. program_name: Antioch Housing Element incentives for lower-income housing (Programs 2.1.6, 2.1.7 and 4.1.3: fee support, land write-downs, expedited processing, density bonus ordinance)
administering_agency: City of Antioch Community Development Department, Planning Division, with CDBG and Housing Programs staff
typical_award_size: Regulatory and discretionary incentives, not a funded program. The certified 2023-2031 Housing Element (HCD certification October 12, 2023) commits the City to encourage extremely low income housing through targeted developer outreach, financial or in-kind technical assistance, fee support, land write-downs and expedited or priority processing, and to offer incentives supplementing state density bonus law (quantified objective: 175 ELI units); to meet at least three nonprofit developers annually and support funding applications; and to keep the density bonus ordinance consistent with state law (Program 4.1.3). Rezoning under the Housing Element raises many sites to 35 units per acre, and the Commercial Infill Housing (CIH) Overlay allows housing on commercial sites. No adopted fee waiver schedule exists; the proposed inclusionary ordinance expressly excluded fee waivers.
affordability_requirement: Case by case; state density bonus thresholds apply; City incentives target extremely low, very low and low income and special needs housing.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; no deadline. Housing Element program review occurs with each Annual Progress Report (April).
layering_notes: Antioch has no local fee waiver ordinance, housing trust fund or in-lieu fund, so these Housing Element commitments are the only local incentives beyond state density bonus law; developers should negotiate fee deferrals, land contributions from the City's surplus list (largest parcel about 5 acres, per the Consolidated Plan) and Housing Successor or PLHA gap loans as part of entitlement. Density bonus and incentives stack with County HOME, Measure X and HACCC PBVs (county records). Programs read from the certified Housing Element Goals, Policies and Programs chapter on the civicplus mirror (source_url) because antiochca.gov returns 403.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Housing Element Programs 2.1.6, 2.1.7 and 4.1.3 contemplate fee support and land write-downs (below-market transfers are public funds under 1720(b)(3)); the density bonus and expedited processing provide no public funds. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Walnut Creek Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Zoning Code Article 9, Sections 10-2.3.903 et seq., amended November 2017) and housing in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing Programs), Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all residential development of one or more units except ADUs and disaster replacement units. New ownership projects: 10% moderate, or 7% low, or 6% very low income units, or pay the in-lieu fee (ownership projects of any size may pay the fee). New rental projects: 10% low or 6% very low income units, or pay the fee (rental units restored after AB 1505). Condominium conversions: 15% low or 11% very low. Fractions of 0.7 or more round up; partial fee payment allowed pro rata; blended income levels allowed. In-lieu fee reset to $18.00 per square foot effective January 1, 2018 with annual construction-price-index adjustments ($19.27 in 2021; about $26.04 per square foot in 2026 per the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide comparison). Walnut Creek Transit Village alone paid over $4 million in in-lieu fees and is expected to generate $6 to 7 million for the City's Housing Trust Fund.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units affordable 55 years and ownership units 45 years; units dispersed on site with the same bedroom mix and comparable quality; one-for-one replacement of demolished low-income units built within 30 years.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee indexed each January. Housing Element Program H-2.D (6th cycle) continues the ordinance and contemplates an updated nexus study; confirm the current per square foot fee with the Housing Division (brynen@walnutcreekca.gov).

administering_agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing and Community Service Grants); contact brynen@walnutcreekca.gov
typical_award_size: Walnut Creek is a CDBG entitlement city in the Contra Costa HOME Consortium. The 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan estimates $2.12 million in federal resources over five years (PY 2025-26 CDBG entitlement estimated around $350,000 to $400,000) plus $4.14 million in general and local funds through the Community Services Grant and Homeless Services Fund; the five-year goal table programs CDBG of $100,000 to $500,000 per goal with $500,000 of local funds per year for several goals and $2.5 million for affordable housing (AH-1). Historically the City sets aside part of CDBG for the Home Rehabilitation Loan and Emergency Grant Program. Awards are competitive on the Consortium's two- and three-year cycle; the FY 2027/28 to 2029/30 NOFA was released October 15, 2026.
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI national objective; Walnut Creek has nine low and moderate income block groups (census tracts 3390.01, 3400.01, 3511.01 to 3511.05) prioritized for area-benefit activities.
next_deadline: Consortium applications due December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM via City Data Services; Walnut Creek Council adopts its PY 2027-28 Annual Action Plan in May 2027 (the PY 2026-27 plan hearing was May 5, 2026).
layering_notes: Walnut Creek's CDBG is small (under $500,000 a year) and mostly funds services and rehab; for development, the City's Local Housing Trust Fund RFP (separate record) and County HOME or Measure X (county records) carry the weight, with HOME requests filed through the same Consortium application the County administers. Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-assisted projects of 8 or more units. Consolidated Plan read from the County-hosted copy (source_url); Consortium NOFA dates and the Walnut Creek contact were read on the City of Antioch's Community Grants page (https://ca-antioch.civicplus.com/993/Community-Grants) because walnutcreekca.gov returns 403.
cycle_notes: three-year cycle; applications due December 7, 2026
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: San Ramon Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Ordinance 520, adopted October 24, 2023; San Ramon Municipal Code Sections C4-175 to C4-183) and Affordable Housing Fund (C4-180)
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division (Lauren Barr, Director; Planning@sanramon.ca.gov, 925-973-2560)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all residential projects of 2 or more units (ADUs excluded). Projects of 2 to 9 units (for-sale or rental) may pay an affordable housing fee equal to 25% of total new livable square footage times the per square foot rate in the City Fee Resolution (about $15.16 per square foot per the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide comparison). For-sale projects of 10 or more units (single-family and multifamily) must build 15% affordable units allocated 20% very low, 30% low and 50% moderate income (must-build added in 2023). Rental projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half very low and half low income. Alternatives (C4-179): voluntary rental units in a for-sale project, off-site construction within San Ramon, preservation of at-risk units with 55-year extensions, land dedication (fully improved with impact fees paid) or combinations. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Fund with an annual report to Council on balance and commitments; the balance was $4.28 million as of March 3, 2022.
affordability_requirement: 55-year affordability (raised from 30 years in 2023) for rental and for-sale units, renewed for 55 years on each resale; resale price capped at purchase price grown by AMI; City first right of refusal on affordable ownership units.
next_deadline: Applies at first approval with an Affordable Housing Plan; Affordable Housing Agreement before final map or building permit. Housing Element Program 8 scheduled a 2024 review of the inclusionary and commercial linkage fee structure; the Council heard a FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule and nexus study update in March 2026, so confirm the current per square foot rate with Planning Services.
layering_notes: San Ramon's 15% rental requirement with half the units at very low income is the deepest in the county among the priority cities and, combined with Bishop Ranch's build-out, produces receiver-site deals: the Canopy (BR 8) Affordable Site Development Agreement introduced January 13, 2026 (Ordinance 536, adopted January 27, 2026) has Sunset Development dedicating a rough-graded site with impact fees paid to Eden Housing for 161 affordable units that absorb the inclusionary obligations of 255 Canopy single-family homes (raised from 15% to 22.5%) and the CityWalk apartments, plus $3,000 per market-rate unit (about $765,000) paid into the Affordable Housing Fund. Dougherty Valley affordable units (Highlands Point, Muirlands, Seville, Valencia, Cornerstone at Gale Ranch and others, about 1,886 affordable units citywide) are governed by Contra Costa County affordability agreements under the Dougherty Valley Settlement Agreement and the County's Chapter 822-4, not this ordinance, and several 20-year moderate-income agreements expire in 2026. Ordinance text read at source_url; the Canopy staff report was read on the City's IQM2 agenda host (https://sanramonca.iqm2.com/Citizens/Detail_LegiFile.aspx?ID=4882).
eligible_project_detail: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 2 or more units (compliance)
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: San Ramon Affordable Housing Commercial Linkage Fee (Inclusionary Housing and Commercial Linkage Ordinance, April 2019) and Affordable Housing Fund
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. A per square foot fee on net new gross floor area of all new commercial construction, including the commercial portion of mixed-use projects, regardless of zoning; exempt: projects adding 5,000 square feet or less, schools and places of public assembly, public facilities, and like-for-like replacement of buildings destroyed by calamity. Developers may instead build affordable units on an appropriate site, dedicate land or provide other housing resources. Mixed-use developments that meet the inclusionary policy are exempt from in-lieu fees. Fees are deposited into the City's Affordable Housing Fund ($4.28 million as of March 3, 2022, before Canopy and other recent payments). The per square foot rate is set in the Master Fee Schedule and was not found on an opened page.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable to the payer; the fund supports very low (including extremely low), low and moderate income rental and ownership housing in San Ramon.
next_deadline: Applies at building permit. Housing Element Program 8 called for a 2024 review of the linkage fee structure to reflect affordable construction costs; the Council considered updated nexus fee studies with the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule in March 2026 (confirm adopted rate).
layering_notes: Bishop Ranch and the City Center office base make this the City's steady fund source; the Affordable Housing Fund has no published NOFA and is deployed by Council through development agreements and project-specific commitments (the City adopted Priority Access System guidelines for City-funded projects), so developers should request Affordable Housing Fund support directly in entitlement negotiations. Stack with County HOME and Measure X (San Ramon is in the Urban County for HOME and CDBG, county records), HACCC project-based vouchers and the City's fee waiver policy (separate record). Read from the HCD-hosted 2023-2031 Housing Element draft (source_url, Sections 11.3.1.4, 11.4.7.1 and Program 8); the adopted element (Resolution 2023-017) is linked from https://www.sanramon.ca.gov/news/what_s_new/adopted_2023_2031_housing_element.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: source is the December 2022 draft Housing Element; it matches the commercial linkage fee scope, exemptions, alternatives and the $4.28 million fund balance as of March 3, 2022. The per square foot rate remains unconfirmed.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: San Ramon Affordable Rental Housing Fee Waiver Policy (adopted October 11, 2022) for 100% affordable rental projects
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning and Building Divisions
typical_award_size: Waiver of development impact fees and a capped waiver of City service fees for rental projects in which all units are affordable to households at or below 80% AMI. Impact fee waiver options: City Traffic Impact Fee, School Age Child Care Fee, Park and Recreation Facility Impact Fee, Private Sector Art and Beautification Fee, Open Space Development Impact Fee, Specific Plan Recovery Fees, General Plan Recovery Fee, Zoning Ordinance Recovery Fee and the Tri-Valley Transportation Development Fee (already waived for affordable units). City service fee waivers (building plan check and inspection, planning plan check, engineering plan check and inspection) capped at 25%. City example: a typical 100-unit affordable project receives about $24,000 per unit in impact fee waivers and $5,865 per unit in service fee waivers, over $2.5 million total. The City counts waived fees as local match for State funding applications; value calculated at building permit.
per_unit_cap: About $24,000 per unit impact fees plus about $5,865 per unit service fees (City example); actual amount depends on unit mix and fees in effect at permit.
affordability_requirement: 100% of units (except managers' units) affordable to households at or below 80% AMI under a recorded affordable housing or density bonus agreement; San Ramon's 2026 rent table caps 80% AMI rents at $2,376 (1 person) to $3,938 (6 persons).
next_deadline: Applies at building permit issuance; no application deadline. The Canopy (BR 8) Eden Housing project (161 units, 2026 entitlements) and Eden's 2453 Camino Ramon project are the first users; confirm the policy remains in the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule.
layering_notes: The only formal fee waiver program among the five priority cities and worth roughly $3 million on a 100-unit deal; combined with Bishop Ranch land dedications it makes San Ramon unusually feasible for 100% affordable 4% credit deals despite high land costs. Waivers are public funds for Labor Code 1720 purposes (prevailing wage) and are reported as local match to TCAC and HCD. Layer with County HOME and Measure X, HACCC PBVs and County conduit bonds (county records); the County has no comparable fee waiver program (county record: development fee waiver for affordable housing, discretionary only). Policy terms read from the HCD-hosted Housing Element (source_url) and confirmed in the January 13, 2026 Canopy staff report on the City's IQM2 host.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Waived fees are public funds under 1720(b)(4), but the de minimis rule in 1720(c)(3) (under $600,000 and under 2% of project cost) and other 1720(c) exemptions decide coverage; the San Ramon policy summary in the Housing Element states no wage term.
audit_note: PW pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on 1720(b)(4) alone; changed to unclear per the consistency rule.

program_name: San Ramon Density Bonus Ordinance (Zoning Ordinance Division D4, Chapter VIII, Sections D4-76 to D4-80) and Priority Access System for City-funded housing
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Chapter VIII implements Government Code 65915 by reference: any changes to state density bonus law supersede local text; waivers of development standards are granted unless specified findings are made; parking may be modified or covered-parking requirements waived for affordable units; a density bonus housing agreement is recorded before final map or building permit; a processing fee set by resolution applies. No local bonus beyond state law. Separately, the City's Priority Access Guidelines give San Ramon residents and workers priority in City-funded affordable projects, and the Housing Element targets 200 very low or extremely low, 200 low and 400 moderate income inclusionary units over 2023-2031 against a RHNA of 5,111 units.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (Gov. Code 65915); density bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary unit count under C4-177, so they stack on top of the 15% inclusionary requirement.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; no deadline.
layering_notes: San Ramon has no city-run NOFA, no RDA successor housing fund (the City never had a redevelopment agency) and its Affordable Housing Fund is deployed by Council through development agreements rather than competitive rounds; local tools are the inclusionary receiver-site model, the fee waiver policy and state density bonus. Most existing affordable stock in Dougherty Valley sits under Contra Costa County affordability agreements (county records: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance Ch. 822-4 and Residential Density Bonus Ch. 822-2) rather than City agreements. Zoning text read on the zoneomics mirror (source_url); the City's code host (qcode) is blocked.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this density bonus ordinance provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any City or County loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on the project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Roseville Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF) gap loans, including Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP) program income NOFA (Resolution 26-404, November 4, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Economic Development Department, Housing Division (316 Vernon Street, Suite 150; 916-774-5270; housing@roseville.ca.gov)
typical_award_size: Project-by-project gap loans from the City's Local Housing Trust Fund, which receives in-lieu fees, affordable purchase loan payoffs and state grant program income. Most recent round: a NOFA released August 31, 2026 offered $1,000,000 of PIP program income (from a $1,050,000 developer loan payoff on the City's 2023 PIP Round 1 award of $1,610,000) for predevelopment of lower-income rental housing; two applications were received (Eden Housing, 505 Royer, 58 senior units; Mercy Housing, Pleasant Grove Apartments Phase II, 49 units) and staff recommended reserving the full $1,000,000 for Pleasant Grove Phase II on November 4, 2026. Earlier LHTF and in-lieu commitments include $4.36M reserved for Junction Crossing (80 units, St. Anton) and, per the City's pipeline report, $6,000,000 for Pleasant Grove Apartments (pipeline PDF returned 502 this pass). The 2021 Housing Element commits the City to re-apply for state LHTF matching funds as rounds open.
per_unit_cap: None published. The PIP award of $1,000,000 for 49 units is about $20,400 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Set by loan documents and an Affordable Rental Housing Agreement; PIP money is limited to lower-income (at or below 80% AMI) rental housing, and the 2026 NOFA targeted 30% to 60% AMI projects with preference for units for persons with disabilities and supportive services. Projects in high opportunity areas or areas at risk of displacement are prioritized (Housing Element Programs 9, 10 and 12).
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026; the August 31, 2026 PIP program-income NOFA closed and $1,000,000 was reserved for Pleasant Grove Apartments Phase II on November 4, 2026. Loan documents return to Council at a future meeting. Watch for the next LHTF or PIP program-income NOFA from the Housing Division.
layering_notes: This is the city layer that stacks under 9% or 4% LIHTC and tax-exempt bonds (county TEFRA via CalPFA, CMFA or CSCDA; the County is not an issuer). Roseville's LHTF is separate from Placer County's in-lieu fee gap loans (Hope Way, Destination at Placer One) and from Housing Trust Placer; a Roseville project can seek all three plus Roseville Housing Authority project-based vouchers. Gap order: LIHTC and bonds first, then City LHTF or PIP reservation, then County or Housing Trust Placer money. Roseville's municipal website (roseville.ca.us, now roseville.ca.gov) opens, but the pipeline PDF and script-rendered agenda pages do not; staff reports were read from the City's CivicClerk API file streams (rosevilleca.api.civicclerk.com).
cycle_notes: as program income is received
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost). The HCD 2024 LHTF NOFA (Section V.D) makes state LHTF matching funds subject to state prevailing wage unless a 1720(c) exception applies, but this record lends local LHTF and PIP program income; the PIP Guidelines and NOFA contain no prevailing wage provision, and the November 4, 2026 staff report states none for these loans. https://hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/lhtf/2024-lhtf-nofa.pdf

program_name: Roseville 10% Affordable Housing Goal in Specific Plan Areas (General Plan Policy LU5.5, Housing Element Programs 6 and 9) with Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements and case-by-case in-lieu fees
administering_agency: City of Roseville Housing Division (compliance) and Development Services Department, Planning Division (specific plans)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Every specific plan area must designate 10% of total units as affordable (General Plan goal since 1989: 20% of the affordable units at middle income up to 100% AMI, 40% low income up to 80% AMI, 40% very low income up to 50% AMI), allocated to specific medium and high density parcels and secured by Development Agreements and Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements recorded before building permits or final small-lot maps. Since 1989 the policy has produced 5,167 affordable units (1,357 very low rental, 2,271 low rental, 427 middle rental, 325 moderate rental, plus 787 purchase units), about 140 per year. The City has no formal in-lieu fee ordinance; in-lieu fees are negotiated case by case ($1,036,410 collected 2013 to 2021). A 2025 Housing Tools Inclusionary Housing Policy Analysis recommended standard fee levels, for example $150,000 per required affordable for-sale unit in projects under 20 units, applied in the East Street Subdivision amendment approved November 4, 2026.
affordability_requirement: Rental units restricted by Affordable Rental Housing Agreements (about 2,700 units under agreement in the 2021 to 2029 period); density bonus (Chapter 19.28) may be assigned by the Regulatory Agreement as part of the subsidy. Sierra Vista Specific Plan: 10% of 8,679 units (about 868) allocated to MDR and HDR parcels, with transfers and credits between parcels allowed by Housing Division approval.
next_deadline: Applies at specific plan and Development Agreement approval; the in-lieu fee option is considered case by case at agreement amendment. The 2021 Housing Element also directs work on a commercial linkage fee (nexus study November 2021, draft ordinance posted, not adopted as of this pass).
layering_notes: The reason Roseville has a steady supply of affordable parcels and developers: specific plan landowners (Sierra Vista, West Roseville, Amoruso Ranch, Villages West and others) carry a 10% obligation and typically deliver dedicated HDR parcels or partner with USA Properties, Mercy Housing, St. Anton, Eden Housing and others. Hope Way and the County in-lieu fee program (County Code Chapter 15.65) apply only in unincorporated Placer; inside Roseville this goal and the Regulatory Agreements govern. In-lieu fees collected flow to the Local Housing Trust Fund (record above). Density bonus units are excluded from the 10% base. Verified from the adopted 2021 Housing Element PDF, the Sierra Vista Specific Plan Affordable Housing chapter and the November 4, 2026 Council packet.
eligible_project_detail: affordable parcels dedicated inside specific plans
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 9, 2026: the Housing Element PDF on roseville.ca.gov returned 403 to curl and exceeded the WebFetch size limit. The November 4, 2026 Council packet (CivicClerk) confirms the 10% affordability requirement applied to new specific plan areas and density-changing rezonings (2013 Housing Element recital), the East Street Subdivision APHA amendment, the 2025 Housing Tools Inclusionary Housing Policy Analysis, the $150,000 per for-sale unit in-lieu fee for projects under 20 units, and deposit of in-lieu fees to the Local Housing Trust Fund. The 20/40/40 income split and the 5,167-unit count were not reread from an opened page this pass. Prevailing wage false is uncited.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(b)(1)-(6) lists the forms public funds take (payments, construction by the agency, below-market asset transfers, reduced or waived fees and loans, contingent loans, credits). A specific plan affordable housing goal and regulatory agreement requirement grants regulatory relief and provides none of those forms of public funds, and the law it rests on imposes no prevailing wage condition, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any City or state funds layered on the same project are tested separately. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Roseville development impact fee deferral for affordable multifamily (Municipal Code Section 4.04.040, Ordinance 6830; Sierra Vista Apartments deferral, Resolution 26-336)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Economic Development Department (Gina McColl, 916-774-5452) with the Finance Department
typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver: city-controlled impact fees are deferred from building permit to final or certificate of occupancy, with interest at the City's pooled rate (ten-year average about 2.23%) and an administrative processing fee per permit. Deferrals of $100,000 or more need Council approval. Example approved September 16, 2026: about $2,987,339 deferred for the 192-unit Sierra Vista Apartments (Greek Orthodox Housing Corporation, parcel JM-30, 4950 Upland Drive), covering fire construction tax, sewer and water connection, drainage, SVSP traffic mitigation, citywide and neighborhood parks, bike trail, public benefit and solid waste fees (about $373,000 per building). For a 100% affordable project (three or more units, all units low, very low or extremely low income, Affordable Housing Agreement under Section 19.28.110, objective design standards, secured promissory note) payment may be pushed up to one year after the first certificate of occupancy. The City's policy is not to waive fees; CSCDA SCIP fee financing is also offered.
per_unit_cap: None; about $15,600 per unit deferred in the Sierra Vista example.
affordability_requirement: Standard deferral is open to any multifamily project on request; the extended one-year post-occupancy deferral requires 100% of units (except managers) affordable to low, very low or extremely low income households under a recorded Affordable Housing Agreement.
next_deadline: Request through the Economic Development Department when fee estimates are prepared; a Council hearing under Government Code 53083 is required for deferrals of $100,000 or more.
layering_notes: Timing relief only; fees are still paid in full with interest, so it does not reduce basis but eases construction-period cash needs. Placer County Capital Facilities fees and traffic fees are not city-controlled and are not deferred; age-restricted projects get reduced traffic and County capital facilities rates. Roseville also made a $571,850 CDBG loan (September 4, 2024) to the same Sierra Vista sponsor for land purchase, showing how CDBG, fee deferral, the Regulatory Agreement and LIHTC stack on one project. Read from the September 16, 2026 City Council agenda packet via the CivicClerk API file stream.
prevailing_wage_basis: No stated rule. The September 16, 2026 Council packet (Sierra Vista deferral, Resolution 26-336) does not address prevailing wage. A fee deferral at the City's pooled interest rate may be a reduced fee or below-market interest rate under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), but 1720(b)(4) alone does not decide coverage; the 1720(c)(3) de minimis test (under $600,000 and under 2% of project cost) and the 1720(c)(5)(E) below-market loan exemption (40% of units at 80% AMI or below for 20 years) may apply, and Roseville's separate CDBG loan to the same sponsor brings its own federal rule.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; only basis is Labor Code 1720(b)(4) and the outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts.

program_name: Roseville Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (SB 341 reports; Housing Element Program 12)
administering_agency: City of Roseville acting as Housing Successor to the former Redevelopment Agency; Housing Division
typical_award_size: Small gap loans and Homeless Prevention and Rapid Rehousing grants. Fund balance $2,379,350 at June 30, 2025 (FY2024-25 deposits $1,032,069, including $737,249 from the 20% share of City loan payoffs; FY2024-25 expenditures $434,196 with $0 for development). affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 targeting: development money must serve households at or below 80% AMI, with at least 30% spent on 30% AMI households and no more than 20% on 60% to 80% AMI; 55-year covenants used; no senior-only restriction issue (0% of assisted units senior-restricted in the last 10 years).

Read from the FY2024-25 SB 341 Report of Required Information posted on the Affordable Housing Funds page.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost). Labor Code 1720(c)(4) also provides that affordable housing paid for solely with former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund moneys (H&S Code 33334.2 and 33334.3) is not paid for out of public funds; whether that carve-out reaches housing successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund money under H&S Code 34176 is not settled in the sources read. The SB 341 report could not be reopened this pass. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Roseville CDBG entitlement and HOME funds (annual Action Plan) and Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) Plan adopted September 2, 2026
administering_agency: City of Roseville Housing Division (Dani Calli, Housing Analyst, 916-774-5277, dcalli@roseville.ca.gov)
typical_award_size: Roseville is a HUD entitlement city; the 2026-27 CDBG award was expected at roughly $700,000 with about $730,000 of prior-year carryover and about $50,000 program income (2026 Action Plan hearing May 6, 2026; 2025-26 CAPER public comment August 29 to September 16, 2026). CDBG is mostly used for owner rehabilitation loans (deferred loans up to $100,000, $5,000 grants for elderly and disabled owners), accessibility work (over $1 million earmarked in 2026 for Sierra Gardens accessibility upgrades) and public services, but it has funded affordable housing land acquisition: a $571,850 CDBG loan to Greek Orthodox Housing Corporation on September 4, 2024 for parcel JM-30 (192-unit Sierra Vista Apartments). HOME funds (state-administered) support first-time homebuyer and rehabilitation programs. PLHA: Roseville's formula allocation under HCD's July 2026 NOFA (about $285 million statewide, five-year term) is programmed in the City's PLHA Plan (Resolution 26-327) for Homeless Prevention and Rapid Rehousing, not development; $1,374,763 of PLHA was budgeted for HPRR in FY2026-27.
per_unit_cap: None; the CDBG acquisition loan example is about $3,000 per unit.

program_name: Roseville Housing Authority (RHA) Project-Based Vouchers and Housing Choice Vouchers (jurisdiction includes Rocklin)
administering_agency: Roseville Housing Authority, a department of the City of Roseville (Housing Division, 916-774-5270, housing@roseville.ca.gov)
typical_award_size: Rental subsidy, not capital. RHA (established October 2, 1974) administers tenant-based Housing Choice Vouchers for roughly 850 households (about 1,600 individuals) at or below 50% AMI in Roseville and Rocklin, plus VASH and Mainstream vouchers. It project-bases vouchers in new affordable developments (the City's news release on The Crawford, 265 units by USA Properties, cites eight RHA project-based vouchers) and runs a Project Based Voucher waiting list (waitlistcheck.com CA1217-4334). Payment standards effective October 1, 2026 and utility allowances effective June 1, 2026 are posted for Roseville (95661, 95678, 95747) and Rocklin.
per_unit_cap: Per-unit PBV contract rents at or below RHA payment standards; the count of PBVs per project is negotiated with RHA (HUD caps apply).
affordability_requirement: HCV income limits: 50% AMI at admission (2026: 1 person $46,000, 4 persons $65,700), with 75% of new admissions at or below 30% AMI; PBV units must meet HUD HQS and the Housing Element directs RHA to expand use in high opportunity areas.
next_deadline: PBV commitments are requested from RHA during predevelopment; RHA reports quarterly to Council (next quarterly status update early 2027). Contact RHA before TCAC or CDLAC applications to secure a PBV commitment letter.
layering_notes: Roseville and Rocklin projects have two voucher sources: RHA (city) and Placer County Housing Authority (county record, PBVs and special-purpose vouchers); Rocklin is covered by both. PBVs raise achievable rents on 30% AMI units and support bond or 4% deals. Not a public works trigger by itself. Verified on the RHA page opened this pass.
prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (HUD PBV development requirements, labor standards): for development activity (new construction or rehabilitation) involving nine or more PBV contract units, the owner and its contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages and the PHA monitors compliance; existing-housing PBV contracts with no development activity do not trigger it. RHA places PBVs in new developments (Voucher Programs page lists The Crawford and Terracina at Winding Creek, 1040 Lower Bank Drive, as under construction), but nearly every RHA PBV property carries exactly 8 PBV units, below the 9-unit threshold; Davis-Bacon applies only if RHA awards 9 or more contract units to a new construction or rehab project. https://www.roseville.ca.gov/departments/affordable_housing/housing_authority/voucher_programs.php https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.153

program_name: Roseville Residential Density Bonus (Zoning Ordinance Chapter 19.28) and Prohousing Designation renewal (Resolution 25-346, November 5, 2025)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Development Services Department, Planning Division (Lauren Hocker, Senior Planner, 916-774-5272)
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 19.28 mirrors Government Code 65915: bonuses of 20% to 50% for very low, lower and moderate income set-asides, 80% (or no limit near major transit) for 100% affordable projects, 20% for senior, foster youth, disabled veteran and homeless housing, 35% for student housing, land donation and child care bonuses, up to four incentives, parking caps (0.5 space per unit for qualifying projects near transit, none for 100% lower-income rental near transit or qualifying senior projects). Applications require a pro forma, an appraisal of the bonus value and a sources and uses statement showing the financing gap. Roseville was among the first ten Prohousing-designated jurisdictions (2022); the designation expired at the end of 2025 and Council authorized renewal on November 5, 2025 (application published for 30-day review through September 29, 2025). The City reports over $1 million in grants attributable to the designation and received $1,610,000 of PIP Round 1 funds in 2023.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, or 100% affordable); Affordable Housing Agreement recorded for 55 years (rental) under Section 19.28.110.
next_deadline: Processed with entitlements; no deadline. HCD action on the Prohousing renewal application was pending at the time of the November 2025 hearing; confirm current designation status with Planning before claiming Prohousing points in MHP, AHSC or IIG applications.
layering_notes: No local enhancements beyond state law other than the explicit pro forma and appraisal submittal requirements. Density bonus units do not count toward the 10% specific plan goal, and the Regulatory Agreement can assign bonus units as part of the City's subsidy. Prohousing status gives bonus points on state NOFAs for projects located in Roseville (not available in Rocklin, Lincoln or Auburn, none of which held the designation as of this pass). Chapter text read on the zoneomics code mirror; Roseville's own code host (ecode360) returns partial PDFs only.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

Read from the September 16, 2026 agenda packet via the CivicClerk API.
cycle_notes: site committed
prevailing_wage_basis: The City sells 505 Royer Street and 300 Taylor Street to Eden Housing at appraised fair market value of $580,000, and the staff report for Resolution 26-331 (September 16, 2026 packet, https://rosevilleca.api.civicclerk.com/v1/Meetings/GetMeetingFileStream(fileId=11713,plainText=false)) states the purchase is not contingent upon City funding; the purchase agreement summary states no wage rule. Labor Code 1720(b)(3) treats a land transfer as public funds only when it is for less than fair market price (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), so the land sale itself does not trigger prevailing wage.
