program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, San Leandro Zoning Code Chapter 6.04 (Ordinance 2004-023, amended 2020-002), in-lieu fee and Affordable Housing Trust Fund (6.04.156)
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department, Housing Services Division, 835 East 14th Street; housing@sanleandro.org, (510) 577-6006
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. At least 15% of units in residential developments must be inclusionary units for moderate, low or very low income households (density bonus units excluded from the base); for-sale projects of 2 to 6 units may pay an in-lieu fee equal to (median San Leandro sales price minus affordable ownership cost) times a fractional unit of 0.30 to 0.90; larger projects may combine fees with off-site alternatives only with approval. Exempt: for-sale projects and condo conversions under 2 units and rental projects under 4 units. Fees, condo conversion fees and loan repayments go to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. FY 2025 AHTF revenue $24,682 (no in-lieu fees), balance $336,166 at June 30, 2025 (FY 2024 restated to $311,484 after audit). Recent BMR production: Centro Callan (10 BMR rental units), Poppy Lane (3 BMR homes).
affordability_requirement: 15% of units for moderate, low or very low income households; rental inclusionary units subject to recorded covenants administered under the BMR Procedural Manual (SLMC 19.172.030).
next_deadline: Applies at map or planning approval; the 2023-2031 Housing Element commits to an economic feasibility study and ordinance amendments during the cycle (not yet scheduled).
layering_notes: The AHTF is too small to fund projects on its own; it has covered predevelopment grants and a site acquisition contribution. The ordinance predates AB 1505 and still exempts small rental projects; developers of rental projects with 4 or more units owe 15% on-site, which is above Hayward's and Fremont's rental percentages and a cost consideration for mixed-income deals. Ordinance text read on the zoneomics mirror (qcode is blocked); fund figures from the FY 2025 AHTF report adopted by Resolution 2025-163 (December 15, 2025).
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check Nov 9, 2026: sanleandro.org DocumentCenter/View/10247 returns 403. The official FY 2025 AHTF report (Legistar 25-434) matches revenue $24,682, balance $336,166, restated FY 2024 $311,484, 2 to 6 unit in-lieu option, Centro Callan and Poppy Lane. The 15% requirement, exemptions and fractional fee formula were checked only on the Zoneomics mirror of Chapter 6.04 (consistent).
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this inclusionary ordinance provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any City or County loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on the project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 The Affordable Housing Trust Fund it feeds would be assessed separately if it funds a project.

program_name: Residential Density Bonus, San Leandro Zoning Code Chapter 6.08, and inclusionary incentives (6.04.136)
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Chapter 6.08 grants the bonus, incentives and concessions exactly as specified in Government Code 65915, processed concurrently with other entitlements and approved if the applicant complies with state law; continued availability of bonus units secured by agreement. Section 6.04.136 allows additional flexibility in density, lot size, yards and parking to accommodate required inclusionary units, but density bonus affordable units are in addition to the inclusionary requirement. Condominium conversions get the 65915.5 bonus (5.32.136).
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; inclusionary 15% must still be met on the base project.
next_deadline: Concurrent with the entitlement application.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law. San Leandro's affordable housing tools beyond density bonus are the inclusionary ordinance, the small AHTF, the HOME/PIP/PLHA RFP and the 2025 park fee exemption; there is no fee waiver for building permits and no local trust fund NOFA with meaningful capital. Code read on the zoneomics mirror.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Park Facilities Development Impact Fee exemption and 50% reduction for affordable units (Administrative Code Section 8.8.121, Council item 25-347, July 2025)
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department and Recreation and Parks
typical_award_size: Park impact fees restructured in July 2025 from per-unit-type ($18,074 per multifamily unit in FY 2024-25) to unit-size tiers: under 550 sq ft $6,052; 550 to 750 sq ft $7,565; 751 to 1,150 sq ft $11,600; 1,151 to 1,650 sq ft $16,140; 1,651 to 1,950 sq ft $20,679; over 1,950 sq ft $25,723 (land acquisition plus improvement components, CPI and ENR indexed). New Section 8.8.121: a residential development is exempt from the park fee if 100% of units (excluding manager units) are affordable and the applicant is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit or controlled by one; any other affordable unit pays 50% of the otherwise applicable rate. ADU fees eliminated by companion resolution.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable (exemption or 50% reduction per affordable unit).
affordability_requirement: Affordable unit per Health and Safety Code 50093 with affordable rent (50053) or affordable housing cost (50052.5) under a recorded restrictive covenant; full exemption requires 100% affordable nonprofit ownership.
next_deadline: No application deadline; the exemption or 50% reduction applies at building permit. Adopted by Resolution 2025-106 on July 21, 2025 (Council item 25-347), effective 60 days after adoption; in effect as of November 8, 2026. Fees index annually.
layering_notes: The only development fee relief among the five priority cities that is written into local code for 100% affordable nonprofit projects (Oakland's AHIF exemption is comparable in effect). Saves roughly $6,000 to $12,000 per small unit. Other City fees (building permit, sewer connection) are not waived; school and EBMUD fees are outside City control. The document read was the draft resolution attached to the July 1, 2025 Council item on Legistar.
cycle_notes: Standing fee relief in Administrative Code Section 8.8.121, not a funding round. Council adopted Resolution 2025-106 (park impact fees and affordable housing waivers), Resolution 2025-107 (ADU street improvement fee exemption) and introduced Ordinance 2025-012 (parkland dedication, second reading September 2, 2025). Resolution takes effect 60 days after adoption.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees waived or reduced by a political subdivision as payment out of public funds, but 1720(c)(3) excludes de minimis subsidies (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost), so coverage depends on project size and other public funds; the San Leandro resolution states no prevailing wage requirement. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: HOME Investment Partnerships Program through the Alameda County HOME Consortium (Cooperative Agreement FY 2027-2029, Council item 26-152) and PLHA
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department, Housing Services Division, 835 East 14th Street; housing@sanleandro.org, (510) 577-6006

affordability_requirement: HOME: 80% AMI and HOME rents; PLHA: per state PLHA plan, Housing First for services.
next_deadline: FY 2028 allocation expected spring 2027; HOME FY 2024 funds must be expended by June 30, 2027. The County may centralize HOME awards under the FY 2027-2029 agreement.

Recent use is rehabilitation of existing affordable stock rather than new construction. Pairs with the County HOME RFP, Measure A1 and 4% credit recapitalizations.

prevailing_wage_basis: HOME: federal Davis-Bacon applies to projects with 12 or more HOME-assisted units (24 CFR 92.354); state prevailing wage depends on Labor Code 1720 facts.

program_name: Stockton Affordable Housing NOFA (annual Housing NOFA; HOME, HOME-ARP, PLHA, LMIHF, NSP, CDBG, HHAP and PIP loan pool)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department, Housing Division (underwriting consultant TDA Consulting Inc.)
typical_award_size: 2025 Housing NOFA released October 30, 2025, closed December 18, 2025: 8 proposals requesting $28.2 million for 522 units; $11,979,838 available after de-obligating $1,614,000 of HOME and LMIHF from Sierra Vista III. Awards: Fairview Terrace (Mutual Housing California, 76 senior units) $2,800,000 gap loan approved March 31, 2026 (Resolution 2026-03-31-1601) on top of $7,037,865 HOME awarded November 19, 2024; Don Shalvey Apartments (Visionary Home Builders, 108 family units, TDC $84.0 million) $5,000,000 and Danny Drive (DCDC, 66 senior units, TDC $39.7 million) $4,179,838 recommended April 2026 after Council deferred them on March 31. 2024 NOFA (January 29, 2024) offered about $16.1 million and funded Fairview Terrace $7,037,865 HOME, Kentfield Apartments rehab $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF, Casa de Mariposa $747,055, plus two HHAP projects. Typical award $0.7 million to $7 million per project.
per_unit_cap: No published cap; 2025 applications ranged from about $27,000 to about $294,000 of City funds per unit. HOME subsidy limits apply when HOME is the source.
affordability_requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement and loan term at 3% simple interest, repaid from residual receipts proportionate to the City share of permanent financing; projects served 30% to 80% AMI (families) and 30% to 60% AMI (seniors). HOME-funded units carry the HOME affordability period inside the 55-year term. Article XXXIV authority: voters allow Council to approve up to 500 assisted units per year.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 9, 2026. The City Housing page posts no 2026 Housing NOFA (it currently lists the Prohousing renewal comment period and the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-27 Action Plan substantial amendments, hearing November 10, 2026). The prior round was released in late October 2025 and closed in mid December 2025; under the Council-approved process (Motion 2025-11-04-1601) the due date is at least 45 days after release, so a release now would close no earlier than early 2027. Confirm timing with hhep@stocktonca.gov, (209) 937-8538.
layering_notes: Stockton is the only city in San Joaquin County running a competitive gap-loan NOFA, and it is the main local soft source after the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (county record). Pool is HUD and state pass-through plus housing successor LMIHF, so awards must fit each source's rules and deadlines; the City requires the full stack to be committed before executing loan documents and de-obligates allocations older than three years that cannot start within three years (Sierra Vista III lost $1.6 million in 2026). Scoring: developer capacity 30, proforma 30, populations served 15, design 15, leverage 10; an AI score was averaged with three human raters in 2025. Stacks with HACSJ project-based vouchers, County HOME (Urban County does not cover Stockton), BHSA and managed care plan grants (county records), the City PFF exemption and the 100% density bonus (records below). 2026 awards included HOME-ARP and PIP as eligible sources. Source documents read through the Stockton Legistar API and Granicus attachments; stocktonca.gov Economic Development pages have moved to /business/economic_development/housing_index.php.
cycle_notes: fall release
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

Award terms (55-year term, 3% residual receipts, HOME 20-year affordability inside the loan term, Article XXXIV 500 units per year) and the $2,800,000 Fairview Terrace loan match the resolution attachment.

program_name: CDBG, HOME and ESG entitlements, City of Stockton (2026-27 Annual Action Plan, CDBG/ESG NOFA and Real Property Acquisition NOFA)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Housing, Homelessness, Events and Parking Department (formerly Economic Development Department Housing Division)
typical_award_size: 2026-27 allocations: CDBG $3,229,216 plus about $350,000 program income, HOME $1,382,561, ESG $284,821. HOME budget: $1,324,906 HOME Housing Loans for multifamily rehab or new construction, $207,384 CHDO set-aside, $150,000 program delivery, $138,256 admin. CDBG largely to public infrastructure ($4,914,998 with carryover) and public services; 2026-27 CDBG/ESG public service NOFA awarded $498,509 CDBG and $262,528 ESG to nonprofits. 2024 Real Property Acquisition NOFA offered about $4,551,524 of CDBG and PIP for nonprofit site acquisition (5 applications, $10.0 million requested; awards included $1,500,000 to Parents by Choice for transitional youth housing at 523 E. Main and up to $800,000 CDBG to STAND for scattered-site acquisition).
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250); no local cap.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and incomes (at or below 60% AMI for rental, 15% CHDO set-aside), CDBG national objective, ESG homeless eligibility. HOME preference policy (2024, in 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan) favors projects serving targeted populations named in the Consolidated Plan.

HOME match is currently 100% waived by HUD. HOME money is the backbone of the City Housing NOFA and has been combined with PLHA, LMIHF, HHAP and PIP in every recent award. CDBG has been used for land acquisition NOFAs for nonprofits, which is unusual in the region. HACSJ has secured City NOFA funds for its DCDC projects (Danny Drive, Sierra Vista). Draft 2026-27 AAP read from the Stockton Legistar attachment; the City housing page lists the same plans.

administering_agency: City of Stockton as Housing Successor; administered by the Housing Division through the Housing NOFA

Recent uses: part of $1,614,000 HOME and LMIHF allocated to Sierra Vista III in 2019 and 2020 (de-obligated March 2026 and returned to the NOFA pool); part of $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF to Kentfield Apartments rehab (2024).
affordability_requirement: Housing successor rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1): 55-year rental covenants, income targeting by statute with at least 30% of expenditures for extremely low income households over each five-year period; City NOFA applies a 55-year regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Deployed only through the City Housing NOFA; no standalone LMIHF application. No open round as of November 9, 2026: no 2026 Housing NOFA is posted on the City Housing page. Check the annual housing successor report filed with the City's HCD Annual Progress Report for the current balance.
layering_notes: Stockton is one of the few San Joaquin County cities with legacy redevelopment housing money; Tracy, Manteca and Lodi records show none in active use. LMIHF is the most flexible source in the Stockton pool (local money, up to 120% AMI, no federal cross-cutting rules) and is usually paired with HOME to cover costs HOME cannot. Treat as a small, lumpy source: the only recent LMIHF commitments were under $1.7 million each. Combine with HACSJ PBVs and SJRHF gap loans (county records). Fund description opened from the Stockton Legistar attachment for the April 2026 award item; the Successor Agency meets concurrently with Council.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Stockton staff report describing LMIHF uses states no wage term. Construction paid solely with low and moderate income housing fund money plus private funds is excluded under 1720(c)(4). Local loans are public funds under 1720(b), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: next_deadline said the next Housing NOFA was expected about October 2026; none is posted as of November 9, 2026, so changed to No open round. The Funding Source Descriptions attachment still describes LMIHF for acquisition, new construction and conversion or rehabilitation up to 120% AMI, matching the record.

program_name: City-Wide Affordable Housing Development Public Facilities Fee (PFF) Exemption Program (with Greater Downtown Residential PFF Exemption; Resolutions 2015-11-17-1602, 2018-02-06-0504, 2018-11-06-1402, 2020-12-15-1105)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department (fee programs) with Community Development Department Permit Center
typical_award_size: Full exemption from seven Public Facilities Fee categories (city office space, libraries, fire stations, parkland, community recreation centers, police stations, street improvements) for qualifying new affordable housing anywhere in city limits; the same categories are exempt for all new residential development in the Greater Downtown area. Dollar value depends on the current PFF schedule (not published on the program page); the program was cited by HCD as a basis for Stockton's 2023 Prohousing Designation. Other PFFs (water, wastewater, air quality, habitat, school fees) and the SJMSCP habitat fee still apply.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable (fee exemption per unit equals the exempted PFF categories).
affordability_requirement: Qualifying affordable housing development as defined in the authorizing resolutions (deed-restricted units); confirm the affordability threshold and covenant term with the Economic Development Department before relying on it.
next_deadline: No application deadline; rolling. Apply before building permit issuance through the Economic Development Department. The exemption sunsets when the City completes its Master Infrastructure Plans and PFF Nexus Study and adopts new fees; as of November 8, 2026 the nexus study is still in progress (Parks Master Plan approved, draft Transportation Master Plan out for comment in 2026), so the exemption remains listed as active.
layering_notes: Most valuable local incentive in Stockton after the NOFA; the exemption reduces per-unit soft costs by the PFF categories listed and the downtown exemption applies to market-rate units too, which helps mixed-income deals. A non-residential short-term PFF deferral program (through December 31, 2027) and the non-residential 5 or 10 year deferral do not apply to housing. Stacks with the Chapter 16.40 density bonus and the Housing NOFA; fee exemptions count as public assistance for Labor Code 1720 analysis, so confirm prevailing wage exposure with counsel. Read from the City Business Assistance page (financial_assistance.php); authorizing resolutions are linked there.
cycle_notes: Rolling fee exemption at building permit. Sunset is tied to adoption of new PFFs after the nexus study, not a fixed date; check the City Public Facility Fees page for nexus study adoption. Pass 3 research also noted a five-year phase-out of the related SESP fee reduction starting 2025 (not stated on the current program page, which still says SESP expires when the nexus study fees take effect).
audit_note: Deadline text fixed (resolution date was being parsed as a past deadline). Prevailing wage left unclear: neither the City program page nor the authorizing resolutions listed there state a prevailing wage rule; Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats waived fees as public funds but de minimis and affordable housing exemptions in 1720(c) make the result project specific, and the statute page on california.public.law returned 403.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. The program fully exempts qualifying affordable housing from seven Public Facilities Fee categories. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Affordable Housing Incentives and Density Bonus Provisions, Stockton Municipal Code Chapter 16.40 (State bonus to 50%, Tier-1 to 75%, Tier-2 to 100%; Ord. 2020-12-01-1502, 2022-07-12-1601-02, 2025-06-03-1601)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. State Density Bonus up to 50%; Tier-1 supplemental bonus 50% to 75% with 30 eligibility points; Tier-2 76% to 100% with 50 points. Points: one per additional percent of very low or low income units, LEED 15 to 30, CALGreen Tier I up to 20, 10% on-site renewable 15, adaptive reuse of historic buildings 20, plus other community benefits. Projects not qualifying for state concessions get three local concessions: setback reduction up to 25%, parking reductions of 25% to 100% scaled to the share of lower income units, lot coverage or FAR increases of 5% to 20%, lot coverage up to 25%, height plus 12 feet or 10%.
affordability_requirement: State law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 100% affordable, senior, moderate for-sale) for the base bonus; supplemental tiers require additional affordable units or community benefits scored under 16.40.050; density bonus housing agreement recorded per 16.40.070.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Title 16 was amended June 3, 2025 and again in 2025-2026 (Chapter 16.20, 16.80.310, 16.244.010) to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element; check the current code before design.
layering_notes: Stockton's 100% bonus exceeds state law and was one of HCD's stated reasons for the Prohousing Designation. Pair with the PFF exemption and the Housing NOFA; the Housing Element also allows duplexes by right in single-family zones. Parking can go to zero for projects with 75% or more lower income units, which matters for downtown and transit sites. Read from the zoneomics code mirror of Title 16 Division 3 because the City's code publisher blocks scripts.
audit_note: Tier 4: zoneomics Title 16 mirror re-read; 16.40.040 tiers, point thresholds, 16.40.050 points and local concessions and the ordinance history match. The next_deadline text cites the June 3, 2025 amendment date, which the script reads as a past deadline; the program is an entitlement provision with no application deadline. prevailing_wage_trigger false is uncited; a density bonus is not a public funds payment.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

administering_agency: City of Tracy Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division

FY 2026-27 notice amounts (CDBG $420,013, HOME $111,278) and eligible activities match.

Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department, Neighborhood Services Division (CDBG administration consultant Michael Baker International)

City guideline: 40% of the award net of admin to community-based organizations. No program income.

affordability_requirement: HUD CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit); Consolidated Plan 2024-2028 goal to preserve and increase affordable housing through rehabilitation, land acquisition or partnerships with housing developers.
next_deadline: 2026-27 applications ran December 8, 2025 to January 27, 2026; the 2027-28 cycle should open about December 2026 with applications due late January 2027 and funds available July 1, 2027. 2025-26 CAPER hearing was September 2, 2026. Contact NeighborhoodServices@lodi.gov.
layering_notes: Lodi is a CDBG entitlement city but not a HOME participating jurisdiction; HOME for Lodi projects comes from the San Joaquin Urban County NOFA (Lodi Commons received $230,024 plus $500,000 program income in 2026-27 and $2 million HOME-ARP, county records). City CDBG contributions to housing are small infrastructure or predevelopment pieces ($115,000 to Salas Park in 2026-27), so treat CDBG as a sub-$250,000 layer. Lodi joined the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund by resolution on July 17, 2024 and gets HHAP Round 4 ($652,126) and Round 5 subrecipient funds for shelter and transitional housing. Read from the City CDBG page and the 2026-27 Annual Action Plan PDF.
cycle_notes: applications December to late January
eligible_project_detail: site acquisition and infrastructure for affordable housing
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Residential Density Bonus, Lodi Municipal Code Section 17.36.050 (Development Code; Housing Element Program 1.1 update pending)
administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. Bonus of 20% to 35% for 10% low income or 5% very low income units, 5% to 35% for 10% moderate income common interest units, 20% for senior projects, additional child care bonus; maximum 35% in the code text, with the code deferring to state law where it conflicts. At least one incentive for qualifying projects of five or more units.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; affordability covenants per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental).
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 1.1 commits the City to update 17.36.050 to the current state tier framework; the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report lists the Development Code amendments as in progress, and the 2025 code amendments (Ordinances 2030 and 2034) did not address the density bonus. No density bonus applications were filed in 2025.
layering_notes: Lodi has no inclusionary ordinance (Housing Element confirms) and no local in-lieu fee, so the density bonus is the only land-use subsidy. Because the code defers to state law, developers can claim the full state bonus despite the outdated 35% text. Pair with County HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and the City surplus land program (next record). Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17 Article 3 because municode blocks scripts.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element on lodi.gov (Constraints, Density Bonuses) describes Chapter 17.36.050 as the record does (five or more units; 5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate common interest, senior, child care; up to 35%; not compliant with the 2020 state tiers; Program 1.1 to amend). The 2025 Annual Progress Report (Legistar matter 2397 attachment) shows Program 1.1 in progress and zero density bonus applications. Official code host codepublishing still returns 403.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: City-owned sites for affordable housing (Housing Element Program 1.16 Surplus Land Act; Salas Park right-of-way with HACSJ; 130 West Century Boulevard)
administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department and City Council
typical_award_size: Land contribution, not cash. Salas Park former right-of-way (about 3 acres rezoned to High Density Residential by Ordinance 2026, August 2024): City agreement with the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin for up to 110 affordable units, first phase Lodi Commons (DCDC Senior Housing at Salas Park, 54 senior units plus manager) funded with County HOME, HOME-ARP, HHAP, Congressional Community Project funds and $115,000 City CDBG. 130 West Century Boulevard (about 2.5 acres, Housing Element capacity 53 lower income units) under Council discussion January 27, 2026 with no decision. Program 1.16 targets 101 lower income units on four City sites, with RFP or sale by 2026, ENA 2026, entitlements 2027-2028, permits 2029.
affordability_requirement: Lower income units counted toward RHNA; Surplus Land Act priority to affordable housing developers (25% affordable minimum under Government Code 54233 when sold for housing).
next_deadline: Housing Element Program 1.16 calls for an action plan to sell or RFP City-owned land for affordable housing by 2026 and incentives for affordable housing on City sites by 2026; watch Council agendas for a Surplus Land Act declaration on 130 West Century Boulevard and the remaining Salas Park phase (56 units).
layering_notes: Lodi's only material local contribution to multifamily deals is land; the City budget has no housing fund and no RDA housing successor fund appears in the Housing Element or in Council items since 2024. The HACSJ partnership shows the working model: City land plus County HOME and HOME-ARP, HHAP, HACSJ PBVs and tax credits (county records). A developer other than HACSJ would need a Surplus Land Act process. Read from the City 2026-27 Annual Action Plan PDF (Salas Park partnership) and the Legistar staff reports for the January 27, 2026 Century Boulevard item.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific rule found. City land conveyed or leased below fair market value is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(3) (transfer of an asset of value for less than fair market price, https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but coverage depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts, for example 1720(c)(1) private residential projects remain covered when built under an agreement with a local public housing authority such as HACSJ. The Surplus Land Act affordability section, Government Code 54233.5, sets 15 percent lower income units at 10+ units and contains no prevailing wage term. Federal HOME or CDBG layered on a given site (for example Lodi Commons) carries its own Davis-Bacon trigger (HOME 12+ assisted units, CDBG 8+ units), which belongs to those funding records, not this land program.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; the only basis is Labor Code 1720(b)(3) below-market land transfer, and the outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and deal terms set in each disposition agreement.

program_name: Lodi Housing Element 2023-2031 incentive programs (Program 1.6 fee waivers, reductions or deferrals for infill at 20 or more units per acre; Program 1.12 incentives for special needs housing; Program 1.5 funding applications)
administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Not yet adopted as a standing program. Program 1.6 commits the City to adopt by 2025 one or more incentives for infill housing at 20 or more units per acre: parking credits, fee waivers, reductions or deferrals when financially feasible, priority processing. Program 1.12 commits to incentives (reduced standards, fee waivers or financial assistance) for housing for persons with disabilities by 2026. Program 1.5 sets a goal of the City securing $1 million in state or federal housing funds by 2028 and $2 million by 2031. Housing Element impact fee estimate: about $18,948 development impact fees plus $11,468 building fees per single-family home; multifamily fees lower per unit.
affordability_requirement: Program 1.6 objective: incentivize 100 extremely low, 200 very low and 200 low income units on infill parcels; Program 1.12 objective 40 special needs units.
next_deadline: No adopted fee waiver, reduction or deferral program as of November 10, 2026. Program 1.6 called for infill incentives by 2025 and Program 1.12 for special needs incentives by 2026; the 2025 Annual Progress Report lists Program 1.12 as not yet started and reports no multifamily or infill applications in 2025. Ask Planning (209) 333-6711 whether a policy is before Council. Lodi is also adding Chapter 15.69 (Agricultural Mitigation Fee) and 15.70 (Parkland Dedication and In-Lieu) in October 2026, which add costs rather than relief.
layering_notes: Lodi has no housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee or housing successor fund; HOME comes only through the County. Until Program 1.6 is adopted, the only fee relief is state law (ADU fee exemptions, SB 937 fee timing). Expect County HOME plus SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and BHSA (county records) to carry gap financing, with City CDBG for off-site infrastructure. Programs read from the adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF on lodi.gov (HCD certified April 11, 2024).
eligible_project_detail: new construction (infill, 20 or more units per acre)
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: certified Housing Element on lodi.gov re-read (Program 1.6 incentives for infill at 20 or more units per acre including fee waivers, reductions or deferrals when financially feasible, establish by 2025; Program 1.5.c $1 million by 2028 and $2 million by 2031; Program 1.12; fee estimates). The 2025 Annual Progress Report (Legistar matter 2397) shows no adopted incentive program and Program 1.12 not yet started; Lodi Legistar matters from 2025 on show no fee waiver or deferral adoption.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Housing Element Program 1.6 commits the City to adopt fee waivers, reductions or deferrals for infill at 20 or more units per acre; not yet adopted. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Affordable Housing Development RFP No. 26-004A (Inclusionary Housing Fund, HOME, HOME-ARP and Housing Successor Agency loans)
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division, 20 Civic Center Plaza M-26, (714) 667-2250; bid contact Jacques Lam, JLam@santa-ana.org; solicitation on PlanetBids portal 20137
typical_award_size: Open RFP issued May 1, 2026 with $17,507,926 available: Inclusionary Housing Funds $2,628,194, HOME $11,533,196, HOME-ARP $715,622 (permanent supportive housing only), Housing Successor Agency Funds $2,630,914, plus Housing Authority project-based vouchers and Housing Successor land. Available funds are republished each quarter in the Housing Division Quarterly Report and added to the RFP by addendum. Recent City awards: Crossroads at Washington $4,600,000 plus 15 PBVs (86 units), WISEPlace $5,200,000 plus 25 PBVs (48 units), Estrella Springs $1,600,000 plus 89 PBVs (89 units), Wellington $920,000 (9 ownership units, approved July 1, 2025), Richard Lehn Intergenerational Housing $2,021,319 HHAP plus 8 PBVs (11 units).
per_unit_cap: None fixed for local funds; HOME subsidy is limited to the HUD maximum per-unit subsidy limits and the City's Affordable Housing Funds Policies and Procedures (amended Aug 18, 2020) cap by-right applications at the HUD per-unit limits.
affordability_requirement: At least 55-year covenants; Inclusionary and Housing Successor funds serve moderate (120% AMI), low, very low and extremely low income households and may fund mixed-income and mixed-use projects; HOME units at High and Low HOME rents with 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; HOME-ARP units are permanent supportive housing only. Priority points for substantial rehabilitation and adaptive reuse (motel and office conversions), homeownership, and by-right or shovel-ready projects.
next_deadline: Quarterly proposal deadlines: January 11, 2027 and May 3, 2027 at 4:00 p.m. (July 1 and October 1, 2026 rounds have passed); question deadlines November 30, 2026 and April 5, 2027. The City's stated objective is to issue one affordable housing RFP per year and finance at least one multifamily project per year.
layering_notes: Santa Ana is the deepest city pool in Orange County: about $17,500,000 in one RFP, mostly HOME, with loans at 3% simple interest, 55-year term, repaid from 50% of residual receipts, TCAC developer fee limits and a Review Panel scoring process under the 2020 Affordable Housing Funds Policies and Procedures (opened). Any City-funded affordable housing project is covered by the June 6, 2023 Community Workforce Agreement (Section 2.2.4, no dollar threshold): contractors sign a Letter of Assent, hire through union hiring halls and pay prevailing wage rates, and the project must reach 30% of craft hours from Santa Ana and Orange County ZIP codes, veterans or MC3 graduates; budget a labor premium even for small or ownership projects that might otherwise be exempt under Labor Code 1720(c). Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units. Stack with County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA loans and OCHA or SAHA PBVs, OCHFT gap loans (WISEPlace took $2,500,000 OCHFT MHSA plus $1,500,000 County ARPA) and 4% or 9% credits. The County NOFA pays $95,000 to $105,000 per unit inside Santa Ana, so the City loan is normally the larger local layer. RFP PDF, RFP page, policies PDF and FY 2025-26 Q4 quarterly report opened on santa-ana.gov and its Google Cloud document store.
cycle_notes: quarterly deadlines under a one-year open RFP
prevailing_wage_basis: RFP No. 26-004A (May 1, 2026), pages 11 to 12: pro formas must assume State prevailing wages and/or Federal Davis-Bacon wages and compliance with the City CWA; HOME and HOME-ARP Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more assisted units (24 CFR 92.354, restated in RFP Exhibit IV page 31). Santa Ana Community Workforce Agreement with the Los Angeles/Orange Counties Building and Construction Trades Council, effective June 6, 2023 (reproduced as Exhibit V of RFP 26-004A, pages 54 to 78): Section 2.2.4 makes 'any Affordable Housing projects that receive City funds' covered Project Work, with no dollar threshold (the $750,000 multi-trade and $100,000 specialty thresholds in 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 apply to public works contracts); Section 5.1 requires covered employees to be paid the hourly rates in the applicable prevailing wage determination; Section 11.2 requires compliance with state prevailing wage law and Santa Ana Municipal Code 33-206. RFP 26-004A Section IV (page 24) and General Terms item (2) (page 19) state the CWA applies to City-funded affordable housing projects, is enforced in the final City agreement, requires union hiring hall referral, and requires at least 30% of craft hours by Santa Ana (Tier 1) or Orange County (Tier 2) ZIP code residents, veterans or MC3 pre-apprenticeship graduates, measured on certified payroll; each proposer signs Attachment H and each contractor signs a Letter of Assent. SAMC 33-206 (emergency ordinance, December 16, 2014) applies state prevailing wage law to City public works as defined in Labor Code 1720, so it adds no coverage beyond state law; the local layer is the CWA. Note: the RFP's Exhibit II sample pre-loan commitment (page 44) leaves the Labor Code 1720 state prevailing wage determination to the developer, but the CWA wage clause applies to all City-funded affordable housing regardless.
audit_note: PW pass B November 10, 2026: read the CWA text in RFP Exhibit V (scanned pages rendered and read) and the 2014 SAMC 33-206 ordinance; basis now cites CWA Sections 2.2.4, 5.1 and 11.2. Trigger stays true.

program_name: Affordable Housing Opportunity and Creation Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 41, Article XVIII.I, Secs. 41-1900 to 41-1909; Ordinance NS-3019) and in-lieu fee to the Inclusionary Housing Fund
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency (inclusionary housing plans) and Community Development Agency Housing Division (Inclusionary Housing Fund)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to projects of five or more units (lowered from 20 by NS-3019, adopted April 19, 2022) that receive a discretionary density or land use increase. Rental projects: 15% low income, or 10% very low, or 5% extremely low, or a 10% mix (5% low, 3% very low, 2% extremely low). For-sale projects: 5% moderate income. In-lieu fee per habitable square foot of the entire project, tiered by size: $6.00 (5 to 9 units), $9.00 (10 to 14), $12.00 (15 to 19) and $15.00 (20 or more) (Sec. 41-1904(c)(1)). Effective January 1, 2026, a project of 20 or more units that elects the $15.00 fee must also sign an enforceable commitment that 30% of the construction workforce is a skilled and trained workforce (Public Contract Code 2601), with at least 35% of those work-hours under City local hire policies; the fee drops to $10.00 at 60% and $5.00 at 90% skilled and trained workforce. From November 16, 2021 through December 31, 2025 the workforce commitment was optional ($10.00 at 30% and $5.00 at 60%, with 20% local hire). The earlier NS-2994 amendment had cut the fee from $15 to $5 per square foot before the 2022 rewrite. Inclusionary Housing Fund receipts since inception: $31,147,483 (FY 2009-2020 $10,800,251; FY 20/21 $3,709,875; FY 21/22 $6,933,320; FY 22/23 $0; FY 23/24 $834,000; FY 24/25 $0; FY 25/26 $1,685,995 from the 408-unit Lowe Enterprises project at 2828 N. Main St.). Fund expenditures to date $20,558,250 for 224 units plus The Link interim shelter ($7,893,866); commitments $1,357,021. Only 35 on-site inclusionary units (25 ownership, 10 rental) have been built since 2011, so the ordinance functions mainly as a fee.
affordability_requirement: On-site units restricted 55 years; fund may be spent on moderate, low, very low and extremely low income rental and ownership housing, shelter and down payment assistance. Sec. 41-1904.1 incentives for on-site production: up to 25% setback reduction, up to 20 feet of added height, and a local density bonus of 1.5% for each 1% of for-sale units above 5% moderate income, up to 35%.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. The in-lieu fee amount is set at issuance of the first building permit and must be paid no later than the first occupancy approval for construction that adds net residential units (Sec. 41-1904(c)(2)). Fee schedule may be changed only by a five-vote Council supermajority. The Housing Element programs commit the City to periodic review of the threshold and fee.
layering_notes: This fee stream feeds the Inclusionary Housing Fund that is offered through the City's annual Affordable Housing Development RFP (record above), which is the only Orange County city in-lieu fund with a regular competitive outlet. Orange County has no county inclusionary ordinance, so this is a city-only requirement. Market-rate developers often use the ordinance's local density bonus with the state bonus; the Housing Element notes the 2022 rewrite was meant to recover fee revenue lost after NS-2994 cut the rate to $5. Ordinance page, NS-3019 PDF and the zoneomics code mirror for Article XVIII.I opened; fund figures from the FY 2025-26 Q4 Housing Division Quarterly Report (opened).
eligible_project_detail: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 5 or more units (compliance)
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: in-lieu fee terms corrected. Old: $15.00 fee for 20+ units reducible to $10.00 or $5.00 with optional local hire (30% of hours) and skilled and trained workforce commitments; fee due before building permit. New: since January 1, 2026 a 20+ unit project paying the $15.00 fee must commit 30% skilled and trained workforce (PCC 2601) with 35% local hire, with $10.00 at 60% and $5.00 at 90%; fee is set at first building permit and due by first occupancy approval. Source: NS-3019 PDF linked from the ordinance page, cross-checked against the zoneomics mirror of Article XVIII.I (official code host blocked). The skilled and trained workforce rule is not a prevailing wage rule, so prevailing_wage_trigger was left false.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana as Housing Successor to the Santa Ana Community Redevelopment Agency)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana as Housing Successor, staffed by the Community Development Agency Housing Division
typical_award_size: LMIHAF ending balance $4,134,871 at June 30, 2025 (FY 2024-25 SB 341 report); $305,772 deposited and $0 spent on development that year. $2,630,914 of Housing Successor funds are in RFP 26-004A. Past commitments: $6,195,000 in 2016 for 69 units and $13,222,740 in 2017 for 118 units. The Housing Successor also ground-leases former RDA sites for 65 to 99 years: 1126 and 1146 Washington (Crossroads at Washington, 86 units, completed October 2024), 801-809 E. Santa Ana Blvd (FX Residences, 16 to 17 PSH units, completed April 2025), 826 N. Lacy (two Habitat homes, 2023). The City and Housing Successor loan portfolio totals $155,432,612 in 344 loans (325 deferred or residual receipts).
per_unit_cap: Subject to the HUD per-unit limits adopted in the City's Affordable Housing Funds Policies for by-right requests; otherwise sized by gap analysis.
affordability_requirement: Low and moderate income (up to 120% AMI) under Health and Safety Code 34176.1; at least 30% of expenditures over each five-year period must serve households at or below 30% AMI (extremely low income test reported for July 2020 to June 2025); senior housing limited to 50% of assisted units over 10 years.
next_deadline: Next RFP quarterly deadline January 11, 2027; land assets are offered when the Housing Authority issues site-specific RFPs.
layering_notes: Small compared with the County's $29,000,000 LMIHAF but flexible: no federal strings, can serve moderate income and mixed-use, and the Housing Authority's land is the real asset (Crossroads and FX Residences were built on 65- and 99-year ground leases). Pair with HOME in the same RFP, SAHA PBVs, County MHSA/BHSA capital and OCHFT. Projects funded through the City RFP are covered by the June 6, 2023 Community Workforce Agreement (union hiring halls, prevailing wage rates, 30% local craft hours), so budget a labor premium even where a Labor Code 1720(c) exemption would otherwise apply. FY 2024-25 Housing Successor Annual Report PDF and the Successor Agency page opened on santa-ana.gov; CWA text read in RFP 26-004A Exhibit V.
cycle_notes: offered through the annual Affordable Housing Development RFP
audit_note: PW pass B November 10, 2026: unclear changed to true. CWA text (RFP 26-004A Exhibit V) Section 2.2.4 covers any affordable housing project receiving City funds and Section 5.1 requires prevailing wage rates; the RFP offers Housing Successor funds under the same terms.
prevailing_wage_basis: Housing Successor funds are offered through RFP 26-004A ($2,630,914), and the RFP states the City CWA applies to City-funded affordable housing projects and is enforced in the final agreement. Santa Ana Community Workforce Agreement with the Los Angeles/Orange Counties Building and Construction Trades Council, effective June 6, 2023 (reproduced as Exhibit V of RFP 26-004A, pages 54 to 78): Section 2.2.4 makes 'any Affordable Housing projects that receive City funds' covered Project Work, with no dollar threshold (the $750,000 multi-trade and $100,000 specialty thresholds in 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 apply to public works contracts); Section 5.1 requires covered employees to be paid the hourly rates in the applicable prevailing wage determination; Section 11.2 requires compliance with state prevailing wage law and Santa Ana Municipal Code 33-206. RFP 26-004A Section IV (page 24) and General Terms item (2) (page 19) state the CWA applies to City-funded affordable housing projects, is enforced in the final City agreement, requires union hiring hall referral, and requires at least 30% of craft hours by Santa Ana (Tier 1) or Orange County (Tier 2) ZIP code residents, veterans or MC3 pre-apprenticeship graduates, measured on certified payroll; each proposer signs Attachment H and each contractor signs a Letter of Assent. SAMC 33-206 (emergency ordinance, December 16, 2014) applies state prevailing wage law to City public works as defined in Labor Code 1720, so it adds no coverage beyond state law; the local layer is the CWA. State law alone would be uncertain: Labor Code 1720(c)(4) excludes housing paid solely from former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund moneys, 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts qualifying below-market residential loans, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The trigger rests on the CWA wage clause, not on Labor Code 1720. Caveat: the CWA says 'City funds'; the RFP treats Housing Successor funds as covered, but a Housing Authority land disposition outside the RFP was not tested.

program_name: HOME Investment Partnerships, CDBG and ESG entitlement (FY 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan)
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division (HOME Participating Jurisdiction since 1994)
typical_award_size: Five-year Consolidated Plan FY 2025-2029 anticipates $41,700,000: CDBG $30,123,118, HOME $9,093,495, ESG $2,504,870. HOME development funds are deployed as loans through the Affordable Housing Development RFP ($11,533,196 of HOME and $715,622 of HOME-ARP available in RFP 26-004A), with 15% of each annual HOME allocation reserved for certified CHDOs. CDBG funds public services, infrastructure, the Residential Rehabilitation Program (grants up to $25,000, closed in Q4 FY 2025-26 when funds ran out) and shelter; HOME also funds the My First Home mortgage assistance program.
per_unit_cap: HOME: HUD maximum per-unit subsidy limits; affordability period 5, 10 or 15 years for rental assistance under $25,000, $25,000 to $50,000, and over $50,000 per unit (20 years for new construction), but the City records 55-year covenants on its loans.
affordability_requirement: HOME rental units at or below 80% AMI at High and Low HOME rents, 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; CDBG national objective benefit to low and moderate income persons.
next_deadline: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring for the July 1 program year; developer requests go through the Affordable Housing Development RFP quarterly deadlines (next January 11, 2027). Public service and CDBG applications are solicited in the winter before the Action Plan.
layering_notes: Santa Ana's HOME grant (about $1,800,000 a year) is larger than the County Urban County HOME grant ($1,244,583) and the City lends most of it to multifamily deals rather than TBRA, which is why HOME is the largest line in the RFP. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units; HOME brings NEPA, Section 3 and a HUD subsidy layering review. HOME-ARP is limited to permanent supportive housing. Santa Ana is outside the County Urban County program, so County HOME is not available inside the city. Consolidated Plan page, CDBG page, HOME page and Grants page opened on santa-ana.gov; RFP PDF supplies the HOME terms.
prevailing_wage_basis: HOME: 24 CFR 92.354 Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units (restated in RFP 26-004A Exhibit IV page 31, also for HOME-ARP); CDBG: Davis-Bacon applies to residential construction of 8 or more units (HCD Act of 1974 Section 110). Local layer: HOME development loans are awarded through RFP 26-004A, and the City CWA (effective June 6, 2023, RFP Exhibit V) Section 2.2.4 covers any affordable housing project receiving City funds, Section 5.1 requires prevailing wage rates, and RFP Section IV (page 24) requires union hiring hall referral and 30% local craft hours (Santa Ana and Orange County ZIP codes, veterans or MC3 graduates). SAMC 33-206 (2014) only adopts state prevailing wage law for City public works.
audit_note: PW pass B November 10, 2026: basis expanded with CWA Sections 2.2.4 and 5.1 read in RFP 26-004A Exhibit V. Trigger stays true.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana (SAHA)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana (Community Development Agency), waiting list hotline (714) 667-2284
typical_award_size: PBVs are committed to City-financed projects through the Affordable Housing Development RFP: Estrella Springs 89 PBVs (89 PSH units, former Budget Inn), WISEPlace on Broadway 25 PBVs (15 set aside for domestic violence survivors), Crossroads at Washington 15 PBVs (43 PSH units of 86), Richard Lehn Intergenerational Housing 8 PBVs (11 units, under construction), plus earlier commitments at Casa Querencia (57 units), Heroes' Landing (75), The Orchard (72) and FX Residences (17). PBV waiting lists for Crossroads at Washington and Andalucia closed April 30, 2026. SAHA received 25 Foster Youth to Independence vouchers in August 2025. Total HCV count not confirmed from an opened document.
affordability_requirement: PBV households at or below 50% AMI at admission (30% of adjusted income toward rent); PSH units generally 30% AMI with Coordinated Entry referrals; HAP contracts up to 20 years.
next_deadline: Request PBVs in the RFP quarterly rounds (next January 11, 2027); SAHA's FY 2026 Annual Plan draft (Feb 17, 2026) was opened but lists no fixed PBV allotment.
layering_notes: Santa Ana is one of four PHAs in Orange County (with OCHA, Anaheim and Garden Grove) and has been the most active in project-basing: 89 PBVs at Estrella Springs is the largest single PBV award in the county. A HAP contract is not itself a prevailing wage trigger but Davis-Bacon applies to new construction or rehab of nine or more PBV units and PBVs bring a HUD subsidy layering review. Combine with City HOME or Housing Successor loans, County MHSA/BHSA capital and OCHFT. The City also receives its own HHAP allocation (Richard Lehn used $2,021,319 HHAP), so the operating stack for PSH can be entirely city-controlled. PSH properties page, Housing Authority page, PBV waiting list notices and the 2025 Affordable Housing Awards release opened on santa-ana.gov.
cycle_notes: requested with or without capital in the Affordable Housing Development RFP
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal Davis-Bacon: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (PBV development requirements, labor standards) requires the owner and its contractors to pay Davis-Bacon wages in the case of development involving nine or more contract units, whether or not completed in stages (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.153). Applies only to PBVs committed under a development agreement for new construction or rehab; PBVs placed on existing housing with 8 or fewer contract units, or no development activity, do not trigger it. State prevailing wage depends separately on other public funds in the deal under Labor Code 1720.
audit_note: Prevailing wage set true per 24 CFR 983.153(c): Davis-Bacon at 9+ PBV contract units in development; existing-housing PBVs are not covered.

program_name: Density Bonus for Affordable Housing (Municipal Code Chapter 41, Article XVI.I, Secs. 41-1600 to 41-1607) and Density Bonus Agreements
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency, Planning Division, (714) 667-2700
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. The local article grants a 25% density bonus plus one additional development incentive under a recorded Density Bonus Agreement, with waivers or modifications of development standards decided under Sec. 41-1607; state law (Government Code 65915) now governs bonus amounts up to 50% or more, up to five incentives or concessions and unlimited waivers, and the City applies the state schedule. The FY 2025-26 Q4 Housing Division report lists the Density Bonus Agreements executed to date, including 415 and 547 rental units restricted under two agreements and smaller sets of 92, 19, 11 and 2 very low income units.
affordability_requirement: State law thresholds: 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, or 100% affordable; local code covenants of 30 years when an additional incentive is granted (state law requires 55 years for rental); a monitoring fee set by resolution applies.
next_deadline: Applies at project application; agreements recorded before building permit.
layering_notes: Santa Ana projects routinely combine the state density bonus with the AHOCO local bonus and the Transit Zoning Code (SD-84) and Metro East overlays; the Housing Element credits the City with 5,130 permits from 2021 to 2024, 152% of its very low, low and moderate RHNA progress through 2025. No fee waiver or impact fee deferral ordinance for affordable housing was found; the County NOFA treats city fee waivers as match but Santa Ana offers none. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; the Q4 quarterly report lists agreements.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Prohousing Designation (HCD Prohousing Designation Program)
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency; designation issued by HCD
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. Santa Ana appears on HCD's list of Prohousing Designated Jurisdictions, which gives projects inside the city bonus points or priority processing in AHSC, Infill Infrastructure Grant, Transformative Climate Communities, SCCP, LPP, TIRCP and STPG, and makes the City eligible for the Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP).
affordability_requirement: Follows the state program applied for (AHSC and IIG serve lower income projects at or below 80% AMI).
next_deadline: Designation is good for four years from award and must be renewed; PIP rounds are announced by HCD. Confirm the designation date with the Planning Division.
layering_notes: The only Prohousing city among the five Orange County priority cities (Anaheim, Irvine, Huntington Beach and Garden Grove are not on the list opened 2026-11-08), so AHSC and IIG applications in Santa Ana carry the designation points. The City's own HHAP allocation, SAHA PBVs and the RFP loans make a full local stack for AHSC-sized projects. HCD designated jurisdictions page opened.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(b)(1)-(6) lists the forms public funds take (payments, construction by the agency, below-market asset transfers, reduced or waived fees and loans, contingent loans, credits). A Prohousing Designation (scoring points and eligibility for HCD programs) grants regulatory relief and provides none of those forms of public funds, and the law it rests on imposes no prevailing wage condition, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any City or state funds layered on the same project are tested separately. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Santa Ana entitlement
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Formula PLHA entitlement, not offered to developers. Santa Ana received $14,360,783 over PLHA Rounds 1 to 4; Round 4 (FY 2023-24 NOFA, HCD Contract 20-PLHA-15193) was a $2,403,595 grant recognized by Council on November 19, 2024. Round 1 paid Santa Ana Navigation Center tenant improvements, Rounds 2 and 3 paid for purchase of that property, and Round 4 funds Navigation Center operating costs and homeless services ($2,283,415 to a subagent, $120,180 staff). The 2021-2029 Housing Element lists PLHA as a funding source for emergency shelter and permanent supportive housing programs.
affordability_requirement: Per PLHA statute: rental production at or below 60% AMI, assistance to persons experiencing homelessness, affordable ownership and workforce housing.
next_deadline: No developer round. Allocations to date are committed to the Santa Ana Navigation Center; confirm with the Housing Division whether any future PLHA year will be set aside for development.
layering_notes: Santa Ana is an HCD PLHA entitlement separate from the County Urban County allocation. All four rounds so far went to the Santa Ana Navigation Center (tenant improvements, property purchase, operations), so developers should not count on City PLHA as gap money unless a later five-year plan amendment shifts funds to rental production. Sources: November 19, 2024 staff report with HCD award letter (Laserfiche WebLink doc 224140) and the September 2022 Housing Element.
cycle_notes: Annual HCD formula allocation to the City; City programs it internally rather than through a developer NOFA.
eligible_project_detail: PSH listed as an eligible Housing Element use but no allocation to development found
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines and Formula Allocation NOFA contain no prevailing wage section (only the Non-Entitlement Competitive NOFA does); Santa Ana has used its share for Navigation Center purchase, tenant improvements and operations, and tenant improvement work would be tested under 1720 on its facts. https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: Anaheim Local Housing Trust Fund (A-LHTF), Ordinance No. 6588; Program Guidelines and Funding Allocation Plan (adopted May 29, 2025, revised June 9, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department, with transfers to the Anaheim Housing Authority by cooperation agreement; 201 S. Anaheim Blvd., Suite 201
typical_award_size: Initial Funding Allocation Plan of $16,000,000: Build More Homes Initiative $5,000,000 (includes $1,000,000 from a federal grant restricted to housing production), First-Time Homebuyer programs $5,000,000 ($50,000 downpayment loans), Housing Stability Program $1,000,000, administration $500,000 (3.12%), reserve $4,500,000. Build More Homes funds pay for site acquisition, site preparation (environmental, demolition, relocation) and gap financing, structured as loans at 4% simple interest repaid from a residual receipts split; A-LHTF money may not exceed 50% of total City investment in a project. Eligible deposits include General Fund, federal PRO Housing grant, state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants, REAP 2.0 (gap financing for infill with at least 65% residential floor area in mixed-use), Development Agreement community benefit payments, philanthropy and in-lieu fees paid under the City's Affordable Housing Ordinance.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized by financial analysis and capped at 50% of City investment per project.
affordability_requirement: Affordability follows the leveraged source (LIHTC, HOME, PLHA); where none applies the City sets project-specific requirements, generally 55-year covenants. Target beneficiaries: workforce households, households experiencing homelessness, active older adults 55 and over, special needs (transition-age youth, persons with disabilities, persons with AIDS). Shelters, transitional housing and group homes are ineligible.
next_deadline: No NOFA. Each expenditure requires a separate Council action; the Funding Allocation Plan is updated in the annual budget cycle (next spring 2027). Approach Housing and Community Development with a site or gap request.
layering_notes: Anaheim's answer to losing $15,000,000 to $17,000,000 a year of redevelopment set-aside: the trust consolidates HOME (FY 2024 $1,314,088), PLHA (about $3,000,000 a year), REAP 2.0 and General Fund into one locally controlled pool, with City gap financing averaging about $6,000,000 per recent project (Finamore Place, Miraflores) before land. The 50% leverage rule means A-LHTF is a secondary layer behind HOME, PLHA, County MHSA/BHSA loans, OCHFT and Anaheim Housing Authority PBVs. The Guidelines are also the City's vehicle for state LHTF matching grants, so expect future rounds to be tied to HCD LHTF deadlines. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis).0 funds carry infill and reporting rules. Guidelines PDF opened via anaheim.gov DocumentCenter (anaheim.net links return 403).
cycle_notes: project-by-project Council actions; annual Funding Allocation Plan in the City budget
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost). The HCD 2024 LHTF NOFA (Section V.D) states that state LHTF matching funds are subject to state prevailing wage unless a 1720(c) exception applies, so a project receiving state LHTF match dollars through the A-LHTF is covered on that basis; local-only A-LHTF dollars carry no stated rule. The A-LHTF Guidelines PDF returned 403 on anaheim.gov and anaheim.net this pass. https://hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/lhtf/2024-lhtf-nofa.pdf

program_name: HOME, PLHA and CDBG entitlement funds used as affordable housing gap financing (Build More Homes Initiative)
administering_agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department (HUD Programs division) and Anaheim Housing Authority
typical_award_size: HOME allocation FY 2024 $1,314,087.60 (down from $2,240,380 in FY 2010 and $1,067,408 in FY 2016); PLHA about $3,000,000 a year since 2019; together about $4,600,000 a year of recurring production money. City cash gap financing has averaged $6,000,000 per project on the last two developments (Finamore Place, completed February 2022, and Miraflores Apartments). The A-LHTF Build More Homes Initiative adds $5,000,000 of the initial $16,000,000 trust fund allocation. Anaheim also administers CDBG, ESG and HOPWA for the region.
per_unit_cap: HOME: HUD maximum per-unit subsidy limits.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and 80% AMI limits with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI; PLHA rental production at or below 60% AMI; City deals have typically been 100% affordable family, senior or supportive housing with 55-year covenants.
next_deadline: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring; developer solicitations are issued per site (recent Housing Authority RFPs covered 212 S. Beach Blvd and State College at Lincoln). Verify the FY 2026-27 HOME and PLHA figures with the department; the City documents page lists only the FY 2022-23 Action Plan.
layering_notes: Anaheim does not run a competitive NOFA; it assembles sites (Beach Boulevard corridor, former motels) and selects developers by RFP, then layers HOME, PLHA, A-LHTF and Housing Authority PBVs. The City is an HHAP direct recipient and a HOPWA grantee for Orange County, so operating subsidies for PSH can come from the same department. Stack order seen in practice: City land lease plus HOME or PLHA loan, Housing Authority PBVs, County MHSA/BHSA or OCHFT loan, 4% credits with CMFA or CSCDA bonds. Davis-Bacon on HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units; state prevailing wage on all City funds. Figures from the A-LHTF Guidelines (amended June 9, 2026), reopened Nov 10, 2026 on anaheim.net with a Chrome user agent. Project details from Pass 3 not reopened in the audit: Miraflores (85 PSH family units, 2024, 60-year ground lease, $3,000,000 HOME loan, 8 vouchers) and Center of Hope (72 PSH units, 2023, $2,000,000 City construction loan, 50 vouchers). anaheim.net HTML pages, Action Plan PDFs and CivicAlerts return 403.
cycle_notes: project-specific RFPs and negotiated agreements; no standing developer NOFA
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).
audit_note: Follow-up Nov 10, 2026: source PDF opened at anaheim.net/DocumentCenter/View/66427 (A-LHTF Guidelines, amended June 9, 2026) and confirms the HOME, PLHA, $4.6M and $6M average gap figures; restored to verified. Miraflores and Center of Hope specifics are from Pass 3 pages not reopened and are flagged in layering_notes.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Anaheim Housing Authority as Housing Successor to the Anaheim Redevelopment Agency)
administering_agency: Anaheim Housing Authority as Housing Successor, administered by Housing and Community Development
typical_award_size: FY 2024-25 Housing Successor Annual Report (dated December 16, 2025): $23,453,030 deposited into the LMIHAF ($13,794 from ROPS items), $22,615,135 spent ($21,423,871 on housing development: $12,312,921 extremely low income units, $2,423,602 very low, $5,205,580 low, $1,481,768 projects pending; $1,191,264 administration), ending balance $16,794,545, all unencumbered, no excess surplus. Prior year-end balances: $38,146,030 (FY 2020-21), $30,063,646, $18,112,239 and $15,956,650 (FY 2023-24). Attachments A and B list many Authority-owned sites (for example 554 S. West Ave., 309 W. Midway, 212 S. Beach Blvd. (Silver Moon), 428 S. Melrose, 883 S. Anaheim Blvd.) marked RFP pending or pending RFP process. Senior test 17% (231 of 1,382 assisted rental units, 2015-2024). Before dissolution the Agency's housing set-aside was $15,000,000 to $17,000,000 a year.

next_deadline: No open round as of November 9, 2026. The FY 2024-25 Housing Successor report lists multiple Authority-owned sites with an RFP pending but gives no release date; watch Anaheim Housing Authority agendas and contact Housing and Community Development.
layering_notes: Anaheim's LMIHAF is active: FY 2024-25 deposits of $23.5 million and housing development spending of $21.4 million, mostly on extremely low income units, with $16.8 million unencumbered at June 30, 2025, plus a large land inventory with RFPs pending. The A-LHTF Guidelines say Trust funds may be transferred to the Housing Authority to combine with other sources for site acquisition. Housing successor funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable units paid for solely from Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund money; other funds in the deal decide coverage (see prevailing_wage_basis). Housing Successor Agency page opened on anaheim.gov; FY 2024-25 report opened on anaheim.net.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost). Labor Code 1720(c)(4) also provides that affordable housing paid for solely with former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund moneys (H&S Code 33334.2 and 33334.3) is not paid for out of public funds; whether that carve-out reaches housing successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund money under H&S Code 34176 is not settled in the sources read. program_name: Affordable Housing chapter: density bonus, by-right review of Housing Element sites, replacement housing and affordable parking ratios (Anaheim Municipal Code Chapter 18.52, Ord. 6627, August 11, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Anaheim Planning and Building Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Sec. 18.52.020.010 adopts Government Code 65915 density bonuses and incentives by reference; Sec. 18.52.020.020 requires affordable housing to be provided under Chapter 17.40 (Inclusionary Housing); Sec. 18.52.020.030 makes review by right (Gov. Code 65583.2(h) and (i)) on Sixth Cycle Housing Element candidate sites for low and very low income units when at least 20% of units are restricted to lower income households; Sec. 18.52.020.040 allows affordable housing on institution-owned property per Sec. 18.38.023. Chapter 17.40 (Ord. 6593, October 29, 2024) requires rental projects of 35 or more units to set aside at least 10% of units onsite (at least 7% low income and 3% very low income) for 55 years, with in-lieu fee, offsite and land dedication alternatives; ownership projects are exempt.

next_deadline: Applies at project application; no deadline.
layering_notes: Anaheim does have a citywide inclusionary ordinance for rental projects: Chapter 17.40 (Ord. 6593, October 29, 2024), cross-referenced in Sec. 18.52.020.020, requires 10% onsite affordable units (7% low, 3% very low income) in rental projects of 35 or more units, with in-lieu fees deposited in the A-LHTF; ownership projects are exempt.
