program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Affordable Housing Implementation Procedure (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Chapter 2-3, Secs. 2-3-1 to 2-3-11; Ord. 04-15, 24-13, 25-16)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services and Housing staff
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects must provide 15% of units as affordable: 5% extremely low or very low income, 5% low income, 5% moderate income (ownership units for very low or low earn 2:1 credit; extremely low units 1.6:1; three- and four-bedroom units 1.4:1 and 1.6:1). Projects with at least 10% very low or extremely low units satisfy the combined 10% lower income requirement. Alternatives (menu option) are allowed only when on-site units are infeasible or in the City's interest: converting market units for 55 years, extending expiring covenants 55 years, in-lieu fees set by Council resolution, transferring units to a nonprofit, buying affordable housing credits (Sec. 2-3-6), alternative housing (SROs, special needs, shelters at 1:1), or dedicating land or resources of at least equal value. Projects up to 100% affordable may be approved in any planning area and can only be denied under Government Code 65589.5(d). Community preference policy in Sec. 2-3-11.
affordability_requirement: Covenants of at least 55 years at the income level provided; bedroom mix must match the market units and affordable units must be dispersed; affordable housing plans and annual compliance reports required; revocation of entitlements for noncompliance.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee amount determined at building permit under the current Council resolution (fee study drafted August 3, 2023; current schedule not confirmed). Chapter last amended June 24, 2025 (Ord. 25-16).
layering_notes: Irvine's 15% requirement is the highest of the five Orange County priority cities and is the engine behind the Irvine Company planning area affordable sites that nonprofits (Jamboree, C&C, Related, ICLT) build with 4% and 9% credits; a nonprofit taking an inclusionary site typically gets the land at low cost plus City or Irvine Community Land Trust support, then layers County MHSA/BHSA, OCHFT and OCHA PBVs. Sec. 2-3-7 states the City has no obligation to provide financial incentives, so there is no guaranteed city subsidy. cityofirvine.gov returned 403 to all fetch methods this pass; the ordinance was read on the zoneomics mirror.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-5.B.3.c; fee set by City Council resolution)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department
typical_award_size: In-lieu fees are deposited in the City's affordable housing fund and used for projects implementing the Housing Element needs assessment or serving low, very low and extremely low income households; the fee is charged per market-rate unit under a Council-approved formula, determined at building permit, and has not been updated since 2011 (a legacy $17,000 per unit rate applied only to pre-2007 Irvine Business Complex filings). A May 2026 Draft Affordable Housing and In-Lieu Fee Analysis was released August 10, 2026; staff recommends keeping the existing formula with updated inputs. Finance Commission reviewed it October 19, 2026; Planning Commission and Council hearings are not yet scheduled. Fund balance and any developer allocation process are not published.
affordability_requirement: Fund uses limited to low, very low and extremely low income households and Housing Element implementation; recipients record 55-year covenants under Chapter 2-3.
next_deadline: No NOFA located as of November 8, 2026. In-lieu fee update pending Planning Commission and City Council hearings (dates TBD). Ask Community Development (cd@cityofirvine.org) for the fund balance and whether a developer round is planned.
layering_notes: Because most Irvine builders provide units on-site or through credits, the in-lieu fund is smaller than Santa Ana's; its visible use is land and loans to Irvine Community Land Trust projects (Salerno, Parc Derian, Doria, Alegre, Sage Park) which then take LIHTC, HOME, OCHFT and County MHSA money. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Code text read on zoneomics because the City-linked Municode page is Cloudflare-blocked; the City In-Lieu Fee Formula Update page (cityofirvine.gov/node/94569) and its September 8, 2026 FAQ were opened and confirm the 15% requirement, the formula-based fee and the update schedule.
eligible_project_detail: land for Irvine Community Land Trust projects
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy (under $600,000 and under 2% of total project cost). Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-5 states no prevailing wage rule for in-lieu fee loans. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: Irvine Community Land Trust (ICLT) land and development partnerships
administering_agency: Irvine Community Land Trust, 501(c)(3) created by the City of Irvine in 2006, 503 Nightmist, Irvine 92618; Board chaired by Ryan Aeh (2026)
typical_award_size: ICLT acquires or receives land (including City conveyances such as the four-acre site reported in the City's FY 2023-25 budget) and ground leases it to development partners so that units stay affordable permanently. Portfolio: Alegre Apartments, Doria Apartments, Parc Derian Apartments, Salerno Apartments (501 Nightmist) and Sage Park (affordable ownership); it reports hundreds of affordable units in Irvine and, since its 2017 mission expansion, elsewhere in Orange County. ICLT finances projects with LIHTC, HOME, Orange County Housing Finance Trust loans, FHLB AHP and HUD programs; dollar values of land contributions are not published.
affordability_requirement: Permanent affordability through recorded ground lease covenants; rental projects have served extremely low to low income households and Sage Park serves moderate income buyers.
next_deadline: No solicitation open as of November 8, 2026; contact ICLT through its partnerships page.
layering_notes: ICLT is how Irvine converts inclusionary land dedications and City-owned parcels into 100% affordable projects without a city loan program; a developer partnering with ICLT gets site control at nominal ground rent and then stacks 4% or 9% credits, County MHSA/BHSA capital, OCHFT (Cypress Village Irvine took $3,500,000 in the 2024 OCHFT round) and OCHA PBVs. ICLT is a nonprofit, not a public agency, so its land alone does not trigger prevailing wage, but City land conveyed through it may. ICLT home, about, history, process, partnerships and properties pages and the September 23, 2026 letter opened on irvineclt.org.
cycle_notes: Partnerships negotiated with ICLT; no RFP or RFQ found on irvineclt.org or by search. Governance note: ICLT directors wrote to the City Council on September 23, 2026 defending Resolution 26-803 (consultant contract), which could affect City-ICLT land conveyances.
audit_note: Deadline text fixed (the extracted date was a governance letter), but no ICLT, City or state rule addressing prevailing wage on ICLT land deals was found on the ICLT process page or by search, so the trigger stays unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The ICLT process page (https://irvineclt.org/our-process/) states no prevailing wage rule. ICLT is a private nonprofit, so its own land alone is not public funds, but City of Irvine land conveyed to ICLT or to a project below fair market value is public funds under 1720(b)(3) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), and the HOME, Orange County Housing Finance Trust and other public loans ICLT layers carry their own rules. Below-market loans can be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), as DIR PW 2019-018 applied (https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf).

program_name: Affordable Housing Credits Program (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-6)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department (credits database and three-party credits agreements)
typical_award_size: Market mechanism, not a subsidy. Projects that build more affordable units than the 15% requirement earn transferable credits in three income categories (extremely low or very low, low, moderate) that they may sell to market-rate projects or mixed projects with a shortfall; credits become available after building permits are issued for the excess units and a completion bond or certificate of occupancy is in place. A three-party credits agreement (buyer, seller, City) must be executed before the buyer's building permits; sale prices are not disclosed to the City.
affordability_requirement: Credits track the income level of the excess units; the receiving project satisfies its required affordable component at that level.
next_deadline: Agreement before building permit; City maintains the credits database on request.
layering_notes: Reclassified from other to regulatory requirement: the credits program is part of the Chapter 2-3 inclusionary procedure (15% requirement, 5% each extremely low or very low, low and moderate) and is a compliance-trading mechanism, not a public subsidy. For a 100% affordable developer it can still be a revenue source: excess units earn credits (for example 2.0 credits per ownership unit sold to lower income buyers, 1.6 extremely low or very low credits per qualifying rental unit, one credit releasing 19 market-rate units) that can be sold to market-rate builders. Confirm with the City how many credits are outstanding and the recent trading range. Read on the zoneomics mirror because the City-linked Municode page is Cloudflare-blocked; the City in-lieu fee page (cityofirvine.gov/node/94569) confirms the 15% requirement and menu options.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Residential Density Bonus Standards (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-10)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 by reference: density bonuses, incentives and concessions, waivers and parking ratios per state law, documented in a density bonus housing agreement recorded as a condition of the discretionary approval; development standards may be modified under Sec. 2-3-10.C for projects providing the Chapter 2-3 affordable units.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable); 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: Applies at project application.
layering_notes: Irvine has no local housing trust fund NOFA, no fee waiver ordinance for affordable units and no city-run developer NOFA; the local tools are the 15% inclusionary requirement, in-lieu fund, credits program, Irvine Community Land Trust and this density bonus section. Irvine receives its own CDBG, HOME, PLHA and HHAP allocations (HHAP Round 6 $5,947,855 per the County record) but those pages could not be opened this pass. Irvine is not a Prohousing designated city per the HCD list opened 2026-11-08.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Affordable Housing (Inclusionary Housing) Ordinance, Huntington Beach Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.26, and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division (Charles Kovac, Housing Manager, charles.kovac@surfcity-hb.org; Gregory Hoang, Senior Housing Analyst, 714-536-5473)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential projects of three or more units (including conversions) must restrict at least 10% of units: rental units at the lower income level (or very low or extremely low at the developer's choice), ownership units at moderate income, with fractional units rounded up or paid as fee. In-lieu fees may be paid by ownership projects of any size and rental projects of 100 units or fewer, per a fee schedule set by Council resolution and indexed annually to Orange County new home prices; fees are paid before building permit (pro rata for phased projects) and deposited in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. Land dedication is allowed at Council discretion. Projects that exceed the requirement on-site are eligible for reduced City fees (the 2025 Annual Progress Report cites over $1,000,000 of development impact fee exemptions for a 78-unit project with 8 ELI, 32 VL and 37 low units). A 6-1 Council vote amended the ordinance and the fee formula to make payment more flexible (date not confirmed).
affordability_requirement: Affordability term at least 55 years for rental and 45 years for ownership; affordable rental units built by a separate affordable developer on a parcel within an ownership project may not request City financial assistance; at least 40% of such units must have two or more bedrooms; interior standards equal to LIHTC minimums.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee per the current Council resolution at building permit. Council must review the Trust Fund and fee within 180 days after each fiscal year end (by late December).
layering_notes: A low 3-unit threshold but a fee-out for all ownership and all rental projects up to 100 units, so in practice most Huntington Beach projects pay the fee; the Trust Fund (next record) is the resulting local source. The ordinance's fee-reduction incentive is the only affordable housing fee relief found among the five cities. Housing Element status matters here: HCD's March 6, 2026 letter found the 2021-2029 element cannot be certified until the Program 2A and 2B rezonings (Affordable Housing Overlay) are complete, and the state litigation over the element continues, which exposes projects to builder's remedy and limits state funding points. Code read on the zoneomics mirror; Legistar attachments (HCD letter, 2025 APR) opened via the Legistar web API.
eligible_project_detail: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 3 or more units (compliance)
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; no NOFA. Council reviews the fund annually within 180 days of fiscal year end. Request the fund balance from the Housing Division.

Huntington Beach Zoning Code Sec. 230.26 states no prevailing wage rule for trust fund loans. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: CDBG and HOME entitlement (FY 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, Resolution 2025-32; annual CDBG Notice of Funding Availability)
administering_agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division (Charles Kovac, Housing Manager; Gregory Hoang, Senior Housing Analyst, gregory.hoang@surfcity-hb.org, 714-536-5473)
typical_award_size: FY 2025-26: CDBG grant $1,121,195 plus $258,868 carryover ($1,380,063 total); HOME grant $538,328 plus $306,100 program income ($844,428 total). HOME uses FY 2025-26: Families Forward TBRA $200,000, Mercy House TBRA $200,000, Mobile Home TBRA $128,841, CHDO Reserve/Affordable Housing $261,754, administration $53,833. CDBG capital: code enforcement $246,506, housing rehabilitation $381,139, TBRA administration $235,000, ADA improvements $125,000; public services $168,179 across six agencies. The 2026-27 CDBG NOFA opened October 2, 2025 with applications due December 11, 2025.
per_unit_cap: HOME: HUD maximum per-unit subsidy limits.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and 80% AMI limits; the City states its HOME CHDO acquisition-rehab rental properties are restricted to households at or below 60% of Orange County AMI for a minimum of 15 years under each CHDO agreement; CHDO reserve for nonprofit-owned or developed affordable housing; CDBG national objectives with at least 70% of funds benefiting households at or below 80% AMI.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 CDBG NOFA open: application packets available October 8, 2026; completed applications due by 5:00 p.m. December 10, 2026 (original signed applications only, postmarks not accepted).
layering_notes: Huntington Beach's HOME is small ($538,328) and goes almost entirely to TBRA; only the CHDO reserve (about $260,000 a year) is available for development, so City HOME is a token layer next to County and OCHFT money. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. The City's Pathways Project (Jamboree Housing ENA extended 18 months in May 2024 for a permanent shelter and supportive housing at the Navigation Center site, Beach and Edinger Corridors Affordable Housing Overlay) was budgeted from IIG, AHSC, TCAC, BHCIP, Community Care Expansion, OCHFT ($2,500,000), OCHA PBVs ($3,720,000) and Behavioral Health Services funds ($5,000,000), illustrating the stack the City expects. Legistar attachments (FY 2025-26 funding tables, 2026-27 NOFA notice, Pathways funding matrix, ENA extension) opened via the Legistar web API; The City CDBG and HOME program page (huntingtonbeachca.gov, opened 2026-11-08) posts the FY 2027-28 NOFA, handbook and application.
cycle_notes: Annual CDBG NOFA each fall with applications due in December for the fiscal year starting the next July; the Citizen Participation Advisory Board reviews applications and the Action Plan hearing is each spring. The FY 2027-28 NOFA covers CDBG only; HOME has gone to City TBRA and the CHDO reserve.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: affordability_requirement said only HOME rents and 80% AMI limits; the City CDBG and HOME page states CHDO-acquired HOME rental properties serve households at or below 60% AMI for at least 15 years, so 60% AMI and the 15 year term were added. program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.14) and Affordable Housing Overlay (Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan)
administering_agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Sec. 230.14 implements Government Code 65915: 20% base bonus for 10% lower income units rising 1.5% per additional 1% to 35%, 5% base bonus for 10% moderate income for-sale units rising 1% per 1% to 35%, one to three incentives or concessions by affordability tier, land donation option under 65915(h). The Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan Affordable Housing Overlay provides non-discretionary review for qualifying affordable projects, and the HBHA Pathways RFQ sought 100% affordable supportive housing at 60% AMI or less with by-right processing for projects with at least 20% affordable units.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; 55-year rental covenants; in-lieu fees under Sec. 230.26 are calculated on units before the density bonus.
next_deadline: Applies at project application. Housing Element Program 2B (expand the Affordable Housing Overlay) is the rezoning HCD requires before certification; Resolution 2026-25 to adopt the element was heard June 2 and June 8, 2026.
layering_notes: Huntington Beach's local code mirrors the pre-2020 state schedule (35% cap), but state law controls and allows larger bonuses; the practical constraint is political and legal (Measure U voter control, State v. City of Huntington Beach over the Housing Element). Until the element is certified, projects may use builder's remedy and the City cannot earn Prohousing points. No local fee waiver ordinance beyond the Sec. 230.26 fee-reduction incentive. Density bonus does not trigger prevailing wage. Code read on zoneomics; HCD March 6, 2026 letter and Legistar matter list opened.

GGHA PBVs are the natural operating layer for a project on the Housing Successor's Civic Center Parcel together with HOME-ARP, County MHSA/BHSA and OCHFT. Housing Authority page and the September 21, 2026 PBV waiting list notice opened on ggcity.org.

Applies only to PBVs committed under a development agreement for new construction or rehab; PBVs placed on existing housing with 8 or fewer contract units, or no development activity, do not trigger it. program_name: Residential Density Bonus and Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements (Garden Grove Municipal Code Chapter 9.60, Secs. 9.60.040 and 9.60.050; Housing Element Program 10)
administering_agency: City of Garden Grove Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Chapter 9.60 implements the State Density Bonus Law, Housing Accountability Act, Housing Crisis Act and No Net Loss law: density bonus, incentives, concessions, waivers and parking ratios per Government Code 65915 and 65915.5 as amended, processed concurrently with the land use application; ministerial review for qualifying housing development projects; replacement of protected units; regulatory agreement required for every affordable unit (Sec. 9.60.050) including a rule that voucher holders pay the affordable rent, not FMR. The 2021-2029 Housing Element reports surveyed projects averaging 183% of base density through bonuses and commits the City to the updated ordinance by 2025 (Program 10) and to study an inclusionary ordinance (Program 11).
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable) with 55-year rental covenants in the City regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Applies at project application. Program 11 inclusionary study was due within the Housing Element cycle; no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee exists as of this pass.
layering_notes: Garden Grove has no inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee, local housing trust fund or affordable housing fee waiver; density bonus plus Housing Element Program 4 (technical and financial assistance for 10 affordable units a year, expedited processing, land write-downs from General Fund, HOME, LMIHAF and PLHA) is the full local toolkit beyond the Housing Successor land and GGHA vouchers. Garden Grove is not a Prohousing designated city. Density bonus does not trigger prevailing wage. Chapter 9.60 read on the zoneomics mirror; 2021-2029 Housing Element PDF opened on ggcity.org.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Program (Municipal Code Chapter 17.36, Ordinance 1252)
administering_agency: City of Hollister Community Development Department, Planning Division and Housing Division (housing@hollister.ca.gov, (831) 636-4360 x1254)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. All for-sale and rental residential projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% of base units (before any density bonus) as on-site inclusionary units: at least 6% very low income, at least 5% very low or low income, and at least 4% very low, low or moderate income (Section 17.36.050). Fractions of 0.25 or more round up. No in-lieu fee option exists; the only alternatives (Section 17.36.060) are affordable rental units inside a for-sale project or acquisition and rehabilitation of existing market-rate units (rehab value at least 25% of pre-rehab value including land, City-approved physical needs assessment, residentially zoned site, applicant-funded relocation). Ordinance 1252 (ZOA 2023-4) adopted August 6, 2024; Housing Element goal of 150 inclusionary units during 2023-2031.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units sold or rented only to very low, low or moderate income households (up to 120% AMI, San Benito County HCD limits) or to the City or its designee; units must average at least 85% of the square footage of market units with the same bedroom count, match unit type proportions, bedroom ratio, finishes and exterior design, and be dispersed on site with equal access to common areas; buyers and renters screened by the Administrator through an open public process (no private selection). For-sale units: affordable price restricted 30 years under a recorded agreement, resetting on resale, owner occupancy within 60 days and at least 10 months a year, no rental. Rental units: affordable for 55 years under a recorded affordable housing agreement.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; an affordable housing agreement is required and inclusionary units must be permitted and occupied in proportion to market-rate units in each phase (Section 17.36.050 F). Exempt: ADUs, projects under 10 units, vesting tentative maps and development agreements in effect at the effective date, complete applications with fees paid before that date, and projects exempted by Gov. Code 66474.2, 66498.1 or other state law. Council may adopt guidelines and administration and monitoring fees by resolution (Section 17.36.080).
layering_notes: Hollister's program is stricter than the San Benito County Chapter 21.03 ordinance (15% on site or 20% off site, with a $30 per square foot in-lieu fee) because it allows no fee payment and requires on-site units for both rental and for-sale projects; as a result the City has no inclusionary in-lieu fund to redeploy as gap financing. Inclusionary units may be used to qualify for a density bonus under Chapter 17.34 (Section 17.36.050 C), so a 15% inclusionary project can stack the state bonus and concessions. The City's Below Market Rate Housing Program (affordable_housing.php) administers waitlists for inclusionary units; all waitlists were closed as of this pass. Hollister's prior Housing Developer Resources page (opened) states the City previously had no inclusionary ordinance; the code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because library.municode.com blocks automated access. Pairs with the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs and the CMFA conduit bonds recorded at the county level (Baler Place, 340 Bridgevale Road, is a Hollister project).
eligible_project_detail: market-rate for-sale subdivisions and condominium projects of 10 or more units (compliance)
market-rate rental projects of 10 or more units (compliance)
acquisition-rehab of existing units as alternative compliance

This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Permit fee waiver program for affordable and special needs housing and reduced multifamily impact fees (Housing Element Policy Action H3.3)
administering_agency: City of Hollister Planning, Building and Finance Divisions and Engineering Department
typical_award_size: Existing: lower sewer and water connection fees and traffic impact fees for multifamily development (per-unit basis; the City is considering a square-foot basis). Committed: a reduction or waiver of permit processing fees for affordable and other special needs housing projects, to be established by August 2026 following the user fee study now underway; the Housing Element also calls for waiving permit fees for ADUs under certain sizes or deed restricted as affordable to lower income households, and the sites strategy table contemplates reducing development fees for key sites. Amounts not yet set.

next_deadline: No application deadline. Policy Action H3.3 set August 2026 to establish the fee waiver program; adoption could not be confirmed. Confirm with the Planning Division before underwriting any waiver.
layering_notes: Hollister has no codified fee waiver today, unlike San Benito County Section 21.03.012, which can reimburse impact fee waivers for 100% affordable projects from county in-lieu fees. Because Hollister collects no inclusionary in-lieu fees, any waiver will be a general fund cost, which is why the City is tying it to the user fee study. Density bonus concessions under Chapter 17.34 remain the only guaranteed path to fee or standard relief until the program is adopted. Recorded as negative information per schema rule 4 and so the August 2026 commitment can be tracked.

A permit fee waiver for affordable and special needs housing is committed in Housing Element Policy Action H3.3 but not yet adopted; lower multifamily connection and traffic fees are part of the general fee schedule. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

administering_agency: City of San Juan Bautista Planning Department (contract planning staff; City Hall 311 Second Street)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of six or more units (the Housing Element describes the rental threshold as five or more) must reserve one affordable unit for every five market-rate units (about 16.7% of base units, calculated before any density bonus) for very low or low income households, for sale or as rentals (Section 11-09-400); fractions may be met with a partial in-lieu fee. In-lieu payment of the whole obligation is allowed only at the City Council's discretion after a Planning Commission recommendation (11-09-500); the per-unit fee formula (11-09-505) is the San Benito County median home sales price for the prior fourth quarter minus the maximum affordable three-bedroom sales price, divided across all project units and paid at building permit. Fees go to a separate interest-bearing account used solely to provide housing opportunities for very low and low income households anywhere in the City (11-09-510). Off-site and joint-venture off-site rental compliance allowed on an infeasibility showing (11-09-600).
affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI) and low (80% AMI) households by San Benito County HUD limits; for-sale and rental reserved units deed restricted for at least 55 years; rental units may not convert to condominiums during the restriction; reserved units must match the design and bedroom and square footage proportions of market units.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; reserved units built before or with market units and in proportion by phase. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (certified by HCD) adds a program to update the inclusionary provisions and notes that most buildable lots fall under the six-unit threshold, so no project has yet triggered the requirement; fee reductions or waivers have been negotiated in development agreements.
layering_notes: The in-lieu account has no reported balance (the ordinance was adopted in 2007 and the Housing Element says the City has no staff or financial resources for a stand-alone housing program), so it is not a realistic gap source. The one-in-five requirement is roughly comparable to San Benito County's 15% on-site standard but with deeper targeting (very low and low only, no moderate). Mixed-use infill in the downtown and gateway districts is the City's moderate-income strategy; exclusively residential new construction on commercial-only Mixed Use parcels is allowed only when 100% affordable, which pairs well with a 100% affordable density bonus project. Layer with San Benito County PLHA (the City passes its own PLHA allocation to the County for homeless services under an MOU), County HHAP and state programs; Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs cover San Benito County. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror.
eligible_project_detail: market-rate subdivisions and multifamily projects of six or more units (compliance)
off-site affordable rental projects satisfying another developer's obligation
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(c)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): private residential projects built on private property are not subject to prevailing wage unless built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or public housing authority. An inclusionary requirement pays no public funds; any spending from the in-lieu account would be a separate public funds question.

program_name: State density bonus implementation and city housing finance capacity (2023-2031 Housing Element programs on density bonus, PLHA and CDBG)
administering_agency: City of San Juan Bautista Planning Department and City Manager's office
typical_award_size: No local enhancement. The adopted and HCD-certified 2023-2031 Housing Element (Final No. 5, January 20, 2026) states the City applies California Density Bonus Law directly (described as up to 35%; current Government Code 65915 allows up to 50% or more) with incentives such as reduced parking, and offers up to a 50% bonus in the Mixed-Use District for special needs and 100% affordable projects. Program 3.8 commits to revising the local density bonus ordinance to match state law by December 2026. Financial resources: the City intends to use over $320,000 of PLHA for an ADU Amnesty Program and has passed part of its PLHA (2019 allocation, $75,999 of a $455,999 2019-2025 plan) to San Benito County for homeless services; it has no CDBG, HOME or redevelopment funds but plans to apply for competitive CDBG and holds inclusionary in-lieu fees.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, senior, 100% affordable); inclusionary units under Chapter 11-09 are counted before bonus units.
next_deadline: No application deadline; state density bonus applies on request. Confirm whether the Program 3.8 density bonus ordinance update (due December 2026) has been adopted.
layering_notes: Explicit negative finding: San Juan Bautista has no local housing trust fund, no fee waiver program, no city NOFA and no city-controlled development funds beyond the Chapter 11-09 in-lieu account. Development capacity is constrained by water and sewer (a sewer force main to Hollister is a City project) and by the 8 to 15 units per acre Mixed-Use zoning; Program 3.13 commits to raising the Mixed-Use designation to 16 to 24 units per acre by December 2026. The only city-level tools are the inclusionary ordinance, state density bonus and SB 35 streamlining; capital must come from San Benito County (PLHA, HHAP, CMFA conduit bonds), Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs and state programs. The City's Housing Element page states the element is adopted and certified by HCD.
eligible_project_detail: mixed-use residential in the Mixed Use district
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Santa Cruz Affordable Housing Trust Fund (AHTF), Resolution NS-26,410, guidelines revised September 10, 2024
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (affordablehousing@santacruzca.gov, (831) 420-5150)
typical_award_size: Construction and deferred-payment permanent loans at simple interest of no more than 3% per year, plus gifts, grants, loan guarantees and credit enhancement. Revenue: Chapter 24.16.030 inclusionary in-lieu fees, the City's PLHA formula allocation (HCD estimate about $1.5 million over five years, deposited directly to the AHTF) and donations. Pipeline list dated September 2024 of 100% affordable rental projects eligible after the first-phase funding review: 136 River Street (For the Future Housing) $1,800,000 loan commitment, predevelopment; 119 Lincoln Street (Eden Housing with For the Future Housing) ground lease plus $5,555,000 loan commitment, predevelopment. Income targets: 30% of funds for extremely low income, up to 70% for lower income, maximum 20% for moderate income, 15% contingency; administrative costs capped at 5%. Fund balance is not published; the 2026 AB 2663 in-lieu fee report (opened) lists fee descriptions but no balance.
per_unit_cap: None published; underwritten by sources and uses and subsidy layering review (Attachment I), with at least 10% equity after completion and promissory-note predevelopment loans limited to 15% of estimated project cost.
affordability_requirement: Rental housing for low (80% AMI) and very low (50% AMI) income households; for-sale housing for moderate, low and very low income; priority first to projects guaranteeing perpetual affordability and second to at least 55 years with recapture; extra points for lowest rents, highest share of affordable units, committed other sources, leverage of tax credits and state and federal programs, and sponsor track record.
next_deadline: No NOFA; requests are reviewed on a rolling basis through a first-phase funding review that places eligible 100% affordable rental projects on the AHTF pipeline list, followed by Council approval of loan commitments. Contact the Housing Division before submitting; the pipeline list was last updated September 2024.
layering_notes: The City's primary local gap source and the usual local match for TCAC, HCD and AHSC applications (the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project secured $33.5M AHSC, $55.1M of tax credits and $55.6M of CDLAC bond authority). Separate from the County of Santa Cruz Housing Funds NOFA (LMIHAF, County PLHA and County AHIF), which covers unincorporated projects only, and from the County's Chapter 17.10 Measure J program; city projects stack AHTF with Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs, City HOME and CDBG (record below) and Prohousing scoring bonuses. In-lieu fee revenue depends on how many Measure O projects pay fees rather than build units, so balances fluctuate; the City also takes land dedications (Anton Pacific dedicated land for the Pacific Station expansion). cityofsantacruz.com now redirects to santacruzca.gov, which returns 403 to scripted fetches; the AHTF page, guidelines PDF, pipeline list and in-lieu report were opened through the WebFetch tool.
eligible_project_detail: conversion of market-rate units to affordable
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on public-funds logic only; no program or local rule found, changed to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. No City of Santa Cruz AHTF NOFA, guideline, resolution or loan term requiring prevailing wage was found (the AHTF page and the 2024 AHTF Loan Guidelines contain no wage term). Loans are public funds under 1720(b)(1) or (b)(4), but qualifying below-market loans may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) and small subsidies under 1720(c)(3). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 The PLHA portion is governed by PLHA formula rules, which are also silent.

program_name: Measure O Inclusionary Housing Program (Municipal Code Chapter 24.16 Part 1, Ordinance 2021-04) and inclusionary in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Housing and Community Development Division, with tenant and buyer eligibility intake by the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz (2160 41st Avenue, Capitola)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Voter-approved Measure O requires residential projects to provide a share of units affordable to very low, low or moderate income households under Chapter 24.16 Part 1 as revised by Ordinance 2021-04 (effective April 13, 2021); units may be built as rental or for-sale and carry long-term or permanent deed restrictions. Before the 2021 revision the ordinance required 15% of new rental units at or below 80% AMI; the City's June 2018 Keyser Marston feasibility analysis tested 15%, 25% and 35% alternatives and Downtown versus non-Downtown subareas under AB 1505, and the revised percentage (reported as 20%) was not confirmed from code text this pass. In-lieu fees under Section 24.16.030(6) are calculated project by project on the affordability gap between market and inclusionary rents (2018 sample: $168,478 gap per unit, $25,271 per market-rate unit or $34.86 per square foot at 15%), are usually paid before building permit issuance and are deposited to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund for new low income units with long-term restrictions or preservation. No refunds or interfund transfers occurred 2021-2025 (2026 AB 2663 report). Measure O rents and incomes are set annually by resolution (2025 schedule effective July 1, 2025, Resolution NS-16,452 series; eight implementing resolutions listed through NS-29,463).
affordability_requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households per the City resolution governing each unit; Measure O rentals restricted to very low and low income tenants or Housing Choice Voucher holders with annual income recertification; eligibility letters issued by the Housing Authority expire after three months; $250 processing fee paid by the seller or landlord.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee due at building permit. Annual rent and income schedules take effect July 1. Confirm the current inclusionary percentage and any Downtown subarea rate with the Housing Division (affordablehousing@santacruzca.gov) because the code publisher (codepublishing.com) and the Measure O resolution PDFs (scanned images) could not be read this pass.
layering_notes: Primary feeder of the AHTF (record above). Compared with the County's Measure J (15% of for-sale projects of seven or more units, rental projects pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee), the City program applies to rental projects, so market-rate apartment developers downtown face either on-site units or a gap-based fee; recent mixed-income downtown projects show the pattern (175 condos with 20 affordable at Front Street Riverfront, 276 market-rate with 37 affordable at 530 Front Street, 233 market-rate with 35 affordable at 130 Center Street). Inclusionary units can qualify for the state density bonus under Chapter 24.16 Part 3. The 2022 ballot Measure O (library and housing site) outcome was not addressed on any City page opened; the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City Lot 4 is under construction with 124 units (all but one manager unit affordable), so the project proceeded. Sources opened: Measure O program page, Resolutions and Ordinances page, FAQ page, For Rent Units page, KMA 2018 analysis PDF and the 2026 in-lieu fee report PDF, all via WebFetch because santacruzca.gov blocks scripted fetches.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check 2026-11-08: Measure O, For Rent Units and FAQ pages confirm very low/low/moderate categories, Ordinance 2021-04 effective April 13, 2021, very low and low income or voucher rentals with annual recertification, $250 fee paid by owner, and 3-month eligibility expiry. Inclusionary percentage still not stated on City pages. prevailing_wage_trigger false has no cited rule in prevailing_wage_basis.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Density bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 24.16 Part 3) and fee deferrals for 100% affordable developments (Part 4, Resolution NS-30,634)
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Planning Division and Housing Division
typical_award_size: Chapter 24.16 Part 4 is now Fee Deferrals for Affordable Units (Sections 24.16.300 Units Eligible for Fee Deferrals and 24.16.310 Procedure for Deferral of Fees). Resolution NS-30,634 (adopted March 10, 2026) lets staff defer development review fees for 100 percent affordable housing projects: Building, Fire, Community Development, Parks, Police, Public Works, Water and similar fees may be deferred up to five years, or until certificate of occupancy if a substantially complete building permit application is filed, then up to about five more years on a payment plan with interest set annually by the Finance Director. Third-party review cost fees are collected in full; impact fees (Gov. Code 66007, SB 937), the Parks and Recreation Facilities Tax and the Quimby Fee cannot be deferred past certificate of occupancy; the Traffic Impact Fee is deferred under separate procedures. Fee waivers are not granted by staff and must still be requested from City Council; Resolution NS-30,635 waivers apply only to projects on City-owned land or buildings. Part 3 density bonus text and the childcare impact fee reduction for 100% affordable projects were not read (codepublishing.com 403).
per_unit_cap: None; deferral covers the eligible development review fees in full, subject to exclusions.
affordability_requirement: 100 percent affordable housing developments for the staff deferral policy; a 2019 City form indicated only very low and low income units were eligible for Part 4 fee relief (not re-confirmed).
next_deadline: Rolling. Submit the supplemental fee deferral application with the 100 percent affordable planning application (or with building plan check if no planning fees apply), then sign a fee deferral agreement and payment plan.
layering_notes: Treat as a cost reduction layered on top of the AHTF loan and Measure O compliance; the County's enhanced density bonus (Chapter 17.12.065, up to 50% for 21% or more low income units) and County AHIF exemption apply only in the unincorporated area. Santa Cruz also created Flexible Density Units in four commercial zones (auxiliary units allowed up to the full floor area ratio regardless of density) and the My House My Home senior ADU program, both cited in the 2023 Prohousing application. Marked needs_confirmation because the code text was not opened; the zoneomics chapter index listing Parts 3 and 4 and the City Prohousing page were. Childcare impact fee: the City Childcare Impact Fee page lists rates with no affordable housing provision; search results suggest Chapter 18.48 exempts 100 percent affordable projects. Confirm before counting it.
cycle_notes: Policy adopted March 10, 2026 (Resolution NS-30,634, Planning Commission recommendation February 5, 2026); eligibility determined by the Community Development Director, payment plan approved by the Finance Director.
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: the fee deferral policy page and Resolution NS-30,634 PDF on santacruzca.gov confirm every deferral term in the record (100 percent affordable, five years or to certificate of occupancy then a payment plan with interest, exclusions for third-party review fees, impact fees under SB 937, Parks tax and Quimby fee). Still unconfirmed: Chapter 24.16 Part 3 density bonus text (codepublishing 403) and the childcare impact fee relief; the City Childcare Impact Fee page lists rates but no affordable housing provision, and search results suggest Chapter 18.48 exempts 100 percent affordable projects rather than reducing the fee. Confirm before relying on the childcare piece. Manual edit Nov 10, 2026: name updated to Part 4 fee deferrals; childcare fee claim removed from name and PW basis.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Chapter 24.16 Part 4 and Resolution NS-30,634 allow deferral of development review fees for 100 percent affordable developments. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Prohousing Designation (awarded August 4, 2023; renewal application 2026, Resolution NS-30,681) and Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City Lot 4
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Economic Development and Housing (Housing Division) with the Planning Division
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. The designation (57 points, 7th highest of 47 jurisdictions as of April 2024) gives City projects scoring preference or priority processing in AHSC, Infill Infrastructure Grant, Transformative Climate Communities and other state programs and made the City eligible for Prohousing Incentive Program Round 2 ($9.5 million statewide pool). Example: the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City-owned Lot 4 (Cathcart, Cedar and Lincoln Streets) received a $33.5M AHSC award, a $55.1M TCAC tax credit award and $55.6M of CDLAC bond authority for 124 units (all affordable except one manager unit) above a new library funded by Measure S, with child care, 240 parking spaces and a $250,000 Economic Development Trust Fund contribution for the farmers market. The 2023 designation expires January 1, 2027; the City applied for renewal in 2026.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable to the designation; the Lot 4 housing is 100% affordable (income levels not stated on the project page; Eden Housing manages the interest list for studio to three-bedroom units).
next_deadline: Renewal decision by HCD pending; current designation valid through January 1, 2027. Lot 4 housing framing was underway on levels 4 through 8 as of the latest project update, with completion dates not stated.
layering_notes: Prohousing points are additive to the AHTF and HOME layers and have been decisive for Santa Cruz downtown projects competing in AHSC. The City disposes of its own land for 100% affordable projects (Lot 4, Pacific Station North 125 units and Pacific Station South 70 units with Santa Cruz Community Health and Dientes, 119 Lincoln Street ground lease) and accepts land dedications from market-rate developers under Measure O (Anton Pacific). Santa Cruz County does not hold a Prohousing designation in the records compiled; Watsonville, Capitola and Scotts Valley pages opened this pass do not mention one. The Prohousing page, the May 2024 Economic Development journal article and the Downtown Library project page were opened; the 2026 resolution PDF returned 403 to scripted access.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Prohousing Designation itself pays no construction cost (Labor Code 1720(a)(1)). The Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project sits on City-owned Lot 4 and is layered with a City-funded library, City land and state awards; any wage obligation comes from those sources, their 1720(b)(3) land terms and award conditions, not from the designation. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true was not tied to a rule; the designation provides no funds and project-level wages depend on the library, land and state award terms. Changed to unclear.

program_name: CDBG and HOME entitlement grants (HUD Consolidated Plan 2025-2030, Annual Action Plan PY 2026-2027)
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (housing@santacruzca.gov)
typical_award_size: PY 2026 (July 2026 to June 2027): $497,393 CDBG and $237,080.42 HOME from HUD, both lower than PY 2025; CDBG total available $512,553 with about $15,000 program income; HOME total available $793,841 including about $100,000 program income and $456,761 of prior-year funds for reprogramming. The City describes typical levels as about $600,000 CDBG and about $400,000 HOME per year. CDBG funds community programs (public services capped at 15%), infrastructure and facility improvements and delivery costs for two housing programs; HOME funds acquisition, homebuyer assistance, homeowner rehabilitation and rental development, with repaid rehabilitation and homebuyer loans automatically reprogrammed to affordable housing. Santa Cruz receives no ESG.
per_unit_cap: HUD HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits apply; none set locally.
affordability_requirement: CDBG benefits households at or below 80% AMI; HOME rental units at or below 60% AMI (High HOME rents) with HUD affordability periods of 5 to 20 years depending on subsidy; Section 3 applies to construction and rehabilitation.
next_deadline: PY 2027-2028 application period open as of this pass; the cycle normally opens in October with applications due mid-December, proposals advertised in November, public review and Council approval February through May, and the Action Plan submitted to HUD by May 15. Applications: online CDBG form, HOME application (DOCX) and CDBG supplemental budget; CBDO certification available. Email housing@santacruzca.gov to join the HUD notification list.
layering_notes: Small but predictable; HOME is the realistic development piece (under $800,000 available in PY 2026) and is typically paired with an AHTF loan and PBVs from the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz. Federal Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units and CDBG projects of 8 or more units. The County administers state HOME and CDBG for the unincorporated area, Watsonville (CDBG entitlement separately), Capitola and Scotts Valley, so Santa Cruz is the only Santa Cruz County city with its own HOME entitlement. Documents opened via WebFetch: HUD Consolidated Plan Documents page and the PY 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan PDF.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 14-46, Ordinance 1480-25 effective October 9, 2025) with in-lieu and commercial fees
administering_agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Housing Division (275 Main Street, Suite 400, (831) 768-3080)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 7 to 50 units: for-sale 15% (5% above moderate, 5% median, 5% moderate), rental 20% (5% low, 5% median, 10% very low or Housing Choice Voucher and other subsidy recipients). Projects over 50 units: 20% for both tenures (for-sale 10% above moderate, 5% moderate, 5% median). In-lieu fees are required from projects of six or fewer units or lots, from new commercial and industrial development over 1,000 square feet (a commercial linkage fee) and from condominium conversions; fees are set by Council resolution and indexed annually at 50% of the Santa Cruz-Watsonville House Price Index change, paid at building permit or final map (14-46.070). FY 2025-26 schedule (effective July 1, 2025, Resolutions 238-01, 72-12 and 136-23): $21,885 per single-family detached unit, $8,419 per multifamily unit for projects of six or fewer units or lots, and $1.75 per square foot for commercial and industrial floor area of 1,001 square feet or more. Income categories use the Watsonville median household income, defined as 70% of the Santa Cruz County median. Federal, state or City-assisted affordable projects meeting the percentages satisfy the chapter in full (14-46.040(c)). Projects with 50% or more affordable units receive priority processing (14-46.080). Release fees for de-restricting units are paid into the affordable housing fund.
affordability_requirement: Rental units 55 years, ownership units 45 years, deed restricted; very low means the lower of 80% of Watsonville median or 50% of county AMI, low up to 100% of Watsonville median or 50% to 80% county AMI, median up to 120% of Watsonville median or 80% county AMI, moderate up to 150% of Watsonville median, above moderate up to 170%; preference for households living or working in Watsonville at least one year; minimum unit sizes and amenity standards in 14-46.060; affordable units built concurrently with market units.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requirement applies at entitlement. No application round as of November 10, 2026. In-lieu fee amounts are in the City's FY 2025-26 affordable housing in-lieu fee schedule; a FY 2026-27 update was not located.
layering_notes: The deepest city inclusionary requirement in Santa Cruz County (20% of rental units with half at very low income or voucher holders) and the only city program with a commercial linkage component; it exceeds the County's Measure J (for-sale only) and Capitola's and Scotts Valley's 15% standards. Because 100% affordable projects satisfy the chapter automatically and get priority processing, tax credit developers face no added inclusionary cost, while mixed-income developers can satisfy the very low tier with Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBV units. Fees flow to the City's Affordable Housing fund (record below). The 2025 code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because codepublishing.com and gocodebook.com returned 403; the City's Affordable Housing page (watsonville.gov/172) was also opened.
cycle_notes: Ordinances 1480-25 and 1481-25 took effect October 9, 2025 and removed the prior exemption for unsubsidized rental projects. Affordable housing agreement approved by Council and recorded before final map or construction.
eligible_project_detail: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of seven or more units (compliance)
small residential projects and commercial or industrial development (fee payers)
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: added FY 2025-26 in-lieu fee amounts from the official watsonville.gov fee schedule (DocumentCenter 27606), which also matches the over 1,000 square foot commercial threshold and HPI indexing. Chapter 14-46 text is still readable only on the zoneomics and gocodebook mirrors (codepublishing.com 403, no Watsonville Legistar client, the Ordinance 1480-25 exhibit not found on watsonville.gov), so confidence stays needs_confirmation.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this inclusionary ordinance (Chapter 14-46) provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any public loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on a project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Inclusionary Housing in-lieu fee Affordable Housing fund, HOME program income and Successor Agency housing assets
administering_agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Housing Division, and the City as Successor Agency to the Watsonville Redevelopment Agency
typical_award_size: The 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan states that inclusionary in-lieu fees under Chapter 14-46 go to the City's Affordable Housing fund and are used for development, acquisition, rehabilitation and preservation of affordable units, and that PLHA, HOME, CDBG, CalHome and in-lieu fees provide gap financing for the First-Time Homebuyer and Housing Rehabilitation programs. The City has no active state HOME grant (last award $1,546,000 in 2011) and holds over $1,850,000 of HOME program income available for future HOME-eligible activities; it has made over 500 FTHB loans and has 280 inclusionary ownership units. The 2025-2029 plan does not mention Successor Agency property and states the City does not anticipate using publicly owned land for CDBG goals. No in-lieu fund balance, multifamily loan terms or application procedure is published.
affordability_requirement: Affordable to households at or below the Chapter 14-46 income categories (70% of county AMI basis) or HOME limits (80% AMI, 60% AMI for HOME rental units) with recorded affordability covenants of 45 to 55 years.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 10, 2026. No NOFA is published; developers negotiate assistance project by project with the Housing Division ((831) 768-3080). Confirm the in-lieu fund balance and the HOME program income balance with the City.
layering_notes: Watsonville's local gap sources are modest and discretionary; the HOME program income (over $1.85 million per the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan) is the largest identifiable pool and carries federal HOME rules and Davis-Bacon for 12 or more units. Stack with the County of Santa Cruz state HOME tenant-based assistance (which covers Watsonville), Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs, HHAP through the Watsonville/Santa Cruz CoC, and City CDBG (record below). Unlike Santa Cruz city there is no adopted trust fund guideline document. Marked needs_confirmation because no fund balance or program guideline could be opened; the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan PDFs on watsonville.gov were read.
eligible_project_detail: first-time homebuyer and owner rehabilitation loans
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan on watsonville.gov re-read; it confirms in-lieu fees go to the Affordable Housing fund for development, acquisition, rehabilitation and preservation, the 70% AMI inclusionary income basis, the $1,546,000 2011 HOME award, over $1,850,000 of HOME program income, over 500 FTHB loans and 280 program units. Removed the former redevelopment agency sites detail, which the plan does not support. The record correctly states that no fund balance, multifamily loan terms or NOFA is published.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. program_name: Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 14-47, Ordinance 1481-25 effective October 9, 2025) with impact fee deferral concession
administering_agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Planning Division (Director approves ministerial projects; Council approves discretionary projects)

Watsonville was certified for its 2023-2031 Housing Element and offers Downtown Watsonville Specific Plan densities; the Specific Plan (Chapter 14-47 of Part 26 on some mirrors) was not opened. program_name: Affordable (Inclusionary) Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 18.02, Ordinance 1062 of 2023) and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department ((831) 475-7300), with buyer intake by the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects creating seven or more for-sale units, residential parcels, mobile home parcels or converted condominiums must restrict 15% of units for sale to moderate, low or very low income households; rental projects are exempt from the inclusionary requirement but pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee under Chapter 18.05 (record below). Alternatives (18.02.050): in-lieu fees at the rate in the Council fee schedule (the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element, Program 2.8, states the inclusionary in-lieu fee and the housing impact fee are both currently $25 per square foot following the 2021 feasibility study), payable at building permit with deferral to certificate of occupancy allowed if the Council finds it aids feasibility and security is provided; off-site units within one mile; land dedication yielding at least 10% more affordable units than otherwise required. In-lieu fees are deposited to the City's housing trust fund for construction of new low and very low income units. Adopted November 2004, amended 2013, 2021 and by Ordinance 1062 (introduced August 24, 2023, adopted September 14, 2023) to update definitions, mobile home sales procedures and eligibility. The City may require more than 15% only when it provides a grant, subsidy, loan, fee waiver or other fiscal benefit.
affordability_requirement: Buyers at or below 120% of Santa Cruz County AMI with assets no more than 1.5 times the income limit (excluding up to $500,000 in retirement plans); affordable price set at 35% of gross income including a 10% down payment; resale restrictions with equity sharing and release payments to the trust fund; condominium conversions of five or more units mitigate through on-site units or in-lieu fees.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee per the schedule in effect at payment. Inventory to date: eight inclusionary condos at Capitola Beach Villas (2008), four other inclusionary homes, seven affordable lots at Turner Lane and 12 new units added citywide in 2025 (69 in the 6th cycle). Housing Element Program 2.8 commits the City to an economic analysis of the inclusionary ordinance during the planning period.
layering_notes: Lighter than the County's Measure J only in scope (same 15%, same seven-unit threshold, for-sale only) and much lighter than Watsonville. Rental developers owe the $25 per square foot Affordable Housing Impact Fee instead, so a 100% affordable rental project in Capitola should seek the impact fee exemption or deferral at entitlement. The ordinance text was read from the Council's Ordinance 1062 packet attachment on the City's public agenda host (mccmeetingspublic) because codepublishing.com returned 403 and the City's own chapter PDF link is dead; the City's Affordable Housing page and 2023-2031 Housing Element (certified August 30, 2024) were also opened.
eligible_project_detail: for-sale subdivisions and condominium projects of seven or more units (compliance)
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this inclusionary ordinance (Chapter 18.02) provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any public loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on a project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: in-lieu fee corrected from $10 per square foot (2021 EPS analysis) to $25 per square foot per the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element Program 2.8; confirm against the current Council fee schedule. Ordinance 1062 terms (15%, seven or more units, assets under 1.5 times the income limit, $500,000 retirement exclusion, 35% of income with 10% down) confirmed.

program_name: Capitola Affordable Housing Trust Fund (established November 2004) and Affordable Housing Impact Fee ($25 per square foot, adopted 2021)
administering_agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department ((831) 475-7300)
typical_award_size: Trust fund balance about $144,000 (2023-2031 Housing Element, certified August 2024); revenue to date has come only from inclusionary in-lieu fees, with donations allowed. Uses: matching funds for state and federal sources, rehabilitation loans and grants, feasibility studies, and acquisition-rehab and new construction gap assistance for households at or below 80% AMI; no loan guidelines, per-project limit or NOFA are adopted. Affordable Housing Impact Fee (adopted 2021 after a nexus study): Housing Element Programs 2.7 and 2.8 state the inclusionary in-lieu fee (ownership projects of seven or more units) and the housing impact fee (projects of fewer than seven units) are both $25 per square foot, and a separate impact fee of $6 per square foot applies to multifamily rental housing, which has no inclusionary requirement (the constraints chapter describes the impact fee generally at $25 per square foot, so confirm the rental rate on the current Council fee schedule). Exemptions or waivers for deed-restricted affordable units are not stated. PLHA: state estimate of $630,557 for Capitola over the 2020-2024 cycle. Capitola imposes no park, transportation, administration or childcare exactions; school fees ($4.08 per square foot) and Central Fire District fees ($0.53 per square foot) apply.
affordability_requirement: Trust fund monies are directed to new low and very low income units (Section 18.02.050) and to affordable units for moderate income and below; the impact fee is used exclusively to facilitate affordable housing development.
next_deadline: No application cycle; requests are negotiated with the Community and Economic Development Director and approved by Council. The 52-unit 100% affordable development at 1098 38th Avenue (building permit application filed, 2025 Annual Progress Report) is the first candidate for City assistance; confirm whether the impact fee is waived or deferred for that project.
layering_notes: Capitola's fund is too small (about $144,000) to serve as gap financing; its value is as a local match or fee offset in a TCAC or HCD application, with capital from the County's Chapter 17.10 AHIF fund being unavailable inside city limits. The $25 per square foot impact fee is a significant cost on market-rate rental projects (the County charges $2 per habitable square foot on rentals), so mixed-income sponsors should model it; the fee feasibility analysis (EPS, 2021) warned rental development was marginal even before the increase. Density increases are available under the mixed-use AHO successor provisions for 20% lower income units (record below). Sources opened: 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF (DocumentCenter 1797), 2021 fee feasibility analysis (DocumentCenter 699) and the March 23, 2026 Annual Progress Report memo. Audit reclassification: funding_type set to loan because Housing Element Program 2.7 states the City uses the Housing Trust Fund to provide loans and grants (Housing Rehabilitation Loan and Grant Program, feasibility studies, and permanent financing of acquisition-rehab and new construction affordable projects); the balance is only about $144,000. The Housing Element also states a $6 per square foot impact fee for multifamily rental housing alongside the $25 per square foot fee, so confirm the rental rate with the City.
eligible_project_detail: acquisition of units for affordable resale
local match for state and federal awards
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Capitola 2023-2031 Housing Element (https://www.cityofcapitola.gov/DocumentCenter/View/1797/Capitola-Housing-Element-Adopted-and-Certified-August-2024) adopts no trust fund loan guidelines or wage rule; its constraints chapter notes only generally that use of state and federal funds triggers relocation and prevailing wage rules. Trust fund loans are public funds under 1720(b)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); a below-market residual receipts loan on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI can be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf), and small subsidies may fall under 1720(c)(3).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing (Below Market Rate) Ordinance (Municipal Code Section 14.01.030, Affordable Housing Committee) and affordable housing in-lieu fee fund
administering_agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department (planningdepartment@scottsvalley.gov, 1 Civic Center Drive) with the Council's Affordable Housing Committee setting project terms
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Within the former redevelopment project area boundary (unchanged since 1990), residential developments of seven or more units (for sale or rental) must set aside 15% of units for very low, low and moderate income households on site, or off site in limited cases; developments of six or fewer units pay an in-lieu fee; projects of seven or more units with average lot sizes over one acre may pay the fee with Council approval. The in-lieu fee equals the median sales price of a home in the project minus the City-determined affordable price. The two-member Affordable Housing Committee recommends unit counts, sizes and affordability levels for each project, subject to Council confirmation. The ordinance has produced 84 affordable rental and 50 affordable ownership units; in-lieu fees from small projects have subsidized smaller rental projects (the City loaned funds to Emerald Hill Apartments, 46 units with MidPen Housing, including impact fee offsets). Exempt: subsidized projects deed restricted through state or federal programs, single homes on existing lots, additions, ADUs and hardship cases. Housing Element Program H-1.8: comprehensive study by July 2026 and a citywide amendment with income-tier standards by January 2027.
affordability_requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households as set per project by the Affordable Housing Committee; inclusionary units carry restricted equity accrual, resale price and rental price limits; subsidized affordable projects meeting the standard are exempt.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; the Affordable Housing Committee meets as special meetings noticed 24 hours ahead. Watch for the July 2026 inclusionary study and the January 2027 citywide ordinance amendment (Program H-1.8), which may change the boundary, percentage and in-lieu formula.

The 15% standard matches Capitola and the County's Measure J but applies to rentals as well; it is lighter than Watsonville's 20%. 100% affordable projects are exempt and instead use Chapter 17.41 ministerial approval and the Chapter 17.62 state density bonus (records below); the 4444 Scotts Valley Drive project is the first 100% affordable project under the 6th cycle element. The 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF (certified April 2, 2024), the City Housing page (scottsvalley.gov/220) and the Affordable Housing Committee page were opened; the municode text of Section 14.01.030 was not (blocked host).
