program_name: Housing Element Opportunity Site Combining District (Municipal Code Chapter 17.41, Ordinance 16.142.1 adopted June 18, 2025): ministerial approval and standards relief for affordable projects
administering_agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department
typical_award_size: Not a subsidy. On Housing Element opportunity sites (Table F-10 sites outside the Town Center Specific Plan), multifamily projects with 20% or more of units affordable to lower income households get by-right approval (objective standards only) with ministerial design review under 17.50.045; other projects follow normal zoning review. Rezone sites carry a 20 du/ac minimum and 40 du/ac maximum, 60% coverage, three stories and a 35-foot top plate (40 feet for vertical mixed use), and at least 16 units are allowed on every site. Any project may request a deviation from a standard that physically precludes its proposed density, limited to the minimum needed. Lot consolidation incentives (deviations from development and subdivision standards) are available only to projects that merge a parcel under one-half acre with an adjacent parcel and are 100% deed restricted for 55 years (rentals at or below 80% AMI, ownership at or below 120% AMI, residential at least 85% of mixed-use floor area). On Mixed-Use Rezone sites residential uses must occupy less than 70% of gross floor area; no affordable exception is stated. Chapter adopted December 4, 2024 (Ordinance 16.142) and rewritten June 18, 2025 (Ordinance 16.142.1) to carry out Housing Element Programs H-1.1 and H-1.2.
affordability_requirement: At least 20% lower income units for by-right approval; lot consolidation incentives require 100% affordable units for 55 years (rental 80% AMI, ownership 120% AMI) on merged parcels that include one under one-half acre.
next_deadline: Available now for sites mapped in the combining district; Program H-1.1 required the rezonings within the Housing Element timeline and Program H-1.2 maintains by-right approval for lower income sites. Confirm site eligibility with the Planning Department.
layering_notes: Scotts Valley's main local incentive for tax credit projects, substituting for the absence of a trust fund or fee waiver; it stacks with the Chapter 17.62 state density bonus and the inclusionary exemption for subsidized projects, and with Housing Authority PBVs and state capital. The 4444 Scotts Valley Drive 100% affordable project (first under the 6th cycle element, using state density bonus and SB 35) is the template. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; the HCD certification letter (April 2, 2024) and the City Housing Element page were also opened.

Any public loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on a project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 The chapter is a local by-right path, not the Gov. administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department and City Manager's Budget Office; Real Property Transfer Tax Fund
typical_award_size: Transfer tax on sales above $2.3 million (threshold indexed from $2 million as of July 1, 2025): 0.75 percent from $2 million to $5 million, 1.0 percent from $5 million to $10 million, 1.5 percent above $10 million. About $225 million collected July 2020 through mid 2023. FY 2025-26 revenue estimate $55.0 million, FY 2026-27 $60.0 million. Original policy (April 2022) directed 40 percent to extremely low income housing, 30 percent low income, 5 percent moderate income, 10 percent homelessness prevention, 15 percent homeless support. The June 10, 2025 revision allows up to 90 percent of revenue after 5 percent administration for homeless sheltering and interim housing, with only the remainder for new or preserved affordable housing; the FY 2025-26 plan puts $0 of new revenue into affordable housing development, and the same June 2025 spending plan programs FY 2026-27 and ongoing revenue ($60.0 million) as $3.0 million administration, $5.7 million homelessness prevention, $51.3 million homeless sheltering and support and $0 for affordable housing. Prior-year Measure E reserves are still being drawn for development, for example $14 million for the Gateway Tower land acquisition (September 2025).
affordability_requirement: When used for development: new or preserved rental housing for extremely low (30 percent AMI) and low income households under City regulatory agreements; previously set by AMI category in Policy 1-18 Section 22.
next_deadline: No standalone Measure E NOFA and no open round as of November 9, 2026. The June 10, 2025 spending plan allocates $0 of FY 2026-27 and ongoing Measure E revenue to affordable housing; any housing share would have to come from a later annual budget (next adoption June 2027). Remaining prior-year Measure E reserves reach developers only through Gap Financing Program awards; verify balances with the Housing Department.
layering_notes: Measure E was the City's largest discretionary housing source from 2020 to 2024 and funded many Gap Financing Program awards. Expect limited new Measure E development money through at least FY 2026-27 because the General Fund shortfall shifted $39.2 million (rising to $42.8 million) of homelessness costs into this fund. Developers should underwrite LMIHAF and inclusionary fee funds first and treat Measure E as upside. A Measure E transfer tax refund pilot for qualifying nonprofit purchases (Section 4.59.230) ran July 2021 through June 30, 2024 with one application; it is now expired. Documents read via Legistar attachments because sanjoseca.gov is blocked. Audit 2026-11-08 funding_type: classed as loan because the development share reaches projects as Gap Financing Program loans (the June 2025 memo cites about $60 million of prior-year Measure E and other housing funds for a Gap Financing NOFA); the shelter share is City-operated spending, not a developer source.
cycle_notes: appropriated through the annual budget and project-specific Council actions
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. The Measure E spending allocation memo contains no prevailing wage term. San Jose Council loan commitment memos read (Capitol Station, Gateway Tower, 318 N. 6th St.) contain no City prevailing wage requirement; sanjoseca.gov NOFA documents returned 403. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: next_deadline said future housing allocations depended on the FY 2026-27 budget (June 2026); the source memo's Table 2 programs FY 2026-27 and ongoing revenue at $0 for affordable housing (all $60.0 million to administration, prevention and shelter), so next_deadline now says no open round as of November 9, 2026 and typical_award_size adds the FY 2026-27 split. No 2026 amendment to Policy 1-18 Section 22 was found in the San Jose Legistar API. Tax rates and the $225 million collection figure are not on this page and were not rechecked.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Housing Successor to the San Jose Redevelopment Agency
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department as Housing Successor
typical_award_size: Ending balance June 30, 2025: $95,884,306. Deposits in FY 2024-25: $22,478,762 (loan repayments and interest). FY 2024-25 expenditures $24.1 million, of which $12.5 million housing development (mostly extremely low income units) and $11.4 million monitoring and administration. Gross value of Housing Successor assets $721 million (loan portfolio and land). Recent LMIHAF commitments: $17.97 million construction-permanent plus $2.17 million acquisition for Gateway Tower, $8.4 million Capitol Station, $5.7 million 1510 North 1st Street.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized through the Gap Financing Program underwriting.
affordability_requirement: Dissolution Law targets: at least 30 percent of expenditures for rental housing at or below 30 percent AMI and no more than 20 percent for 60 to 80 percent AMI, measured over five-year periods; City covenants of 55 years or longer.
next_deadline: Funds are awarded through the rolling RFP and NOFA addenda described in the Gap Financing Program record; next addendum expected 2026. Annual Housing Successor report is presented each March with the Housing Element APR.
layering_notes: The largest and most stable local pool in the county at about $96 million, replenished by about $20 million per year of loan repayments as older RDA loans mature. Draws require a Council appropriation from the Housing Project Reserve. Stacks with County Measure A, SCCHA project-based vouchers, 4 percent credits and CalHFA MIP. Program income rules make it less flexible than inclusionary fee funds for moderate income units. sanjoseca.gov blocked; the Housing Successor Annual Report was read as an attachment to the March 2026 APR Council item.
cycle_notes: through the Gap Financing Program rolling RFP
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. Labor Code 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable housing paid for solely from the former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund; whether that reaches housing successor LMIHAF money is not settled in the sources read. The Housing Successor report read contains no prevailing wage term. San Jose Council loan commitment memos read (Capitol Station, Gateway Tower, 318 N. 6th St.) contain no City prevailing wage requirement; sanjoseca.gov NOFA documents returned 403. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Municipal Code Chapter 5.08, in-lieu fees and Surplus Credits Exchange (2026 amendments)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential developments of 10 or more units (threshold lowered from 20 in 2021). On-site rental options after the January 27, 2026 amendments: 5 percent at 60 percent AMI, 5 percent at 80 percent AMI and 5 percent at 110 percent AMI (15 percent total); the former 10 percent at 30 percent AMI alternative was removed. For-sale: 15 percent at 120 percent AMI with the price cap raised to 120 percent AMI. Off-site rental: 30 percent (10 percent each at 60, 80 and 100 percent AMI); off-site for-sale 25 percent at 110 percent AMI. In-lieu fee is set per square foot in the annual Schedule of Fees; about $50 million in in-lieu fees collected from 15 fee-only projects since March 2021 ($38.2 million fee-only plus $12.4 million mixed compliance). Fees flow to the Inclusionary Fee Fund, which is a Gap Financing Program source ($4.3 million committed to Gateway Tower in 2025). Pipeline: 73 projects, 12,900 units, 1,900 affordable.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary rental units restricted for 55 years (reduced from 99 years in 2026 to match TCAC and state density bonus terms). 100 percent affordable developments at or below 100 percent AMI now comply by recording an abbreviated City covenant that mirrors their TCAC, HCD or CDLAC regulatory agreements instead of a full Inclusionary Housing Agreement.
next_deadline: Ordinance adopted January 27, 2026 and effective in 2026. The Surplus Credits Exchange (Section 5.08.540) will get a 12-month performance review; check the Housing Department for exchange rules and current in-lieu fee rates (set each June in the Schedule of Fees and Charges).
layering_notes: For affordable developers the key uses are: (1) the Inclusionary Fee Fund as a gap source, (2) the 2026 Surplus Credits Exchange, where a 100 percent affordable or mixed-income project that exceeds its requirement can sell credits (room-count equivalency) to market-rate projects, a potential new equity-like revenue stream, and (3) streamlined compliance for 100 percent affordable projects. Alternative Financing Model 1 (August 2026) pairs Gap Financing loans with deeper inclusionary set-asides (for example 10 percent at 50 percent AMI) in tower and wrap projects. Market-rate projects in the Multifamily Housing Incentive Program pay a $0 in-lieu fee if they provide 5 percent at up to 110 percent AMI on site, which reduces fee revenue to the fund. State density bonus can be layered on inclusionary units. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo and ordinance read from Legistar.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Chapter 17.14, suspended 2021) and Commercial Linkage Fee (Chapter 5.11)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. AHIF: $17.00 per livable square foot on market-rate rental projects at adoption (2014), escalating 2.4 percent a year to $20.08 when suspended for projects first approved on or after June 29, 2021 (Resolution 80149). Cumulative AHIF revenue and interest $25.6 million; fund balance $11.4 million at June 30, 2025, all to be committed through the Gap Financing Program. CLF (Ordinance 30475, September 22, 2020): FY 2025-26 rates are $17.86 per square foot for office at or above 100,000 square feet downtown and nearby (lower tiers for smaller office), hotel $5.95, industrial over 100,000 square feet $3.57, warehouse $5.95, residential care $7.15, with reduced rates outside downtown. Cumulative CLF revenue $6.1 million, to be allocated through the Gap Financing Program.
affordability_requirement: Fee revenue funds housing for extremely low, very low, low and moderate income households under City regulatory agreements (55 years or longer).
next_deadline: No direct application; the funds are awarded through the Gap Financing Program rolling RFP. Next Mitigation Fee Act annual report due to Council in late 2026.
layering_notes: Both funds are small relative to LMIHAF and are blended into Gap Financing awards. The CLF was adopted at well below the Keyser Marston nexus maximum and office construction has been weak, so expect only a few million dollars a year. The AHIF was replaced by extending the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance to rental projects of 10 or more units. Compare with Mountain View and Sunnyvale, whose commercial linkage fees have generated far larger balances. sanjoseca.gov blocked; the FY 2024-25 annual report memo was read from Legistar.
cycle_notes: AHIF suspended for new projects; CLF continues to accrue and is deployed through the Gap Financing Program
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The fee ordinance itself is a requirement on private development and provides no public funds under 1720(a)(1), but the fee revenue is lent to affordable projects; those loans are public funds under 1720(b) and may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans, 40% of units at 80% AMI for 20+ years) or 1720(c)(3) de minimis. No City NOFA or ordinance wage requirement was found. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 The San Jose AHIF/CLF report read contains no wage term.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: Multifamily Housing Incentive Program (MHIP), construction tax reductions and inclusionary in-lieu fee waiver (Municipal Code Sections 4.46.039.13 and 4.47.098)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department with Planning, Building and Code Enforcement, Public Works and Finance
typical_award_size: Phase I (projects that apply by February 28, 2027 and pull building permits by that date, capacity expanded from 1,800 to 3,600 units on January 27, 2026): 50 percent reduction of the Building and Structure Construction Tax (1.54 percent to 0.77 percent of valuation), 50 percent reduction of the Commercial, Residential and Mobile Home Park Construction Tax (2.42 percent to 1.21 percent), reduced inclusionary requirement of 5 percent of units at 100 percent AMI (or up to 110 percent AMI) and a $0 inclusionary in-lieu fee. Phase II (after capacity or March 2027): 25 percent Building and Structure tax reduction (to 1.16 percent) plus the inclusionary benefits. Approved waivers range from $4.07 million (498 West San Carlos, 278 units) to $6.93 million (3896 Stevens Creek Phase 1, 311 units, September 2026). Five projects with 1,444 units started construction under the program by January 2026.
per_unit_cap: Roughly $14,000 to $22,000 per unit in waived taxes and fees in approved projects.
affordability_requirement: Market-rate high-density projects (50 or more units per acre in growth areas) providing at least 5 percent of units affordable at up to 100 or 110 percent AMI; recorded affordability restriction required. Financial infeasibility finding under Municipal Code Section 14.10.310 and the 2025 Cost of Residential Development Study.
next_deadline: Phase I application deadline February 28, 2027; building permit must be obtained by February 28, 2027 for the 50 percent reductions. Each waiver requires a Council public hearing under Government Code 53083.
layering_notes: Not a subsidy for 100 percent affordable projects, which generally are exempt from these construction taxes anyway, but it is the City's main production incentive for mixed-income market-rate towers and wraps and it shapes the inclusionary pipeline (lower on-site percentages, zero in-lieu fee revenue). Alternative Financing Model 3 (August 2026) pairs MHIP incentives with master-lease financing so that a public or nonprofit master lessee can take down units at 80 to 110 percent AMI. Developers combining MHIP with state density bonus should confirm the 5 percent at 100 percent AMI units count toward density bonus moderate income thresholds. sanjoseca.gov blocked; staff memo read from Legistar.
cycle_notes: first come first served with tiered readiness prioritization
eligible_project_detail: high-density market rate with on-site workforce units
prevailing_wage_basis: The MHIP staff memo does not address prevailing wage. Construction tax and in-lieu fee reductions are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (fees reduced or waived by a political subdivision), but coverage depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts; no DIR determination or City rule on MHIP was found.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; only basis is Labor Code 1720(b)(4) fee waivers, outcome depends on 1720(c) and project facts.

program_name: Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds, City Council Policy 1-16 (City as conduit issuer)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department and Finance Department
typical_award_size: City-issued tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds and notes for 4 percent LIHTC projects, for example Berryessa TOD (March 2026), 525 North Capitol (June 2025) and La Moraga refunding (July 2025). Policy 1-16 was amended April 28, 2026 to streamline readiness requirements, financing team selection, private placements and alternative structures, and to prioritize developments leveraging substantial non-City subsidy, preservation of at-risk units and permanent supportive housing. City fees and procedures are moving to an administrative procedures document.
per_unit_cap: Limited by CDLAC allocation and project debt capacity, not by City policy.
affordability_requirement: Federal 20 percent at 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at 60 percent AMI minimum under Section 142(d), plus City regulatory agreement; City prioritizes deeper affordability and PSH.
next_deadline: Applications track CDLAC allocation rounds (typically three per year); submit the City inducement request at least one Council cycle before the CDLAC deadline. Check the revised administrative procedures with the Housing Department.
layering_notes: San Jose is one of the few cities in the county that issues its own bonds rather than relying solely on CMFA or CSCDA, which avoids JPA issuer fees but adds City fees and Council timing. Alternative Financing Model 2 (August 2026) contemplates private activity bonds with master-lease financing for projects without 4 percent credits. County TEFRA approvals cover unincorporated projects only. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar.
cycle_notes: tied to CDLAC rounds
prevailing_wage_basis: DIR public works coverage determinations PW 2006-001 (Horizons at Indio, March 12, 2007, citing PW 2004-016 Rancho Santa Fe, publicly offered conduit bonds) and PW 2006-006 (Tracy Place Senior Apartments, July 11, 2006, privately placed CDLAC bonds bought by a bank) hold that conduit multifamily bond financing is not payment out of public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) because proceeds and repayments never enter public coffers, and that LIHTCs are not public funds. San Jose acts as conduit issuer under Council Policy 1-16, and the April 28, 2026 Policy amendment memo imposes no prevailing wage requirement. Other public subsidy layered on the project (City or County loans, land, fee waivers) is analyzed separately and can still trigger prevailing wage. Sources: https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-001.pdf ; https://www.Dir.Ca.Gov/OPRL/coverage/year2006/2006-006.pdf

program_name: Alternative financing frameworks for affordable housing (Gap Financing plus IHO, PAB plus master-lease, production incentives plus master-lease)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: Council resolution of September 1, 2026 authorizing the Housing Director to implement four mixed-financing models: (1) Gap Financing Program loans in exchange for deeper inclusionary set-asides (example: 10 percent of units at 50 percent AMI instead of 5 percent at 60 and 5 percent at 80); (2) private activity bonds combined with master-lease financing; (3) production incentive programs (MHIP) combined with master-lease financing; (4) master-lease financing combined with the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance. Target rents 40 to 110 percent AMI. No new dollars; uses existing Gap Financing, bond and incentive tools.
affordability_requirement: Varies by model; 40 percent AMI up to 110 percent AMI with recorded restrictions; Model 1 limited to tower and wrap projects already paying prevailing wage.
next_deadline: Housing Director may implement without further Council action subject to funding approvals; individual loan or master-lease commitments still return to Council. No deadline.
layering_notes: Relevant to developers of mixed-income towers (prevailing wage already assumed) and to nonprofit or public master lessees. Models borrow from the Bay Area Housing Finance Authority and CalHFA middle-income work; they will compete with the Multifamily Housing Incentive Program pipeline for the same market-rate projects. Prohousing: San Jose applied for HCD Prohousing Designation in June 2023 (memo read); current designation status was not confirmed this pass, verify on HCD's designated jurisdictions list. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar. Audit 2026-11-08 funding_type: classed as loan because Model 1 is a Gap Financing loan and the master-lease models use City funding expected to be repaid on exit; no new grant dollars.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. The Alternative Financing memo mentions prevailing wage only as a cost assumption for tower and wrap projects (where prevailing wage labor is already in the financing model), not as a City requirement; conduit private activity bonds are not public funds under DIR PW 2006-001. https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-001.pdf
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: HUD entitlement grants (CDBG, HOME, ESG, HOPWA), FY 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 entitlement estimate $13,743,769: CDBG $7,445,057, HOME $2,484,924, ESG $658,211, HOPWA $1,869,366, HOPWA-PSH $1,286,211. Total available with prior-year balances and program income $36,340,762, including HOME $23.16 million (prior-year balance $18.99 million) available for affordable housing development. The adopted plan (Table 8) does not leave the HOME balance open to general pipeline projects: $22,371,942 is a reserve for motel acquisition, rehabilitation and new affordable housing development project(s) (the Department is exploring acquisition and rehabilitation of two motels for conversion to SRO units), $372,738 is the 15 percent CHDO set-aside and $217,422 is administration; funds are reprogrammed (for example to preservation) if the selected projects cannot meet HOME compliance and timeliness.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits (HUD 221(d)(3) based) apply.
affordability_requirement: HOME: at least 90 percent of assisted tenants at or below 60 percent AMI, 20 percent of units in projects of five or more at 50 percent AMI, HOME affordability periods of 5 to 20 years; City layers its 55-year covenant.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 Action Plan hearings expected March to April 2027 with HUD submittal by May 15, 2027. Developers access HOME through the rolling RFP rather than the Action Plan.
layering_notes: San Jose is its own entitlement jurisdiction and HOME participating jurisdiction, separate from the County Urban County CDBG and HOME Consortium (see county record). The large HOME balance (about $22.4 million) is reserved in the FY 2026-27 plan for motel acquisition and SRO conversion project(s) plus a CHDO set-aside, so it is a near-term opportunity mainly for motel conversion or CHDO sponsors that can meet HOME timeliness and environmental review. HOME triggers federal cross-cutting rules (Davis-Bacon for 12 or more HOME units, URA, environmental review). sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar.
cycle_notes: public services and capital through the Action Plan; housing development funds flow through the Gap Financing Program
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: entitlement and balance figures match ($13,743,769 new, $36,340,762 total, HOME $23,162,102). Old: HOME typically committed to Gap Financing developments and the $19 million balance described as open to construction-ready PBV projects. New: Table 8 reserves $22,371,942 of HOME for motel acquisition, rehabilitation and new development project(s) (two motels for SRO conversion being explored) plus a $372,738 CHDO set-aside and $217,422 administration.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of San Jose formula entitlement (Rounds 4 and 5)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: $6,585,489 for PLHA Rounds 4 and 5 (grant agreement authorized March 24, 2026), part of the City's 2019 to 2023 five-year allocation plan. The Round 4 and 5 allocation is designated for emergency shelter operations, not development. Earlier rounds supported housing programs under the 2020 plan.
affordability_requirement: PLHA statute allows households up to 120 percent AMI (150 percent in high-cost areas); San Jose's current plan uses the funds for shelter operations.
next_deadline: The 2024-2028 PLHA formula cycle will require a new five-year plan; watch for a Council action in 2026 or 2027 that could redirect future rounds to development.
layering_notes: Not a developer-facing source in San Jose today. Contrast with Mountain View, which routes PLHA to specific developments. The County's PLHA record covers the Urban County allocation. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar.
cycle_notes: allocated to shelter operations under the five-year plan
eligible_project_detail: new construction (eligible but not currently funded)
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines and Formula Allocation NOFA contain no prevailing wage provision (only the separate Non-Entitlement Competitive NOFA does). https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf San Jose currently uses PLHA for emergency shelter operations, which are not construction under 1720(a)(1).
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: Below Market Rate Housing Program, City Code Chapter 36 Article XIV Division 2 (moving to Chapter 46), 2026 amendments and in-lieu fee schedule
administering_agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 7 or more units: 15 percent BMR for rental and non-townhome ownership, 25 percent for rowhouse and townhouse projects; projects under 7 units pay fractional in-lieu fees with a new graduated reduction for 1 to 6 units. Rental BMR units at over 50 to 80 percent AMI with a 65 percent AMI weighted average; ownership at over 80 to 120 percent AMI (100 percent weighted average) plus a further 10 percent of townhome units at 120 to 150 percent AMI. Affordable in perpetuity; rents may rise at most 3 percent a year. In-lieu fees (now only a valuation yardstick for alternative compliance, since Council removed fee payment as a compliance option): rental $118 per net new habitable square foot in 2025 falling to $98 in FY 2026-27; townhome $153 to $118; other ownership $67 to $91; escalated by the California Construction Cost Index. Alternative compliance (land dedication, off-site units, or acquisition and preservation of existing housing) requires Council approval and a $32,000 cost-recovery fee.
affordability_requirement: Rental 65 percent AMI weighted average (range over 50 to 80 percent AMI); ownership 100 percent AMI weighted average; perpetual affordability; 15 percent of BMR units (or one unit) to be accessible under the 2026 amendments.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requirement applies at entitlement. No application round as of November 9, 2026.
layering_notes: BMR in-lieu fees historically funded the City's NOFA (for example $10 million to 1012 Linda Vista in 2023 and $6.3 million to Lot 12), so removing fee compliance will shrink the BMR Housing Fund over time; the City seeded the Affordable Housing Initiative Fund with $1 million from this fund in January 2026. The new acquisition and preservation compliance path lets a market-rate developer buy and deed-restrict existing units, a potential partnership for nonprofit preservation buyers. Precise plan areas (North Bayshore, East Whisman) carry their own affordability and land dedication requirements (North Bayshore six land dedication sites, Middlefield Park two sites); those plans were not opened this pass. State density bonus is available on top of BMR units. mountainview.gov returns 403 to automated access; Council reports were read from the Legistar attachment host.
cycle_notes: Phase 2 BMR amendments: EPC hearing March 4, 2026; Council first reading May 12, 2026 with second reading set for June 9, 2026 (adoption not confirmed in the Nov 2026 audit); updated in-lieu amounts take effect through the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule; Council to relocate the program to Chapter 46 before the end of 2026.
audit_note: Tier 4 Nov 9, 2026: May 12, 2026 Council report matches on 15 and 25 percent requirements, AMI ranges and weighted averages, in-lieu fee table ($118 to $98 rental, $153 to $118 townhome, $67 to $91 other ownership), removal of in-lieu fees as a compliance option, $32,000 alternative compliance fee and graduated small-project reduction. Past first reading date moved from next_deadline to cycle_notes. prevailing_wage_trigger false is uncited; a regulatory requirement with no public funds.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Affordable housing over-the-counter Notice of Funding Availability (Housing Impact Fund, BMR In-Lieu Fees Fund, Local Housing Trust Fund grant)
administering_agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department and Council NOFA Review Committee
typical_award_size: Over-the-counter (first come, first served) NOFA since 2014 funded by the Housing Impact Fee on office, high-tech, hotel and retail development, BMR in-lieu fees, and state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants. Since 2014 the City has invested $119 million in affordable housing. Examples: Lot 12 (120 units, Alta Housing and Related California) $23.45 million total City commitment, revised October 14, 2025 to $3.1 million BMR in-lieu, $3.31 million Housing Impact Fees, $1.0 million Successor Agency funds, $8.0 million SB 129 grant, $2.2 million Rental Housing Impact Fund, $3.2 million LHTF, $1.86 million HOME and $0.78 million HOME-ARP; 96 West El Camino Real (79 units, Danco) Housing Impact Fund $6.73 million plus $1.27 million PLHA; 1012 Linda Vista $10 million reservation (2023) returned to the funds in October 2025 pending a new NOFA application for a 53-unit version. City funding is targeted to 20 percent of total development cost (a $1 City to $4 other leverage ratio). Housing Element Program 4.3 commits about $40 million over the cycle; the pipeline gap was estimated at $50 million in 2024.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap; City target is 20 percent of total development cost. Recent commitments equal roughly $85,000 to $195,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Multi-Family Rental Underwriting Guidelines (2022); deed restrictions for extremely low, very low and low income households; priority to projects that leverage County Measure A, PBVs and state funds and that serve unhoused and special needs households.
next_deadline: Applications accepted at any time; City-owned sites (Lot 12, 87 East Evelyn) are awarded by RFQ/RFP instead. An online application portal was targeted for late 2025. The Housing Impact Fee update is underway through a County collaborative nexus study; watch for a 2026 or 2027 fee action.
layering_notes: Mountain View has the strongest city housing fund in the county outside San Jose thanks to office linkage fees. Stack order used by staff: County Measure A or SHDF, SCCHA PBVs, 4 percent credits and CMFA bonds, state LHTF, PLHA and PIP pass-throughs, then City Housing Impact Fund and BMR funds last. The 2019 City-County MOU allocates Measure A to the City pipeline. The City also committed $4 million toward a $20 million acquisition and preservation pool for CSFRA rent-stabilized units (March 2024), contingent on $16 million in outside partners. mountainview.gov blocked; memos read from Legistar.
cycle_notes: over-the-counter, five-step review to NOFA Review Committee then Council
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. The Mountain View NOFA staff report contains no prevailing wage term. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: over-the-counter NOFA, 20 percent of total development cost target and $119 million since 2014 confirmed. Old: Lot 12 commitment shown as including $6.3 million BMR in-lieu and $5.95 million Housing Impact Fees. New: the October 14, 2025 Council report reduced these to $3,100,000 BMR and $3,306,673 Housing Impact Fund, with the $23.45 million total made up of those plus $1.0 million Successor Agency, $8.0 million SB 129, $2.2 million Rental Housing Impact Fund, $3.2 million LHTF, $1,862,056 HOME and $781,271 HOME-ARP. January 2026: the City seeded a $1 million BMR-funded Affordable Housing Initiative Fund with the Los Altos Mountain View Community Foundation (not a developer NOFA).

program_name: Mountain View Affordable Housing Initiative Fund (partnership with Los Altos Mountain View Community Foundation)
administering_agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department and Los Altos Mountain View Community Foundation (fiscal sponsor)

Eligible uses: new construction in the City pipeline (priority), acquisition, preservation or rehabilitation of existing housing, homebuyer programs, other projects approved by the City. 3 percent LAMVCF administrative fee on the City contribution; City approves all expenditures and may claw back its grant if donations lag.
affordability_requirement: City-identified affordable housing priorities; projects must meet the City's affordability restrictions when funds are used for development.
next_deadline: New fund; donor engagement beginning 2026. No application process published yet; contact the Housing Department (Wayne Chen, Housing Director).
layering_notes: Small today but the only city-sponsored philanthropic housing fund in the county. Most useful as predevelopment or gap top-up for projects already in the City NOFA pipeline. Treat as unclear for prevailing wage because donated funds passed through a nonprofit may not be public funds, while the City seed grant is. mountainview.gov blocked; Council report read from Legistar.

City money is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1), but philanthropic donations through the Community Foundation may not be, and coverage depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts; no stated rule found.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; no fund guidelines yet, outcome depends on fund source and 1720(c) exemptions.

administering_agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department

cycle_notes: public services biennial; capital and housing funds allocated directly through the Action Plan

CDBG: Davis-Bacon applies to residential projects of 8 or more units under HCDA Section 110 and 24 CFR 570.603.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check: December 5, 2024 HRC memo confirms 65 percent CDBG capital minimum, direct allocation of capital and HOME funds as loans, biennial public services NOFA, $171,000 General Fund under Council Policy A-8, HOME for low and very low income, and HRC Feb/Mar, Council April, HUD May 15 timing. program_name: Conduit tax-exempt multifamily bonds (CMFA TEFRA approvals) and City-owned or dedicated land for affordable housing
administering_agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department; California Municipal Finance Authority as issuer
typical_award_size: City is a CMFA member and holds TEFRA hearings for 100 percent affordable projects: 334 San Antonio Road (Castellan, 100 units, up to $50 million authorization, about $18.75 million expected, September 2026), 96 West El Camino Real and 87 East Evelyn Avenue (May 2026), 1020 Terra Bella (January 2026), 424 Bryant Street Lot 12 (August 2025). Land: City-owned Lot 12 (ground lease to Alta/Related), VTA site at 87 East Evelyn (City ground lease since 2021, Affirmed Housing, AHSC Round 9 award of $5.5 million for City streets and bus shelters in 2026), and precise plan land dedication sites (North Bayshore six sites, Middlefield Park two sites) delivered by master developers.

next_deadline: TEFRA hearings scheduled on request ahead of CDLAC rounds; land dedication sites become available as North Bayshore and Middlefield Park phases proceed (three North Bayshore sites expected during the Housing Element period). Developer selection for City sites is by RFQ/RFP.
layering_notes: Mountain View does not issue its own bonds; CMFA is the default issuer (CSCDA also acceptable). Dedicated land from the precise plans is the City's largest non-cash subsidy and is paired with City NOFA loans, County Measure A and SCCHA vouchers. mountainview.gov blocked; Council report read from Legistar.
prevailing_wage_basis: Mixed record. The CMFA conduit bond component is not public funds per DIR determinations PW 2006-001 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2007/2006-001.pdf) and PW 2006-006 (https://www.Dir.Ca.Gov/OPRL/coverage/year2006/2006-006.pdf). The City land component (ground leases and dedicated sites) can be public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(3) if conveyed below fair market value, and coverage then depends on 1720(c) exemptions and deal terms; the Council report does not address prevailing wage.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear because the land component depends on 1720(b)(3) and project facts; bonds alone do not trigger it. Consider splitting bonds and land into separate records.

program_name: Inclusionary Below Market Rate Housing Program, Municipal Code Chapters 19.67 (ownership) and 19.77 (rental), BMR in-lieu fees (Council Priority Project HO-9)
administering_agency: City of Sunnyvale Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. 15 percent of units must be deed-restricted BMR units distributed through the project: rental projects of 3 or more units (5 percent very low income and 10 percent low income) and ownership projects of 7 or more units (all 15 percent moderate income); 100 percent affordable projects are exempt. The 2026 Strategic Economics feasibility study found 20 percent is not supportable, so staff recommend keeping 15 percent and converting fees: ownership in-lieu fee from 7 percent of sales price (about $70 per square foot) to $93 per square foot for 7 or more units; rental in-lieu fee from $33 to $93 per square foot for 7 or more units and from $16.50 to $46.50 per square foot for 3 to 6 units; four-year review cycle added to Council Policy 2.3.3. Fees deposit to the Housing Mitigation Fund. Alternative compliance plans require Council approval (2025 examples: 777 Sunnyvale-Saratoga Road, 1124 West El Camino Real). Ordinance 3239-25 (March 2025) allows reduced requirements for qualifying retail preservation projects in low and moderate resource areas. Inventory: 366 BMR rental, 516 BMR ownership and 1,768 units in 100 percent affordable developments.
affordability_requirement: Rental BMR units: 15 percent of units, split 5 percent very low income and 10 percent low income, for projects of 3 or more rental units. Ownership BMR units: 15 percent of units at moderate income for projects of 7 or more ownership units. MTC TOC policy minimums (15 percent, rental average 80 percent AMI or less, ownership average 120 percent AMI or less) are met.
next_deadline: City Council hearing on the in-lieu fee conversion and Policy 2.3.3 amendment scheduled November 10, 2026 (Planning Commission October 12, HHSC October 28, 2026); fees take effect 60 days after adoption. Next full review in four years.
layering_notes: The in-lieu fee increase (nearly triple for rental) will push more market-rate projects to build units on site and will enlarge the Housing Mitigation Fund NOFA pool in the meantime. Affordable developers benefit indirectly through the NOFA and through BMR alternative compliance partnerships (off-site units). State density bonus applies on top of the 15 percent. Sunnyvale also reduced park dedication in-lieu fees for affordable and DUO projects in 2024. sunnyvale.ca.gov returns 403 to automated access; the report was read from the Legistar attachment host.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: Old: 15 percent applies to rental and ownership projects of 7 or more units, fewer than 7 exempt, rental BMR units at low income. New: Table 2 of the October 12, 2026 report shows rental applies to 3 or more units (15 percent on site: 5 percent very low income, 10 percent low income; small rental in-lieu fee $16.50 per square foot for 3 to 6 units, $33 for 7 or more) and ownership to 7 or more units (15 percent moderate income, in-lieu 7 percent of sales price). Proposed fees and the November 10, 2026 Council hearing date confirmed.

program_name: Non-Residential Housing Mitigation Fee (Housing Impact Fee), Municipal Code Chapter 19.75
administering_agency: City of Sunnyvale Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee on new office, R&D, industrial, retail and lodging square footage in any zone since 2015; over $47 million collected 2015 to 2022. January 24, 2023 action (BAE nexus study) raised office and R&D to $11 per square foot for the first 25,000 square feet and $22 per square foot above that, left retail, lodging and industrial unchanged, and kept CPI indexing; one legacy project pays $13 per square foot versus the prior $19.50 standard rate. Revenue funds the Housing Mitigation Fund, which supplies the biennial NOFA ($16 million in 2022, $29.5 million awarded in 2024, $18 million offered in 2026).
affordability_requirement: Projects funded from the Housing Mitigation Fund are restricted to lower income households for at least 55 years.
next_deadline: Current FY 2026-27 rates are in the City's Master Fee Schedule (not opened this pass); confirm with the Housing Division. No fee update is pending beyond annual indexing.
layering_notes: Sunnyvale's linkage fee, driven by Moffett Park and Peery Park office growth, is the engine behind one of the county's largest city housing funds. Fee revenue will slow with the office downturn, so the 2026 NOFA ($18 million) is smaller than 2024. Compare with San Jose's CLF ($6.1 million cumulative) and Mountain View's Housing Impact Fee. sunnyvale.ca.gov blocked; staff report read from Legistar.
cycle_notes: fee paid at building permit; funds deployed through the NOFA
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The fee ordinance itself is a requirement on private development and provides no public funds under 1720(a)(1), but the fee revenue is lent to affordable projects; those loans are public funds under 1720(b) and may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans, 40% of units at 80% AMI for 20+ years) or 1720(c)(3) de minimis. No City NOFA or ordinance wage requirement was found. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 The Sunnyvale Housing Mitigation Fee staff report discusses but does not adopt a prevailing wage fee discount.

program_name: Housing Mitigation Fund and BMR In-Lieu Fund biennial Notice of Funding Availability
administering_agency: City of Sunnyvale Community Development Department, Housing Division (Housing and Human Services Commission advisory)
typical_award_size: Biennial NOFA. 2022: $16 million to four developments. 2024 (issued May 2, 2024, due June 6, 2024): $29,533,000 awarded August 13, 2024, including $14.03 million to MidPen's 1171 Sonora Court (172 units; $12.5 million City acquisition of the site plus $1.53 million predevelopment, about $84,500 per unit with earlier PLHA), $1.5 million predevelopment to MidPen's 295 South Mathilda (126 units, City-owned site bought for $7.3 million in 2023), and $14 million to Pacific Companies and Miramar's 352 East Java Drive (308 units, about $45,000 per unit). 2026 NOFA released January 2026 for $18 million with awards announced spring 2026; priorities include senior and age-friendly projects and units for people experiencing homelessness. Minimum award $500,000; FY 2024-25 budget appropriated $32.5 million.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap; 2024 awards ranged from about $45,000 to $85,000 per unit (excluding land).
affordability_requirement: Deed restricted to lower income households for a minimum of 55 years; scoring favors deep affordability, homeless-serving units (at least 20 to 25 percent in recent awards), high resource locations, readiness and leverage. Funding agreement must be executed within two years of award.
next_deadline: 2026 round awards were expected spring 2026; next NOFA expected in FY 2027-28 (about early 2028), when 295 South Mathilda is expected to seek about $7.5 million in construction funds and 1171 Sonora about $12 million. Confirm award results and the next release with the Housing Division (NOFA documents are posted on the City housing page, which is blocked to scripts).
layering_notes: The best-funded city NOFA in the county after San Jose. Awards are structured as predevelopment, acquisition (with the City taking title and ground leasing, which locked in TCAC High Resource status for 1171 Sonora) and construction loans, and are meant to leverage County Measure A or SHDF, AHSC, IIG, BAHFA and 4 percent credits. Sunnyvale's HHSC scoring sheet is public. Also uses PLHA for predevelopment ($500,000 to 1171 Sonora in 2022). sunnyvale.ca.gov blocked; APR and award reports read from Legistar.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. City acquisition and ground lease below market value is also public funds under 1720(b)(3). The Sunnyvale document read contains no prevailing wage term; sunnyvale.ca.gov NOFA pages are blocked. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. Labor Code 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable housing paid for solely from the former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund; whether that reaches housing successor LMIHAF money is not settled in the sources read. program_name: Density Bonus Ordinance (2008) update and affordable housing fee deferrals and waivers, Housing Element 2023-2031 Programs 16, 20 and 21

typical_award_size: The 2008 Density Bonus Ordinance was replaced by Chapter C.12 (Density Bonus for Affordable Housing Developments) of the new Zoning Ordinance, Title XIII, adopted September 2, 2025 and effective October 2, 2025. It grants density bonuses, incentives, waivers and parking ratios per state law, and allowed incentives include waived, reduced or deferred City fees (plan check, permit and development impact fees), direct financial aid by loan or grant, and density beyond state law, with additional incentives decided case by case; eligibility requires full on-site compliance with the 15 percent Affordable Housing Ordinance. audit_note: Audit 2026-11-08: verified against the adopted Zoning Ordinance and Housing Element; corrected the claim that no updated density bonus chapter exists. Prevailing wage left unclear: neither Chapter C.12 nor the Housing Element states a prevailing wage rule for fee waivers or deferrals, and no City policy on point was found.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Fee waivers and deferrals are available only as negotiated density bonus incentives under Zoning Ordinance Chapter C.12 or case by case; the density bonus itself provides no public funds (1720(a)(1)). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: City of San Diego Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Fund and Inclusionary Housing Fund, SDMC Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 5) and SDHC Affordable Housing and Permanent Supportive Housing NOFA (FY27 NOFA-27-01)

typical_award_size: FY27 NOFA-27-01 (released November 6, 2026) makes up to $22 million available (HOME plus Affordable Housing Fund) as residual receipts loans for new construction rental housing. FY 2027 Annual Plan: about $42.5 million AHF available July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 ($5.4M new fees and loan repayments plus $37.1M fund balances, of which $22.4M is already committed); Rental Housing Production allocation $30.39M including a $9.0M AHF share for the FY27 NOFA. HTF: at least 60 percent of funds for very low income (up to 50 percent AMI), no more than 20 percent for low income, no more than 10 percent for median income. The City's Bridge to Home LMIHAF and PLHA NOFA (separate record) is run by the Economic Development Department, not SDHC, and projects commonly take both. HOME funds awarded to the City are administered by SDHC and folded into the same NOFA. AHF also funds ADU construction loans up to $250,000 at 3 percent for low income homeowners (7 year affordability) and homeless programs. FY27 plan and FY25 annual report read on sdhc.org.
cycle_notes: Annual NOFA subject to SDHC budget approval. FY27 NOFA-27-01 draft guidelines public comment closed October 29, 2026; NOFA released November 6, 2026 with up to $22 million (HUD HOME awarded to the City plus the City Affordable Housing Fund) for new construction of affordable rental homes, rents affordable at or below 60 percent AMI for at least 55 years, awarded as low-interest residual receipts loans.

The FY27 NOFA itself is on PlanetBids and could not be read. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
