program_name: Affordable housing fee deferral loans (deferral of development impact, water and sewer connection and building permit fees; Housing Element Program 7)
administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department and City Council (case-by-case resolution)
typical_award_size: Case-by-case Council approval of long-term deferral of City water connection, sewer connection, development impact and building permit fees, structured as General Fund loans repaid several years beyond occupancy. Oak Park Public Housing (Paso Robles Housing Authority) phases one through four received fee deferral loans of $1.018 million (Resolution 12-031), $889,000 (14-019), $999,423 (17-019) and $1,438,160.71 (Resolution 18-020, 2018). Resolution 18-020 terms: promissory note repaid over up to 30 years from building permit at 3.75% simple interest from residual receipts, secured by a deed of trust. News reports (not agency sources) describe a March 2026 Council resolution deferring water, sewer, development impact and building permit fees for affordable housing, a 30-year deferral of about $1.2 million for Highland's Senior Affordable Apartments (298 Niblick Road), a 30-year deferral of about $1.8 million for Sunrise Villas Apartments, a roughly 50% impact fee waiver for a nine-unit Habitat for Humanity project on Vine Street, and February 2021 deferrals for a 79-unit senior project at Woodland Plaza II.
affordability_requirement: Units affordable to lower-income households (Health and Safety Code 50079.5), including extremely low income; City practice requires a recorded affordability covenant for the longest feasible time and not less than 30 years (Resolution 18-020).
next_deadline: Rolling; no open round or deadline as of November 8, 2026. Requests go to Council with the entitlement or before building permit; contact Community Development at (805) 237-3970 or planning@prcity.com.
layering_notes: This is the only City-controlled financial tool in Paso Robles; it substitutes for a housing trust fund. City fee deferrals have been the local match for Paso Robles Housing Authority tax credit deals (Oak Park) and are expected to pair with County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund awards, HASLO or Paso Robles Housing Authority vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund loans and the Urban County HOME NOFA (county record). The City receives about $165,000 per year of CDBG through the Urban County, which cannot fund new construction or impact fees. The 2026 resolution and project-specific deferrals were found only in local news; the City's eScribe agenda host (pub-pasorobles.escribemeetings.com) renders listings in JavaScript and returns 403 on document downloads, so the HCD-hosted 2020-2028 Housing Element is the agency source. Paso Robles is now preparing its 7th cycle Housing Element (consultant RFP due September 8, 2026).
cycle_notes: No NOFA. Housing Element Program 7 (Affordable Housing Support) commits the City to offer impact fee deferrals for lower-income units and allow deferral of fees several years beyond occupancy; each deferral is approved by Council resolution.
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: facts confirmed. The program_name cites Housing Element Programs 8 and 9, but in the adopted 2021-2028 Housing Element the fee deferral commitment is Program 7 (Affordable Housing Support); Program 8 is the Uptown/Town Centre Specific Plan and Program 9 is homelessness resources. The Element lists the Oak Park phase four loan as $1,438,461 (record cites $1,438,160.71 from Resolution 18-020), not material.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Paso Robles Housing Element (Programs 8 and 9) states no wage term for fee deferral loans. Waived, reduced or deferred fees are public funds under 1720(b)(4) (fees or loans charged at less than fair market value), but 1720(c)(3) de minimis and other 1720(c) exemptions decide coverage. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Inclusionary housing ordinance and local affordable housing fund (none adopted; Housing Element finding)
administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department, Housing Programs Division
typical_award_size: None. The 2020-2028 Housing Element states the City of Paso Robles does not have an inclusionary ordinance, and the City holds no inclusionary in-lieu fund, local housing trust fund or RDA successor housing fund for development. The Housing Programs Division's development support is limited to CDBG (about $165,000 per year through the Urban County), applying for County-administered HOME funds, fee deferrals and liaison with the Paso Robles Housing Authority. A November 2025 townhouse proposal offered a voluntary in-lieu payment tied to the County's Title 22 point system for use in a future tax-credit project, which indicates ad hoc negotiated contributions rather than a program.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: Not applicable; no program exists as of November 8, 2026. Watch the 7th cycle Housing Element update for any inclusionary or local housing fund program.
layering_notes: Negative finding recorded so the gap is visible: Paso Robles is the largest North County city and offers no local gap funding beyond fee deferrals. Developers must rely on County Title 29 and the new Regional Housing Fund (county records), HASLO and Paso Robles Housing Authority vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund and state programs. The 2020 Housing Element workshops listed a possible local housing fund (General Fund, TOT, in-lieu fees) as an option but none was adopted. prcity.com pages and the HCD-hosted Housing Element were opened; the 2025 Annual Progress Report could not be located on prcity.com.
audit_note: Kept funding_type other: this is a negative finding with no deployable fund; the Housing Element states the City has no inclusionary ordinance and lists only General Fund fee deferral loans, Urban County CDBG and HOME, and the private SLO County Housing Trust Fund as resources.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds; Paso Robles has adopted no inclusionary ordinance or local housing fund (Housing Element finding), so there is no program that could pay public funds or trigger prevailing wage. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) city allocation through the San Luis Obispo Urban County
administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department, Housing Programs Division (County of San Luis Obispo is lead agency)
typical_award_size: City page states about $165,000 per year, but the County's 2027 Action Plan NOFA estimates Paso Robles' 2027 CDBG share at $295,492 ($192,070 available for project applications after admin and the 15% public services cap). At least 70% must benefit low income persons (80% AMI or below), no more than 15% for public services, up to 30% for blight elimination; projects must complete within about 1.5 years. CDBG cannot pay new housing construction costs or development impact fees; eligible uses include land acquisition for low income housing, street improvements serving low income housing, rehabilitation and public facilities.
affordability_requirement: Beneficiaries at or below 80% of county median income; HOME and CalHome recipients must be low income.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The County runs one combined Action Plan NOFA each fall; the next round (2028 Action Plan) is expected to open in late September 2027.
layering_notes: The City recommends use of its own CDBG share but the County Board adopts the Action Plan (county record: Urban County Action Plan NOFA). HOME and ESG are not allocated to the City; the City may apply to the County for HOME annually, and County HOME has funded Peoples' Self-Help Housing projects in Paso Robles (Canyon Creek, Creekside Gardens). Useful only for acquisition, site work or rehab components and must be paired with other local or state sources for construction. Davis-Bacon applies.
cycle_notes: City CDBG requests run on the Urban County Action Plan calendar: RFP late August or September, applications mid to late October, City Council recommendations November to February, County Board hearing in spring. The 2027 Action Plan NOFA applications were due October 30, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. via Neighborly. Contact City Housing Programs at (805) 237-3970.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal Davis-Bacon Act applies to CDBG-assisted construction (24 CFR 570.603; residential projects with 8 or more units). The County 2027 Action Plan NOFA Section B and the City CDBG page both state the federal prevailing wage requirement.

program_name: Interim Inclusionary Housing Policy (Council policy adopted June 24, 2003, amended November 25, 2003) and inclusionary in-lieu housing fund
administering_agency: City of Atascadero Community Development Department (fund and resale administration by Administrative Services, affordablehousing@atascadero.org)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies only to residential projects needing legislative approval (planned developments, subdivisions, rezones). 20% of units affordable; in multifamily and mixed-use areas split 20% very low, 37% low, 43% moderate (single-family areas 100% moderate). Projects of 1 to 10 units may pay the in-lieu fee or build; 11 or more units must build unless Council approves fees. In-lieu fee equals 5% of the construction valuation of the market-rate units; fractional units up to 0.499 pay fees. Collected fees sit in the City's inclusionary (in-lieu) housing fund, which has helped Peoples' Self-Help Housing (Atalaya Street 24 homes, Triangle parcel 11 units) and Corporation for Better Housing (60 very low and low income units). Housing Element Program 2.C commits the City to adopt a policy for using the in-lieu funds.
affordability_requirement: Deed restriction of 30 years under the policy (County Affordable Housing Standards used for income limits, rents and prices); inclusionary units are treated as density bonus units not counted against maximum density. Projects using the state density bonus and second units are exempt.
next_deadline: Not applicable. The 2022 EPS nexus study recommended replacing the policy with a citywide affordable housing impact fee (nexus-justified maximum $38.71 to $75 per sq ft, adopted fee to be set well below) and lowering inclusionary to 10% to 15% for large discretionary projects; no ordinance had been adopted as of the pages read.
layering_notes: Still an interim policy more than 20 years on; it only reaches discretionary legislative projects, so most by-right multifamily pays nothing. A 100% affordable LIHTC project is effectively exempt and can request the in-lieu fund as gap money; the fund balance is not published and should be requested from Administrative Services at (805) 470-3428. Pair with the City's impact fee deferral program and state density bonus (separate records), County Title 29 and Regional Housing Fund awards, HASLO vouchers and the Urban County HOME NOFA (Atascadero is a participating city). atascadero.org opens to scripts; the policy PDF, Housing Element and EPS nexus study were read directly.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Salinas Local Housing Trust Fund (Fund 2603) and Multifamily Housing NOFA gap financing (FY 2025-26 round, Resolution 23358)

Blocked: cityofsalinas.org and salinas.gov return 403 to scripts; all material was read from the Salinas Legistar web API and legistar2.granicus.com attachments (staff report of October 20, 2026, Legistar file 26-494, and the September 10, 2024 LHTF staff report, file 24-480).

No FY 2026-27 or later NOFA found in Salinas Legistar items through November 8, 2026. Rounds have been issued when HOME, LHTF, PLHA and HSA balances accumulate rather than on a fixed annual date.

The State LHTF Round 5 NOFA (https://hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/lhtf/2024-lhtf-nofa.pdf) says LHTF Program funds are subject to state prevailing wage law unless a Labor Code 1720(c) exception applies as determined by DIR, which restates 1720. Local loans and grants are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) and (b)(5) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market interest rate loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (applied to an NPLH loan in DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf), and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidies (under $600,000 and under 2 percent of project cost). Federal wages attach by source: HOME at 12+ HOME-assisted units (24 CFR 92.354, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354) and CDBG at 8+ units (24 CFR 570.603, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/570.603), which several NOFA awards carry.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Salinas Municipal Code Chapter 17, Sections 17-8 to 17-13), rental housing impact fee, inclusionary housing trust fund and 2026-27 ordinance update (EPS study)
administering_agency: City of Salinas Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Current ordinance (2017 amendment and guidelines): on-site inclusionary units apply only to for-sale developments of ten or more units, with three standard options (20% with 4% very low, 8% low, 4% moderate and 4% workforce at 160% AMI; 15% with 6% median, 6% moderate and 3% workforce ownership units; or 12% with 8% very low and 4% low rental units). Rental developments instead pay a per-square-foot rental housing impact fee set by fee resolution and must offer 12% of units to Housing Choice Voucher holders, unless they voluntarily provide affordable units in exchange for a City benefit. For-sale developers may pay a per-square-foot in-lieu fee at building permit. All fees go to the inclusionary housing trust fund. Exemptions include 100% affordable projects with 30-year restrictions and the Downtown (Central City Overlay) exemption added in 2022 (Section 17-8(d)). The City hired Economic and Planning Systems on February 1, 2026 to update the ordinance with a nexus and in-lieu fee study, a Technical Advisory Committee and a cost-recovery review fee; draft ordinance targeted for May 2027.
affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80%), median (100%), moderate (120%) and workforce (160%) tiers depending on option; inclusionary units must be comparable to market units and dispersed; first preference to Salinas residents and workers.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fees due at building permit at the rate in the fee resolution then in effect. Housing and Land Use Committee received the update report October 20, 2026 (file 26-506); TAC outreach runs through spring 2027 and a draft ordinance is expected May 2027. Developers with pending projects should track the Phase 2 Zoning Code Update (mid-2027) as well.
layering_notes: Fee revenue feeds the inclusionary housing trust fund that, with the state LHTF award and HSA money, capitalizes the City's multifamily NOFA (record above). An inclusionary requirement (Chapter 17.32, https://www.zoneomics.com/code/seaside-CA/chapter_3) obliges a private developer to restrict units and pays nothing toward construction, so it does not trigger prevailing wage. In-lieu fee revenue later lent or granted by the City, or a land dedication site conveyed below market, would be public funds under 1720(b)(1) or (b)(3).

program_name: Affordable Housing Incentives (Zoning Code Chapter 17.33, density bonus)
administering_agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 17.33 grants density bonuses by Council determination on the state sliding scale (10% lower income units earn 20%, rising to 35% at 20%; 5% very low income units earn a 20% bonus on a parallel scale), with incentives and concessions, reduced parking (17.33.050), child care bonuses (17.33.060), processing rules and a recorded density bonus agreement (17.33.100). Bonus units do not count toward the 20% inclusionary requirement. The fifth cycle Housing Element (Program 13) acknowledged the chapter had not been updated to current state law and committed to do so in the comprehensive zoning update.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; affordability terms per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental).
next_deadline: Not applicable; state law controls where the local chapter is less generous. Check for the Seaside 2040 zoning update adoption before relying on local tables.
layering_notes: No local fee waiver, trust fund NOFA or city NOFA was found for Seaside beyond the inclusionary in-lieu fund and CDBG (records above and below). Seaside is a CDBG entitlement city (about $365,000 a year per the fifth cycle Housing Element; FY 2026-27 funding plan adopted March 2026 with about $581,000 including carryover, unverified) and is not in the Urban County. Water connection moratorium relief (Council July 2026) matters more than zoning for multifamily feasibility. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because the City site is JavaScript-only for agendas.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: CDBG entitlement, Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fund and Successor Agency properties (Housing Element funding resources)
administering_agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department (Housing and CDBG administration); Successor Agency to the Seaside Redevelopment Agency
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan (draft, City CDBG page): about $275,000 CDBG entitlement plus $256,750 program income and $49,250 prior year funds, $581,000 total, allocated by Council on March 19, 2026. The FY 2026-28 NOFA anticipated $525,000 (FY 2026-27) and $500,000 (FY 2027-28) and caps planning and administration at 20% and public services at 15%, with the remaining 65% for public facilities and infrastructure; public service grants are guided to $5,000 to $12,000. New housing construction is ineligible except by Community Based Development Organizations, and FY 2026-27 awards went to public services and facility projects (including the Elm House transitional housing roof). The fifth cycle Housing Element (HCD review draft, March 2020) reported an Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fund of about $2.6 million as of 2017, historically granted to nonprofit developers to buy existing housing or build new affordable units; no current balance was found. Successor Agency Long Range Property Management Plan sites were identified for residential and mixed use sale.
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI benefit; in-lieu fund projects serve very low, low and moderate income households under Chapter 17.32 covenants.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The next two-year CDBG NOFA (FY 2028-30) is expected in late 2027 if the City repeats the prior cycle timing; in-lieu fund awards are ad hoc.
layering_notes: Seaside controls three small local layers (CDBG entitlement, in-lieu fund, successor agency land) but CDBG is used for public services and public facilities, not new housing construction, so it is not a gap source for multifamily development. A developer should approach Community Development about the in-lieu fund or sites such as Campus Town (about 297 planned affordable units), the North 40, Parker Flats and 1620 Broadway; the Action Plan also cites the Seaside Housing Collaborative for acquisition and rehabilitation. County HHAP, County Housing Trust Fund and HACM project-based vouchers (county records) are the larger sources. CDBG figures come from the City's CDBG page, the draft FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan and the FY 2026-28 NOFA; the in-lieu fund figure is from the 2020 Housing Element draft hosted by HCD.
cycle_notes: CDBG runs on a two-year funding cycle: the FY 2026-28 NOFA was issued November 10, 2025 with a mandatory workshop December 10, 2025 and applications due January 9, 2026; Council approved FY 2026-27 allocations March 19, 2026. In-lieu fund awards are ad hoc by Council action.
eligible_project_detail: public facilities and infrastructure, including nonprofit-owned housing facilities
in-lieu fund grants for acquisition or new affordable construction (ad hoc)
Successor Agency sites for residential sale
audit_note: Audit 2026-11-08: the City CDBG page (ci.seaside.ca.us/262) now opens and links the draft FY 2026-27 Action Plan (DocumentCenter View 16790) and the FY 2026-28 NOFA (View 16456). The prior record overstated CDBG at $365,000 a year for acquisition and rehabilitation; current CDBG is public services and facilities. In-lieu fund balance is a 2017 figure.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing (Municipal Code Section 17.48.030 as amended by Ordinance 2025-07) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Section 17.48.090)
administering_agency: City of Marina Community Development Department, Planning Services Division; City Manager's Office, Housing
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Ordinance 2025-07 (introduced May 20, 2025, adopted June 3, 2025, effective 30 days later, implementing Housing Element Program 2.4 with General Plan Amendment Resolution 2025-48) lowered the threshold from 20 to 5 or more units and set a citywide 20% requirement for new or substantially rehabilitated for-sale or rental housing: 6% very low, 7% low, 7% moderate, plus a voluntary incentive-based 10% middle income (up to 135% AMI for-sale) tier; existing occupied housing on the former Fort Ord also 20% (6/7/7), down from 40% (15/15/10). Market-rate density bonus units are exempt. Alternatives approved by Council (17.48.030(D)): land dedication, acquisition and rehabilitation, preservation of at-risk units, conversion of market-rate units, special needs housing, or a tailored program for 500-unit specific plan projects. No in-lieu fee is codified; the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (17.48.090) receives only enforcement recoveries. Rental units restricted 55 years (in perpetuity if allowed), for-sale resale restrictions 45 years, rents capped at 90% of comparable market rent.
affordability_requirement: 20% of units: 6% very low (rent at 30% of 50% AMI), 7% low (30% of 60% AMI rental), 7% moderate (30% of 110% AMI rental); middle income tier voluntary.
next_deadline: Applies with the first discretionary application (affordable housing plan required). Housing Element objective: 200 lower income units through inclusionary and density bonus by 2031.

Minor fix to adoption date; APR reference (93 Dunes BMR units occupied 2024) moved out of next_deadline because its past date was being read as a deadline.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Affordable Housing Overlay fee waivers and deferrals (Municipal Code Section 17.48.130, Ordinances 2023-01 and 2023-12) and state density bonus adopted by reference (Section 17.48.040, Ordinance 2023-07)
administering_agency: City of Marina Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Projects on Affordable Housing Overlay (AHO) sites mapped for Housing Element opportunity sites receive ministerial administrative approval by the Community Development Director (no hearing), AHO development standards instead of the base zone (42-foot height, 48 feet on Reservation Road and Del Monte Boulevard), and one of three incentives: waived, reduced or deferred planning, plan check or construction permit fees; deferral of City construction and impact fees to completion or occupancy; or payment of construction and impact fees over twelve months or longer after completion. Section 17.48.040 adopts Government Code 65915 to 65918 by reference and caps bonuses, concessions, waivers and parking at the state maximums unless a development agreement provides more. Approvals lapse after two years with a one-year extension.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable; fee relief sized to the project's actual City fees.
affordability_requirement: To use the AHO a project must restrict at least 12% of units to very low income or 15% to low income households (Section 17.48.130(F)(1)(b)) under an agreement of at least 55 years executed before building permit; minimum density 30 units per acre. Inclusionary ratios in Table 17.48.030-1 still apply. Density bonus target units above the inclusionary requirement are restricted 30 years.
next_deadline: Not applicable; ministerial on AHO-mapped sites. Housing Element Program 2.3 committed the City to evaluate its incentives by end of 2024 and strengthen them by end of 2026 if 200 lower income units are not on track.
layering_notes: The AHO is the only fee relief program found among Monterey County priority cities and was cited in Marina's August 2025 Prohousing Designation application (Enhancement Category 3). Fee deferral to occupancy helps construction-period cash flow on tax credit deals such as Lightfighter Village (EAH and Veterans Transition Center, 71 units) and future Dunes and Downtown Marina AHO sites. It does not waive school, water (Marina Coast Water District) or Fort Ord Reuse Authority successor fees. Code read on the zoneomics mirror (Title 17, Chapter 17.48) because marina.municipal.codes returns 403.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific rule found. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees that are reduced, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, but 1720(c)(3) excludes de minimis subsidies (under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost) and 1720 does not address fee deferrals; the outcome depends on the size of the waiver and other project funding. Marina Code Chapter 17.48 (zoneomics mirror) contains no prevailing wage provision.
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: affordability_requirement changed from a general reference to the overlay's very low and low income emphasis to the stated minimum of 12% very low or 15% low income units with a 55-year agreement (Section 17.48.130(F)(1)(b); Zoneomics mirror used because the official code host is blocked). Fee incentives, 42 and 48 foot heights, ministerial approval and the two-year lapse are confirmed. Section 17.48.130(E)(2) still says inclusionary requirements apply at twenty units, which conflicts with the five-unit threshold set by Ordinance 2025-07.

administering_agency: City of Soledad (requesting agency) with Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department (Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager, (831) 755-5391)

On March 16, 2026 the County Health, Housing, Homelessness and Human Services Committee considered Soledad's request to use the County's reserved AOWH funds, about $1,680,063, to buy land in Soledad for homes sold to moderate income households under a 45-year resale restriction, with the City selecting a developer; staff would amend the County PLHA plan with HCD and memorialize the City's obligations. Soledad's own 2024-2028 PLHA allocations also flow to the County (about $289,000 a year across the three delegating cities). audit_note: Spot check Nov 9, 2026: committee report 26-261 (introduced March 16, 2026, hearing dated March 26, 2026) confirms the 2024 delegation by Carmel-by-the-Sea, Greenfield and Soledad, the $1,680,063 AOWH reserve, the moderate-income for-sale land purchase with 45-year resale restriction, plan amendment with HCD and RHNA credit to the City. No later Board of Supervisors item on the Soledad request was found in the Legistar API through November 2026. prevailing_wage_trigger true is uncited. PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true changed to unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf) contain no prevailing wage, Davis-Bacon or Labor Code 1720 provision; the HCD PLHA FAQ (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/cycle-2-nofa-faq.pdf) says only that HCD programs require compliance with applicable law including prevailing wages unless the project meets a Labor Code 1720(c) exception as determined by DIR. PLHA loans and grants are public funds under 1720(b)(1) and (b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), 1720(c)(5)(C) (mortgage, down payment or single-family rehab aid to a household) and 1720(c)(3) de minimis can apply. Davis-Bacon applies only if HOME (12+ HOME units, 24 CFR 92.354) or CDBG (8+ units, 24 CFR 570.603) is layered. The request is to use County PLHA AOWH funds to buy land for moderate-income for-sale homes built by a City-selected developer (report 26-261, https://legistar.granicus.com/Monterey/attachments/3aa10ea9-740a-42ea-afbd-7ee3960877e7.pdf; Attachment A, https://legistar.granicus.com/Monterey/attachments/e454e9b4-bab8-4d6a-9ba5-85cd8ae39ceb.pdf). Land acquisition is not construction, and down payment aid to buyers is exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C), but a land write-down to the developer is public funds under 1720(b)(3).

The CPF grant passes through the County to buy the City site and install manufactured units that HACM will own (report 26-251, https://legistar.granicus.com/Monterey/attachments/446cbf52-6318-4730-8963-e4693920468c.pdf); whether federal pass-through funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and whether a housing authority-owned project falls outside the 1720(c)(5) private-project exemptions are project facts (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720).

program_name: City of Madera HOME Investment Partnerships (new participating jurisdiction) and CDBG entitlement, 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan
administering_agency: City of Madera Grants Division (Finance), Grants Administrator Marcela Zuniga, (559) 661-3692
typical_award_size: HOME: about $353,555 per year (5-year estimate $1,767,777). The first allocation, in 2024, was $372,065, plus a one-time City match of $127,935, for $500,000. Over 2025-2029 the ConPlan housing goal budgets HOME $1,590,999.90, CDBG $322,982 and PLHA $1,361,913. CDBG: about $989,791 per year. The PY 2027/28 tentative allocation is about $990,000 (up to 20% admin, up to 15% public services, about $643,500 capital).
per_unit_cap: HOME federal per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250); no local cap published.
affordability_requirement: HOME rental rules (24 CFR 92.252): HOME rents for households at or below 60% AMI, with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more units. CDBG must benefit households at or below 80% AMI.
next_deadline: CDBG PY 2027/28 applications opened November 2, 2026 and are due January 29, 2027 by 5:00 p.m. via grantsinfo@madera.gov. No HOME rental NOFA found; request HOME gap funding directly from the Grants Division ahead of tax credit rounds.
layering_notes: Madera became a HOME participating jurisdiction in June 2024, so HOME is now the City's only recurring federal source that can fund new rental construction. The ConPlan lists owner rehab or new affordable housing as HOME uses. The amounts are small (about $354K per year), so the City would likely save several years of HOME for one gap loan, as the City of Merced does. Stack with PLHA (separate record), Housing Authority of the City of Madera project-based vouchers (county record) and 4% or 9% credits. Federal Davis-Bacon wages apply at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. HOME also requires NEPA review, and grants from 2024 on carry Build America Buy America requirements. The CDBG NOFA mostly funds public services and public improvements, but CDBG can pay for acquisition and site work for new housing. Sources read: 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, PY 2027/28 CDBG Notice of Funding (media-001-us.cdn.govstack.com/madera-003-us/media/guann5xv/notice-of-funding-final.pdf) and the 6th Cycle Housing Element.
cycle_notes: CDBG application window opens early November; no open developer NOFA found for HOME

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Madera Municipal Code Chapter 10-3-5.1) with Housing Element incentives: fee reductions (Program B-7), impact fee waivers (MMC 10-8.17) and fee waivers or deferrals (Program A-4)
administering_agency: City of Madera Community Development Department, Planning (Planning Manager David Brletic, (559) 661-5433)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The density bonus follows state law; the chapter was amended in February 2025 to track recent state changes, including parking for 100% affordable projects near transit. Program B-7 fee reductions: downtown projects and vacant or aging buildings get up to 100% off Engineering fees and 75% off Planning and Building fees. Non-profit buildings get up to 50%, with building fee reductions capped at $4,000. MMC 10-8.17 lets the Community Development Director approve impact fee adjustments, waivers or exemptions. Program A-4 offers fee waivers and deferrals for affordable projects as technical assistance.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (for example 10% lower income or 5% very low income units); 55-year affordability for bonus units.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. The Housing Element commits to local density bonus standards beyond state law by Q1 2028 and to fee reductions for at least 20 qualifying projects by Q3 2026.
layering_notes: Madera has no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fund. These fee tools are the only local cost reductions beyond HOME and PLHA. Program B-7 targets downtown revitalization, so it fits best for an affordable rental project downtown. Elsewhere, use the Director's waiver authority in MMC 10-8.17 and ask for a deferral under A-4. A fee waiver is a public subsidy and, depending on its size, can trigger state prevailing wage. The 6th Cycle Housing Element was adopted February 4, 2026. Madera County's density bonus (county record, Chapter 18.114) applies only in unincorporated areas.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Program B-7 fee reductions, MMC 10-8.17 impact fee waivers and Program A-4 fee waivers or deferrals come with the density bonus; the bonus itself provides no public funds (1720(a)(1)). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

Housing successor asset fund money is public funds under 1720(b); 1720(c)(4) names only the former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund, not the housing asset fund, and housing successor land conveyed below fair market value is public funds under 1720(b)(3). Below-market residual receipts loans may fall under the 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption (below-market loan, at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI; DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

cycle_notes: City applies to HCD state CDBG and HOME rounds

program_name: Housing Density Bonus and Other Incentives (Chowchilla Municipal Code Chapter 18.58) and Housing Element Program 3.e impact fee deferral
administering_agency: City of Chowchilla Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Chapter 18.58 implements State Density Bonus Law (Gov. Code 65915) with no local enhancements. Program 3.e (adoption targeted for Q1/Q2 2025) would let developers pay a small portion of impact fees at permit and defer the rest for up to 30 years as a recorded note. The note would be due on sale, refinance or loss of affordability.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds. The deferred fee note becomes due if multifamily rents stop being affordable.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. Program 3.k will amend Chapter 18.58 to match current state law. Confirm whether the Program 3.e fee deferral resolution was adopted.
layering_notes: Chowchilla offers nothing beyond state density bonus law and a proposed fee deferral. The adopted 2024-2032 Housing Element says the City has no inclusionary, affordable housing or other local housing ordinances, and there is no local trust fund, fee waiver fund or NOFA. If adopted, the deferral works like a soft second loan that can sit under tax credit financing. A deferral may count as public funds for prevailing wage purposes. ADU builders can use free pre-approved Cottage Home plans (funded by SB 2). cityofchowchilla.org opened directly; the code was read on the zoneomics mirror.
prevailing_wage_basis: Density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of development standards, not public funds; Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) covers only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011, Gov. Code 65912.130). Chapter 18.58 offers City financial incentives (subsidies, land, fee waivers) only at the City discretion. The Program 3.e impact fee deferral is proposed, not adopted; if adopted, a deferral is a fee reduction or loan under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) and would be tested against 1720(c)(3) de minimis.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: false kept for the density bonus; revisit if the fee deferral program is adopted.

layering_notes: This is the main route into City land and City-sponsored state applications in Los Banos. The City's current PLHA funds operate a second bridge home, so little PLHA is free for capital. Los Banos is not a CDBG entitlement city; it applies to the state CDBG NOFA (code enforcement in 2015, planned 2025 rehab application) and does not fund multifamily development. A related RFP for a joint homeless housing applicant closed April 26, 2024. Merced County CoC CA-520 HHAP and Housing Authority of the County of Merced vouchers (county records) are the other layers.
cycle_notes: RFQ issued January 2024, no deadline
prevailing_wage_basis: No stated rule. The RFQ (issued January 25, 2024, no deadline) contains no prevailing wage or labor standards clause. Conveying City parcels below fair market value is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(3), but coverage depends on 1720(c) exemptions and on whichever state or federal sources are layered in, each with its own rule.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; the RFQ PDF served at the source_url was read and has no labor standards terms.

program_name: Atwater Housing Element Program 7 (Facilitating Affordable Housing Development): density bonus ordinance to be adopted, fee waivers, reductions or deferrals, and city-built off-site improvements
administering_agency: City of Atwater Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The Housing Element finds the Atwater Zoning Code does not address density bonus and is not in compliance with State Density Bonus Law. The Code was to be amended by January 31, 2026 (end of 2026 in the Program 7 timeline); state law applies directly in the meantime. Incentives: possible fee waivers, reductions or deferrals; expedited review; and off-site improvements (traffic, street, sewer) built by the City as capital projects, case by case.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. Density bonus ordinance due by end of 2026. A water and sewer priority policy for affordable housing (SB 1087) is due by end of 2026, and the infrastructure fee study and fee schedule update by June 2026; verify status.
layering_notes: Atwater has no local density bonus ordinance yet, and no inclusionary ordinance, trust fund or city NOFA. The goal is entitling at least 100 subsidized units with nonprofit partners during the planning period. The City-built off-site improvements are the most tangible local subsidy and would count as public funds. Source is the July 2026 MJHE version of the Atwater Housing Element on the MCAG mercedmjhe.com site; adoption status not confirmed.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Program 7 offers fee waivers, reductions or deferrals and City-built off-site improvements, which are construction by a political subdivision under 1720(b)(2); the density bonus itself provides no public funds (1720(a)(1)). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Atwater PLHA allocation (ADU loans and rental assistance) and state CDBG and HOME grants (non-entitlement)
administering_agency: City of Atwater Community Development Department
typical_award_size: PLHA ADU loans of up to $40,000 per qualified applicant. PLHA mortgage, rent and utility assistance of up to $5,000 per household (up to six months). The City received no CDBG in the 5th cycle but by 2026 had state CDBG and HOME awards for owner-occupied rehab. No multifamily allocation identified.
affordability_requirement: Lower income households under PLHA, CDBG and HOME rules.
next_deadline: Set by HCD state NOFAs; unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Atwater's housing money is small and aimed at owners, ADUs and tenants, not multifamily gap financing. A multifamily developer should treat Atwater mainly as a co-applicant for state CDBG or HOME and a source of letters of support. Merced County's surplus land at Castle Commerce Center in Atwater (county record) is the relevant site lead.
cycle_notes: City applies to state CDBG, HOME, CalHome and PLHA; Program 7 commits to annual applications starting 2026
prevailing_wage_basis: No single stated rule. Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(C) exempts assistance to a household for rehabilitation of a single-family home, and the HOME (12 or more units) and CDBG (8 or more units) federal thresholds do not reach owner-occupied rehab, but PLHA ADU loans fund new construction that 1720(c)(5)(C) does not clearly cover, so the outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Atwater Housing Plan has no labor standards language.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; program mixes ADU construction loans, rental assistance and owner rehab with no stated program rule.

program_name: Atwater Housing Successor to the former Atwater Redevelopment Agency (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund)
administering_agency: City of Atwater as Housing and Non-Housing Successor Agency
typical_award_size: No active lending. The City's FY 2026-27 budget (adopted June 8, 2026) confirms the City is the Housing Successor Agency and lists the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (fund 3065) with FY 2024-25 unaudited revenue of $42,457 (interest) and $3,396 of professional services, an FY 2025-26 amended budget of $10,000 interest and $20,000 professional services (municipal code update), and no FY 2026-27 appropriations. No housing loans are budgeted and the fund balance is not stated.
affordability_requirement: Housing Asset Fund rules (HSC 34176.1).
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Recorded so the asset fund is not missed. The budget shows interest income but no housing loans or grants, so do not assume cash is available without asking the City; request the latest SB 341 report, the fund balance and any housing successor-owned parcels. atwater.org opens directly; the successor agency page lists only 2012-2015 ROPS and oversight board documents.
cycle_notes: no published process
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: successor agency page re-read; the FY 2026-27 adopted budget book confirms the housing successor role and shows the asset fund with interest income only and no housing expenditures. The latest posted ACFR (FY 2021-22) does not break out the fund. No SB 341 report found on atwater.org.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Atwater successor agency page (https://www.atwater.org/successor-agency/) lists only ROPS and oversight board documents and states no wage rule; housing successor funds under HSC 34176.1 carry no wage rule of their own. Loans from the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund are public funds under 1720(b) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); a below-market residual receipts loan on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI can be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf).

program_name: Affordable Housing Development and Substantial Rehabilitation NOFA (HOME, HOME-CHDO and HOME-ARP), City of Fresno PY 2026-2027
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (Housing Finance)
typical_award_size: PY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan programs $2,804,486.73 HOME for affordable development or rehab (entitlement $2,766,057.28 plus $500,000 program income and $229,944 prior year) and a $414,909 HOME CHDO set-aside. Recent awards: $3,000,000 HOME to Sarah's Court II (120 units, 11 HOME units, January 2026). City HOME-ARP allocation was $11.9 million (HOME-ARP supportive services NOFA closed April 13, 2026). Five-year Con Plan years 3 to 5 HOME estimate $8.3 million.
per_unit_cap: HUD HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits apply; no separate City cap published.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and incomes (at or below 80% AMI, with HOME rent limits on assisted units); 55-year City regulatory agreement typical for rental loans; priority for projects in areas of opportunity.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The 2026-2027 AHD NOFA (PlanetBids No. 2026/12602307) closed August 31, 2026. The separate PY 2027-28 HUD CPD NOFA (tentative release December 14, 2026, applications due January 22, 2027) follows the Consolidated NOFA model covering ESG, HOPWA, public services, infrastructure and owner-occupied repair, not HOME rental development. Expect the next AHD NOFA in mid-2027; verify with HCDD at (559) 621-8300.
layering_notes: City of Fresno is its own HUD entitlement (CDBG $6.9M, HOME $2.77M, ESG $624K, HOPWA $1.27M in PY 2026) and is not part of the Fresno Urban County, so City projects do not compete in the County HOME/PLHA NOFO and vice versa. The AHD NOFA is separate from the Consolidated NOFA (CDBG, ESG, HOPWA public services and infrastructure, due January 23, 2026). City HOME is usually layered with City PLHA, LHTF and Housing Successor funds and with 4% or 9% LIHTC; HOME triggers Davis-Bacon at 12 or more assisted units and federal NEPA review before choice-limiting actions. Fresno Housing (county record) PBVs and bonds stack on top. The PlanetBids NOFA document itself could not be opened by script; figures come from the City HCD page and the PY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan.
cycle_notes: summer, posted on PlanetBids
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: City of Fresno Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF), Resolution 2021-201 and Revised Program Guidelines 02
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing Finance Division
typical_award_size: Dedicated $1,500,000 per year from the City Real Estate Transfer Tax, plus General Fund contributions, Prohousing Incentive Pilot Round 1 ($2,064,891) and State LHTF matching grants (about $8.5 million received to date, including $1,797,373 appropriated January 2026). Recent loans: $5,000,000 Cesar Chavez Apartments (54 units, 2024 commitment) and $3,727,000 The Park at South Stadium (15 LHTF units of 174, approved June 18, 2026; includes $156,800 Housing Successor funds). City applied for PIP Round 4 (up to $2,000,000) to recapitalize the fund.
per_unit_cap: None published; South Stadium works out to about $248,000 per LHTF-restricted unit.
affordability_requirement: Local funds (Guidelines 02) serve households at or below 80% AMI (State match dollars follow State LHTF rules, with at least 30% to extremely low income); 55-year affordability covenants on rental loans. Eviction Protection Program uses are exempt from income verification since July 1, 2025.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The LHTF Multi-Family New Construction NOFA (PlanetBids No. 12601837) released April 24, 2026 and closed May 25, 2026 with 11 applications; no new LHTF NOFA is posted on the City housing page. Next NOFA depends on the FY 2027 transfer-tax allocation and any PIP Round 4 award; verify with Housing@fresno.gov.
layering_notes: One of the few city-controlled flexible local sources in the Central Valley. Loans are 3% simple interest, 55-year, residual receipts, and accept third or fourth lien position behind construction/permanent debt and other public loans, so they fit as gap under 4% LIHTC and tax-exempt bonds. Guidelines 02 were rewritten in 2025 (Resolution 2025-270) and a technical amendment in April 2026 restored multifamily new construction as eligible after it was inadvertently dropped; check the current guidelines before applying. Competes for the same transfer-tax dollars as the Eviction Protection Program. County has no equivalent trust fund (see Fresno County PLHA and HOME records).
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The State LHTF Round 5 NOFA (https://hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/lhtf/2024-lhtf-nofa.pdf) says LHTF Program funds are subject to state prevailing wage law unless the project meets a Labor Code 1720(c) exception as determined by DIR, which restates 1720 rather than setting a separate rule. The City LHTF loan agreement for The Park at South Stadium (Section 7.14, https://agendas.fresno.gov/api/v1/attachments/cmqb6fzd1sw39pe4bj1bxdmdt/file) makes the developer responsible for prevailing wage only to the extent local, state and federal law require, and applies HOME 24 CFR 92.354 only as applicable. Local loans and grants are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) and (b)(5) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market interest rate loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (applied to an NPLH loan in DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf), and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidies (under $600,000 and under 2 percent of project cost). LHTF loans are 3% residual receipts loans, so 1720(c)(5)(E) can apply where they are the only public participation.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true changed to unclear; City agreement Section 7.14 defers to applicable law.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Fresno 2024-2028 Five-Year Plan and PLHA development loans
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing Finance Division
typical_award_size: Estimated $14,949,413 over 2024-2028 (first allocation $2,391,906, second $2,562,083). 45% of each year to multifamily rental development, 50% to owner-occupied rehab and down payment assistance, 5% admin. Recent award: $1,600,000 PLHA to Helm Lofts (9 restricted units of 98, conditional award February 9, 2026).
per_unit_cap: None published; Helm Lofts was about $178,000 per restricted unit.
affordability_requirement: Rental activity up to 120% AMI under State rules, with a portion of units reserved at or below 60% AMI; 55-year regulatory agreement; loans are low-interest deferred (Helm Lofts: 3% simple, 55-year term).
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. Last standalone PLHA NOFA ran August 1 to August 29, 2025. The draft 2024-2028 PLHA plan (public comment September 21 to October 10, 2026; hearing November 5, 2026; Council adoption pending) states PLHA rental funds are offered through the City's Affordable Housing Development and Substantial Rehabilitation NOFAs, the latest of which closed August 31, 2026. Expect the next round with the mid-2027 AHD NOFA; verify with Housing@fresno.gov.
layering_notes: Separate from the Fresno County PLHA (county record covers the unincorporated area and participating cities, not the City of Fresno). The City plan devotes only 45% to rentals, so expect roughly $1.1M per year available for multifamily. PLHA is used as soft gap alongside City HOME and LHTF and with LIHTC; it was also paired with the market-rate-oriented Revolving Loan Fund on Helm Lofts. State PLHA funds count as public funds for prevailing wage purposes.
cycle_notes: Delivered through the City's annual Affordable Housing Development and Substantial Rehabilitation NOFA per the draft 2024-2028 plan.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf) contain no prevailing wage, Davis-Bacon or Labor Code 1720 provision; the HCD PLHA FAQ (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/cycle-2-nofa-faq.pdf) says only that HCD programs require compliance with applicable law including prevailing wages unless the project meets a Labor Code 1720(c) exception as determined by DIR. PLHA loans and grants are public funds under 1720(b)(1) and (b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), 1720(c)(5)(C) (mortgage, down payment or single-family rehab aid to a household) and 1720(c)(3) de minimis can apply. Davis-Bacon applies only if HOME (12+ HOME units, 24 CFR 92.354) or CDBG (8+ units, 24 CFR 570.603) is layered. The City draft 2024-2028 PLHA plan (https://www.fresno.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Draft-2024-to-2028-PLHA-5-Year-Plan-Document-10w1852.pdf) is silent on prevailing wage, and half the allocation funds owner-occupied rehab and down payment assistance, which 1720(c)(5)(C) exempts.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true changed to unclear. The layering note that state PLHA funds count as public funds is correct under 1720(b) but does not by itself make a project a public work.

program_name: Housing Successor to the Redevelopment Agency of the City of Fresno, Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF) program income and FHS-owned sites
administering_agency: City of Fresno in its capacity as Housing Successor (FHS) and Fresno Revitalization Corporation
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 budget $4,188,073 (carryover $4,138,073 plus about $50,000 program income); unencumbered and available for development $2,523,599, all restricted to units at or below 30% AMI because FHS exceeded the 20% cap for 60-80% AMI. LMIHAF assets under management $28.9 million; FY 2024-25 ending balance $6,856,360. Historic per-unit contributions range from about $25,000 to $331,000; recent uses include Heritage Estates ($1.2M), B Street ($836,200 encumbered) and 33 E Atchison ($275,000).
affordability_requirement: HSC 34176.1: at least 30% of funds for extremely low income (30% AMI) rentals, no more than 20% for 60-80% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI; 55-year covenants for rentals.
next_deadline: No standalone NOFA as of November 8, 2026. Funds and FHS-owned parcels are committed through City NOFAs, RFPs and disposition agreements (FY 2026-27 program income budget approved June 11, 2026; $2,523,599 unencumbered, restricted to 30% AMI rentals). Contact the Housing Successor.
layering_notes: Small cash pool but useful for deep (30% AMI) targeting and as a match: PLHA allows LMIHAF dollars to be matched into a housing trust account. FHS land is being paired with LHTF, RLF and PRO Housing applications in Downtown and Chinatown (South Stadium used $156,800 FHS plus FHS parcels at 829 and 835 Fulton). Excess surplus test is met (unencumbered $4.08M versus $6.24M threshold at FY 2024-25), so there is no pressure to transfer funds to HCD.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Labor Code 1720(c)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) provides that affordable units built or rehabilitated under Health and Safety Code 33334.2(a)(5) or (a)(7) and paid for solely from the Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (or that fund plus private funds) are not paid for out of public funds; whether that carve-out reaches housing successor LMIHAF dollars and the deal structure is a project fact. Mixed with other public sources, LMIHAF loans fall under 1720(b), subject to 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans. The FY 2026-27 Housing Successor report item (https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-26-752-21456) states no prevailing wage rule.

program_name: Downtown and Chinatown Housing Development NOFA, City Revolving Loan Fund (RLF) construction loans
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
typical_award_size: Construction gap loans of up to $8,000,000 per project from the City Revolving Loan Fund (Round 2 awards: Helm Lofts $8M, Uptown Apartments $8M, The Park at South Stadium $8M). 60-month term, variable rate estimated at 4.81%, secured by deed of trust.

affordability_requirement: None required for RLF dollars; market-rate projects are eligible (Uptown is 48 market-rate units). Affordability comes from layered sources or Surplus Land Act terms (South Stadium 70 of 174 units restricted to very low and low income for 55 years).

layering_notes: Short-term construction money, not permanent soft debt: it must be taken out at conversion, so it suits 4% LIHTC or mixed-income deals with a permanent loan sized to repay. Pairs with City PLHA, LHTF and FHS land in the Downtown/Chinatown area, and with the TOD height and density bonus. RLF capital is State money: $20 million of the State's $250 million Downtown Fresno appropriation (FY 2025-26 installment, Resolution 2025-256) plus a further $5 million appropriated in 2026 for a $25 million fund (Council item 25-1713). The executed RLF Agreement form (item 26-440) nonetheless contains boilerplate federal compliance language; confirm with the City whether any federal cross-cutters attach.
cycle_notes: round-based NOFA, awards on a rolling basis
prevailing_wage_basis: No program rule found. The City RLF Agreement form (Council item 26-440, Park at South Stadium) requires compliance with prevailing wage laws only 'as may be applicable' (sections 5.4 and 7.14) and the staff reports and resolutions for Helm Lofts, Uptown and South Stadium are silent. Coverage then rests on Labor Code 1720(b) (public funds, including below-market loans) and depends on 1720(c) facts, such as (c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with 40% of units at 80% AMI or less for 20+ years and (c)(3) de minimis, so it is project-specific. https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-26-440-21137 ; https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear. RLF Agreement says prevailing wage applies 'as may be applicable'; outcome depends on Labor Code 1720(b) and 1720(c) project facts. The Round 2 NOFA document itself (PlanetBids 12601560) was not readable.

program_name: HUD Section 108 Affordable Housing Development Loan Pool (Substantial Amendment 2025-02)
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Community Development Division
typical_award_size: $15,000,000 pool (City borrowing capacity $15,494,680) for land acquisition and acquisition of manufactured housing units; no minimum or maximum loan; loans generally forgivable at end of affordability term. City repays HUD over 20 years from future CDBG (estimated 3.94% rate).
per_unit_cap: None; sized to demonstrated financing gap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit developers only. At least 51% of units on land acquired with the pool for low and moderate income households (80% AMI), or at least 20% for non-elderly multifamily rental where CDBG share is proportional; 100% LMI for manufactured units; up to 55-year covenants. Borrower must secure outside senior financing and commit up to 10% equity.
next_deadline: Council hearing to adopt Substantial Amendment 2025-02 and authorize the HUD application scheduled November 12, 2026 (ID 26-1506). If approved, a NOFA will be posted on PlanetBids; timing unknown, verify with the Community Development Division.
layering_notes: Land acquisition gap, so it fits early in the stack ahead of LIHTC applications, and can help secure site control for TCAC/CDLAC rounds. CDBG/Section 108 rules apply (Davis-Bacon at 8 or more units for assisted construction, NEPA, URA relocation). Competes with future City CDBG public infrastructure spending because CDBG is pledged for repayment. Separate from the City's earlier $20M Section 108 loan for the Senior Activity Center.
cycle_notes: City NOFA after HUD approval
prevailing_wage_basis: Program rule: the City of Fresno Section 108 Loan Guarantee Program Underwriting and Servicing guidelines (May 2026, Prevailing Wage section, page 12 of 58, in the Section 108 application, https://www.fresno.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Section-108-Loan-Guarantee-Application-Affordable-Housing-Development-Loan-Pool-10w1789.pdf) state that housing development projects are a public work for federal purposes including Davis-Bacon and Related Acts and for State purposes under Labor Code 1720 et seq., absent a contrary written determination by HUD, DIR or a court, and that developers shall perform project work as a public work. Federal basis: Section 108 is assistance under Title I of the Housing and Community Development Act, and 24 CFR 570.603 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/570.603) applies Davis-Bacon to construction financed with that assistance, for residential rehabilitation only at 8 or more units; the guidelines checklist applies Davis-Bacon to projects with more than 11 assisted units.

program_name: City-owned and surplus land contributions with conditional City funding commitments (Surplus Land Act RFPs, Land Bank)
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
typical_award_size: Land at nominal cost plus conditional funding. Examples: Vantage Blackstone senior modular (100 units) gets a 1.21-acre parcel on a 55-year ground lease at $1 per year plus $4,300,000 loan/grant (approved October 22, 2026); Parkview Apartments (98 units, Cesar Chavez Foundation) gets three Parkway Drive parcels plus $10,500,000 conditional commitment (December 2025); Ventura Family Apartments land contribution.
affordability_requirement: Per SLA and Gov. Code 37364 exempt-surplus terms: at least 40% of units at or below 80% AMI with half at or below 50% AMI, regulatory agreement of at least 30 years; recent deals carry 55-year covenants and 30% to 80% AMI targeting.
next_deadline: Site by site; Vantage Blackstone commitment expires September 30, 2027 if financing is not secured. Watch City SLA notices and RFPs on PlanetBids.
layering_notes: City land plus a conditional funding resolution is the standard Fresno package for TCAC 4% and HCD MFSN applications (commitments are reissued each round, as with Parkview since 2024). Funding sources behind the commitments vary (CDBG-acquired land on Blackstone carries CDBG national objective requirements). Below-market ground leases count as public subsidy for prevailing wage. The City also adopted a Land Bank program to acquire sites for future reuse.
cycle_notes: site-specific RFPs and SLA notices of availability
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Transfer or lease of public land below fair market value is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(3) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); coverage then depends on 1720(c) exemptions and the other public sources in the deal. 1720(c)(5)(E) covers only below-market loans, so it does not by itself exempt a below-market ground lease. The Vantage Blackstone item (https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-26-1294-21998) and its draft resolution state no prevailing wage term. Projects that also take City HOME (12+ HOME units, 24 CFR 92.354) or CDBG-funded construction (24 CFR 570.603) carry Davis-Bacon by those rules.

next_deadline: Likely expired: the City application form (July 2025 update) states the waiver is not valid on building permits issued after June 30, 2026 and only when backfill funds exist. layering_notes: Market-rate and affordable infill both qualify, so it is not affordable-specific, but it lowers impact fees for downtown and BRT corridor projects that also use the TOD bonus. Applied at certificate of occupancy, not at permit, so the full fee must be carried in the construction budget. Use near zero in FY 2025 suggests limited backfill funding. Fee waivers backfilled with City funds may be public subsidy under Labor Code 1720.
cycle_notes: First come, first served at building permit, subject to annual backfill funding; form sunset for permits issued after June 30, 2026.
audit_note: Program sunset per application form June 30, 2026; no extension located. Prevailing wage left unclear: neither the form nor the fee waiver report states a prevailing wage rule; Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats waived fees as public funds but applicability to a given project was not confirmed.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. The program waives City park, police, fire and street impact fees (FMC Article 12-4.16) and reimburses up to 50 percent of curb, gutter and sidewalk costs, which is also a payment under 1720(b)(1). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Affordable housing development impact fee deferral to certificate of occupancy (uncodified Ordinance 2008-51)
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department and Public Works Department
typical_award_size: Defers payment of all adopted City development impact fees (street, water, sewer and others) on qualifying affordable units from building permit to certificate of occupancy. Deferral only, no reduction.
affordability_requirement: Inside the Central Area (bounded by SR 180, 99 and 41): any unit in a development with at least 15% of units restricted; outside the Central Area: restricted units only. Covenants of at least 55 years for rental and 30 years for ownership.
next_deadline: Ongoing; request at building permit.
layering_notes: Construction-period carry savings only; fees are still due before occupancy. Stacks with the Infill Incentive waiver where both apply and with density bonus concessions. Ordinance dates from 2008; confirm current implementation with Public Works since it is uncodified.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program rule found; Ordinance 2008-51 (fee deferral to certificate of occupancy) says nothing on prevailing wage. Coverage would rest only on Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (fees or obligations paid, reduced, waived or forgiven), and whether a deferral with no reduction counts, plus the 1720(c)(3) de minimis test ($600,000 and 2% of project cost), depends on project facts. No DIR determination on point was located. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear. The only basis is Labor Code 1720(b)(4); a pure deferral may not be a reduction or waiver, and the de minimis exemption in 1720(c)(3) may apply. Project-specific.

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (FMC Chapter 15, Article 22) with TOD Height and Density Bonus (Article 21) and Housing Element Program 9 by-right approval
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department

next_deadline: Not applicable; applied with entitlements.
layering_notes: Local text predates recent State amendments, so the State statute controls bonus percentages and concessions. TOD stacking is a Fresno-specific advantage on Blackstone and Ventura/Kings Canyon BRT corridors. No density cap on mixed-use zones since 2022. No inclusionary fund exists to tap. Code read on the zoneomics mirror (City code host not used).
audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: library.municode.com and api.municode.com (Fresno's official code host) still return 403, and a fresno.gov media search found no Development Code PDF with Articles 21 and 22, so the code text remains mirror-only and confidence stays needs_confirmation.

Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

administering_agency: City of Oxnard Housing Department (Housing Director) and Community Development Department

The April 8, 2020 Harris and Associates nexus study proposed per-unit fees of $36,000 (single-family for-sale), $35,000 (multifamily for-sale) and $28,000 (multifamily rental), replacing 2006 fees of $7,000, $5,500 and $7,735; fees are indexed every July 1 since 2021 to the ENR Building Cost Index (Los Angeles). Rental: at least 5% very low income (50% AMI) plus 5% lower income (80% AMI), proportional by bedroom size. Covenants of at least 20 years; Oxnard-resident preference list required. Off-site units or land dedication (MAI appraisal) can substitute for the payment with Council approval. Payments go to the City's Affordable Housing Trust Fund (see separate loan record). Projects in the -AHP/-AHD additive zones must provide units and cannot pay in lieu. The 20-year covenant is far shorter than TCAC's 55-year term, so a tax credit deal on the same site carries the longer restriction. Ventura County has no adopted inclusionary ordinance (postponed June 2026), so Oxnard's requirement is local only. Oxnard's Prohousing application was pending as of April 2026. oxnard.gov HTML pages return 403 (Cloudflare) to scripts, but wp-content PDFs open directly.

The City's HOME match surplus was $21.5 million at September 2025, so local funds are not needed for HOME match. Housing Successor (former Oxnard CDC) LMIHAF funds are subject to SB 341 income proportionality (at least 30% of development spending to 30% AMI); the City's SB 341 report was not located this pass. County-level sources (HTFVC loans, County NOFA) stack on top. The fund balance figure comes from the HUD Action Plan, not a fund statement.

No City of Oxnard in-lieu fund NOFA, guideline, resolution or loan term requiring prevailing wage was found (the FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan mentions state prevailing wage only as a barrier to affordable housing). Loans are public funds under 1720(b)(1) or (b)(4), but qualifying below-market loans may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) and small subsidies under 1720(c)(3). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 Housing Successor funds are not covered by 1720(c)(4), and PLHA formula rules are silent on prevailing wage.

administering_agency: City of Oxnard Housing Department, Grants Management Division

program_name: Oxnard Affordable Housing Additive Zones, -AHP (by-right) and -AHD (discretionary) (City Code Chapter 16, Division 7C, Ordinance No. 2999)
administering_agency: City of Oxnard Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Zoning entitlement, not a subsidy: adds the right to build multifamily or mixed use at up to 30 units per acre on Housing Element sites; ministerial site plan review in -AHP; lot merger fees waived when merging parcels under 0.5 acre. The FY 2026-27 Action Plan cites an inventory of 2,466 potential units in these zones.

layering_notes: Commercial or office space capped at 15% of floor area for by-right treatment. Impact fees still apply (Sec. 16-420D(D)), so fee relief must come from Policy H-4.2 waivers negotiated separately. State density bonus (Division 7A) can be layered for more density. Useful for 100% affordable tax credit projects seeking ministerial certainty on smaller sites.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this additive zone (by-right or discretionary multifamily entitlement under Division 7C) provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any public loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on a project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 The lot merger fee waiver for parcels under 0.5 acre is a 1720(b)(4) item but far below the 1720(c)(3)(B) de minimis threshold (under $600,000 and under 2% of project cost). The -AHP path is a local by-right path, not Gov. Code 65913.4.

program_name: Thousand Oaks Development Impact Fee Deferral Program (temporary Council resolution, October 2023)
administering_agency: City of Thousand Oaks Community Development Department and Finance Department
typical_award_size: Deferral, not a waiver: a developer that has not yet paid City development impact fees may defer them from building permit to certificate of occupancy, paying interest at the current five-year Treasury rate. Applies only to the City's own impact fees (13 active fees), not planning or building permit fees, school, Quimby (CRPD) or fire district fees. Dollar value depends on project fee load (staff noted larger projects can reach $5.0 million in City impact fees).

next_deadline: Status unconfirmed as of November 10, 2026: the program was set to expire after one year and no extension was found. Confirm with Thousand Oaks Finance or Community Development before underwriting.
layering_notes: Improves construction-period cash flow and reduces construction loan interest, but interest is charged on the deferred amount; does not reduce permanent sources needed. School district, park district, fire district and permit processing fees are not covered.
cycle_notes: Council authorized staff on October 10, 2023 to implement a temporary program by staff report (not by resolution); the staff report says it would expire after one year. A March 19, 2024 Council item approved a deferral for one project under the program. The 2024 APR (March 25, 2025) describes it as in effect until a date uncertain, while the 2025 APR omits it, and no extension item was found in Council or Planning Commission agendas from 2023 to 2026. State law (Gov. Code 66007) separately defers most residential impact fees to final inspection or certificate of occupancy.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees that are reduced, waived or forgiven as public funds and 1720(b)(5) covers loans repaid on a contingent basis, but the statute does not address a pure deferral; no City or DIR rule on this deferral was found.
