layering_notes: Fee deferral, not forgiveness: fees plus interest come due later, secured by a deed of trust, so lenders and TCAC underwriting must carry the deferred obligation. Ventura Housing Authority CEO Jeff Lambert said the program lets sponsors plan ahead (Ojai Valley News, October 2024). Fee relief is local public funds for prevailing wage purposes. Needs confirmation because cityofventura.ca.gov returns 403; the 2021-2029 Housing Element (HCD site) and the Ojai Valley News report were opened, and ordinance details come from search excerpts of city PDFs (DocumentCenter 41962 ordinance language, 41976 Planning Commission packet, 42235 October 22, 2024 agenda item, 44572 May 13, 2025 agenda item).
cycle_notes: Chapter 4.240 adopted October 2024 (second reading October 22, 2024). Used for Arrive Ventura (297 units, 104 affordable; Council action May 13, 2025, Quimby fee excluded) and requested for College Community Courts (February 25, 2025 Quimby fee deferral).
eligible_project_detail: new residential construction with at least 50% lower income units (deferral)
100% affordable developments (partial waiver, development agreement fee exemption)
audit_note: Follow-up Nov 10, 2026: Chapter 4.240 adoption confirmed by Ojai Valley News (unanimous first reading, second reading October 22, 2024); eligibility, fee list, deed of trust and 55-year term rest on search excerpts of city PDFs that return 403. Stays needs_confirmation until the code text or ordinance is opened.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. 100 percent affordable projects are exempt from a City development fee, and Housing Element Program 29 calls for fee deferral and a partial fee waiver. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

Code 54222.5, https://california.public.law/codes/government_code_section_54222.5; 54233, https://california.public.law/codes/government_code_section_54233) impose affordability, not wages. program_name: Ukiah Housing Trust Fund (UHTF) NOFA, funded with PLHA, Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP) and housing successor funds
administering_agency: City of Ukiah Community Development Department, Housing Services Division (Housing and Grants Manager, housing@cityofukiah.com, 707-463-6708)
typical_award_size: Most recent round: June 10, 2024 NOFA for about $1,000,000 to acquire infill parcels for affordable housing, combining a $455,000 Prohousing Incentive Pilot award (October 2023) with up to $617,000 of the City's 2019-2022 PLHA allocation. Loans at 0 to 3% simple interest, 55-year term, repaid from residual cash flow after operating costs, senior debt, reserves and deferred developer fee; due on sale or refinance. Acorn Valley Plaza (DANCO, 74 units, opened March 2025) was built with UHTF funds.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized as gap funding after all other sources.
affordability_requirement: Units affordable at or below 60%, 80% or 120% AMI with a recorded 55-year rent or resale covenant; bonus points for units at 0 to 30% AMI. Funding-source rules (PLHA, PIP) add restrictions.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The 2024 round closed July 8, 2024 and no newer NOFA is posted on the Housing Services page as of 2026-11-08. Projects must deploy UHTF funds and start construction within two years of award.
layering_notes: Ukiah is the only priority city in Mendocino County with a standing local trust fund and was the first rural Northern California city with a Prohousing Designation (April 2023), which earns state Prohousing points on AHSC, IIG and similar applications. The 2024 round targeted parcels in TCAC High and Highest Resource areas and favored scattered-site or non-traditional infill. The Housing Element says the fund exists partly to supply local match points for tax credit applications. Stacks with County HOME program income (about $351,767, for example the Marigold Villas request in Ukiah) and the City's own state HOME awards; County PLHA is a separate formula pool. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis).
cycle_notes: irregular; issued when state funds are awarded
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The June 2024 UHTF NOFA (https://cityofukiah.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024-HTF-NOFA.pdf) states no prevailing wage term. HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf) contain no prevailing wage, Davis-Bacon or Labor Code 1720 provision; the HCD PLHA FAQ (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/cycle-2-nofa-faq.pdf) says only that HCD programs require compliance with applicable law including prevailing wages unless the project meets a Labor Code 1720(c) exception as determined by DIR. PLHA loans and grants are public funds under 1720(b)(1) and (b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), 1720(c)(5)(C) (mortgage, down payment or single-family rehab aid to a household) and 1720(c)(3) de minimis can apply. Davis-Bacon applies only if HOME (12+ HOME units, 24 CFR 92.354) or CDBG (8+ units, 24 CFR 570.603) is layered. The HCD Prohousing Incentive Program guidelines and Round 4 NOFA (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/pip-final-guidelines-2026.pdf, https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/pip-round-4-nofa.pdf) contain no prevailing wage provision. UHTF loans are 0 to 3 percent residual receipts loans, so 1720(c)(5)(E) can apply (https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf); land acquisition alone is not construction under 1720(a)(1).

program_name: Ukiah Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF)

affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1(a)(3)(A): after allowed administration and homeless prevention spending, remaining LMIHAF funds must be spent developing housing for households at or below 80% AMI, with at least 30% for rental housing at or below 30% AMI (extremely low income) and no more than 20% for households between 60% and 80% AMI, tested in five-year compliance reports. Housing successor income targeting (two-thirds at 60% AMI or below) is stricter than the UHTF NOFA's 120% AMI ceiling, so the City will steer LMIHAF dollars to lower-income units. Balance and five-year expenditure deadlines should be confirmed from the City's latest Housing Successor annual report, which was not located on the City site this pass. cycle_notes: deployed through UHTF NOFAs
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Labor Code 1720(c)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) provides that affordable units built or rehabilitated under Health and Safety Code 33334.2(a)(5) or (a)(7) and paid for solely from the Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (or that fund plus private funds) are not paid for out of public funds; whether that reaches housing successor LMIHAF dollars depends on the deal. Mixed with other public sources, LMIHAF loans fall under 1720(b), subject to 1720(c)(5)(E). The 2019 Housing Element (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/ukiah-6th-adopted102819.pdf) states no prevailing wage rule for the fund.

program_name: Ukiah density bonus (Zoning Code Section 9253) and development fee deferral for affordable housing
administering_agency: City of Ukiah Community Development Department, Planning Services

Section 9253 (Ord. 945, 1993) grants at least the bonus and incentives in Government Code 65915 and lets the City deliver them through Planned Development zoning regardless of parcel size or a Council variance waiving development standards. The 2019 Housing Element reports a fee deferral program for housing developers (water and sewer hookups are the largest fees; typical multifamily fees about $12,500 per unit, 9.5% of development cost) and that affordable developers may receive funding and fee deferrals for infrastructure.

layering_notes: Ukiah has no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee; the 2019 Housing Element removed the inclusionary program and the nexus study, relying on the trust fund and by-right zoning instead. Fee deferral terms were not found in a current resolution, so confirm amounts and timing with Planning (707-463-6268). Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Fort Bragg Inclusionary Housing Requirements and Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund (Coastal LUDC Chapter 17.32 and Inland LUDC Chapter 18.32; Ordinance 1029-2026)
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Non-subdivision projects of 5 to 10 units (rental or for-sale) must make 20% of units affordable by design; for-sale projects of 11 to 20 units 10% inclusionary and 21 or more units 15%; rental projects over 10 units owe inclusionary units only when they request a density bonus or incentive. Alternatives: land donation, small secondary units (two per inclusionary unit in 11 to 30 lot subdivisions), in-lieu fee set by Council resolution. In-lieu fees and resale equity recapture go to the Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund (17.32.090), restricted to affordable housing acquisition, construction and reimbursement of excess affordable units. Fund balance not published.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units: half at 80% AMI and half at 120% AMI, with priority for essential public service employees; rental affordability term 25 years. For-sale units: 15-year resale control with equity sharing back to the Housing Trust Fund. Affordable projects restricted at least 15 years are exempt.
next_deadline: Ordinance 1029-2026 (coastal zone amendments to 17.31 and 17.32) passed in September 2026 and takes effect upon California Coastal Commission certification; verify certification date with the City.
layering_notes: A 2023 City Attorney memo notes Fort Bragg's 20% requirement for 5 to 10 unit projects and no requirement for larger rental buildings without a bonus. A November 12, 2024 hearing on an inclusionary in-lieu fee resolution and nexus study is referenced in a City notice, but city.fortbragg.com returned 502 errors and timeouts this pass, so the adopted fee amount was not confirmed. Trust fund money could serve as local gap funding for tax credit projects but no NOFA or award process was found. The County repealed its inclusionary ordinance; Fort Bragg runs its own. Ordinance read from the City's Legistar attachment host (Legistar web API client 'cityfortbragg').
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check 2026-11-08: Ordinance 1029-2026 text matches the record on thresholds, rental AMI split (80% and 120%), 25-year rental and 15-year for-sale terms, and effectiveness upon Coastal Commission certification. For-sale inclusionary units are split half at 100% AMI and half at 120% AMI (17.32.040), which the record omits.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority. This requirement is imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Spending of in-lieu fee revenue is a separate public funds question. Loans or grants from the Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund would be tested separately.

program_name: Fort Bragg Density Bonuses and Affordable Housing Incentives (CLUDC Chapter 17.31, ILUDC 18.31) and Council preliminary pre-approval of inclusionary incentives (17.32.070)
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg City Council and Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a cash subsidy. State density bonus implemented locally, with a voluntary pre-application step: a developer can ask Council to pre-approve density bonus, incentives and waivers at a public hearing within 90 days, before filing entitlements. Examples: Hazelwood Senior Apartments (49 units, 30 to 60% AMI) received pre-approval on February 24, 2025 for a height incentive (7 feet 8 inches over the 35-foot limit), reduced parking (75 stalls versus 114) and a 9% density bonus; Fort Bragg Apartments (1151 South Main, 83 units with 8 very low income) received pre-approval in November 2024.
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915; regulatory agreement under 17.31.060.
next_deadline: Not applicable; letter of request may be filed any time before the entitlement application.
layering_notes: In the coastal zone every bonus or incentive must also be consistent with the certified LCP and avoid adverse impacts on coastal resources, a constraint beyond state law; Ordinance 1029-2026 updates 17.31 to current state law pending Coastal Commission certification. Pre-approval is non-binding but de-risks tax credit applications. Hazelwood was approved May 2025 but missed 2025 tax credits and planned to reapply in 2026. 1151 South Main is in CEQA litigation after the Coastal Commission denied an appeal.
audit_note: Nov 9, 2026 spot check: February 24, 2025 staff report matches (49-unit Hazelwood senior project, 7 feet 8 inches over the 35-foot limit, 75 stalls versus 114, 9% density bonus, 90-day Council review under 17.32.070). The same report notes CLUDC 17.32.040 requires 15% affordable units in developments over 7 units; that requirement is carried in record a40ff77cbc.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: City of Fort Bragg state HOME, PLHA and CDBG applications (City as State Recipient), including Hazelwood Senior Apartments HOME request
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg Economic Development Department (Grants Coordinator)
typical_award_size: May 12, 2025 Council authorized a $4,600,000 FY24 State HOME application ($4,500,000 loan to AMG Associates for Hazelwood Senior Apartments, 49 units at 30 to 60% AMI, $25 million total cost; $50,000 soft costs; $50,000 admin). Repaid HOME loan proceeds stay in the City Housing Trust Fund. PLHA: formula allocation committed to Housing Mendocino Coast (community land trust); 2021 competitive PLHA award with DANCO for the Plateau project; 2024 competitive PLHA considered for homeless services because no development project was ready. The 2025 CDBG application targets sidewalks, not housing; $570,000 of CDBG program income is encumbered for business loans.
per_unit_cap: HCD HOME per-unit limits; FY24 State Recipient cap $4.5 million per multifamily project plus soft and admin costs.
affordability_requirement: HOME: 55-year state affordability for new construction (20-year federal); PLHA competitive rental: at or below 60% AMI for 55 years.
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The City's FY24 State HOME application for Fort Bragg Senior Apartments (Hazelwood, $4,550,000 requested) is not on HCD's final FY24 awardee list dated June 10, 2026, and the City did not apply in the HOME 2025 Projects NOFA (due March 30, 2026). HCD has not posted the next HOME Projects NOFA date. 2025 State CDBG applications were due April 3, 2026 and the City's application targets sidewalks, not housing.
layering_notes: City sponsorship is the practical path to state HOME for small coastal projects since Fort Bragg is not a HUD participating jurisdiction. HOME triggers Davis-Bacon at 12 or more HOME units. AMG planned 9% tax credits after HOME. County PLHA and HOME program income are separate County pools; Fort Bragg holds its own PLHA formula share. Staff reports were read from the Legistar attachment host because city.fortbragg.com was down.
cycle_notes: HCD State HOME Projects NOFA, roughly annual (2025 NOFA released January 29, 2026, due March 30, 2026, awards expected July 2026). City sponsors one developer project per round as State Recipient. PLHA formula share is committed to Housing Mendocino Coast.
audit_note: Hazelwood (Fort Bragg Senior Apartments) HOME request was not funded in the FY24 round; developer would need to reapply in a future HOME round.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: Housing Mendocino Coast community land trust partnership (ARPA housing funds and PLHA), 251 S. Franklin Street
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg City Manager's Office with Housing Mendocino Coast (501(c)(3) community land trust)
typical_award_size: Council obligated $800,000 in ARPA funds to housing (Resolution 4859-2024); about $50,000 went to the Prohousing Designation application. June 22, 2026 staff recommended $350,000 of remaining ARPA housing funds for HMC's acquisition of 251 S. Franklin Street (about 1 acre, 12 to 13 workforce units) and working capital, under an MOU to be drafted in summer 2026. HMC reports about $1.39 million in existing funding. The City previously used SB 2, LEAP, REAP and PLHA funds to form HMC.
affordability_requirement: Households up to 120% AMI; CLT ground lease (typically 99 years) with resale restrictions; possible priority for City employees and local workforce.
next_deadline: MOU and funding documents were to be prepared in summer 2026; ARPA funds must be expended by December 31, 2026 under federal rules, so verify status with the City Manager.
layering_notes: Not a general NOFA; the City routes funds to its incubated CLT. Useful as a land and ownership partner for small workforce projects rather than a gap lender for tax credit rentals. The staff report states $300,000 in the recommendation and $350,000 in the discussion; confirm the final amount. Fort Bragg also references a Prohousing Designation application funded with ARPA; designation status was not confirmed this pass.
cycle_notes: one-time ARPA allocation
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The June 22, 2026 staff report (https://legistar1.granicus.com/cityfortbragg/attachments/f234af69-08d5-4b5d-bbaa-9dd829b93041.docx) states no prevailing wage term for the ARPA and PLHA support to Housing Mendocino Coast. Land acquisition and working capital are not construction under Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); later construction on land bought with City funds is a 1720(b) question, and down payment or mortgage aid to ownership households is exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C). HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf) contain no prevailing wage, Davis-Bacon or Labor Code 1720 provision; the HCD PLHA FAQ (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/cycle-2-nofa-faq.pdf) says only that HCD programs require compliance with applicable law including prevailing wages unless the project meets a Labor Code 1720(c) exception as determined by DIR. PLHA loans and grants are public funds under 1720(b)(1) and (b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), 1720(c)(5)(C) (mortgage, down payment or single-family rehab aid to a household) and 1720(c)(3) de minimis can apply. Davis-Bacon applies only if HOME (12+ HOME units, 24 CFR 92.354) or CDBG (8+ units, 24 CFR 570.603) is layered.
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true changed to unclear.

program_name: Willits Density Bonus ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.67) and Housing Element affordable housing incentives (Program HE-2C and related)
administering_agency: City of Willits Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 17.67 (updated September 2018) implements Government Code 65915 for projects of five or more units, with concessions that can include City fee waivers or publicly owned land. The 2019-2027 Housing Element commits to project-by-project fast-track processing, density bonuses, flexible standards, reduced parking, fee subsidies when feasible and fee deferrals for mixed-use projects with affordable multifamily units, plus water allocation priority for lower-income projects (HE-1.G).
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Willits must adopt its 7th cycle Housing Element by 2027.
layering_notes: Willits has no local housing trust fund, no inclusionary ordinance (Program HE-3.D only committed to study feasibility by spring 2020) and no city-run NOFA for multifamily. Fee subsidies and deferrals are discretionary and General Fund dependent; if granted they likely count as public funds for prevailing wage. Multifamily gap money must come from County HOME program income, state programs and tax credits. Code text read from the zoneomics mirror; Housing Element read from the HCD-hosted copy (willits-6th-adopted121719.pdf).
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Chapter 17.67 concessions can include City fee waivers or publicly owned land (below-market land is public funds under 1720(b)(3)); the density bonus itself provides no public funds (1720(a)(1)). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Willits Owner-Occupied Housing Rehabilitation Program (PLHA and CDBG funded)
administering_agency: City of Willits Community Development Department
typical_award_size: 0% interest deferred loans of $25,000 to $50,000 per home (current application packet), with the program page citing up to $100,000, funded by the City's PLHA allocation; Council authorized a CDBG application in November 2022 for about $554,000 to seed a revolving housing rehabilitation loan program. The City also holds CDBG business loan program income.
per_unit_cap: $50,000 to $100,000 per home depending on source.
affordability_requirement: Owner-occupants at or below 120% AMI (household of four $112,700 under the City's April 23, 2025 income limits in the current PLHA application packet; the program page still lists $108,500).
next_deadline: Open intake by appointment with Community Development (707-459-7112); subject to funding availability.
layering_notes: Shows that Willits commits its PLHA formula share to single-family rehab rather than multifamily gap financing, so no city PLHA is available for affordable rental projects. Recorded as negative information for multifamily layering. Developers should look to Mendocino County HOME program income and the Community Development Commission of Mendocino County for project-based vouchers.
prevailing_wage_basis: Not triggered for this program. California Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(C) states that, unless otherwise required by a public funding program, rehabilitation of privately owned residential projects is not public works where assistance is provided to a household for the rehabilitation of a single-family home (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines contain no prevailing wage requirement (searched, no match). For the CDBG-funded portion, 42 U.S.C. 5310(a) applies Davis-Bacon to rehabilitation of residential property only if it contains 8 or more units, so single-family owner-occupied rehab is exempt (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/5310).
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: affordability_requirement used the older four-person limit of $108,500; the current City PLHA application packet sets it at $112,700 (120% AMI, limits as of April 23, 2025) (old: $108,500, new: $112,700). Loan terms match: 0% deferred loans of $25,000 to $50,000 in the packet, up to $100,000 on the program page.

program_name: Truckee Inclusionary Housing (Development Code Chapter 18.214) and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee (Section 18.210.100; Resolution 2024-65) with dedicated in-lieu fee account
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department and Department of Neighborhood Services and Sustainability (Housing)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. 15% of all new units in residential projects (and subdivisions of seven or more lots) must be affordable, built no later than the market-rate units; density bonus units are excluded from the base. Alternatives: off-site units in the Truckee region, land dedication, purchase of inclusionary credits, or deed-restricting existing units. In-lieu fee by Council resolution with annual update: $136,851 per required affordable unit under Resolution 2024-65 (up from $115,517 under Resolution 2023-63); projects of six or fewer units or lots pay a scaled fee (Exhibit A1) at the developer's option. Larger projects may pay in lieu only if the review authority finds it furthers affordable housing equally or better. Fees go to a separate interest-bearing account and must be used for Town affordable housing programs that create housing in the Truckee region, not studies (Resolution 2024-65 Exhibit A).
affordability_requirement: Ownership inclusionary units: 100% moderate income, or one-third each low, moderate and above moderate. Rental units: 100% low income, or one-third each very low, low and moderate. Affordability controls under Chapter 18.210 with locals preference; in perpetuity per the Town's Housing Resources page.
next_deadline: Fee is reset annually by resolution; a November 2025 staff report reportedly recommended not adopting an update, so confirm the fee in effect for 2026 with the Town before underwriting.
layering_notes: Inclusionary units can receive Homegrown Housing payments only where the project qualifies for the new Chapter 18.213 non-monetary incentives; otherwise required units are ineligible. In-lieu fee revenue supports Town housing programs (Homegrown Housing, THAP, Lease to Locals and similar) rather than a traditional tax credit gap loan NOFA; no Town multifamily NOFA was found. Separate from the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund, which Truckee does not belong to (members are the County, Grass Valley and Nevada City). Code text from the October 12, 2023 Article VII PDF on the Town site.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority. This requirement is imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Spending of in-lieu fee revenue is a separate public funds question.

program_name: Truckee Workforce Housing Ordinance for non-residential development (Development Code Chapter 18.216)
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy (commercial linkage). Commercial, industrial, institutional, recreational, residential resort and other non-residential projects must build workforce housing for a share of the full-time equivalent employees they generate (Table 7-7; commercial projects of 3,500 square feet or less and industrial of 7,000 square feet or less, or under 7 FTEE, are exempt). Fractions and approved cases may pay the same in-lieu fee ($136,851 per required unit under Resolution 2024-65) or use alternative equivalent actions such as land dedication.
affordability_requirement: Workforce units restricted under Chapter 18.210 affordability controls; occupancy by employees in the Truckee region.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Draft 7th cycle Program H-2.E calls for reviewing the ordinance and an affordable housing credit bank by December 2029.
layering_notes: Creates partnering opportunities: commercial developers needing workforce units can buy inclusionary credits from, or dedicate land to, affordable projects. The Edmunds Lofts site came to the Town through a land dedication by High Altitude Fitness under this ordinance. No county equivalent exists.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority. This requirement is imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Spending of in-lieu fee revenue is a separate public funds question. Land dedicated to the Town under the ordinance and later conveyed below market would be public funds under 1720(b)(3) for that project.

program_name: Truckee Homegrown Housing Program, Monetary Incentives (formerly Deed Restriction for New Housing Development)
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Housing Division; program operator Sierra Business Council (info@sierrabusiness.org, 530-582-4800)
typical_award_size: Per-unit payment for a 55-year deed restriction on newly built units, paid at certificate of occupancy after recording: studio $100,000, one bedroom $150,000, two bedroom $225,000 for units restricted to 180% AMI; studio $116,000, one bedroom $174,000, two bedroom $261,000 for units restricted to 120% AMI. Guidelines approved June 23, 2026. Town Council has committed $3,600,000 to deed restriction payments, after moving site-acquisition funds into the program in September 2025.
per_unit_cap: $261,000 per two-bedroom unit at 120% AMI; studios through two bedrooms only.
affordability_requirement: Occupants must work within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary; household income at or below 180% AMI (rent or price capped at 120% AMI affordability) or at or below 120% AMI (capped at 80% AMI affordability); 55-year non-renewing restriction; no short-term rental; one dedicated parking space per unit.
next_deadline: Open; apply after a complete Planning application. Milestones: building permit application within 9 months of entitlement, permit issued within 18 months, first inspection within 24 months, certificate of occupancy within 30 months, or the award is cancelled.
layering_notes: Designed for missing-middle workforce units, not tax credit deals: projects entitled under State Density Bonus Law are ineligible, and funds cannot be combined with other assistance that imposes an equivalent 55-year income and workforce restriction. Eligible only in VMT Exemption Areas. Payment at C of O means it works as permanent-loan paydown or equity replacement, not construction financing. A January 27, 2026 BAE valuation analysis informed the revised amounts. Town funds count as public funds under Labor Code 1720.
cycle_notes: first come, subject to available funds
prevailing_wage_basis: The June 23, 2026 Homegrown Housing Program Guidelines do not address prevailing wage, and whether a post-completion deed restriction payment makes a privately owned residential project a public work under Labor Code 1720 was not confirmed by any cited rule.
audit_note: Redirect resolves to the same June 23, 2026 guidelines PDF; payment table, AMI tiers, 55-year term, density bonus exclusion, VMT area and milestone deadlines match. Prevailing wage changed from true to unclear because no stated rule supports true. The $3,600,000 Council commitment is not in the guidelines and was not re-checked.

program_name: Truckee Deed-Restricted Housing Incentives (Development Code Chapter 18.213, Ordinance 2026-06) and Density Bonus (Chapter 18.212)
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Non-monetary incentives, not a subsidy. Ordinance 2026-06, adopted April 28, 2026 and effective about May 28, 2026, implements 2040 General Plan Action LU-2.B: a Town-specific workforce and affordable housing bonus with streamlined review and flexible design standards for projects with deed-restricted units, with income criteria set by Council resolution. Chapter 18.212 separately implements state density bonus law, including a Development Bonus for Partnered Commercial Projects (18.212.160).
affordability_requirement: Deed-restricted units meeting the Council-adopted income criteria (workforce levels up to 180% AMI under the companion Homegrown program); state density bonus thresholds for Chapter 18.212.
next_deadline: In effect; requested with the Planning application.
layering_notes: Choose one path: projects using State Density Bonus Law cannot take Homegrown payments, while projects using Chapter 18.213 can also draw Homegrown payments, even for their inclusionary units. Draft 7th cycle Program H-3.D adds fee deferrals, land write-downs and incentives beyond state density bonus for acutely and extremely low income, senior and disability housing. The Housing Development Incentives page text says the ordinance was introduced April 7, 2026 with second reading April 28; the Council work plan page reports adoption on April 28, 2026.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011). Chapter 18.213 incentives are non-monetary; Homegrown Housing payments are a separate Town program tested on their own, and draft Program H-3.D fee deferrals are not adopted.

program_name: Truckee existing-stock deed restriction programs: Truckee Home Access Program (THAP), Lease to Locals, Rooted Renters and Short-Term Rental Workforce Housing Token pilot
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Housing Division
typical_award_size: THAP pays buyers up to $150,000 (maximum $937,500 purchase price), sellers and local businesses for permanent workforce deed restrictions on homes (cap 245% AMI). Lease to Locals pays owners up to $18,000 to convert homes to long-term local rentals; Rooted Renters pays up to $26,000 to lock in below-market rents. The STR Token pilot gives short-term rental certificates in exchange for 15-year workforce deed restrictions (150% AMI average per adult; applications closed June 20, 2024). Results to date: 871 deed-restricted units (6.2% of stock), 33 THAP homes, 276 Lease to Locals conversions, 76 Rooted Renters units, 37 ADUs created through grants and loans.
per_unit_cap: THAP $150,000 per home; Lease to Locals $18,000; Rooted Renters $26,000.
affordability_requirement: Occupants must work locally; income caps vary by program (THAP 245% AMI; Token 150% AMI per adult).
next_deadline: Open; THAP parameters under review with revisions targeted for Q4 2026.
layering_notes: Not a source for new affordable multifamily, but signals the Town's local revenue priorities: its housing dollars go mainly to deed restrictions of existing stock and middle-income production. The Town's goal is 10% of housing stock deed restricted by 2032. The Council work plan lists a potential housing revenue measure and draft Program H-2.F targets at least $300,000 per year of added local funding (additional TOT, business, sales or transfer tax). Mountain Housing Council of Tahoe Truckee (Tahoe Truckee Community Foundation) is the regional partner for AMI tiers above 120%.
audit_note: Spot check Nov 9, 2026: Town pages and THAP Guidelines confirm THAP up to $150,000 with $937,500 maximum price and 245% AMI cap, Lease to Locals up to $18,000, Rooted Renters up to $26,000, and the STR Token pilot (applications closed June 20, 2024; 15-year deed restriction; 150% AMI average per adult). Program result counts (871 units and others) were not on the pages read. prevailing_wage_trigger false is uncited.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction, alteration, demolition, installation or repair paid with public funds; THAP, Lease to Locals, Rooted Renters and the STR Token pilot pay for deed restrictions or occupancy commitments on existing homes and fund no construction, and buyer payments are homebuyer assistance exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Truckee Town-owned land public-private partnerships (Edmunds Lofts) and Railyard Master Plan affordable housing obligations
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Planning Division and Town Manager
typical_award_size: Edmunds Lofts: Town-owned 0.5-acre site (APN 018-580-052, dedicated by High Altitude Fitness) to be conveyed to Paradigm8 / Sagemodern under a Development and Disposition Agreement for 12 deed-restricted workforce units; entitlements granted in 2025 and building permits under review (75% complete at December 31, 2025). Railyard: Council work plan item 6.3 will move inclusionary and workforce housing obligations from the Railyard Development Agreement into the Railyard Master Plan (late 2026 to early 2027); the Town made a significant financial contribution to the earlier 66-unit Truckee Artist Lofts in the Railyard. Draft 7th cycle Program H-2.H directs annual review of all Town-owned and partner-agency land (TTUSD, Caltrans, Tahoe Forest Hospital, Truckee Donner PUD) for housing.
per_unit_cap: Land contribution; no cash figure published.
affordability_requirement: Deed-restricted workforce units per the DDA; Railyard units per the Development Agreement.
next_deadline: No open RFIQ as of 2026-11-08. Council removed the pilot to find another site from the 2025-2027 work plan on September 9, 2025. Watch the Railyard Master Plan amendment (late 2026 to early 2027).
layering_notes: Land write-downs of public land are public subsidy for prevailing wage purposes and trigger Surplus Land Act review. Coldstream Commons (48 units at 60% AMI, nine HUD 811 units) is an existing affordable project in the Coldstream Specific Plan area; no new Coldstream affordable commitment was found this pass. Prohousing Designation status for Truckee was not confirmed.
cycle_notes: no open solicitation; RFIQ issued October 16, 2024
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Conveying Town land below fair market value is public funds under 1720(b)(3), but no Town or program prevailing wage rule was found, and for a small project like Edmunds Lofts (12 units) coverage depends on the land value against 1720(c)(3) de minimis limits and other 1720(c) exemptions. The Surplus Land Act (Gov. Code 54221, 54233) adds affordability rules but no prevailing wage requirement. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

program_name: Grass Valley Affordable Housing Density Bonuses and Incentives (Development Code Chapter 17.32)
administering_agency: City of Grass Valley Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Local chapter tracks Government Code 65915: one incentive at 10% lower income, 5% very low or 10% moderate (common interest) units, two at 17% lower or 10% very low, and so on; parking reductions (17.32.050) and childcare bonuses (17.32.060); Council grants requested incentives unless it makes written findings. The 2024 Annual Progress Report says no density bonus has been requested and the City planned updates to the ordinance.
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915; density bonus agreement under 17.32.100.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested before or with the project application.
layering_notes: Grass Valley has no inclusionary ordinance, no city housing trust fund of its own and no city NOFA; its local money flows through the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund and the regional PLHA plan administered by Nevada County HCS (see county records). Code text read from the zoneomics mirror; grassvalleyca.gov returns a JavaScript shell to scripts, so the City's meeting-host attachments were used for the APR.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Grass Valley Housing Element affordable housing programs: fee deferral on request (Program 28), state and federal funding support (Program 13), tax-exempt bonds (Program 14)
administering_agency: City of Grass Valley Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Fee deferral for affordable housing is available on request, but the City reports it has received no requests. Program 13 commits the City to apply for grants and support developers seeking funding (objective 25 very low and 40 to 60 low income new units in 2019-2027); Program 14 supports tax-exempt bonds and mortgage credit certificates. The City won a $2 million DTSC Equitable Community Revitalization Grant in 2024 to clean up a brownfield site of interest to affordable developers, and expedited a Habitat for Humanity SB 9 lot split for three deed-restricted homes.
affordability_requirement: Lower income units per the funding source; Program 28 targets units at or below 30% AMI with Nevada County and the Regional Housing Authority.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The 7th cycle Housing Element is due in 2027.
layering_notes: Deferral terms are not codified in a published resolution; negotiate case by case. City sites have historically attracted County-sponsored supportive housing (Brunswick Commons, 41 units) and RHA projects. The City joined the October 30, 2025 regional housing workshop with the County, Nevada City, Truckee and HCD. Source is the 2024 General Plan Annual Progress Report (March 2025) on the City's meeting host; a 2025 APR was not located this pass.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Fee deferral or reduction can be public funds under 1720(b)(4), but the Housing Element programs state no prevailing wage rule and deferrals are often de minimis under 1720(c)(3). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: Nevada City density bonus and affordable housing incentives (Housing Element Program 24; Zoning Code update pending)
administering_agency: City of Nevada City Planning Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. The City grants density bonuses and incentives per state law; Cashin's Field (51 units, opened 2023) used an 80% density bonus and reduced parking. The 2025 Annual Progress Report says the City will update its density bonus regulations in 2026 to match current state law. Nevada City has not raised development impact fees since 1993 and is considering a fee study in 2026.
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915.
next_deadline: Not applicable; 7th cycle Housing Element (2027-2035) update underway with workshops July 30 and September 10, 2026.
layering_notes: Nevada City has no city housing trust fund, no city NOFA and no city-run CDBG or HOME program; the 2025 APR states the City's limited resources preclude its own rehabilitation program. Local gap money comes through the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund and regional PLHA (the City allocated PLHA to Cashin's Field). Zoning code density bonus chapter not found on the zoneomics mirror; source is the City's 2025 Housing Element APR.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: Nevada City subdivision affordability requirement (30% of homes 1,500 square feet or smaller; Section 17.80.220 lower income share)
administering_agency: City of Nevada City Planning Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The 2025 Housing Element APR describes two layers. Housing Element Program 5 requires that 30% of homes in new subdivisions be 1,500 square feet or smaller and affordable to moderate and below income households, through deed restriction or an affordable housing plan approved by the Planning Commission or Council (size limits, rental units, second units); the Zoning Code was amended in 2009 to carry this out and 34 lots have been approved under it (none built yet). The same APR entry states that Municipal Code Section 17.80.220 requires 20% lower income units in developments. The code text was not available, so whether 17.80.220 is the 2009 implementing section or a separate requirement, and its unit thresholds, are not confirmed.
affordability_requirement: Per the 2025 APR: Program 5 targets moderate and below income (30% of subdivision homes, 1,500 square feet or smaller); Section 17.80.220 is described as requiring 20% lower income units. Confirm the code text before relying on either figure.
next_deadline: Not applicable.
layering_notes: Functions as a light inclusionary rule with no in-lieu fee or fund found. Section 17.80.220 is not on the zoneomics mirror (Chapter 17.80 page loads without section text) and gocodebook returns 403; ask the Planning Department for the current section and whether the 30% size rule and the 20% lower income rule both apply.
audit_note: Follow-up Nov 10, 2026: APR reread. The 30%/1,500 sq ft figure is the Housing Element Program 5 objective; the APR separately cites 17.80.220 as requiring 20% lower income units. Record now states both as the APR does; code text still unconfirmed.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

program_name: Nevada City fee waiver for deed-restricted low income ADUs and reduced ADU impact fees (Municipal Code 17.72.026)
administering_agency: City of Nevada City Planning Department
typical_award_size: Waiver of mitigation fees and utility hook-up fees for deed-restricted low income accessory dwelling units; reduced AB 1600 impact fees for all ADUs and none for ADUs under 750 square feet. Pre-approved ADU plans available. Objective of 8 affordable second units in the cycle.
affordability_requirement: Low income deed restriction on the ADU.
next_deadline: Not applicable.
layering_notes: Small-scale tool only; no equivalent waiver is codified for multifamily. Recorded so the market's lack of multifamily fee relief is visible.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Waived fees are public funds under 1720(b)(4), but an ADU fee waiver is likely de minimis under 1720(c)(3) and no Nevada City rule states prevailing wage applies. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: no program rule found stating prevailing wage applies; changed true to unclear because only the general 1720(b) public-funds definition supports it.

program_name: Riverside Local Affordable Housing Trust Fund (LAHTF), created by Council resolution March 12, 2024
administering_agency: City of Riverside Housing and Human Services Department
typical_award_size: Construction and permanent loans at simple interest of no more than 3% per annum, with repayments recycled into the fund. Seeded with a $1,500,000 transfer of PLHA funds; ongoing revenue from HOME, NSP, CalHome, PLHA and ARPA affordable housing program income (ARPA affordable housing allocation was $1,388,797) plus 50% of future sale proceeds of City-owned land bought with General Fund money. City applied for a $1,000,000 HCD Local Housing Trust Fund match (August 2024). Staff cite typical gap requests of $3M to $4M for 65 to 80 unit projects.
affordability_requirement: Low to moderate income households. Committee recommendations at creation: 99-year affordability term, priority for seniors and justice-involved people, and eligibility for market-rate developers that restrict 10% of rental units (or 5% of for-sale units). Loans funded with PIP Round 4 money require 55-year first-position covenants at or below 50% AMI.
next_deadline: No LAHTF NOFA issued as of 2026-11-08. The March 24, 2026 PIP Round 4 staff report says residual receipts from PIP loans will flow to the trust fund and staff will issue a NOFA once enough has accumulated. Contact Housing and Human Services (Agripina Neubauer, Housing Project Manager).
layering_notes: City-controlled gap layer that sits ahead of County HOME/PLHA (the County CDBG/HOME record covers the Urban County, which excludes the City of Riverside as its own entitlement grantee). Stacks with the City's own HOME, PLHA and PIP loans (separate records) and with 4% or 9% LIHTC. Capitalized mainly from recycled program income, so the balance is small relative to need; expect it to be combined with HOME and PLHA on the same project. If the LHTF state match was awarded it carries HCD LHTF regulatory terms. City pages on riversideca.gov are thin; staff reports were pulled through the Legistar web API (client riversideca).
prevailing_wage_basis: No LAHTF rule found; the March 12, 2024 staff report is silent on prevailing wage. City loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose public participation is below-market interest rate loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20+ years at or below 80% AMI (applied in DIR PW 2016-035, Spring Park Senior Villa). Where a loan is drawn from HOME program income, HOME rules (24 CFR 92.354, Davis-Bacon at 12+ HOME-assisted units) follow that money. Outcome is project-specific.
audit_note: Leave unclear: only basis is the general Labor Code 1720(b) public funds definition; coverage turns on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Searched LAHTF staff report, Labor Code 1720 and DIR coverage determinations 2026-11-08.

program_name: Housing Authority of the City of Riverside, Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Riverside (Housing Successor to the former Redevelopment Agency)
typical_award_size: FY 2023-24 (latest report found, dated April 1, 2025): $9,403,323 deposited, $2,899,271 spent ($1,597,196 on housing development across ELI, VLI and low income units), ending cash balance $2,547,069. Portfolio $35.6M ($34.9M loans receivable, $685K real property). The Housing Authority also owns 104 units managed by RHDC under a 2024 operating agreement.
affordability_requirement: LMIHAF rules (HSC 34176.1): at least 30% of spending for ELI (30% AMI) and no more than 20% for 60 to 80% AMI over each five-year period; 55-year rental covenants typical.
next_deadline: No standing NOFA. Funds and Housing Authority land are committed project by project through Council and Housing Authority actions; contact Housing and Human Services.
layering_notes: Separate from the County housing successor (HACR) record; only for projects inside city limits. Used alongside City HOME/PLHA and land write-downs (see Housing Authority land record). Ending balance is modest, so treat as a supplemental source. A FY 2024-25 report was not found on the City site (404) and should be requested.
audit_note: PW citation pass 2026-11-09: true was uncited and no program-specific rule was found; set unclear per Tier 3 rule (1720(b) alone does not support true).
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Housing successor loans and land are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and (b)(3) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); 1720(c)(4) exempts only Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund money under Health and Safety Code 33334.2 and 33334.3 and does not name housing successor asset funds, and 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts below-market loans where at least 40% of units are restricted to 80% AMI for 20 years. No program rule, NOFA or agreement term stating prevailing wage was found.

program_name: Housing Authority and Successor Agency land write-downs and surplus land dispositions (e.g., 2882 Mission Inn Avenue DDA, 11049 Bogart, 8733 Indiana)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Riverside; Successor Agency to the Redevelopment Agency of the City of Riverside

prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Below-market land transfers are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(3) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The Surplus Land Act sections read (Gov. Code 54233, https://california.public.law/codes/government_code_section_54233; 54233.5, https://california.public.law/codes/government_code_section_54233.5) impose affordability covenants only, not prevailing wage. No DDA or program term stating prevailing wage was found. The 2882 Mission Inn DDA also pairs $900,000 City HOME; HOME Davis-Bacon (24 CFR 92.354) applies only if 12 or more units are HOME-assisted, which the DDA staff report does not state.
audit_note: PW citation pass 2026-11-09: true was uncited and no program-specific rule was found; set unclear per Tier 3 rule (1720(b) alone does not support true).

program_name: City of Riverside HUD entitlement funds: HOME Infill Residential Development Program and CDBG (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
administering_agency: City of Riverside Housing and Human Services Department
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 HUD allocations total $9,050,906: CDBG $2,749,768, HOME $981,735 (of which $883,561 to the Infill Residential Development Program, plus about $200,000 HOME program income), ESG $250,428, HOPWA $5,068,975 (City is the HOPWA EMSA grantee for both Riverside and San Bernardino counties). Recent HOME loans: $1,508,234 Sunrise at Bogart (22 PSH units), $1,550,443 Mulberry Gardens Family (11 HOME units). HOME-ARP also used ($3,000,000 Mulberry Gardens Senior).
affordability_requirement: HOME: at or below 80% AMI with HOME rent limits; 20-year minimum HOME period for new construction, City typically records 55 years.
next_deadline: Public notice of funding availability released each December (last one December 2025) for the following July program year; FY 2027-28 notice expected about December 2026. Action Plan due to HUD by mid-August.
layering_notes: City is its own HUD entitlement and is outside the Riverside Urban County CDBG/HOME pool in the county record. HOME is small (under $1M a year), so it functions as a slice of the local gap. Federal Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. The draft Action Plan says the City dedicates its direct PLHA allocation to affordable housing development as additional leverage.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

program_name: City of Riverside Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) direct formula allocation, development loans
administering_agency: City of Riverside Housing and Human Services Department
typical_award_size: Five-year PLHA plan (adopted July 7, 2020) estimated $9,732,750. CY 2023 application $2,456,509 (March 2025). Development loans to date: $1,000,000 Golden Pierce (79 units), $1,053,907 The Aspire (32 youth PSH units), $380,562 Sunrise at Bogart (22 PSH units), $250,000 proposed for Grapevine (10 units). A large share also goes to homeless case management ($1,384,134 City Net).
affordability_requirement: PLHA rules: rental units at or below 60% AMI (up to 120% AMI for owner units), 55-year covenants.
next_deadline: Awarded through Council-approved loan agreements; uncommitted amounts may be transferred to the Local Affordable Housing Trust Fund ($1.5M already moved). Contact Housing and Human Services.
layering_notes: City receives its own PLHA formula share separate from the County PLHA record, so City projects can carry both a City and a County PLHA loan. Commonly stacked with City HOME and PIP on the same project (Sunrise at Bogart used PIP $1.44M, PLHA $380K and HOME $1.51M).
prevailing_wage_basis: HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines contain no prevailing wage or Labor Code 1720 provision, and the City staff report is silent. PLHA loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but the 1720(c)(5)(E) below-market loan exemption (40% of units at or below 80% AMI for 20+ years) can apply, as in DIR PW 2016-035. Outcome depends on project facts and other layered sources (City HOME triggers Davis-Bacon at 12+ HOME units under 24 CFR 92.354).
audit_note: Leave unclear: only basis is the general Labor Code 1720(b) public funds definition; coverage turns on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. PLHA guidelines and City staff report searched for prevailing wage 2026-11-08 with no hit.

audit_note: Leave unclear: only basis is the general Labor Code 1720(b) public funds definition; coverage turns on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. PIP guidelines (Round 4 and 2026) and City staff report searched 2026-11-08.

program_name: Riverside density bonus, Municipal Code Chapter 19.545

A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

program_name: University Avenue Density Transfer Pilot Program (Housing Element Program HE-EJ-7-2)
administering_agency: City of Riverside Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Not a cash subsidy. Creates a unit bank seeded with residential capacity from City-owned surplus parcels in the University Avenue Specific Plan; receiver sites (City surplus and Housing Element sites) can withdraw extra units first-come first-served, with priority to City surplus sites, and may combine withdrawals with Chapter 19.545 density bonuses.

next_deadline: Land Use Committee recommended approval; the Council item (Legistar 52587, March 2026) showed status Agenda Ready with no recorded vote in the API. Verify adoption with Planning before relying on it.
layering_notes: Most useful when paired with a City surplus parcel disposition (see land write-down record). Pilot limited to the University Avenue Specific Plan area; may expand if successful.
audit_note: T4 spot check 2026-11-08: staff report matches on bank seeding, receiver eligibility, first-come priority and density bonus stacking; program also allows a Direct Transfer method. Council hearing was April 21, 2026 (Legistar 52587, intro March 24, 2026); API still shows Agenda Ready with no recorded action, so adoption remains unconfirmed. Prevailing wage false is uncited; zoning tool with no public funds.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) require construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds; a density transfer from a City unit bank is an entitlement, not a payment, fee reduction or land transfer, and 1720(c)(1) excludes private residential projects on private property. Any City surplus land conveyed to a receiver site is a separate 1720(b)(3) question.

program_name: Moreno Valley density bonus program, Municipal Code Section 9.03.050 (with impact fee reductions)
administering_agency: City of Moreno Valley Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Implements state density bonus law plus a local fee incentive: 50% reduction of the development impact fee and parkland impact mitigation fee for VLI units and 25% for lower income units (Section 9.03.050.I.2). Up to four concessions; projects within half a mile of a major transit stop also get up to three more stories or 33 feet.
affordability_requirement: Gov. Code 65915 thresholds (5% VLI, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% lower income with up to 20% moderate, and special populations); 55-year affordability agreement for rental units.
next_deadline: Applied at entitlement; last amended by Ord. 1035 (December 16, 2025).
layering_notes: The fee reduction is a real local enhancement beyond state law and can be requested as an additional incentive. A City fee reduction may count as public funds under Labor Code 1720. No local housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee fund was found for Moreno Valley. Code read on the zoneomics mirror.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Section 9.03.050.I.2 reduces the development impact fee and parkland fee 50 percent for very low income units and 25 percent for lower income units; the density bonus itself provides no public funds (1720(a)(1)). Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

program_name: Corona Housing Authority Housing Fund (Fund 291) loans and Housing Authority land (Corona 2nd Street Family Apartments DDA)
administering_agency: Corona Housing Authority (Housing Successor), Community Services Department, Housing Services
typical_award_size: Example August 21, 2024 DDA for 115 family units: Authority cash loan $7,535,280 (Housing Fund 291) plus a land loan at the higher of appraisal or $2.8M; City loans of $529,875 HOME-ARP, land at the higher of appraisal or $1.2M, and up to $2,000,000 in deferred development impact fees. Local subsidy about $99,731 per unit, 18.5% of a $62.0M total cost ($539,301 per unit). Loans amortized and repaid over 55 years.
per_unit_cap: None published; about $100K per unit local subsidy on the 2nd Street deal.
affordability_requirement: All units except the manager unit affordable in perpetuity at 30%, 50% and 80% of median income (rents at 30 to 60% with caps to 70% under tax credits); 20-unit preference for homeless families.
next_deadline: No NOFA cycle; the Authority uses RFQ/RFP for its sites. A second phase of about 25 PSH units on the same site is planned. Housing Fund balance was not found; request the latest SB 341 housing successor report from Housing Services.
layering_notes: Corona's main local gap source. Layered with 4% LIHTC, City CDBG and HOME-ARP and a DIF deferral note. Land was bought from RCTC under the SLA with $600K CDBG and $1.4M Housing Fund; repayment splits 30% to CDBG program income and 70% to the Housing Fund. Corona's Legistar (client corona) has no matters after August 2024, so newer Council items were not reachable through the API.
audit_note: PW citation pass 2026-11-09: true was uncited and no program-specific rule was found; set unclear per Tier 3 rule (1720(b) alone does not support true).
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Housing Authority Fund 291 loans and land loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and (b)(3) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); 1720(c)(5)(E) may exempt below-market loans with at least 40% of units at 80% AMI for 20 years. The 2nd Street DDA read states no prevailing wage term. The separate City HOME-ARP loan would carry Davis-Bacon only at 12 or more HOME-ARP units (24 CFR 92.354).

program_name: Corona development impact fee waiver or deferral for affordable housing
administering_agency: City of Corona (City Council; Housing Services and Planning)
typical_award_size: Case by case. On the 2nd Street Family project the City deferred up to $2,000,000 in development impact fees into a promissory note repaid over 55 years.
affordability_requirement: Tied to the affordability terms of the project's DDA or density bonus agreement.
next_deadline: Requested at predevelopment and approved by Council resolution with the project agreement. The FY 2026-27 Action Plan commits staff to educate affordable developers on how to request a waiver or deferral.
layering_notes: No standing fee deferral ordinance was found; treat as negotiable. Deferred fees held as a City loan count as public funds for prevailing wage. Useful to reduce the gap at construction closing.
prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Fees reduced, waived, deferred or reimbursed are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); whether a project is covered depends on 1720(c)(3) de minimis (under $600,000 and 2% of project cost) and other 1720(c) exemptions. No program rule stating prevailing wage was found.

program_name: Corona CDBG, HOME and HOME-ARP (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
administering_agency: City of Corona Housing Services Division
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 CDBG and HOME investment $1,844,570 (draft plan sized on 2025-26 allocations of $1,085,264 CDBG and $409,306 HOME); about $8.9M expected over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan. HOME is mostly programmed to tenant-based rental assistance ($656,979 TBRA, 20 households). HOME-ARP allocation $1,801,873 (as amended July 2025) with $1,531,592 for affordable rental housing; the August 6, 2024 2nd Street DDAs commit $529,875 to the Family project and $1,000,000 to the PSH project, so the HOME-ARP rental allocation is effectively fully committed.
affordability_requirement: Low and moderate income (at or below 80% AMI); HOME rent limits.
next_deadline: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring for a July 1 program year; FY 2027-28 cycle expected to start winter 2026-27. Little HOME is left for development after TBRA; ask Housing Services before counting on it.
layering_notes: Corona is its own entitlement, not part of the County Urban County. CDBG has been used for land acquisition for housing ($600K on 2nd Street). Corona does not qualify for a HOME match reduction. The Action Plan also lists SB 2 PLHA as a resource.
prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).
audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: typical_award_size said HOME-ARP was only partly committed to 2nd Street ($529,875). The August 6, 2024 staff reports show $529,875 to 2nd Street Family plus $1,000,000 to 2nd Street PSH, about $1,529,875 of the $1,531,592 rental allocation, so no HOME-ARP is left for new projects. Other figures match the draft 2026-27 Action Plan.

program_name: Corona Affordable Housing Overlay Zone (AHO), Municipal Code Chapter 17.31
administering_agency: City of Corona Planning and Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. By-right approval for housing projects on AHO-designated parcels that reserve at least 20% of units for lower income households; mixed use allowed if at least 51% of floor area is residential; density per General Plan designation; objective design standards apply.
affordability_requirement: At least 20% of units for lower income households at affordable rent or cost, regulatory agreement for at least 30 years.
next_deadline: Ongoing. Adopted by Ord. 3360 (2023). The Action Plan also proposes a General Plan change to allow 100% residential in Mixed-Use designations with the AHO overlay.
layering_notes: By-right status removes CEQA and discretionary risk, useful for TCAC readiness. Can be combined with Chapter 17.87 density bonus. The 30-year minimum term is shorter than TCAC's 55 years, so the tax credit term governs.
audit_note: T4 spot check 2026-11-08: Chapter 17.31 text (Ord. 3360, 2023) matches on 20% lower income, 51% residential floor area for mixed use, General Plan density, 30-year regulatory agreement. Projects of 4+ units still go through Development Plan Review (17.31.060(B)); tract or parcel maps remain discretionary. Official codepublishing host returns 403, so text read via zoneomics reproduction. Prevailing wage false is uncited; zoning tool with no public funds.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

layering_notes: Nine-county Bay Area after the 2021 revisions (lower leverage requirement, up to $6 million convertible to forgivable debt, fund term extended to 20 years). Borrowers need 5 years of experience and 4 completed comparable projects (or a qualifying JV partner). Repayment at sale or refinance; pairs with county preservation funds, the City of Oakland and San Francisco small sites programs and BAHFA's separate Housing Preservation Loan Pilot ($17.8 million REAP 2). MTC public capital in Notes B and C, so prevailing wage is marked unclear.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program rule found: the MTC BAPP page, the March 2022 BAPP Loan Term Sheet and MTC Resolution 4454 BAPP program revisions (May 2021) contain no prevailing wage or labor standard. MTC capital in Notes B and C may be public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but coverage depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (BAPP finances acquisition of occupied buildings, with rehab scope varying).
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; no BAPP term sheet or resolution language on prevailing wage; only basis is general Labor Code 1720(b), outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and rehab scope. Confirm with Enterprise, LIIF or MTC.

program_name: Bay Area Transit Oriented Affordable Housing (TOAH) Fund predevelopment and acquisition loans

affordability_requirement: Affordable housing and neighborhood assets near transit in the San Francisco Bay Area.
next_deadline: Rolling through the originating CDFIs.
layering_notes: Oldest of the MTC-seeded regional funds and the model for GSAF and BAPP. Confirm remaining capacity and current terms with LIIF or an originator before relying on it; terms were not available on the page opened this pass. MTC seed capital may be public funds for Labor Code 1720 purposes.
prevailing_wage_basis: No program rule found: the LIIF national funds page, the MTC TOAH page, the TOAH and BAPP brochure, and the TOAH II acquisition and predevelopment loan term sheets (April 2024, bayareatod.com) contain no prevailing wage or labor standard. MTC seed capital may be public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but coverage depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts, and TOAH loans finance acquisition and predevelopment rather than construction.
audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; TOAH II term sheets and MTC and LIIF pages state no prevailing wage rule; only basis is general Labor Code 1720(b). Current TOAH II term sheets are posted at bayareatod.com.

jurisdiction: Five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa)
program_name: Partnership for the Bay's Future: Bay's Future Fund (BFF) loans
administering_agency: LISC Bay Area (fund manager and originator) with Corporation for Supportive Housing and Capital Impact Partners as originators; San Francisco Foundation convener; contact Asha Rao, Senior Director of Investments, LISC Bay Area
typical_award_size: $500 million loan fund; structures from predevelopment to mini-permanent; interest typically 4% to 5% set by AMI served, term and originator; loan size up to $7.5 million; loan to value up to 150% for high-impact projects; loans must mature by August 2030.
affordability_requirement: Rental housing serving households at 0% to 120% AMI with deed restrictions.
next_deadline: Rolling through LISC Bay Area, CSH or Capital Impact; all loans must mature by August 2030.
layering_notes: Covers San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. Seeded by Chan Zuckerberg Initiative ($40 million first-loss), Facebook/Meta, Genentech, Kaiser Permanente, the San Francisco Foundation and others; underwriting tolerates more risk, including for emerging developers of color. The August 2030 maturity limit makes this a bridge product; the companion Community Housing Fund provides the long-term 2% money. The deployment goal was $500 million by end of 2025, so confirm remaining availability.
audit_note: Nov 8, 2026 spot check: the family of funds page does not state the five-county geography.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(b) defines public funds as money, assets, loans or reduced obligations provided by the state or a political subdivision (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). LISC Bay Area, managing the Bay's Future Fund, lends private capital (philanthropic and corporate capital such as the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, Meta, Genentech and Kaiser Permanente), which is not state or political subdivision money, and the program page (https://www.lisc.org/bay-area/areas-of-work/affordable-housing/partnership-bays-future/family-of-funds/) states no prevailing wage term, so the loan does not itself trigger state prevailing wage. Public sources layered in the same deal (city, county, HCD or other public loans) are tested separately under their own rules; if a loan relends state or local public money, that money's rule applies instead.
