program_name: Public Lands Unlocking Sites (PLUS) predevelopment guaranty program, LISC Bay Area
administering_agency: LISC Bay Area with a Chan Zuckerberg Initiative-backed guaranty
typical_award_size: $10 million guaranty that lets LISC provide predevelopment funding for affordable housing on surplus public land without borrower collateral; goal of over 800 affordable units by 2029 across 12 Northern California counties. Loan sizes and pricing are not posted.
affordability_requirement: Multifamily housing for households earning up to 80% AMI on surplus or public land.
next_deadline: Rolling; contact LISC Bay Area lending (no public application posted).
layering_notes: Reclassified from other to loan: the guaranty is a credit enhancement that backs LISC Bay Area predevelopment funding to developers, so the deployable product is a predevelopment loan without borrower collateral (LISC lending products page; LISC 2023 Bay Area annual report). Designed for Surplus Land Act and other public-site dispositions where developers cannot pledge collateral before site control. Example cited: a 127-unit project on a 2-acre city and transit district site in Santa Cruz. Combine with BAHFA Priority Sites predevelopment loans and county or city surplus land programs. Public land involvement makes prevailing wage status project-specific.
audit_note: Guaranty amount, 800-unit goal, 12 counties and 80% AMI come from the LISC 2023 Bay Area annual report; the lending products page confirms PLUS provides predevelopment funding with no collateral but posts no terms.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(b) defines public funds as money, assets, loans or reduced obligations provided by the state or a political subdivision (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). PLUS lends LISC Bay Area predevelopment capital backed by a private Chan Zuckerberg Initiative guaranty, which is not state or political subdivision money, pays predevelopment costs rather than construction, and the LISC lending products page (https://www.lisc.org/bay-area/how-we-work/lending-products/) states no prevailing wage term, so the loan does not itself trigger state prevailing wage. The public land the program targets is tested separately: a below-market land transfer is public funds under 1720(b)(3), and other public loans in the deal carry their own rules.

program_name: Faith and Housing program predevelopment grants and technical assistance, LISC Bay Area
administering_agency: LISC Bay Area; contact Evita Chavez, Senior Program Officer, Housing; funders include Alameda County HCD, BMO, Capital One, Crankstart, First Republic Foundation, San Francisco Foundation, Silicon Valley Community Foundation, Sobrato Family Foundation and Wells Fargo
typical_award_size: Cohort program since 2019: technical workshops, a development coach, grant funds for predevelopment activities and a participation stipend for faith-based and community-based landowners; grant amounts not posted.
affordability_requirement: Affordable housing on faith-owned land, typically through a joint venture with an experienced developer.
next_deadline: Next cohort date not posted; join the mailing list on the program page.
layering_notes: Useful for developers partnering with congregations under SB 4 (Affordable Housing on Faith and Higher Education Lands Act). Grants cover early feasibility before Housing Trust or CDFI predevelopment loans. Alameda County HCD is a funder, so Alameda projects may have a direct county tie-in.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers only construction, alteration, demolition, installation or repair work paid for in whole or in part out of public funds (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The Faith and Housing program funds technical workshops, a development coach, predevelopment grants and participant stipends (https://www.lisc.org/bay-area/areas-of-work/affordable-housing/faithandhousing/); it funds no construction, so it does not trigger prevailing wage even though Alameda County HCD is among its funders. Construction financing for a resulting project is tested separately.

No direct capital.

jurisdiction: FHLBank San Francisco district (California, Arizona, Nevada)
program_name: FHLBank San Francisco Affordable Housing Program (AHP) General Fund competitive grants
administering_agency: Federal Home Loan Bank of San Francisco (member-sponsored applications; the project sponsor applies through an FHLBank member bank, credit union, insurer or CDFI)
typical_award_size: 2026 competition: $60.1 million in General Fund grants awarded June 22, 2026 to 39 projects (2,676 units) in California and Arizona from 125 applications; 2026 awards total $66.3 million including the Nevada Targeted Fund, up nearly one-third from 2025. Per the 2026 Implementation Plan, maximum request is the lesser of $2,000,000 or 50% of total project costs, and no more than $65,000 per income-restricted rental unit (scored on a declining scale from $30,000 to $65,000). Four years from award to complete construction and draw funds. Since 1990, $1.48 billion awarded for nearly 160,000 homes.
per_unit_cap: $65,000 per income-restricted rental unit and $2,000,000 per project (lesser of $2,000,000 or 50% of total project costs)
affordability_requirement: Rental projects must reserve at least 20% of units for households at or below 50% AMI with a 15-year retention period; owner-occupied projects serve households at or below 80% AMI (5-year retention).
next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. 2026 General Fund awards announced June 22, 2026; FHLBank San Francisco has not posted 2027 competition dates.
layering_notes: A grant that flows through a member institution, so line up a member bank or CDFI sponsor (Housing Trust Silicon Valley, Community Vision and Clearinghouse CDFI are members that sponsor awards) early. Scoring favors homelessness and special needs set-asides, ELI units, lower subsidy per unit and donated or discounted property; 2026 awards included $27.9 million for 19 supportive housing developments and more than $20 million for 12 senior developments. Loan pools and revolving funds may not apply to the General Fund. AHP funds are private bank-system money and do not by themselves trigger state prevailing wage, though federal AHP regulations apply. Grants are typically sized at $30,000 to $65,000 per unit and used as gap equity alongside LIHTC and state soft debt.
cycle_notes: Annual General Fund competition under the yearly AHP Implementation Plan (2026 plan effective January 1, 2026). 2026 awards announced June 22, 2026. The AHP and Apply pages invite unfunded applicants to reapply in the 2027 competition but give no application window; the 2026 Implementation Plan sets no round dates. Check for the 2027 Implementation Plan and window, which on past cycles would fall in the first half of the year (not stated by the Bank).
audit_note: Tier 2 deadline audit 2026-11-08: no 2027 round dates posted. 2026 Implementation Plan confirms $2,000,000 or 50% of total project cost cap, $65,000 per rental unit cap and 20% at 50% AMI.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(b) public funds are money or equivalents provided by the state or a political subdivision (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). AHP grants are paid from the earnings of the Federal Home Loan Bank of San Francisco, a member-owned cooperative, under 12 U.S.C. 1430(j) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/12/1430), which contains no prevailing wage or Davis-Bacon term, and the AHP page states none (https://www.fhlbsf.com/products/community-programs-grants/ahp). AHP alone therefore does not trigger state prevailing wage; other public sources in the deal are tested separately.

jurisdiction: CommonSpirit Health hospital markets in California
program_name: CommonSpirit Health (Dignity Health) Community Investment Program below-market loans
administering_agency: CommonSpirit Health Community Investment Program, San Francisco; cip@commonspirit.org; expression of interest form on the program page; local Dignity Health hospitals act as community liaisons
typical_award_size: Loans up to $10.0 million, tenor up to 10 years, secured or unsecured, concessionary interest benchmarked to inflation, flexible repayment; structures include bridge, line of credit and term. $400 million allocation; $263 million approved across 94 investments as of March 31, 2025; 398 loans and $502.5 million approved since 1990, with affordable housing about 45% of the portfolio. Dignity Health's Homeless Health Initiative has invested nearly $36 million across its California sites since FY2019, including $375,000 in May 2026 for two Yolo County projects ($125,000 Freeman Garden Court, Woodland, 12 units; $250,000 Choice Neighborhoods and Tupelo project, 73 units) and more than $3 million in Yolo and Sacramento Counties to date.
affordability_requirement: Mission-oriented projects addressing social drivers of health, including affordable and supportive housing for low income communities; must show community support and partnership with a CommonSpirit hospital.
next_deadline: Rolling expression of interest.
layering_notes: Place-based: investments are tied to CommonSpirit (Dignity Health) hospital markets, which in scope include Sacramento (Mercy General, Mercy San Juan, Methodist, Mercy Folsom, Woodland Memorial in Yolo), Stockton (St. Joseph's, San Joaquin), Merced, Grass Valley (Sierra Nevada Memorial, Nevada County), Redwood City (Sequoia, San Mateo), Santa Cruz (Dominican), San Luis Obispo and Santa Maria, Ventura (St. John's) and the Inland Empire. Loans often go through a CDFI or linked deposit; CommonSpirit also guarantees loans. Dignity Health is a financing partner of the Monterey Bay Housing Trust. Patient, concessionary money that fits predevelopment or gap positions in supportive housing with co-located services.
eligible_project_detail: bridge and lines of credit to developers and CDFIs
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: program PDF matches loan size up to $10.0M, 10-year tenor, concessionary rate, $400M allocation, $263M and 398 loans/$502.5M as of March 31, 2025 (the web page text shows an older 386 loans/$454M). Page lists inquiry email cip-inquiry@commonspirit.org. Homeless Health Initiative figures were not re-checked on this source.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(b) defines public funds as money, assets, loans or reduced obligations provided by the state or a political subdivision (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). CommonSpirit Health, a private nonprofit health system, lends private capital (its own investment allocation), which is not state or political subdivision money, and the program page (https://www.commonspirit.org/impact/community-health-initiatives/community-investment-program) states no prevailing wage term, so the loan does not itself trigger state prevailing wage. Public sources layered in the same deal (city, county, HCD or other public loans) are tested separately under their own rules; if a loan relends state or local public money, that money's rule applies instead.

jurisdiction: Kaiser Permanente Northern California service area (Bay Area, Sacramento, Central Valley)

administering_agency: Kaiser Permanente National Community Health (impact investing) with Enterprise Community Loan Fund and Enterprise Community Partners as fund partners

layering_notes: Reclassified from other to loan: Kaiser's housing page says the Thriving Communities Fund provides capital and long-term loans to acquire, develop and maintain multiunit properties; RxHome is a $100 million debt fund with Enterprise Community Loan Fund (Enterprise blog, December 18, 2023). The Housing for Health Fund is a separate preservation equity vehicle; earlier passes reported it at $85 million with Enterprise and JPMorgan Chase in the Bay Area and Sacramento, but those figures were not confirmed on pages opened in the Nov 10, 2026 audit. audit_note: NC audit Nov 10, 2026: Kaiser housing security page confirms $400 million, 30,000 units by 2030 and Thriving Communities Fund long-term loans; Enterprise blog (December 18, 2023) confirms RxHome terms and 7,167 units. Housing for Health Fund dollar figures moved to layering_notes as unconfirmed.

administering_agency: Destination: Home (Santa Clara County public-private partnership nonprofit), San Jose; fund seeded by Cisco ($50 million, 2018) and Apple ($50 million, 2019)

affordability_requirement: Supportive housing and extremely low income (30% AMI) housing for formerly homeless households in Santa Clara County.
next_deadline: Open funding opportunities are posted on the fund page; otherwise rolling by invitation.
layering_notes: The private counterpart to the County's Measure A and the Housing Trust Supportive Housing Fund. Zero or low interest acquisition money lets sponsors tie up sites before County Measure A, Homekey+ or NPLH awards. Destination: Home is also a founding partner of the Bay Area Housing Innovation Fund (separate record) and funded a dedicated San Jose planner for supportive housing projects. audit_note: Tier 4 spot check: fund page confirms Cisco $50 million (2018) and Apple $50 million (2019), over $96 million invested, no or low interest acquisition and predevelopment financing for 42 ELI and supportive developments with more than 4,100 units, capacity grants to 8 developers (1,600 units) and to Campbell, Morgan Hill, Mountain View and San Jose. Open Funding Opportunities page says funding is by RFP or invitation. prevailing_wage_trigger false has no cited rule; private philanthropic funds are not public funds, but no ruling on point was opened.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) and (b)(1) to (b)(6) define public funds as payments, asset transfers, fee or loan reductions and credits by the state or a political subdivision; the Destination: Home Supportive Housing and Innovation Fund (established with a $50 million Cisco gift plus Apple funds) lends or grants privately raised capital, which is not public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Public sources layered in the same deal (for example state LHTF funds, which the 2024 LHTF NOFA section V.D makes subject to prevailing wage unless a 1720(c) exception applies, https://hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/lhtf/2024-lhtf-nofa.pdf) are assessed separately. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

jurisdiction: Santa Clara, San Mateo, San Francisco, Alameda and Santa Cruz Counties
program_name: Bay Area Housing Innovation Fund (Housing Accelerator Fund with Apple, Sobrato Philanthropies and Destination: Home)
administering_agency: Housing Accelerator Fund (San Francisco nonprofit lender), with founding partners Apple, Sobrato Philanthropies and Destination: Home; later investors Valhalla Foundation, Harry and Jeanette Weinberg Foundation and individual philanthropists
typical_award_size: $100 million fund (launched July 2024 at $50 million, doubled December 2025). Mezzanine construction-to-permanent loans (September 2025 term sheet): up to $20 million per project, higher on request; construction period interest about 3% to 5% fixed; permanent period subordinate debt repaid from residual receipts and refinance proceeds to a 5% target annualized return; total term up to 20 years; origination up to 1%. Construction-to-permanent first mortgage loans (August 2025 term sheet) with the same $20 million cap, 3% to 5% construction pricing and 20-year maximum. Loans to date: $16 million for 1633 Valencia, San Francisco (Mercy Housing California, 145 PSH units, 19-month build, about $525,000 per unit) and $11 million for Harvey West Studios, Santa Cruz (Housing Matters with MidPen, 120 PSH units).
per_unit_cap: Total development cost caps excluding land: under $575,000 per unit for studio projects, $650,000 for small-unit projects, $700,000 for all one-bedroom projects and $775,000 for family projects
affordability_requirement: Net new permanently affordable units up to 120% AMI with preference for 50% and 30% AMI; nearly half of pilot homes reserved for formerly homeless or extremely low income households.
next_deadline: Rolling after entitlement; a NOFA is forthcoming (sign up on the fund page). Construction must start within 12 months of commitment and reach certificate of occupancy within 3 years.
layering_notes: Eligible counties: Santa Clara, San Mateo, San Francisco, Alameda and Santa Cruz. Intended to let projects skip the LIHTC queue: it funds construction and permanent debt for projects that commit to cost and time targets about 40% below Bay Area averages, with a third-party evaluator documenting the approach. Entitlements must be in hand before commitment. Pairs with county Measure A or local gap funds, Homekey+ and project-based vouchers; residual receipts split must follow local public agency policy where applicable.
audit_note: Tier 4 spot check November 8, 2026: term sheets match $20M cap, 3% to 5% construction pricing, 5% mezz target return, 20-year term, TDC caps, 120% AMI with 50% and 30% preference, five counties, entitlement and 12-month start rules. Perm loan sheet also states about 6% permanent period rate. Fund page now lists 1633 Valencia at $540,000 per home (record says about $525,000) and Harvey West at $530,000 per home.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) covers construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(b) defines public funds as money, assets, loans or reduced obligations provided by the state or a political subdivision (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720). The Housing Accelerator Fund, through the Bay Area Housing Innovation Fund, lends private capital (Apple, Sobrato Philanthropies and Destination: Home capital), which is not state or political subdivision money, and the program page (https://www.sfhaf.org/bay-area-housing-innovation-fund/) states no prevailing wage term, so the loan does not itself trigger state prevailing wage. Public sources layered in the same deal (city, county, HCD or other public loans) are tested separately under their own rules; if a loan relends state or local public money, that money's rule applies instead.

program_name: Marin Community Foundation CommunityFirst Loan Fund (nonprofit site acquisition and affordable housing loans)
administering_agency: Marin Community Foundation, 5 Hamilton Landing Suite 200, Novato; director for community investment performs due diligence; Finance Committee approves loans under $5 million, board approves larger
typical_award_size: Loans to Marin nonprofits generally $500,000 to $5 million; short or long term; uses include site acquisition, construction and rehabilitation for Marin County affordable housing and capacity-building bridges; 0% default rate over 20 years; repayments revolve. Example: $1.35 million loan plus $500,000 grant for Stinson Beach affordable housing. Rates not posted (a 2017 fund report cited 4.0% fixed).

Pair with the Marin County Affordable Housing Fund and city in-lieu funds (San Rafael, Novato, Mill Valley); MCF money can close acquisition gaps ahead of County awards.

Stinson Beach example and 2017 rate are not on the page. Prevailing wage false is uncited (private loan).

The CommunityFirst Loan Fund lends Marin Community Foundation (private foundation) money (https://www.marincf.org/marin-community/how-we-support-nonprofits/community-first-loan-fund), so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage; public sources layered in the same project are analyzed separately.

program_name: We Lift: The Coachella Valley's Housing Catalyst Fund (revolving loan fund managed by Lift to Rise and LIIF)
administering_agency: Lift to Rise (Palm Desert) with Low Income Investment Fund as fund manager; partners include the County of Riverside, Rural Community Assistance Corporation and about 70 community partners

audit_note: Leave unclear: only basis is the general Labor Code 1720(b) public funds definition; coverage turns on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. We Lift page searched 2026-11-08; no loan term sheet or guidelines published.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Anaheim Municipal Code Chapter 17.40, Ord. 6593, October 29, 2024) and In-Lieu Fee Schedule (Resolution No. 2024-126)
administering_agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department (Affordable Housing Development Division), with the Planning and Building Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental residential or mixed-use projects of 35 or more units must provide at least 10% of units onsite as affordable rentals: at least 7% at or below low income (80% AMI) and at least 3% at or below very low income (50% AMI) (Sec. 17.40.050.0201). Alternatives (Sec. 17.40.060): in-lieu fee, offsite construction (only if the Director finds onsite production economically infeasible; within Anaheim, reasonably close, built before or with the market-rate project), or land dedication in Anaheim zoned for the required units with value comparable to the in-lieu fee. In-lieu fee per Resolution No. 2024-126 (adopted November 19, 2024, effective 60 days after adoption): $10.00 per square foot of total habitable/leasable space in the entire project. City example: 240 units x 875 sq ft = 210,000 sq ft x $10.00 = $2,100,000, or $87,500 per required inclusionary unit (24 units). Fractional units: round up, or pay a fractional fee of $20 to $100 per square foot of one unit (0.2 to 1.0 of a unit; example 0.7 of a unit x 875 sq ft at $70.00 = $61,250). Fees are paid before the first building permit (pro rata by phase allowed) and deposited in the Anaheim Local Housing Trust Fund.
affordability_requirement: 10% of units in rental projects of 35 or more units: at least 7% at or below 80% AMI (low income) and at least 3% at or below 50% AMI (very low income), Orange County AMI per HCD; affordable rent is 30% of the applicable AMI percentage adjusted for household size (H&SC 50052.5) minus mandatory tenant-paid housing costs. Covenant of at least 55 years for rental units; after 55 years the covenant may be removed only if the property is redeveloped to a non-residential use. Affordable units must be built concurrently with or before market-rate units, match market-rate unit size (up to 15% smaller with approval), with proportional bedroom mix, comparable finishes and amenity access, dispersed, and no separate entrances. Ownership projects are exempt, so there are no for-sale set-asides.
eligible_project_detail: rental residential or mixed-use projects of 35 or more units (compliance)
onsite affordable rental units in mixed-income projects
offsite affordable units or land dedication as alternative compliance

exempt: projects under 35 units, ownership projects of any size, condo conversions, disaster reconstruction, additions and remodels, and projects under development agreements (pre-ordinance, or later ones with comparable affordable housing obligations)
cycle_notes: Applies to residential or mixed-use projects of 35 or more units whose planning application (or building permit application for by-right projects) was formally submitted on or after October 8, 2024, the date of first reading. Ord. 6593 was adopted October 29, 2024 and took effect 30 days after final passage. The in-lieu fee resolution was adopted November 19, 2024 and took effect 60 days later. A draft inclusionary housing plan and agreement are submitted with the planning application; the agreement is recorded before any final or parcel map or building permit, and is not required where the obligation is met by in-lieu fee (the plan and agreement section also does not apply to land dedication). The fee schedule is to be adjusted periodically by Council resolution; no update after Resolution 2024-126 was found.
next_deadline: Applies at project application; no deadline. In-lieu fees are due before issuance of the first building permit.
prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority. This requirement is imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Spending of in-lieu fee revenue is a separate public funds question.
layering_notes: Rental only: Anaheim exempts ownership projects of every size, unlike the Santa Ana (587c1bf887) and Huntington Beach (adbbe8ef1b) ordinances in this database, which also reach for-sale housing. The $10 per square foot fee (about $87,500 per required unit in the City example) is the main alternative most market-rate developers will price against onsite units. Under Sec. 17.40.090, units provided for a state density bonus (Chapter 18.52, record 2db1a1727f) count toward this requirement if they also meet Chapter 17.40 standards, so a project with 10% low and very low units can satisfy both. Projects under a development agreement with comparable affordable obligations are exempt, which matters in the Platinum Triangle and other DA areas. In-lieu fees go to the Anaheim Local Housing Trust Fund (record ec67d2dea0), which redeploys them as gap loans through the Build More Homes Initiative; this is the City's own fund, not a County of Orange program, and no County inclusionary requirement applies inside Anaheim. Ord. 6593 recitals note it replaced a voluntary Housing Ambassador approach that had raised $561,000. Ordinance and fee resolution read in the City Clerk Laserfiche portal (records.anaheim.net); code text cross-checked on the gocodebook mirror because amlegal returns 403.
audit_note: Sources read November 9, 2026: City Affordable Housing page (anaheim.gov/5190), Ordinance 6593 (records.anaheim.net DocView id 5538865), Resolution 2024-126 with Exhibit A fee methodology (records.anaheim.net DocView id 5575892), and the Chapter 17.40 code text on gocodebook. No in-lieu fee update after 2024 was found; confirm the current rate with Housing and Community Development before underwriting.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Integrated Plan FY 2026-29: housing interventions, rental and operating subsidies and capital development (Carriage Court Studios)
administering_agency: Placer County Health and Human Services, Behavioral Health (Adult System of Care; Amy Ellis, Director of Behavioral Health; Primary Housing Interventions Contact Jamie Gallagher, 530-889-7283); 11434 B Avenue, Auburn
typical_award_size: Housing Interventions is 30 percent of the BHSA base allocation (no exemption or transfer): $6,810,046 (FY 2026-27), $7,745,005 (FY 2027-28) and $8,270,067 (FY 2028-29), plus $1,000,000 a year of unspent MHSA carryover, for $7,810,046, $8,745,005 and $9,270,067 ($25,825,118 over three years). Total BHSA allocations are $22,700,154, $25,816,683 and $27,566,891. Planned BHSA and MHSA housing spending by year: capital development $1,952,000, $1,750,000 and $2,317,000 ($6,019,000 total; 25%, 20% and 25% of the component); permanent-setting rental subsidies $949,000, $1,110,218 and $1,383,768; permanent-setting operating subsidies $1,603,378, $1,770,912 and $1,185,232; interim rental subsidies $144,473 to $156,473; interim operating subsidies $2,357,780, $2,569,541 and $2,817,758; outreach and engagement $546,703 to $648,705 (7%); landlord outreach and mitigation $0, $354,000 and $300,000; participant assistance $50,000 to $200,000; housing navigation and tenancy sustaining $50,000 to $75,000; admin $156,200 to $185,413. Half of the component is dedicated to the chronically homeless. The one named capital project is Carriage Court Studios (Homekey): 55 total units, 10 funded with Housing Interventions, capacity 54, expected cost per unit $284,855, units available April 1, 2027. Plan targets 285 people a year on rental subsidies (367 units) and 463 people on operating subsidies (280 units).
per_unit_cap: BHSA Housing Interventions capital may not exceed $450,000 per unit (DHCS policy manual C.10.1); Carriage Court Studios lists an expected cost per unit of $284,855. Capital is capped at 25 percent of the Housing Interventions component.
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible adults and families with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk of homelessness, prioritized through the CA-515 Coordinated Entry System; at least 50 percent of component funds for chronically homeless people. BHSA is payer of last resort and cannot pay for housing services covered by Medi-Cal managed care plans.
eligible_project_detail: capital development for permanent supportive housing (one project: Carriage Court Studios, Homekey)
project-based and tenant-based rental subsidies in permanent and interim settings
operating subsidies for PSH, adult residential facilities, transitional housing and peer respite
participant assistance, housing navigation, tenancy sustaining services and outreach
cycle_notes: Three-year BHSA Integrated Plan, FY 2026-27 through FY 2028-29, with annual updates. Draft released March 31, 2026; comment period closed April 30, 2026; Behavioral Health Advisory Board public hearing April 27, 2026. Behavioral Health Director certification signed June 19, 2026; Board of Supervisors certification signed by Chair Shanti Landon dated June 25, 2026 (the Board meeting agenda item itself was not located). No NOFA or competitive round.
next_deadline: No NOFA. Capital in this plan period is committed to one project (Carriage Court Studios). Developers or operators of PSH serving BHSA clients should contact Placer County Behavioral Health housing staff (Jamie Gallagher, 530-889-7283) about rental or operating subsidies; new capital projects would need to be added in an annual update.
prevailing_wage_basis: Capital development is funded ($6,019,000 over three years, Carriage Court Studios), so BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720); whether a project is covered depends on 1720(c) exemptions, for example 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market interest rate loans on projects with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Neither the Placer County 2026-2029 BHSA Integrated Plan Capital Development Projects section (https://www.placer.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/114232/Placer-County-2026-2029-Integrated-Plan_Final-PDF) nor the DHCS BHSA County Policy Manual capital development section C.10 (https://policy-manual.mes.dhcs.ca.gov/behavioral-health-services-act-county-policy-manual/V1.0.0/7-bhsa-components-and-requirements) states a prevailing wage rule. Rental and operating subsidies are not construction under 1720(a)(1).
layering_notes: Classified grant: the plan funds housing capital (Carriage Court Studios) and rental and operating subsidies for housing. Placer County Behavioral Health has run its own housing team for about 20 years and braids BHSA with Homekey (Sun Rose Apartments, Carriage Court Studios, Brown Bear Studios), BHCIP, BHBH, HHAP, CDBG, County general fund, ARPA, opioid settlement funds, IGT revenue, Transitional Rent and Housing Trio Community Supports, HUD CoC and HCV/VASH vouchers. BHSA operating subsidies support CoC-funded PSH sites such as Timberline and Placer Street. Partners are AMI Housing (AMIH) and The Gathering Inn. The plan expects a 40 percent cut in HUD PSH renewals and BHSA to backfill about 100 households. For a developer, BHSA here is mostly an operating or rental subsidy source for PSH units serving BHSA clients, not open gap capital; the County Executive Office Economic Development and Housing Division runs the in-lieu fee gap loans and PLHA, and the Placer County Housing Authority (HHS) supplies project-based vouchers. Capital share (20 to 25 percent of the component) is higher than Nevada (0) and similar to Fresno.
